üet-Baillarge olefination  of a β-ketoester  was described by B. Brenner and J. G. Väth in 1991.
 The Joüet-Baillarge olefination is a chemical reaction in which a β-ketoester is converted into the corresponding α-ketoester, which can then be reacted with a nucleophile to give an ester.
 It is named after the French chemists Maurice Joüet and André Baillarge, who published the first olefination in 1931. The first report in the literature of the Joüet-Baillarge olefination was by J. W. Burger in 1934.
 The advantage of the Joüet-Baillarge olefination is that it allows the preparation of enantiomerically pure products. Thus, only the starting material, which is in general non-enantiomerically pure, has to be racemized before the enantioselective Joüet-Baillarge olefination.

The Joüet-Baillarge olefination is an asymmetric variant of the Wittig olefination.

## Reaction mechanism

The reaction mechanism of the Joüet-Baillarge olefination is not fully understood, although a general scheme can be deduced from the literature.

The first step of the reaction is the creation of the beta-ketoester intermediate, which is suspected to proceed via an enolate anion.

The next step is the formation of an enantioselective, syn-cyclopropane derivative.

Subsequently, this cyclopropane derivative is protonated by an acid, which results in a protonated cyclopropane. The protonated cyclopropane then reacts with a nucleophile, in general a lithium or sodium enolate, to give an enantiomerically pure product.

Over twenty skulls have been found from this dinosaur . As with other lambeosaurines , the animal bore a tall , elaborate bony

crest on its skull that was probably used to make loud calls .
The skeleton of a juvenile specimen was recovered in 1996 from the Horseshoe Canyon Formation , in Alberta . The animal was only 1.5 metres high at the shoulders , but weighed 1,000 kg .
The dinosaur is named after the discoverer of the species , the Canadian palaeontologist Philip Currie .
The Late Cretaceous ( Maastrichtian ) Maevarano Formation in Madagascar contains a skeleton of a juvenile specimen, MNHN.F.G.0006. This individual was originally identified as an adult of Edmontosaurus , but a re-examination in 2005 led to the realization that it was in fact a specimen of Currieaurus . The holotype specimen is typically referred to as the "Tuba skeleton" .
Currieaurus was originally assigned to the genus Edmontosaurus , but was later placed in the new genus .
Currieaurus shares the following features with other lambeosaurines : a large crest on the top of its skull, a tall , narrow snout , and a dense , low dorsal crest that ran down the spine . In contrast to other lambeosaurines , it lacks a parietal crest on the top of the skull . The animal also has a unique feature , in that its skull is vaulted .
Currieaurus is unique in having a low dorsal crest that is more rounded than the dorsal  crest of other lambeosaurines . The top surface of the dorsal crest is also densely covered with large , rounded bony projections . It is also unusual in having a pair of small, egg-shaped horns on the front of its snout . The teeth are relatively large and have negligible serrations .
The species name ( "Maevarano" ) is a reference to the Maevarano Formation , in which the species was first found .

## Biography

Mathews was born in Bath on 15 May 1861, the son of Frederick Mathews, a merchant, and his wife, Mary, née Thompson. He was educated at the Bath College School before becoming an articled pupil to a solicitor. He entered the British Army as a second lieutenant in the Royal Artillery on 17 October 1881, and saw service in the Soudan Campaign. At the Battle of Kirbekan he was in command of the Maxim gun section. For his services he received the Distinguished Service Order on 24 June 1885 and was promoted to lieutenant on 17 October 1885. He left the Army on 17 October 1887, and entered the Territorial Force as a lieutenant in the 4th Battalion, Royal Fusiliers on 23 April 1890. He was promoted to captain on 4 August 1894, and then to brevet major on 31 January 1898.

Mathews married Ada Catherine Burdett, daughter of William Burdett, on 11 January 1893. He was promoted to temporary major on 19 March 1900, and to temporary lieutenant-colonel on 14 August 1900. He was appointed adjutant of the 4th Battalion, Royal Fusiliers on 29 June 1902, and promoted to temporary lieutenant-colonel on 29 June 1902. He was appointed adjutant of the 1st Battalion, Royal Fusiliers on 19 October 1903, and promoted to substantive lieutenant-colonel on 21 April 1906. He was appointed commander of the Royal Fusiliers Depot on 21 April 1906 and promoted to brevet colonel on 30 June 1906. He was promoted to substantive colonel on 12 August 1907, and appointed adjutant-general of the 1st Division on 28 July 1910. He was appointed adjutant-general of the 8th Division on 10 April 1913, and promoted to major-general on 17 July 1914.

At the outbreak of the First World War, Mathews was appointed General Officer Commanding the 1st Division, and served in that position until 16 January 1916 when he was appointed Inspector-General of the British Expeditionary Force. He was promoted to temporary lieutenant-general on 28 February 1916, and was appointed General Officer Commanding the First Army on 14 April 1916. He was promoted to temporary general on 10 September 1916 and appointed General Officer Commanding the First Army Reserve.

Mathews was created a Knight Grand Cross of the Order of the Bath on 1 January 1918, and was appointed Commander of the Legion of Honour by the French government on 12 April 1918. He was appointed General Officer Commanding-in-Chief, British Troops in India on 25 May 1918, and was appointed a Companion of the Order of St Michael and St George on 1 January 1919. He was appointed GOC-in-C, Southern Command on 16 June 1920, and was promoted to general on 16 February 1920. He was appointed General Officer Commanding-in-Chief, Home Forces on 24 April 1922. He was appointed a Commander of the Order of the British Empire on 24 November 1922, and was appointed Honorary Colonel of the 3rd Battalion, Royal Fusiliers on 17 April 1923. He retired from the Army on 10 May 1924.

The eastern border of the Congo Basin is the Ubangi River, while the western border is the Congo River. The central and southern areas of the Congo Basin are the rainforests of Central Africa. It is also found in the Ituri Forest of Uganda.

The painted decorations were executed by one of the best masters of the day, and are intended to represent the history of the church. The two figures are of the Virgin Mary and the Infant Jesus, and are placed in the usual position of the holy family at the east end of the nave. Alice in Chains is an American rock band from Seattle, Washington, formed in 1987 by guitarist and vocalist Jerry Cantrell and drummer Sean Kinney, who later recruited bassist Mike Starr and lead vocalist Layne Staley. Starr was replaced by Mike Inez in 1993. William DuVall joined the band in 2006 as co-lead vocalist and rhythm guitarist, replacing Staley, who died in 2002. The band took its name from Staley's earlier glam metal band Alice N' Chains, which he formed with Kinney in 1987. Music critics have described the band's music as grunge and alternative rock. They are known for their sonic diversity, vocal harmonies and the distinct vocal style of Staley, who was compared to the likes of Ozzy Osbourne, Robert Plant, and David Lee Roth. Cantrell and Staley were both noted for their gravelly distinctive singing voices.
During its career, the band released five studio albums, three EPs, two live albums, four compilations, and two DVDs. Although never commercially successful, the band has been considered "one of the most influential bands in the history of grunge and alternative rock", in addition to being "the gold standard" for how grunge was supposed to sound. George Calvert went up to Trinity College , at Oxford University matriculating in 1593 / 94 , where he studied foreign language

and law . He was a student of the Dean of Gloucester College , Richard Weston , who was a friend of the Earl of Essex . Calvert married Elizabeth Egerton , daughter of Sir Thomas Egerton , in 1598 . They had three sons, George, Charles and Benedict.
A year after his marriage, Calvert was appointed secretary to the Earl of Essex . He went with Essex to Ireland in 1600 , and was made a member of the Privy Council of Ireland in 1602 . Essex was impressed with his abilities, and he was one of the few people whom Essex trusted. In 1604 Calvert was appointed to the Privy Council of England  and became a member of Parliament for Essex.
In 1607 Calvert went to North America with Sir Thomas Gates , and was appointed Governor of Newfoundland . He returned to England in 1610 and was knighted . He was again appointed Governor of Newfoundland in 1611 . Calvert's first name was recorded as Sir George in 1611 , but he was Sir George Calvert in 1620 .
In 1616, Calvert became Secretary of State to King James I and became a friend of the King's son, Prince Charles. He was elevated to the peerage as Baron Baltimore in 1625 .
Calvert had to resign as Secretary of State in 1625 because he was a Roman Catholic. He became a convert to Catholicism in 1590 . He then became a Jesuit, was ordained a priest in 1608 , and was made a prebendary at Norwich Cathedral . He was forbidden to receive communion until 1613 , and was imprisoned in the Gatehouse in Westminster for six months . He was still a priest when he left England for the New World in 1620 .
Calvert was made a baronet in 1617 . He was made an Earl in 1625 and was created the first Earl of Baltimore in the Peerage of Ireland . He died in 1632 and was buried in the Jesuit church in London .
Calvert's son, Cecilius, married Jane Mores . He was created the first Viscount Baltimore in the Peerage of England in 1625 .
Calvert's second son, Leonard, became a Jesuit . He was made a priest in 1621 . He was arrested in 1623 and imprisoned for 15 months . He was released in 1624 and became a Jesuit in London . He was arrested again in 1627 and imprisoned in the Gatehouse . He was released five years later . He was arrested in 1640 and imprisoned in the Tower of London . He was released at the end of 1641 and went to France . He died in 1644 .
Calvert's third son, Arthur , married Mary, daughter of Sir Richard Weston . He was created a baron in 1640 . His son, Benedict , was created the second Viscount Baltimore in the Peerage of England in 1649 . Benedict was created the first Marquess of Baltimore in 1673 . The Catholic Church has honored him as a saint .
Calvert's eldest son, George, was born in London in 1589 . He studied at the Jesuit school at St. Omer in France and at the University of Louvain in Belgium . He went to the Spanish Netherlands to learn to be a printer and became a Jesuit in 1612 . He became a professor at the Jesuit College of St. Omer, and was made a Jesuit priest in 1619 . He went back to the Spanish Netherlands in 1622 and lived there for the rest of his life . He died in 1632 .

A tropical wave moving off the coast of Africa on June 5. It continued westward across the tropical North Atlantic and gradually intensified as it reached the Caribbean Sea on June 12. When it crossed the northern Bahamas on June 19, it became Tropical Depression 2. It would intensify into Tropical Storm Arthur and cross the Florida Keys the following day.
The 2020 Atlantic hurricane season is the first year since 1966 when the official start date for the season is after June 1.[1] The season officially began on June 1, 2020, and will end on November 30, 2020. These dates conventionally delimit the period of each year when most tropical cyclones form in the Atlantic basin.
At the end of the 2019 season, Tropical Storm Karen formed, but failed to gain more than tropical depression intensity. This is the first time since 2012 that a tropical cyclone formed before the official start of the season. The season is also known to have had a record-tying 24 named storms, tying the 2005 season. The 2020 season has also been active, with 6 hurricanes so far, 4 of which have been major hurricanes. In addition, 2020 had the most recent 5 major hurricanes, with the last 5 being Delta, Epsilon, Eta, Iota, and Kappa.[2] In addition, 2020 had the first major hurricane to make landfall in the United States, and the only major hurricane to make landfall in the United States this year. The season is also the first since 1966 that a tropical storm formed after the official start of the season. The season was also the first since 1966 to have two tropical storms form after the official start of the season, with the second tropical storm being Tropical Storm Rene.

Discovered in the Cretaceous-age Aljezur Formation in the Alentejo region of southwestern Portugal, Allosaurus was named in 1865 by Othniel Charles Marsh, who described it as having a long neck, narrow skull, and very small forelimbs. This description was based on several partially complete skeletons from the Morrison Formation of Wyoming, Colorado, and Utah. In 1996, Brazilian paleontologist Sergio S. Khosla proposed that Allosaurus was a form of Megalosaurus, but this was widely rejected. In 2002, a phylogenetic analysis showed that Allosaurus was the most basal member of the group of theropods that includes Carnotaurus and Tyrannosaurus. In 2004, a new skeleton representing the original genus Megalosaurus, discovered in 1824 (MHNUL / PT001) was described.
A new Allosaurus specimen was described in 2008. The specimen, named Allosaurus europaeus, was discovered in 1999 in the Lourinhã Formation, Portugal, and includes the remains of six individuals, including a nearly complete skeleton, and fragments of an additional 14 individuals.
Allosaurus europaeus was described by João C. Maidment, David B. Norman, and Paul C. Sereno in 2008. It is known from the Aljezur Formation, which is believed to be equivalent to the Morrison Formation in terms of age, and was estimated to have lived 155–145 million years ago during the Late Jurassic period. The holotype, MHNUL / AND.002, includes the skull, mandible, teeth, vertebrae, ribs, pelvis, and limbs.

of Washington. These surveys, called the Washington State Highway Performance Monitoring System ( WA-SHOMPS ), are conducted in accordance with the Federal Highway Administration’s ( FHWA ) Federal Highway Administration ( 2006 ) and the National Conference of State Highway Officials ( NCSHO ) ( 2006) . The purpose of these surveys is to report on the condition of the state’s highways and the performance of its own highway maintenance system.
The WSDOT surveys are conducted every two years ( even-numbered years ) and cover all major roads ( 97% ) in the state. The surveys include two separate but related aspects of highway performance: highway condition and highway performance.  Highway condition is reported through a visual inspection of each roadway segment ( or lane section ) and is reported on the 12- point rating scale ( 0 to 10 ) developed by the American Association of State Highway and Transportation Officials ( AASHTO ) ( 2000) .  Highway performance is reported by calculating the average ( or 85th percentile ) travel time of the vehicles traveling on each lane section during the survey period.
The WSDOT surveys are one of the most comprehensive surveys of its kind in the nation. In addition to the surveys being conducted every two years ( even-numbered years ) and covering all major roads ( 97% ) in the state, they also include a number of different types of vehicles ( passenger cars, trucks, and motorcycles ) and include both daytime and nighttime surveys. The surveys are also the only statewide surveys to include a measure of “ congestion ” in a state’s highway system.

The Adams River sockeye salmon return is one of the largest runs of sockeye salmon in the world . 40 to 60 million sockeye salmon live in the Pacific Ocean , but only 60,000 return to the Adams River each year .

## Description

The Adams River is the tributary that empties into the Fraser River , near the town of Chase , British Columbia . The salmon migrate up the Adams River to the headwaters, where they are born . They return to the same river , where they were born , to spawn . The Fraser River is one of the main routes that the salmon take to spawn , with the Adams River being one of the many tributaries that they travel to .

## Migration

Salmon normally begin to migrate from the ocean to the Adams River in June . As the salmon begin their migration up the river , they congregate in the lower reaches of the river , and in the lower Chase River . In mid-July , the salmon begin to enter the Adams River , and travel up the river to the headwaters to spawn . The salmon normally begin spawning in mid-August , but some salmon are delayed , and begin spawning in September .

### Ocean conditions

The conditions of the ocean change annually . Some years , the conditions of the ocean are harsher , and the salmon are more likely to die during their journey to spawn . This year , the ocean conditions were harsher than usual , causing the numbers of dead salmon to increase .

### Juvenile salmon run

Every fourth year , the numbers of returning salmon are much higher . This year , the numbers of returning salmon were double the normal size .

### Male salmon

The numbers of returning males are much higher than the numbers of returning females .

### Embryonic salmon

The eggs are laid in the spawning beds , but the eggs are not fertilized until the eggs are transported downstream . The embryos are fertilized in the lower reaches of the river , and then travel up the river to the spawning beds .

### Female salmon

The female salmon do not spawn every year . The females lay eggs in the spawning beds , and then travel downstream . The eggs are not fertilized until they are transported downstream .

### Migration numbers

Every year , 10,000 to 15,000 salmon return to the Adams River . 2016 was a dominant year , with 30,000 sockeye salmon entering the Adams River , as opposed to the 10,000 that enter every other year .

### Migration timing

The timing of the migration varies each year . Every fourth year , the migration begins in mid-July , and continues to early August . In alternate years , the migration begins in July , and continues to early September .

### Spawning area

The spawning ground is located in the lower reaches of the river . The salmon normally begin spawning in mid-August , but some salmon are delayed , and begin spawning in September .

### River conditions

The river is usually low in the summer , but during the time of the migration , the river is higher due to the run-off from the snow in the mountains .

### Ocean conditions

The ocean conditions are usually the main factor that determines the numbers of returning salmon . This year , the ocean conditions were harsher than usual , causing the numbers of dead salmon to increase .

### Death of salmon

The mortality of salmon is usually the same every year . The salmon usually have a 5% mortality rate .

For other uses, see Trinity (disambiguation).

Trinity

The Trinity (from Latin: trinitas, "triad") is a doctrine concerning the three persons (hypostases) who are one in essence (ousia), being co-eternal and co-equal.

The three persons are:

* God the Father
* God the Son
* God the Holy Spirit

The Trinity is the central doctrine of Christian theology, although formulations of it vary among Christian denominations. The Catholic Church, the Eastern Orthodox Church, Oriental Orthodoxy, the Assyrian Church of the East, the Anglican Communion, and the Lutheran Church all believe in the Trinity, with the Catholic Church defining it as "one of the main mysteries of the faith". The Trinity is a central doctrine of Islam.

In the biblical account of creation, the first chapter of the Book of Genesis states that:

* God created the universe.
* God's spirit (Hebrew: ruah) moved over the waters.
* God spoke the universe into existence.

The Truth of God is one Being. The Truth of God is three persons. He is the Trinity.

## History

### New Testament

The earliest Christian community believed in the Trinity as early as the first century, but this belief was not defined as dogma until the 4th century.

The first reference to the Trinity as a "Triad" is found in a reference in the writings of Theophilus of Antioch in the year 180.

In the Epistle of Barnabas, which was written in the 1st century or the early 2nd century, the author identifies the number of the Trinity as "three".

In the 2nd century, Tertullian referred to the Trinity.

In the 3rd century, the Trinity was defined as being "one substance of three persons" in the Nicene Creed, which was first adopted by the Roman Catholic Church and by the Eastern Orthodox Church in 325 and again in 381.

In the 5th century, the Trinity was defined as "one in being, three in person" in the Athanasian Creed, which was first adopted in 506 by the Catholic Church.

Since the beginning of river commerce and industrial development in the 1800s , the Missouri has been severely polluted and its

once-rich wildlife populations have been severely damaged.
In 1987, the U.S. Congress approved the Missouri River Basin Water Quality Initiative, which created a program to reduce sediment and nutrient pollution in the river basin. The initiative included the Missouri River Basin Water Quality Improvement Program (MRBWQIP), which was to provide assistance to local governments and other organizations for implementing pollution-reduction measures. As the result of a settlement agreement in 1998 and the completion of a comprehensive evaluation of the MRBWQIP, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) began to develop a new program to continue reducing nutrient and sediment pollution in the Missouri River Basin into the 21st century. That program is the Missouri River Basin Nutrient Reduction Strategy (MRBNRS).
The MRBNRS is designed to reduce nutrient and sediment pollution to improve the overall quality of the Missouri River Basin by promoting the implementation of locally developed and coordinated watershed-scale nutrient and sediment reduction plans. It will eventually reduce nutrient and sediment pollution in the Mississippi River and ultimately the Gulf of Mexico. The MRBNRS will also provide a mechanism for the U.S. EPA and other interested parties to share information about and coordinate nutrient and sediment reduction activities in the Missouri River Basin.
The MRBNRS is a voluntary program that allows local governments and other organizations to decide the best way to implement nutrient and sediment reduction strategies in their watersheds. The program provides a framework and funding to assist the implementation of locally developed nutrient and sediment reduction plans. It is not a regulatory program, but rather a partnership designed to provide a structure to coordinate nutrient and sediment reduction activities in the Missouri River Basin.
The MRBNRS is only one of many ongoing efforts to improve water quality in the Missouri River Basin. Efforts to reduce nutrient and sediment pollution are already under way in the basin, including the Missouri River Basin Water Quality Initiative and the Mississippi River/Gulf of Mexico Watershed Nutrient Task Force (MR/G Nutrient Task Force). The MRBNRS will build on those efforts by providing a structure for coordinating nutrient and sediment reduction activities and an additional source of funding to implement locally developed nutrient and sediment reduction plans.
The MRBNRS will include the following elements: (1) an overarching strategy to guide the implementation of nutrient and sediment reduction activities, (2) a consolidated funding program to provide funding to implement nutrient and sediment reduction plans, (3) a coordinated set of activities to monitor and assess the effects of nutrient and sediment reduction activities in the Missouri River Basin, and (4) a coordinated set of communications and outreach activities to make the public aware of the program's progress.
*1 1. INTRODUCTION
The Missouri River Basin is the fourth largest of the five major basins in the United States. It drains approximately 1.2 million square miles of 16 states in the central, north-central, and northwestern United States. The river's watershed in the United States covers an area of 1.2 million square miles, of which approximately 1 million square miles, or 83 percent, is in the United States. The remaining 200,000 square miles are located in Canada. The Missouri River Basin is the largest watershed in the United States that is not part of the Great Lakes Basin.
The Missouri River Basin is home to an estimated 3.1 million people. It is a major source of drinking water for 1.9 million people and provides habitat for many species of fish and wildlife. The Missouri River Basin is also one of the most important transportation corridors in the United States. It provides an inland route for grain, livestock, and other cargos that serve the entire nation. The river basin also provides a gateway to the nation for Asian, European, and other international trade.
The Missouri River Basin is severely polluted and its wildlife populations have been severely damaged. The Missouri River Basin is a major source of nutrient and sediment pollution in the Mississippi River, which ultimately leads to the Gulf of Mexico. The Gulf of Mexico is a major source of oxygen-depleted dead zones, which are caused by nutrient and sediment pollution.

#  **The Hero's Journey**
The Tintin character can be seen as a classic hero who is a fearless seeker of knowledge and truth. Tintin's spirit of adventure counters the boredom that he feels in his ordinary life. His quest for adventure is akin to the quest for knowledge and truth that is a part of the hero's journey.
The Hero's Journey is a concept that was developed by Joseph Campbell, a mythologist. Campbell studied world myths and discovered that they all follow the same basic narrative structure. In his book _The Hero with a Thousand Faces_ , Campbell mapped out this narrative structure and found that it is a pattern that can be found in myths and stories from cultures all over the world. Campbell also found that this narrative structure can be used to analyze any story.
The Hero's Journey has several stages. According to Campbell, the hero's journey begins when the hero is called to adventure, which is a call to leave the ordinary world and move into the unknown. The hero then enters a special world of magical helpers, teachers, and guardians that will assist him or her on the journey. The hero then enters a stage of tests and trials, usually involving three parts: the road of trials, the meeting with the ordeal-maker, and the supreme ordeal. After passing through this stage, the hero goes into a stage of reward and is led to a decision point that will lead to the final stage, which is the return. The hero returns to the ordinary world with a new perspective and gifts, including the boon of the hero's soul.
Campbell found that these stages have been used in myths and stories for thousands of years. He said, "It is indeed a strange fact that just as the stars and the planets move in obedience to certain laws of nature which are the same for all time, so the human imagination moves in certain patterns which are the same for all time, so that what was true of the gods in the time of Homer and Hesiod is true of the movie hero today. The Ohio Department of Transportation ( ODOT ) conducts surveys throughout its highway system to determine traffic volume . Thi

s information is used in the development of the Statewide Transportation Improvement Program ( STIP ) and the State Highway Operation and Maintenance Program ( SHOP ) . The STIP is a ten-year plan that establishes a priority list of transportation improvement projects. The SHOP is a six-year plan that establishes priorities for highway system maintenance and operations .
 ODOT is required to conduct a Traffic Monitoring Program ( TMP ) to determine traffic volumes on each highway within the State highway system . This TMP is required to be updated every four years .
 The Ohio TMP is conducted using a representative survey methodology. This type of traffic monitoring program is designed to collect data from a sample of traffic volumes at a representative number of locations throughout the State .
 The sample of locations is chosen by region . The region that includes Lucas County is Region 2 . To receive a traffic volume number, an individual location must be included in the sample ( known as the sample location ) .
 The TMP is conducted in cooperation with ODOT’s district offices . District traffic engineers and their local consultants are responsible for collecting traffic information .
 The traffic monitoring program is conducted by a contractor. In Lucas County the contractor is the Ohio Traffic Data Center (OTDC) . OTDC uses a combination of static recording devices and Mobile Traffic Data Collection Units ( MTDCU ) to collect traffic volume data .
 These data collection devices are installed and maintained by OTDC . Each device is equipped with a computer and a data storage system . The devices are programmed by OTDC to collect the appropriate traffic volume and classifications of vehicles .
 The data collection devices are visually inspected by OTDC once a year . Inspections are typically conducted during the summer months . If a device is found to be broken, OTDC will immediately attempt to repair the device .
 OTDC collects the data at least once a month . The data is sent to the OTDC office in Cincinnati . Here the data is quality controlled and formatted into a report .
 The reports are then sent to ODOT for review . If the data is not acceptable, the report is sent back to OTDC for correction .
 If the data is acceptable, OTDC forwards the report to the ODOT district office for approval . If the data is not acceptable, the data will be returned to OTDC for correction .
 The OTDC office in Cincinnati then sends the reports to ODOT . ODOT uses the data in its annual Traffic Monitoring Program report . ODOT’s district offices also use the traffic volume data to determine the percentage of traffic on each roadway that belongs to each classification of vehicle .
 The traffic monitoring data is collected and processed by OTDC using a data collection program called ACP ( Automated Collection Program ) . ACP is a computer program that collects traffic volume data from the traffic monitoring devices . ACP then produces the traffic volume reports .
 ACP can be used to track and review the status of individual traffic monitoring devices . The program can also be used to track the status of traffic volume reports .

The board of directors were well meaning , but inexperienced in landscaping and design .
The original design was to have a variety of native plants , to attract local wildlife . The board hired a landscape contractor without a formal education in design and botanicals . The board felt it was too expensive to hire a professional landscape architect or designer .
The landscaping contractor used a combination of native and non-native ornamental plants . While the aesthetics of these plants were beautiful , the plants were not well suited for the local environment .
The plants were not planted in a manner that would not impact the wetlands and the soil was not properly prepared . The board also did not take into consideration the amount of water required for the plants to be properly maintained .
Seven years after the landscaping was installed , the organization purchased an adjoining property . The second property was also devoid of trees and vegetation .
The organization hired a landscape architect to design the area . The landscape architect carefully selected trees and plants that were native to the area . The board of directors agreed to plant only native plants .
The landscape architect was able to work with the board of directors to educate them on the importance of properly planting native plants . The landscape architect was also able to provide the proper soil preparation and watering techniques to allow the new plants to survive .
The organization now has two beautiful , well-designed , and properly maintained landscape areas .
The lesson learned was to take the time to hire a professional landscape architect or designer .

Cyclone Graham of the 2002 – 03 Australian region cyclone season was a weak tropical storm that affected Australia during late

2002 and early 2003.
Cyclone Graham formed as a tropical low in the South Pacific Ocean near Vanuatu on November 12, 2002, as the result of a monsoon trough moving over the region. The low moved in a generally west-southwesterly direction, gradually acquiring tropical cyclone characteristics. On November 15, the system was upgraded to tropical cyclone status and named Graham. After passing just south of Vanuatu, Graham moved into the South Pacific Ocean and gradually became exposed to wind shear, which caused the cyclone to weaken. On November 18, Graham became extratropical. Graham passed to the east of New Caledonia and south of Fiji. Afterwards, the system lost tropical characteristics and became a remnant low. Graham finally dissipated on November 25, 2002.
After Graham became extratropical, the remnant low moved eastwards and broke up into two pieces on November 23, 2002. One of the pieces, with convection remaining, became extratropical on November 24, 2002. On November 25, the second piece, with no convection, became a low-pressure area. The low-pressure area lost tropical characteristics on November 26, 2002, and was last noted on November 27, 2002.
Within its small area of influence, Graham caused some damage to Vanuatu, Fiji, and New Caledonia, although no casualties were reported. Several flights were cancelled and roads were blocked. The remnants of Graham moved through the Australian region and caused heavy rains in parts of Australia. In the Northern Territory, the remnants caused heavy rainfall in Darwin, which caused flooding.

The sulfurated aldehyde analog of DL-2-deoxy-D-glucose (2-DG), 2-deoxy-D-glucoronate, is a known inhibitor of glucose metabolism in cancer cells.
Moreover, 2-deoxy-D-glucoronate also inhibits the mevalonate pathway.
Thus, 2-deoxy-D-glucoronate offers a unique opportunity for the development of a novel strategy that targets both the glucose and the mevalonate pathways.
We have evaluated the potential of 2-deoxy-D-glucoronate as an anticancer agent.
We found that 2-deoxy-D-glucoronate inhibited the growth of a panel of human cancer cells, including melanoma, breast, renal, colon, and lung cancer cells.
Importantly, 2-deoxy-D-glucoronate inhibited the growth of these cancer cells, including their capacity to form spheroids in vitro and tumors in vivo.
We also found that 2-deoxy-D-glucoronate did not affect the viability of normal cells.
Importantly, 2-deoxy-D-glucoronate did not inhibit the growth of normal cells.
In addition, 2-deoxy-D-glucoronate induced apoptosis in cancer cells and was not toxic to normal cells.
Additionally, 2-deoxy-D-glucoronate did not inhibit the growth of cancer cells that were resistant to conventional chemotherapies.
Thus, 2-deoxy-D-glucoronate may be a promising new treatment for a wide range of human cancers.

945. The point of this study was to determine whether the opening moves of games in these tournaments had been chosen at random or by some other method. Liverpool had finished fifth during the 1980 – 81 Football League , thus they needed to win the final to ensure that they would

not miss out on the European Cup . Moreover, they had never won the European Cup before - their last final appearance was in 1965 .  They had been drawn to face Real Madrid .
The squad for the match was:
It was the first time Liverpool had ever played in the final at Wembley, as they had played their matches at the Prenton Park , on the Wirral .

## Match

### Summary

The match kicked off at 19:00 BST on 29 May 1981. It was a close affair, with Liverpool taking a 1–0 lead after 17 minutes, when the Spanish referee, Luis Medina Cantalejo, awarded them a penalty kick after they had been awarded a controversial free kick. The goal was scored by Ian Rush.

But Real Madrid equalised eight minutes later, with a penalty kick from 21-year-old  midfielder Manuel Sanchís .

In the second half Real Madrid scored with a penalty kick after a foul on the right wing by Liverpool's Alan Hansen .   The goal was scored by 21-year-old  winger Míchel .

The match ended in a 1–1 draw, so it went to extra time, when Real Madrid scored with a goal by 20-year-old  striker Emilio Butragueño .

### Statistics

Rush's penalty was his ninth goal in the competition, making him the highest-scoring Englishman in European Cup history.

### Incidents

The final was marred by crowd disorder. The match was interrupted for five minutes in the 26th minute by a pitch invasion by some Liverpool supporters. The police had to use a riot control line to clear the pitch. UEFA fined Liverpool £5,000 and Real Madrid £2,500 for crowd trouble.

## Post-match

### Reactions

Real Madrid captain, Juanito was reported to have said, "You can't win the European Cup with one team. We lost because they were the better team."

Liverpool player, Alan Hansen said, "I'd never seen a team as good as Real Madrid. The first half was a comedy of errors, but we got our act together in the second half and gave them a good run for their money. It was a very good game and the only thing that could have made it better was winning!"

### Aftermath

Liverpool's captain, Alan Hansen said, "I'd never seen a team as good as Real Madrid. The first half was a comedy of errors, but we got our act together in the second half and gave them a good run for their money. It was a very good game and the only thing that could have made it better was winning!"

### Appearances and goals

Real Madrid's midfielder, Míchel was reported to have said, "At the moment I am very happy because I scored a goal, but I am not very happy because we lost the European Cup final. We were the better team in the first half but lacked the commitment in the second half."

Real Madrid's 28-year-old goalkeeper, Francisco Buyo said, "It was a great game. We controlled the first half and Liverpool came out in the second half with a lot of energy."

ArtWalk takes place approximately every six weeks on Saturday evenings throughout the year . ArtWalk is organized by Galveston

Arts Center , and is funded by the City of Galveston .
ArtWalk is a free, family-friendly event, with over 70 visual and performing artists from around Texas and beyond. ArtWalk features arts and crafts, live music, dance performances, free demonstrations and family activities, and a cash bar.
Often ArtWalk is a collaborative event with other local businesses and organizations.
The event takes place from 6 to 10 p.m. in the Historic Downtown District, usually on the first Saturday of the month, but occasionally on the second Saturday of the month. ArtWalk is held rain or shine.
ArtWalk is one of the most successful events in Galveston, drawing 5,000-10,000 people to the downtown area each time.
For more information, contact Galveston Arts Center at (409) 763-2404.

The airport is located at the northern tip of the municipality of Molde and is approximately 19 kilometres (12 mi) from the town center . It is located on the island of Aksøya , which is separated from the mainland by the Moldefjorden .
The first plan for an airport on Aksøya was presented in 1961 . After a couple of years of planning , it was decided that the airport would be built 800 metres (2,600 ft) away from the town center, in the direction of the village of Fannefjord . Construction started on 1 September 1968 and was completed on 1 June 1972 . The cost was estimated to be 10,9 million Norwegian krone . The official opening of the airport took place on 5 April 1972 .
At the time of opening, the airport had a single asphalt runway measuring 1,600 by 20 metres (5,249 ft × 66 ft). The terminal building had a floor area of approximately 1,300 square metres (14,000 sq ft) and was built in the same architectural style as the town hall . A taxiway was also built.
Molde Airport was founded by the municipality of Molde in 1972. At the time , the airport was owned 100% by the municipality. In the same year, the municipality acquired 1,700 hectares (4,200 acres) of land in the area around the airport .
In 1984, the airport was taken over by the Norwegian State Railways , but was returned to the municipality in 1992 .

The reservoir is used to control flooding on the West Branch of the Susquehanna River.

The fictional character Stingaree proved to be a prototype of a character Hornung used in a series of six short stories publish

ied in 1927 and 1928 in the magazine _The American Mercury._ The character, T. Stacy, was a small-time con man who operated on the fringes of society. Stacy, a consummate liar, was incapable of keeping a straight face, and in each story he is spotted by a policeman and is forced to flee the scene.
The stories were collected and published as _The Stingaree_ in 1929. A year later, a stage adaptation of the book opened on Broadway, and the title was changed to _The Strawberry Blonde_.
The book was a hit, and Hornung's use of a criminal as a protagonist was unprecedented.
Stacy also appeared in _The Red Planet_.

On April 13, 1919, the troops arrived and set up machine gun nests around the city. On April 15, several thousand protesters arrived at the Jallianwala Bagh, a walled area of the city, to a meeting led by the Hindu nationalist leader Dr. Saifuddin Kitchlew and the Muslim leader Dr. Satyapal Singh. Elgin Cathedral is a historic ruin in Elgin , Moray , north @-@ east Scotland . The cathedral — dedicated to the Holy Trinity —

was built between 1224 and 1318 on the site of an earlier abbey . The last service was held in the choir in 1560 and the church fell into disuse. The building remains along with the surviving chapel of St Mary and St John (1322–24) and the monumental staircase (1385).
The cathedral was begun in 1224 by Bishop Henry de Moravia and was completed by his successor Bishop William de Lamberton. It was consecrated in 1242 but the completed building did not have an architectural style. It is probable that the earliest parts of the cathedral were built by the master mason William de Whittington who also built the collegiate chapel of St Giles in Edinburgh . This scheme of building was continued in the 13th century and the choir was completed in 1250. The nave was begun in 1260 and the crossing tower was finished in 1287. The abbey had to be enlarged when it became a cathedral in 1318. There were enlargements in the 15th and 16th centuries but the cathedral was never finished. The glass in the windows was replaced by plain sash windows in the 17th and 18th centuries.
The ruins are now in the care of Historic Scotland and are open to the public.

Dollo 's specimens allowed him to show that Owen 's prehistoric pachyderms were not correct for Iguanodon . He instead modelled

Iguanodon on an elephant-like shape, and used the name to cover a whole group of very dissimilar animals. In fact, few features of Iguanodon were shared by these animals. They had all been found in rocks from the Late Jurassic of Europe and America, and had long, thin, tapering teeth, so it was natural to assume they had similar diets and therefore similar lifestyles. Dollo now made them all into Iguanodon .
Iguanodon was the first dinosaur to be named in the twentieth century, and it was a revolutionary idea to 'unify' the fragmentary remains of extinct animals. The fossils of Iguanodon were collected by other, less well-known scientists than Owen and Dollo, and so the remains of the first dinosaurs were not named by the people who knew the animals best. In fact, the first dinosaur remains named were not even dinosaurs. The remains were placed in a museum collection and not identified as belonging to a dinosaur until the 1920s.
The very origins of the term 'dinosaur' are based on a confusion, a mistake. The first dinosaur fossils were discovered in Switzerland in 1842, and were named _Iguanodon_. The name comes from the Greek words _iguana_ (meaning 'iguana') and _odon_ (meaning 'tooth'). The fossils were first found by a Swiss palaeontologist, Louis Agassiz, who was intrigued by the similarity of the teeth to those of modern iguanas. At that time people were not sure about the age of the rocks in which the fossils were found, and so Agassiz believed they were relatively recent. Therefore he assumed the teeth were from an iguana-like lizard, so he named it _Iguanodon_.
In 1847 Agassiz was proved wrong. The rocks had been found to be much older than he had thought, and so the fossils could no longer be seen as recent. When they were found to be from a period of geological history known as the Jurassic, an age of dinosaurs, the name _Iguanodon_ was used for the dinosaur. But it was not until 1878 that the fossil was properly described as a dinosaur, by the German scientist Christian Erich Hermann von Meyer.
It was a man named Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins who first suggested the name _Dinosauria_ for the group of animals we now call dinosaurs. Hawkins was an English sculptor who lived from 1807 to 1889, and made models of dinosaurs and other prehistoric animals. The first models were made in 1853, and made him famous. He also became a scientific adviser to the Crystal Palace, a glass structure built to house the Great Exhibition of 1851.
Hawkins was asked to make a series of models for the Crystal Palace, and had to decide how to portray the dinosaurs. He decided on models that were based on actual fossils. He was able to make models of the animals from fossils discovered in the 1840s by the palaeontologist Gideon Mantell. The actual fossils were from Sussex in southern England, and included bones from teeth, skulls and limbs.
Hawkins had been tipped off by a friend that the fossils were not from a giant lizard, as Mantell believed, but from an extinct group of animals. Hawkins created models of the animals, and to ensure his work was scientifically accurate, he asked the geologist Henry De la Beche to consult Mantell and other experts. De la Beche encouraged Hawkins to call the animals by a new term, _Dinosauria_ , and so the group of animals we now call dinosaurs was named by a sculptor.
In 1840 Gideon Mantell had made a discovery that would change the way people thought about the world. He found a set of fossils that he believed to be from a giant lizard. He called the animal _Iguanodon_ , and so began our love affair with dinosaurs.
Mantell was a palaeontologist, a person who studies fossils, and he was interested in the geology of the south of England. He was also an amateur artist, and was looking for fossils to draw. The eastern box turtle is highly variable in appearance, and many subspecies are now considered separate species. Eastern box turtles may grow to more than 4.5 inches (12 cm) in length, with a carapace length of 3.25-5.5 inches (8.3-14 cm).
The eastern box turtle is found along streams, in ponds, and in marshes. It is often found in oak forests. Some populations are found in savannas.
The eastern box turtle begins to breed in March or April. The female lays 3 to 12 eggs. The incubation period is 75 to 95 days. The young hatch in late May or early June.
The eastern box turtle is omnivorous. It feeds on insects , mollusks, carrion , fruits, and shrubs.
The eastern box turtle is preyed upon by raccoons, red-tailed hawks , and great horned owls .
The eastern box turtle is one of the few box turtles to be completely terrestrial. They move quickly on land, and are capable of a top speed of 10 miles (16 km) per hour.
The eastern box turtle is endangered in Illinois, Massachusetts, Michigan, New Jersey, New York, and Pennsylvania, and threatened in Florida. It is fully protected in North Carolina, and listed as a species of special concern in Kentucky, Mississippi, Missouri, and Tennessee.

Once war was declared , Darwin began to receive more attention from military planners . In June 1940 , No. 12 Squadron was " ca

nt a ried " to Darwin for duty . This was an unusual event . The Squadron was not a Fighter Squadron , but a " Bomber Reconnaissance " unit . It had been based in India at the start of the war , and had flown not only reconnaissance missions but also had attacked German shipping . In Darwin it would be used to patrol the seas and airspace around Timor , and to " protect " the Northern Territory .
The No. 12 Squadron officers who had served in India were not the best of men , and the Australians who were sent to Darwin to take over the Squadron had little respect for them. They were a " rough lot " , with a reputation for being " uncouth , untidy and downright rude " . They seemed to be " determined to use Darwin as a dumping- ground for slackers " , and the officers and men of No. 12 Squadron were not the sort of people the Australians liked to deal with.
Some of the Australians mentioned that they had " drafted in " some of the " roughest " men from Darwin to fill places that the Squadron could not fill with its own personnel. Their stated reason was that the Australians could " do without " the disliked and not very competent No. 12 Squadron personnel .
The Australians found that their complaints were taken seriously , and the No. 12 Squadron personnel were transferred to other units. " The Aussie squadrons don't dig no holes in the sand ."
In early July 1940 , No. 12 Squadron and No. 100 Squadron were flying in Darwin. One of the officers of No. 12 Squadron was Pilot Officer Chisholm. He was a young man who had been in England for about a year, and who had then been posted to the Far East. He had been in Burma , and had been made an officer in the Royal Indian Air Force. During the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor , he was flying a patrol when he saw a large Japanese fleet which he reported to Darwin . When he returned to Darwin , he was given a new aircraft and told to patrol the Northern Territory .
When No. 12 Squadron was ordered to Darwin , Pilot Officer Chisholm had been put into a single-seater aircraft which he found extremely difficult to fly. He was told to fly over Timor to determine if there were any Japanese ships in the area.
He was never seen again.
It is not known if Pilot Officer Chisholm's aircraft was shot down by Japanese fighters , or if he crashed into the sea.
Darwin's reputation grew as a " dumping-ground " for " slackers " and " rough " people .
In mid-November 1940 , No. 12 Squadron was sent to Port Moresby to help protect Australia's northern coast from possible Japanese invasion. No. 100 Squadron was sent to Ambon , to be nearer the Japanese fleet.
For those who believed that No. 12 Squadron was the cause of the air raids on Darwin and the Northern Territory , it was a further blow that No. 12 Squadron did not suffer any losses while in Darwin.
During the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor , Darwin's air defences were overwhelmed . It took several years for the air defences to be improved .
Darwin was defended by two squadrons of Curtis Hudsons , and one squadron of Lockheed Hudsons . These were not modern aircraft , and were not capable of defending Darwin. They were also not armed against fighters or bombers.
The few aircraft that the RAAF had were simply not enough to defend Darwin .
In Darwin , there was a strong belief that the Japanese were going to attack , and the people of Darwin were deeply concerned about the defence of the city. They were told that the defences would be strengthened , but they knew that these were not enough. When the air raid sirens sounded , the people of Darwin did not go to the shelters , because they knew that there was no shelter that would protect them from the bombs.
During the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor , the RAAF's defences were so weak that they were unable to fly fighter patrols . The RAAF ordered that all aircraft had to be flown to Darwin . This was an impossible order , and the aircraft arrived in Darwin too late to be effective.
The people of Darwin were told that the Japanese would attack , but the Australians were not prepared.

5. The episode acquired a Nielsen rating of 7. 7, with a 12 share.  It was the sixth highest-rated show on the Fox network that week, following The X-Files , Married... with Children , Beverly Hills, 90210 , Melrose Place , and Living Single .

IGN's Chris Carabott wrote that "'Bart vs. Australia' is a classic Simpsons episode. It's funny, it's touching, and it's just a little bit sad. It's a perfect example of a classic Simpsons episode." He also added that "Bart's anger at Homer is not only a great source of comedy, it's a great source of drama. Bart's distrust and hatred of his father is palpable, and the episode does a great job of exploring that. Bart's just been laid off, so he's in a bad mood anyway, but when he sees Homer's new job in the paper, he loses it. It's a testament to the writing that it's not just a shouting match between Bart and Homer, but we also see the hurt and pain in both characters."
In 2011, "Bart vs. Australia" was nominated for an Annie Award for "Outstanding Achievement in an Animated Television Production for Children" at the 38th Annie Awards.

000 rice cakes, 250,000 gallons of rice wine, and more than 500,000 pounds of rice. The Khmer Rouge had stockpiled vast quantities of rice and other foodstuffs, and, in anticipation of the NVA and Pathet Lao offensives, had destroyed massive amounts of rice which would otherwise have been available to the people of Cambodia.
With the NVA and Pathet Lao on the move, the Cambodian resistance forces, along with the U.S. and South Vietnamese forces, began the battle to blunt the communist thrust.
#  **The Cambodian People**
The Cambodians are truly a gentle and proud people. They have been subjected to the cruelest of tyrannies for more than a decade, but have never offered the least resistance to their tormentors. Their intransigence is a result of the indoctrination of the Khmer Rouge, who have propagandized their people into believing that the Khmers, the Cambodian people, are the only true people of Cambodia.
The Khmer Rouge brainwash Cambodians with the following statements:

Before the Democrats had even finished their convention, Nixon was already assembling his ticket. On July 9 , Nixon announced that Connecticut 's Governor John D. Rockefeller, Jr. He had served as chairman of the Democratic National Committee and was the first cousin of the former Democratic nominee for President, Tennessee Senator Estes Kefauver.
Rockefeller's selection was a surprise to many, including Nixon's campaign manager, John Mitchell. He had lobbied for former New York Governor Nelson A. Rockefeller, the son of another oil tycoon and a popular governor, but had been rebuffed. The younger Rockefeller would be the first major party vice presidential candidate with no political experience. Critics charged that the selection of Rockefeller as a running mate was a political payoff for Rockefeller's financial support of the Republican Party. Nixon and Rockefeller had met only once before, at a New York City dinner at the home of the mayor, John Lindsay.
After accepting the nomination, Nixon quickly moved to gain control of the Republican Party. In 1968, the Republican National Committee (RNC) had created a special committee to coordinate the party's efforts in the 1972 presidential election. This committee was headed by Richard Nixon's old friend, former New York Governor Thomas Dewey, and had been designed to keep Rockefeller from gaining control of the party. Dewey was a close friend of Nelson Rockefeller. With the nomination of Nixon, the RNC chose to disband the committee, and took control of the party's presidential campaign.
The 1972 Republican National Convention was held in Miami Beach , Florida . Nixon had expected to be nominated on the first ballot, but his opponent, South Dakota Governor George McGovern, was putting up a strong showing. The Democrats had nominated McGovern on the first ballot in Miami, and the Republicans also expected to be able to nominate their man without going into a second ballot. The convention was held from August 21–23, but on the first day of the convention, it quickly became clear that the Republicans were headed for a long battle.
Initially, the delegates who had supported Nixon were divided between those who supported him and those who supported Rockefeller. The Nixon delegates were united in their support for their man but the Rockefeller delegates were divided between supporters of the Connecticut governor and those who were willing to wait to see what happened in the "Rockefeller caucus." On the first ballot, Nixon was not able to gain the two-thirds of the vote necessary for a nomination.
On the second ballot, a series of shifts in support occurred. Those who supported Rockefeller dropped their support, as did those who had been divided between Rockefeller and Nixon. This shift allowed Nixon to win the nomination on the second ballot.

The interior of the church is also a quiet and tranquil space which is light and airy. There is a simple nave with an aisle on the north side. There are two windows in the nave and four in the aisle. The chancel has a plain rectangular ceiling with a plain stone arched recess. The nave is fitted with pews and has a paved floor. The windows are all plain with no stained glass.
The church has a small cheerful bell on top of a short tower. The bell was rung every day to call the congregation to worship and to give the time of day. During the 19th century the church was known for its 'special services', which were performed by the Revd John Henry Newman and the Revd Frederick William Faber. Newman and Faber were both Anglican priests who later became Roman Catholic priests. They favoured the Oxford movement, a movement within the Church of England which promoted the restoration of Anglo-Catholic ritual and practices.

The athletics competition at the first Olympics featured a men 's long jump competition and a women 's competition was introduced at the 1932 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles.
No others were added for the 1932 Games. The original 1924 Olympic long jump competition was a straight jump (without a run-up) from a grass mound. The programme of the 1932 Games reserved the grass mound for the women, who jumped from a distance of 5.50 m (18 ft 1 in). The men jumped from a distance of 6.67 m (21 ft 11+3⁄4 in). The two distances were changed to 5.40 m (17 ft 8+3⁄4 in) and 7.20 m (23 ft 7+1⁄2 in) for the 1936 Games. In 1948 and 1952 the women 's distance was increased to 5.95 m (19 ft 6 in).
The women 's long jump world record was first set in 1933 and has been set 31 times since then. The men 's world record has been set 32 times since 1923.

berta Naas , who was there, told me, "It was the biggest press event I have ever seen. I mean, Tom Cruise was there, and so were a lot of the other big stars in the film. There were helicopters, photographers, throngs of people, and the police were on the street. It was quite amazing."
 Naas , a film and Broadway reviewer for the _Wall Street Journal ,_ has seen and written about many film premieres, but she had never encountered the kind of crowd that turned out for the premiere of _Valkyrie._ "The buzz was tremendous," she said. "It was the hottest ticket in town. For the first time in a long time, I felt that the excitement and anticipation of a new Tom Cruise film were actually reflected in the way people responded to it."
 The film has been getting rave reviews, including this one from _USA Today_ : "It is a grand, sweeping, tense and dramatic film, with a cast that does it justice. The characters are rounded and flawed, and we see the tragedy of what they are attempting to do. It is a film that deserves a wide release. This is a film that will entertain and educate the public about the horrific events of history."
 I asked Naas if she thought the film might change public perception about the German role in World War II. "Yes, I do," she said. "The film shows that the Germans were very complex people, and it is a reminder of how much more difficult it is to know who your friends are, and who your enemies are, than it seems."
 _Valkyrie_ has been a long time coming. It was originally announced in 2006, but filming didn't begin until 2008. It was filmed in Europe, primarily Germany. (The scene where Cruise is being chased by Nazi soldiers through the woods was filmed on the grounds of the former Nazi concentration camp at Buchenwald .) The film was originally scheduled to be released in December 2009, but the release date was pushed back to January 2010 to give the film a better chance for Oscar nominations.

 I asked Naas if the film was a cautionary tale. "I think it is," she said. "The film shows what happens when people get so desperate for a change that they are willing to do extreme things. And, of course, it also shows what happens when people misjudge who their enemies are, and fail to see the consequences of their actions."

In the second part of Helen Who Couldn 't Help It Busch attacks Catholic pilgrimages . The childless Helen goes on a pilgrimage

to the Marian shrine at Lourdes and Busch again uses the technique of contrasting 'real' and 'fake' events . A small group of pilgrims , including Helen , crosses the border into Spain on their way back from Lourdes and are captured by Franco 's forces . Busch satirizes the Spanish Inquisition and uses Helen as a mouthpiece to expose the hypocrisy of the Church .
 Home and Private Life . Busch 's attack on the Church is not the only instance of religious criticism in this play . She also attacks the Judeo-Christian tradition and the family . The play opens in the front room of the McNulty home with Helen , the youngest of four sisters , preparing to go on her pilgrimage . A group of friends and neighbors visit for drinks and a discussion of the war in Spain . During this conversation , Helen 's parents discover that one of their daughters , the middle sister , is expecting a baby and another is engaged to be married . Likewise , Helen 's aunts and uncles have had children and are now pursuing their grandchildren . The traditional values of the Catholic home are being destroyed by the 'new ' generation . The McNulty parents are shocked and disappointed that their daughters are not following the path of marriage and motherhood . Helen feels that the news of her unwed pregnancy is a ' disaster ' for her family and plans to marry the father of her child . The confrontation between the traditional and the nontraditional values is apparent in the conversations that follow . Helen and her friends are of the opinion that the war in Spain is a war for democracy and that the Church should support the Spanish Republic . The parents and aunts and uncles are in favor of Franco and believe that Lourdes is a pilgrimage for 'suckers ' . Helen and her friends , being older and more radical than their parents , have been exposed to leftist writers and philosophers and are strong supporters of the new socialism . The parents and their relatives are old fashioned and traditional in their thinking . All the characters are unhappy with the present state of affairs in their lives . The McNulty family , as a whole , are unhappy with the political and social climate in the world . The parents are also unhappy because their oldest daughter , Rose , has married and left home and their youngest daughter , Helen , is pregnant and a 'sinner ' . Helen is unhappy because she has been rejected by her boyfriend and because she is not married . The play ends when Helen returns from Lourdes and proclaims an unwanted child .

## Background

As Manet entered his twenties he began a series of small oil paintings that he would continue to paint for the rest of his life. This was in addition to his more ambitious and larger-scale works. He made little money from these paintings, and the sales never exceeded a few hundred francs. He showed them at the Salon of 1859, where they were poorly received by the critics. Art historian John House wrote, "In the 1860s he painted a number of small canvases, which he referred to as esquisses. They were studies, sketches, or experiments in painting. They ranged from the tiny 18 x 12 cm (7 by 5 in) Les cloches (The Bells) to the large 23 x 17 cm (9 by 7 in) L' Ancien musicien (The Old Musician)." These small canvases are now considered among the most important in Manet's oeuvre.

### Portraits

Manet painted a number of portraits in the 1860s, and these are the most popular of all his esquisses. The first was his mother, Suzanne Manet, painted in 1862. The model for the young man in A Bar at the Folies-Bergère is unknown, but Manet painted him in a number of other works. It was probably his brother-in-law Eugène Boch. The other portraits are of men, who are rarely identified. Some of these were painted in cafés, while others are in the artist's studio.

### Seascapes

Manet painted a number of seascapes in the 1860s. These were painted in the Normandy coast, and include both landscapes and scenes of a man fishing from the shore. A number of these feature fishermen pulling in their nets. These were small paintings, and Manet had a difficult time selling them, as collectors preferred larger works.

### Cafés and taverns

Manet painted many scenes of cafés, taverns and bars during the 1860s. These were usually taverns in Le Havre, where he spent some of his childhood. He painted a similar theater scene as well. These generally show bourgeois or peasant men, although some of the paintings do show young women.

### Military subjects

Manet painted a number of military subjects in the 1860s. He painted many of these during his summer trips to Le Havre, where he spent some of his childhood. Many of them are scenes of soldiers in military camps, but he also painted a number of paintings of battle scenes. These are very small paintings, and Manet had a difficult time selling them.

### Interiors

Manet painted a number of small interior scenes during the 1860s. Many of these were painted in the cafés and taverns he frequently visited in Le Havre. Manet was fascinated by the people he saw there, and he made a number of studies of them. Some of the scenes are of people playing cards.

### Luncheons

Manet painted a number of small luncheon scenes during the 1860s. These scenes show bourgeois or peasant men eating at taverns, or in their homes. Some of the paintings show women as well, but many are of men.

### Boycarriages

In the 1860s Manet painted a number of small paintings of boycarriages. These were small carts drawn by children. The carriages are painted in red or blue, and are often decorated with flowers. The children who pull the carts are usually dressed in red or blue.

From the Middle Ages, Arab Christians were divided into two main groups, the Melkites and the Jacobites. The name Melkite comes from the Greek word _megalykos_ , which means "imperial." The Melkites thus designate Christians from countries that were part of the Byzantine empire. They are today concentrated in Lebanon, Syria, and most of the countries of the Arab world, as well as in Egypt and in the regions of the eastern Mediterranean that were part of the Ottoman Empire.
The term Jacobite is used in reference to Syrian Christians who adhere to the Church of the East. They are today concentrated in Iraq, Iran, Pakistan, and India.
The twenty-five centuries of Christianity in the Arab-speaking world have been marked by a series of trials and setbacks. In their history, the Christians of Arabia came face to face with the "Arab" conquerors who came from the Arabian Peninsula, and their fate was closely linked to the history of the Arab-Muslim world.
From the time of the Arab conquests in the seventh century until the twentieth century, Arab Christians, by and large, were citizens of the Ottoman Empire. This has had several consequences. First, they were all in Turkey, Egypt, and the Arab countries of the Peninsula. Second, they were all under the hegemony of the Ottoman Empire, which imposed Islamic law on the Muslims and the Christians of its territories. Third, they all spoke Arabic. They were Arabs, Muslims, and Christians who were divided by religion and language.
The Arabs and the Christians did not have a common history. The Arabs and their culture were different from the _Mashriq_ (the countries of the eastern Mediterranean) and their culture. They were Arabs of the _Mashriq_ , and they shared the same culture. The Arabs of the Peninsula were Muslims, but the Arabs of the _Mashriq_ were Christians.
The Arab-Christian relationship has not been easy. The Christians of the _Mashriq_ were subjected to different kinds of oppression, tyranny, and persecution by the Arabs. But they were also exposed to other kinds of oppression and persecution, such as the Crusades and the Inquisition.
The Arab-Christian relationship was not always peaceful. The Crusades and the Inquisition were periods of conflict and war between the Christians of the East and the Arabs. ­nity . The country is experiencing a devastating spread of the HIV/ AIDS virus, which has struck hardest in the nation’s poorest communities. On the eve of the state of emergency, more than 40 percent of the adults in Swaziland were living with HIV/AIDS. But by the end of 2005, the country’s total population was just under one million, meaning that 400,000 Swazis were living with the virus. This book offers a case study of the South African government’s AIDS response, focusing on the activities of the South African National AIDS Council (SANAC) and how it has helped shape South Africa’s AIDS policy and programs. As a case study, the South African AIDS response provides a powerful example of how a centralized, coordinated national response can reduce the impact of HIV/AIDS on a nation. And, as the Swaziland case study shows, the South African AIDS response offers crucial lessons for other countries, such as Swaziland, that are confronting their own AIDS crises.
By way of background, the AIDS response in South Africa is a powerful example of how coordinated centralized leadership and resources can be harnessed to reduce AIDS’ impact on a nation. In South Africa, the government and the private sector have come together to combat the spread of HIV/AIDS, and this book assesses the role played in this effort by SANAC.
In 1999, the South African government established SANAC in order to coordinate the AIDS response across the country. SANAC is the first of its kind in Africa, and its creation demonstrates the commitment of the South African government to combating the spread of the virus. The South African AIDS response has been an innovative model of how to effectively and efficiently deliver services, and the SANAC model has been widely emulated throughout Africa and the world.
AIDS is a global pandemic. It affects people everywhere, but its impact is uneven. The disease has varying impact on different countries, communities, and people. In South Africa, the impact of AIDS is uneven, as well. The virus has struck hardest in places where poverty is rampant, where the health care infrastructure is weak, and where there has been a breakdown in the social structure.
South Africa is one of the poorest nations in the world, and AIDS has hit hardest in the country’s poorest communities. In many ways, the South African AIDS response is a microcosm of the global AIDS response. South Africa’s AIDS crisis has been unevenly distributed throughout the country. In KwaZulu-Natal and the Eastern Cape, for example, infection rates are higher than in other provinces.
Part of the reason for the uneven impact of the virus in South Africa has been the weakness of the country’s health care system. In the early 1990s, health care in South Africa was in a state of collapse. The legacy of apartheid, which had established a system of separate hospitals for black and white patients, had left the country’s health care system without the resources to care for its population. At the same time, South Africa’s social services were in disarray, as the country struggled to reverse the legacy of apartheid.
These challenges, combined with the spread of the AIDS virus, have created a significant crisis in South Africa. There is a critical shortage of health care workers, especially in the country’s most impoverished provinces. Health care services are not accessible to the poorest communities, and the capacity of the health care system is not sufficient to meet the demand.
South Africa’s AIDS response has been organized around the concept of decentralized care. This approach has been a major factor in the success of the country’s AIDS response and has helped to ensure that the virus has not led to the destruction of the social fabric.
The decentralized care approach was created in response to the breakdown of the social fabric in South Africa, which has been exacerbated by the spread of the AIDS virus. The approach is based on the idea that access to health care is an essential part of the country’s AIDS response. The approach is also based on the idea that access to health care is an essential part of economic development in South Africa.

## Plot summary

The novel's narrator is a woman called Anna K. who is not a terrorist, although she is married to one. She and her husband, Jonathan, are members of an organization called the Cell. The story begins with a scene of terrorism: a bombing in a restaurant in the centre of London. Anna is a sometimes troubled but still passionate woman who is determined to understand what the Cell is all about. She is a person who has lost her faith and is looking for another. She is searching for meaning and a purpose to her life. She is willing to go to extremes to find the answers to her questions.

The narrative begins with Anna on a train, reflecting on what she has been doing and where she is going. She has been staying in London for two years, and has been involved with the Cell for almost that long. In the course of the novel, the train ride forms the frame story of the whole. Anna's husband, Jonathan, is a member of the Cell. The Cell is a terrorist organization, and their aim is to terrorize the public into making changes in society. They use a variety of violent tactics, including bombings and kidnappings.

Anna and Jonathan meet and fall in love at first sight at a demonstration in London, where they were both protesting the British government. They are both radicals, and they are both very committed to finding a way to change society. They are both very political, and their politics are very similar. Their commitment to changing society is what makes them fall in love. They are both very committed to the cause, and they are willing to do whatever it takes to achieve their goals. They are both very idealistic, and their idealism is what makes them fall in love. Anna and Jonathan are the only two people in the Cell who are completely committed to the cause. sp. Other theories such as the presumed domestication of the Sorraia by the Iberians are not supported by any scientific research, and the relationship of the Sorraia to the African wild horse remains mostly speculative.

## Breeding

The Sorraia is a small horse breed, generally weighing about 500 kg (1,100 lb) and standing about 14 hands (56 in, 142 cm). It's the only breed that does not have a specific standard for its conformation. However, the breed is characterized by its dappled grey color, small head and ears, long legs, and robust, muscular body.

## History

Mares of Sorraia

Until 1998, the Sorraia breed was called the Iberian pony, but was renamed after the discovery that there were no ponies in the breed's ancestry. According to the breed registry, it is a wild horse native to the Iberian Peninsula. The theory was that the Sorraia was not descended from domesticated horses, but from the extinct wild horse of the Iberian Peninsula, Equus quagga bozasi. The Sorraia was described as similar to the extinct Iberian wild horse, Equus albidus, and was considered to be a subspecies of that wild horse.

Despite the lack of a definitive history, the Sorraia is considered to be one of the oldest horse breeds in the world.

The Sorraia has been cultivated since the 1970s in Portugal, and is a symbol of the region. The breed is also recognized in Spain, France, and in the United States and Canada, where the breed association was founded in 1998.

There is a wild Sorraia population in the Iberian Peninsula, in the Spanish province of Salamanca. It is also possible that the Sorraia could be a hybrid of the Iberian wild horse and the domestic horse, but no scientific research has been conducted.

An important pathophysiological mechanism of leukemogenesis in AML is the epigenetic induction of dedifferentiation by genetic

mutations. The most important of these is the FLT3-ITD mutation, which is present in about 30% of AML cases and correlates with a poor prognosis. Using mouse models, we have shown that FLT3-ITD mutation induces AML by increasing PI3K/AKT signaling through constitutive activation of the PI3K/AKT pathway.1,2 We hypothesize that this increase in PI3K/AKT signaling is mediated by the loss of the transcriptional repressor MeCP2.
 Mutations in the gene encoding methyl-CpG binding protein 2 (MeCP2) have been associated with several diseases, including autism, Rett syndrome and X-linked intellectual disability.3,4 These mutations have been proposed to cause disease by increasing transcription of genes affected by the mutation. However, the mechanism is not fully understood and no therapeutic intervention is currently available.
 We propose that FLT3-ITD mutation causes AML through a MeCP2-dependent mechanism. Inhibition of PI3K/AKT signaling has been shown to be effective in the treatment of AML.5 We propose that therapeutic inhibition of PI3K/AKT signaling would be effective in treating AMLs caused by mutations in MeCP2.
 The specific aims of this proposal are to: 1) develop and validate a novel mouse model for MeCP2-associated diseases; 2) determine the mechanism by which MeCP2 mutations cause AML; and 3) determine the effectiveness of the novel therapeutic approach for treating MeCP2-associated diseases. We have successfully established and validated a novel mouse model of MeCP2-associated disease. We have also determined that MeCP2 mutations cause AML by increasing PI3K/AKT signaling. We are currently investigating the effectiveness of the novel therapeutic approach. These studies will provide the necessary preclinical data for the clinical development of this novel treatment.
