The fort is designed as a defensible battery , rather than a defensive strongpoint . The faces of the fort join to form a half

circle .
The fort's circumference was 1000 feet (305m); it is 150 feet (46m) wide, and 17 feet (5m) high, and is built of brick. The roof was flat and was used as a parade ground.
The fort was built by John Waller, and it is possible that it was used by the Parliamentarian forces to defend against a Royalist attack during the Civil War.
The fort is now a scheduled monument and a Grade II listed building .
The fort is located in a field between Hatcham Park Road and St Johns Road, near the junction with Church Road. The site is fenced off.
Hatcham Park Road (A205) runs from New Cross to Blackheath Road (A204). The site is 350 metres north east of New Cross station.

Seo Taiji (Korean: 서태지; born Lee Seok-hyun on September 2, 1972), is a South Korean singer, producer, songwriter and rapper. As the frontman of the pioneering Korean hip-hop group Seo Taiji and the Boys, he is often regarded as the "Father of Korean Hip Hop". Seo was also one of the most prominent figures in the Korean Wave movement of the late 90s and early 2000s.
In the late 1990s, Seo Taiji and the Boys took the Korean music industry by storm with their hip hop sound and innovative style, which was different from the typical K-pop at the time. Their style of music brought a newfound popularity to the genre that had previously remained niche, and they became the first Korean music act to garner international success, bringing Korean music to the international stage. They were also the first K-pop group to incorporate rock and jazz elements into their music. Seo Taiji and the Boys were among the most influential acts in Korean hip hop history, with many subsequent groups being heavily inspired by their music.
In 1999, Seo Taiji and the Boys split up to pursue solo projects. Seo continued his career as a solo artist, and emerged as a prominent figure in the Korean wave of the early 2000s. In 2004, he announced the end of his solo career to form a new hip hop group, Se7en, and in 2005, he began a solo career under the moniker Se7en. In 2010, he reunited with Lee Juno and Yoon M. B to form Seo Taiji and the Boys once again.

In the 2009 Friends Provident Trophy , the first one @-@ day competition in the English domestic calendar , Somerset showed a m

aturity and skill that belied their youthful line-up. They reached the final with a commanding victory over Nottinghamshire, and in the final they overcame a spirited attempt by Middlesex to win the game, and with it the trophy.
 Nottinghamshire's chief spin bowler in the match was Ben Phillips .
 Somerset did not have to wait long for the first of what would prove to be a series of major county victories in 2009, the Friends Provident Trophy. In an early season one-day competition, the Trophy is the first of the season for the counties, and Somerset's chances of success were boosted by the news that the match was to be played at the Weston-Super-Mare ground, which was being renovated to meet the ECB's new ground-grading criteria. The ground had been closed to cricket since 2007, but now had a new seating area, a new scoreboard and a new dressing room.
The key decision facing the skipper was the selection of a fast bowler. Matty Spriegel was expected to be the first choice, but he had suffered a back injury during the winter and was not yet fit enough to play. That left Steve Kirby, a man who had been written off by many of the Somerset supporters, as the only possible candidate.
Middlesbrough, on the other hand, had the luxury of choosing from a number of candidates. James Fuller was selected to open the bowling, supported by Stuart Meaker and New Zealander Chris Martin . The 'Boro had been to the final in 2008, and were desperate to win the trophy.
 Michael Yardy has been selected as one of the Wisden Cricketers of the Year.
 Somerset's plan to attack Fuller and Meaker from the beginning was thrown into disarray when Meaker was taken out of the attack after only six overs. Meaker was forced to retire hurt, and with him went the 'Boro's best chance of taking an early wicket.
Somerset's top run-scorer in the match was Jonathan Bailey, who made 76 not out to help Somerset reach a total of 226-6. Middlesbrough were able to make only a token fight of the chase, with the impressive Davies taking 5-24 as they were all out for 140.

Ireland has an ancient industry based on peat ( known locally as " turf " ) as a source of energy for home fires . A form of bi

omass , peat has been harvested in Ireland for at least 5,000 years  and was a major fuel source for homes ( as well as for horticulture ) in the 19th century . Today, peat is being used to generate electricity .

## Background

Ireland has an abundance of peat, with up to 500 million tonnes ( 492 million long tons ; 550 million short tons ) of peat having been harvested in the past 100 years. This is generally mined in cutaway areas rather than dug out.

Ireland's peat-based industry is concentrated in three main areas:

* North-east Ireland (primarily County Fermanagh and County Cavan )
* West-midlands Ireland (primarily County Offaly and County Galway )
* South-west Ireland (primarily County Clare and County Westmeath )

The industry has declined over the 20th century as coal and oil replaced peat as the main source of fuel.

## Modern use of peat

### Power generation

Ireland has a network of 18 peat-fired power stations, operated by ESB, which produce 20–25% of the country's electricity. The first peat-fired power station, at Ardnacrusha, began operating in 1929. The remainder of the stations were constructed during the 1980s and 1990s. The first of these was the Moneypoint power station in 1984.

The peat-fired plants have a combined capacity of 3,200 MW. Peat is a relatively inexpensive fuel, selling for less than €15/t . However, the use of peat is politically controversial because of the environmental impact of harvesting the resource.

### Heating

Peat is the traditional fuel for home fires in Ireland, with peat briquettes sold in supermarkets and the traditional " turf " still used in many homes. Peat is more expensive than coal, but is available locally and does not have the seasonal variation that coal has.

### Horticulture

Peat is still harvested to a limited extent to grow horticultural plants and flowers.

## Environmental impacts

Peat extraction is a significant source of atmospheric nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas with a global warming potential 300 times that of carbon dioxide. The extraction of peat is also causing air pollution, noise pollution and visual pollution. Peat extraction may also cause soil erosion.

### Environmental impact of power generation

The environmental impacts of peat-fired power generation are significant. Peat is a carbon-rich fuel whose burning produces smoke and carbon monoxide. Peat-fired power generation plants have been estimated to produce 20% of Ireland's nitrogen oxide emissions. Peat-fired power generation produces 10% of Ireland's sulfur dioxide emissions, and 14% of Ireland's carbon dioxide emissions.

### Environmental impact of electricity generation

Peat is a fossil fuel. This means that it will eventually run out.

### Environmental impact of heating

Peat is a carbon-rich fuel whose burning produces smoke and carbon monoxide. Harvesting peat for home fires releases nitrous oxide, carbon dioxide and methane.

## Sustainability

The Irish peat industry is largely sustainable. It is estimated that the amount of peat harvested in Ireland is less than the amount naturally generated by the bogs.

amed as the " Band " ( Robbie Robertson , Rick Danko , Richard Manuel , Garth Hudson , and Levon Helm ) . This tour was followed by one of the most influential albums in rock history , _Blonde on Blonde_ , which included the hit single " Rainy Day Women # 12 & 35 " .
On August 28 , 1966 , the Byrds released a version of Dylan's " Mr. Tambourine Man " , which reached number one in the charts . By December 1966 Dylan and the Band had recorded their first album together , _The Basement Tapes_ , which was released in 1975.
After a motorcycle accident in 1966 , Dylan spent four years touring and recording less frequently while writing songs in his home in Woodstock , New York , including the three songs on the soundtrack to the film _Pat Garrett & Billy the Kid_ ( 1973 ) and the triple album _Planet Waves_ ( 1974 ) .
The 1975 album _Blood on the Tracks_ was inspired by Dylan's separation from his second wife , Sara Dylan , and featured the song " Tangled Up in Blue " , which was covered by both the Band and the Beach Boys . In 1976 , he received a Grammy Award for Best Country Song for " If Not for You " .
In 1978 , Dylan released the album _Street-Legal_ , which was his first to reach the Top 10 on the U.S. album chart . Although the album was a commercial success , Dylan's touring schedule began to suffer due to exhaustion and his voice being repeatedly damaged during live performances. After a summer tour of North America , Dylan took a year off from touring .
In 1981 , he released the album _Shot of Love_ , followed by _Infidels_ in 1983 . In 1984 , Dylan underwent a conversion to Christianity and released two albums: _Slow Train Coming_ and _Saved_. In 1985 , he released _Empire Burlesque_ , and in 1986 , he released _Knocked Out Loaded_. In 1987 , he released _Down in the Groove_ , which was followed by _Oh Mercy_ in 1989. In 2000 , Dylan released _Love and Theft_ , which was nominated for Best Contemporary Folk Album at the Grammy Awards . In 2001 , he released _Things Have Changed_ , which was nominated for Best Song Written Specifically for a Motion Picture or for Television at the Grammy Awards . In 2003 , Dylan released _Modern Times_ , which was nominated for Album of the Year at the Grammy Awards and for Best Contemporary Folk Album at the Grammy Awards . In 2006 , he released _Together Through Life_ , which was nominated for Best Contemporary Folk Album at the Grammy Awards . Dylan's most recent studio album , _Tempest_ , was released in 2012 .

 "The Egyptians knew only one moon god, and he was Sin"
 It is not difficult to find a wide variety of sources that will tell you that the Egyptians' one and only moon god was Sin, but that does not mean those sources are correct.
 The problem is that Sin is a Sumerian word that means "moon." Some scholars have argued that the Egyptians borrowed the word and used it as a name for the god (probably because he was indeed the moon god). Hornung and others have argued that Sin came to Egypt and was given an Egyptian name, but the evidence for that is very weak.

The thirty-three-year-old de Moravia had the task of carving out an institutional framework out of the loose community of Marian devotees which, by the time of Honorius's bull, had more than 200 members.
The new order, which was to be known as the Brothers of the Blessed Virgin Mary of Mount Carmel, was to be a male-only religious order. The men were to be celibate, living lives of poverty, chastity, and obedience. Each brother was to dedicate himself to prayer and to a life of penance. One of the brothers was to be designated the superior, who was to be chosen by a group of brothers from among their number and then approved by the bishop. Particular care was to be shown to those who were sick or infirm.
De Moravia himself was to be the superior, and the order was to have its headquarters in the small village of Mount Carmel in the Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem. The site of the order's monastery was symbolically important: it was on the slopes of Mount Carmel, in the very place where Elijah had encountered the Lord. The order of Carmel was thus intended to be a continuation of Elijah's prophetic witness to God's power and faithfulness.

Ian McCall was born on this day in 1962 in Dunfermline , Fife . After working as an apprentice joiner he signed his first professional contract at Rangers at the age of 16 in 1980, and made his debut in August 1983. He stayed at Ibrox until 1992, making 342 appearances and scoring 17 goals. During his first spell at Rangers Ian McCall won the Scottish Premier Division title in 1984–85 and 1987–88 and the Scottish Cup in 1983–84, 1985–86 and 1987–88.
In 1992 McCall signed for Bradford City , winning promotion from Division Three in his first season. After Bradford's relegation to Division Three in 1994 he moved back to Rangers, where he remained until his retirement in 1998. When McCall left Rangers in 1998, he was appointed as Bradford City manager and took the club to the Division One play-off final, where they lost to Wigan Athletic . After the disappointment of the play-off final McCall moved to English Division Two club Lincoln City , where he stayed for two seasons. In 2001 McCall moved to Scottish third division side Clyde, leading the club to promotion in 2003. Leonard was educated at Kempston High School in Bedford , England . He made his debut for London Irish in 1989, and was signed by Bath for £200,000 in 1991. He moved to Wigan in 1993, and the following year went on to be named the Rugby Football League's "man of steel" in the 1994-95 season. In 2000, Leonard was named in the Rugby Union Hall of Fame . He was inducted into the England Rugby Football Union Hall of Fame in 2008 .
Leonard's career was plagued by injury problems. In the 1997 World Cup final, he broke his arm in the first minute of play. In 2001, he broke a rib in a match against Northampton. He was diagnosed with a torn ankle ligament in a 2002 match against Gloucester. He was named in the England squad for the 2003 World Cup, but did not play a single match, and later retired from the game.

In 1989 , three of the parish 's buildings — the church , the rectory , and the rectory 's garage — were added to the National

Register of Historic Places .
 
\n

Holy Family Church , a brick Romanesque Revival structure, is located at the junction of Mill and Main Streets in downtown Riverdale. It was built in 1892 and expanded in 1926. Holy Family is a single-story structure, with a gabled roof and a 125-foot (38 m) tower. At the center of the front facade is a semicircular arch. The interior of Holy Family church contains an altar, pews, a pulpit, and a baptismal font. The church also houses a very large pipe organ.

The rectory, also a brick structure, is located on Mill Street. It is a three-story structure with a gabled roof. A front porch extends across the entire front facade, supported by two posts. The rectory 's interior contains a living room, a dining room, a kitchen, and a fireplace.

The rectory 's garage is located to the rear of the rectory . It is a one-story structure built in 1988, constructed of concrete block. The garage 's interior contains a large drive-through bay.

contains significant amounts of thorium and uranium .

The name is derived from the Greek word monazitēs , "single stone",as it is found as a single mineral .

## Composition

Usually monazite contains variable amounts of lanthanides and yttrium , along with significant amounts of thorium and uranium . The lanthanides are concentrated near the rims of the crystal, with the higher atomic number elements preferentially located towards the center. Monazite's chemical composition can be expressed as 

( La , Ce , Nd , Pr , Sm , Eu , Gd , Tb , Dy , Ho , Er , Tm , Yb , Lu , Y )  +  ( Th , U )  +  ( Ca , Fe , Mn , P )  +  ( F , Cl , Br , I ) 

In some rare cases, all the lanthanides are concentrated in the crystal's outer rim, resulting in a product known as bastnäsite . Monazite is a common mineral in placer deposits, but in many cases the lanthanides have been separated from the other minerals. When this is the case, the monazite is considered an ore of the lanthanides.

Monazite is the only known natural ore of thorium .

## Occurrence

Monazite is usually found in placer deposits as a heavy mineral sand . The monazite of placer deposits is usually a mixture of lanthanides . Lanthanide placer deposits are found along the coasts of India, Australia, the United States and Canada . They also occur in many other countries, including China and Brazil .

Monazite has been found in alluvial sands in the southeastern United States since the 1930s.

Monazite also occurs in beach placers in Florida, Georgia, and South Carolina .

Monazite crystals were discovered in the 1950s in the northern part of the Central Plateau of New South Wales, Australia . Researchers assumed that they were monazite, but it was actually a new mineral, but the name was already used.

### Minor

Monazite occurs as a minor mineral in pegmatites, carbonatites and other igneous rocks . It is found in many areas of the world, including the United States, Brazil, Canada, India, Sri Lanka, Russia, Madagascar, Egypt, and Australia.

## Uses

Monazite is mined and processed for its rare earth elements .

Monazite is used to make monazite concentrate .

Monazite is used in the preparation of rare earth elements .

Monazite is used in ceramic glazes and as a source of phosphorus.

Groening thought that it would be funny to have a baby character that did not talk and never grew up , but was scripted to show

"the most important things in life from the child's point of view." The writers also wanted to contrast the zany antics of the show's main characters with the sweetness of the baby. The show's writers stated that the ideas for the character came from their childhood, when a baby in the family would cry whenever the adults fought. They thought that this was a very innocent and honest reaction. In the episode "Lisa on Ice," Homer gets angry and explodes at Bart, but Lisa, the innocent baby, is convinced that her brother is a robot. The writers thought that it would be funny to have a baby that was so innocent that she believed her brother was a robot.

The character's design is based on the actress Elizabeth Taylor. Groening said that they wanted to have a "beautiful but weird and unattractive" baby. The baby is voiced by Maggie Roswell. The original test animation for Maggie was a combination of "a little baby and a little chicken." Roswell also originally voiced Helen Lovejoy and Mona Simpson. She was replaced as the voice of the characters in 1998, so that she could be a cast member of the sitcom Grace Under Fire and the CBS soap opera The Young and the Restless.

In 1849 James Goodhue began publication of the Minnesota Pioneer newspaper in Saint Paul ( the paper would later be renamed the

Minnesota Pioneer and Democrat). The newspaper's masthead carried the name of the Goodhue brothers, James and Andrew, who had acquired the title of the St. Paul Land Company in 1839 and 1840. The newspaper was a vehicle for promoting the sale of lots in the new town of St. Paul, and by 1852 the brothers had acquired title to most of the land within the area covered by the newspaper.
As the city of St. Paul grew, the Minnesota Pioneer and Democrat became the region's preeminent newspaper. As a result, the newspaper was used to publicize the city's first steamboat, the St. Paul, built in 1854. James Goodhue was the city's first mayor, serving from 1854 to 1855.
The paper's name was changed to Minnesota Pioneer in 1856, when Goodhue sold the paper to Henry C. Gilbert and John S. Pillsbury. In 1860 Minnesota Pioneer was purchased by S. W. Pillsbury and W. L. Merriam.
In 1877, the paper merged with the St. Paul Times and the St. Paul Press to form the St. Paul Daily Press.

Hannah de Rothschild was born in 1851 into a world of great wealth and luxury . She was the granddaughter of Baron Nathan Mayer

de Rothschild, the American-born British banker with the broad-shouldered gait, who had built up his fortune by investing in railway companies and British government bonds. The family business was now a worldwide banking empire, controlling more than a third of the gold reserves of the Bank of England, and a majority of its shares. The Rothschilds had a reputation for being the most prudent and conservative of financiers, but they were also known as shrewd businessmen who made a fortune from government bonds, which were issued during the Crimean War to help pay for the British war effort in the 1850s.
Hannah's father, Lionel Nathan de Rothschild, was a man of great ambition, who was determined to become a leading politician. At the age of twenty-three he had established a flourishing banking business in London, and in 1849, to the astonishment of his family, he had married a beautiful young woman, Annie Rothschild, who was the daughter of his uncle, Salomon Mayer, and as such a first cousin. The marriage had not been approved of by the Rothschilds, and for many years Lionel and Annie were forced to live apart from their children, who were brought up by a nanny in a house in Kensington. In 1856, however, the Rothschilds, who were always willing to make concessions to the younger generation, relented. Dylan has won many awards throughout his career including eleven Grammy Awards , one Academy Award and one Golden Globe Award .

The Pulitzer Prize Board on April 15, 2016, awarded Dylan a special citation for "his profound impact on popular music and American culture, marked by lyrical compositions of extraordinary poetic power." In May 2012, Dylan received the Presidential Medal of Freedom from President Barack Obama. Dylan has sold more than 100 million records, making him one of the best-selling music artists of all time. He has also received numerous honorary doctorates, including one from Princeton University, for his contributions as a musician and a writer.
In 2010, Dylan was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, for "having created new poetic expressions within the great American song tradition." His work has influenced many other musicians, and he has been inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, Minnesota Music Hall of Fame, Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame and the Songwriters Hall of Fame.
Early life and musical beginnings
Dylan was born Robert Allen Zimmerman on May 24, 1941, in Duluth, Minnesota. His father, Abraham Zimmerman, worked for the Standard Oil Co., and his mother, Beatrice Stone, was a homemaker. Dylan's paternal grandparents, Zigman and Anna, emigrated from Odessa, in the Russian Empire (now Ukraine), and changed the family name from "Zimmerman" to "Zimmerman" upon arriving in the United States. Dylan has said: "It's a small town. Everybody knows everybody. The accent is definitely not Minnesota. There's a strong Jewish influence there."
Dylan's father, an Orthodox Jew, changed the family name from "Zimmerman" to "Dylan", after the Welsh poet, Dylan Thomas, when Robert was 6 years old. Dylan has said that the change was probably made "to satisfy an ancestral jones on my father's part", and that he prefers to use the name Dylan. His parents took him to Hibbing to live with his maternal grandparents, Abe and Clara Stone, for several years, where he was influenced by the music of Hank Williams, Little Richard and Elvis Presley, as well as by the political activism of the Civil Rights Movement.
Dylan played the harmonica and the piano as a child, and at the age of 10 he began performing in Hibbing, playing John Lee Hooker numbers and other blues standards. He sang and played piano and harmonica in a trio, the Golden Chords, with two school friends in Hibbing, and began performing in Duluth in local clubs. In the summer of 1959, he went to see John Lee Hooker in Duluth, and afterward, Hooker gave him a harmonica. The following spring, Dylan had formed a band, the Golden Chords, with two school friends in Hibbing, and in the autumn of 1959 they performed at the Ten O'Clock Scholar, a local club in Duluth.
In January 1960, at the age of 19, Dylan went to New York City, initially to be near his musical idols Woody Guthrie and Little Richard, and to perform at clubs on the Lower East Side. His main ambition at that time was to become a folk singer, but he also had aspirations to be a comedian. In New York, Dylan began performing at clubs on the Lower East Side, playing solo acoustic numbers with a harmonica rack around his neck. He began going to clubs to hear blues musicians such as Big Joe Williams, Son House, Howlin' Wolf and Willie Dixon, and he went to his first folk club, Gerde's Folk City, where he heard Fred Neil and Odetta. He also went to the clubs where the emerging performers of the New York folk scene were playing, such as The Bitter End, Gerde's Folk City, Café Wha?, The Gaslight Coffee House and The Village Gate, where he was influenced by the music of Dave Van Ronk, Ramblin' Jack Elliott and Carolyn Hester. He also went to the Broadside Ballads dance, where he was influenced by the music of Eric von Schmidt and the Clancy Brothers.

That's the thing I'm most proud of."  He has occasionally stated that his biggest regret was not being able to achieve his goal of creating a "zero-fatality" Formula One.  Along with other FIA presidents, Mosley has been criticized for his perceived top-down paternalism,  and he has been described as "a master of the universe"  and "the dictator of Formula One"  and of having "absolutely no tolerance for dissent." 

## Personal life

Mosley is a keen enthusiast of vintage cars, particularly Bugattis and pre-war Bentleys. He is also an enthusiast of polo and, for many years, owned a polo team.

Mosley is a keen amateur photographer who has exhibited his work.

### Relationships

Mosley has been married twice. His first wife, Caroline, was killed in a car accident in 1977, aged 29. He married his second wife, former model Lady Helen Windsor, in 1980. They have three daughters and one son. The couple divorced in 2008. In 2012, a judge in Madrid ordered Mosley to pay Lady Helen £12.5 million in damages and £600,000 in legal costs. Mosley appealed, the decision was upheld in 2015, and in 2016, Lady Helen's lawyers completed the process by ensuring that the money was paid.

### Adult parties and spanking

Mosley has been the subject of legal action by civil liberties groups after revelations that he ordered police to stop photographers, claiming that he was attending "adult parties" and that his sexual activities were "private and consensual". He has also stated that he has arranged to be spanked on occasion by his wife.

### Nazism

In 1986, Mosley was sentenced to three months in prison, suspended for two years, and ordered to pay a £6,000 fine for assaulting a protester outside a meeting of his National Front organisation in 1981. In 2001, he was criticised by the Daily Telegraph for having expressed admiration for the Nazi Party in a 1983 interview with the New Statesman. He was also criticised for having attended a white-supremacist rally in 1974. Mosley's response to these allegations was that he had "tried to understand fascism" as a teenager, and that the "whole Nazi thing was a catastrophe for the world", but that the Nazi Party in the 1930s had "some good ideas" and that he had learnt "nothing from them". In an interview with the BBC in 2002, he stated that he believed there were "absolutely no grounds" for maintaining that he was a racist. He also stated that "I was a twit at the time and I'm not proud of it, but I think it's a mistake to judge people who did their wrong things in the twenties and thirties by today's standards".

### Allegations of paedophilia

In 2008, a claim was made that a friend of Mosley's, a former Conservative MP, had sexually abused a 12-year-old boy. Mosley was questioned by police about the matter, but was not arrested. In 2012, Mosley's second wife, Lady Helen Windsor, obtained a private ruling from a judge in Madrid that Mosley should pay her a £12.5 million settlement in compensation for the breakdown of their marriage, and that he should also pay her £600,000 in legal costs. The court heard that Mosley had been involved with a woman who was a convicted paedophile (who had been sentenced to 18 months' imprisonment in 1979 for having sexual intercourse with a 13-year-old boy). In 2016, the Court of Appeal upheld the decision of the lower courts, with Mosley appealing the decision to the Supreme Court. The assaults on Zeebrugge and Ostend were eventually launched on 23 April , after twice being delayed by poor weather . The Ost

end raid was cancelled, but a raid on Zeebrugge was launched the following day. The raid took place at dawn on Sunday, 23 April, in a thick fog that made it difficult for the ships to find the harbour. The Germans on the other hand had been able to set up a barrage of guns to fire on the approaching British ships and to sink the destroyers that were to have protected the torpedo boats from enemy fire.
The battle had started when the destroyers _Hampshire_ and _Icarus_ had been sunk by the German gunfire. The remaining destroyers and torpedo boats had then managed to break through the barrage and enter the harbour, where they were fired on by the shore batteries. The British ships had dropped their sea anchors to stop them being dragged too fast by the current. However, the current was stronger than expected and they were swept by a strong tide beneath the bridge that led to the outer harbour, where they were stuck fast. The commanding officer of the _Vindictive_ , Commander Godfrey Place, had managed to get his ship close to the mole, and had ordered that the sea anchors be released to try and refloat the ship.
However, the first sea anchor was released too soon and became entangled in the bridge. The ship was now so close to the mole that the Germans on the shore batteries could see that they had to act quickly if they were to save the ship. The sea anchor was cut and a second line released. This time the sea anchor was released at the right moment and the ship was refloated, but was now moving too fast to be controlled.
The Germans opened fire on the ship from the shore batteries and the _Vindictive_ was hit several times. Many crew members were killed and wounded. The ship was hit again by a shell as it tried to manoeuvre into a position to land the storming party. A large hole was made in the ship and sea water began to pour into the ship. The Germans were now aiming directly at the bridge. The surviving bridge crew tried to control the ship's movements, but were hit and killed.
The _Vindictive_ was heading straight for the mole when Lieutenant Commander Philip Louis Vian, who was overall in command of the raid, ordered the engines stopped and the ship to be steered in the opposite direction. The steering had become extremely difficult as many of the bridge crew were now dead or wounded. The _Vindictive_ was now heading straight for a German barge, moored to the mole. The crew on the barge were now trying to escape the ship, but were pulled back when a shell from the _Vindictive_ struck the barge. The explosion killed the crew and the barge was now caught in the propeller of the _Vindictive_ , which was now heading directly at the mole.
The ship was now only a few metres from the mole. Commander Vian now ordered the crew to abandon the ship. Only the storming party was left on the ship. The ship's stern crashed into the mole and the storming party began to climb down the ropes to the shore. They were followed by the wounded who had not been able to leave the ship. However, there were still many Germans on the mole and they began to fire on the party. They were now exposed to the fire from the shore batteries and many of the storming party were hit. They were still trying to make their way to the shore when the German batteries opened fire on the shore and the ship.
However, the Germans had not counted on the fact that the _Vindictive_ had been hit so badly that the ship began to list to starboard. The storming party and the wounded were now pushed towards the shore. Many of the storming party had been hit by shrapnel or bullets and were unable to move. On November 8, 2007, the National Hurricane Center (NHC) began monitoring a non-tropical low pressure area located over the Bahamas for potential tropical development. The low was initially thought to lack sufficient tropical characteristics to be classified as a tropical cyclone, but a tropical cyclone formation was still possible due to upper-level outflow. By November 9, the NHC began to classify the system as a subtropical cyclone; the system was designated as Tropical Depression Twenty-Eight on November 10. The depression quickly intensified into Tropical Storm Brenda, becoming the first named storm of the 2007 Atlantic hurricane season. It became a hurricane on November 12, becoming the first hurricane of the season to form after the seasonal end of the Atlantic hurricane season on October 31.

Brenda's motion was initially toward the northeast, in response to a subtropical ridge to the north of the system. By November 13, the ridge had shifted to the east, pushing Brenda toward the southeast. On November 14, the ridge weakened, allowing Brenda to begin a northward progression. On the same day, the NHC began to issue advisories on Tropical Storm Beryl, which was located farther east in the central Atlantic. Brenda moved rapidly away from the United States coastline, and on November 15, the NHC issued its last advisory on the storm. The storm was absorbed into a strong extratropical cyclone over the Atlantic Ocean on November 16.

## Impact

Earlier in the season, the National Hurricane Center (NHC) was criticized for not issuing advisories on any named storms in the tropical Atlantic prior to the seasonal end on October 31. As a result, the NHC began issuing tropical cyclone forecasts in early November. Brenda was the first system to be named, but no other tropical cyclones were named after it. Brenda was the only named storm of the season to attain hurricane strength.

In early November, Brenda produced heavy rainfall and flooding in the Caribbean. Brenda was the first storm of the 2007 season to affect the United States. Marshall McLuhan was a colleague of Innis 's at the University of Toronto . As a young English professor , McLuhan was flattere

d by Innis 's invitation to join i nnis in the formation of the summer school. Innis was in turn impressed by McLuhan 's intelligence, his wide reading, and what Innis perceived as the young man's ability to "cut through" to the essences of things. According to the more often told version of events, McLuhan came to the summer school one year, and after a few days of lectures he announced that he had been "revolutionized." He left for Europe and returned the next summer as a thoroughly changed man, a "convert" to the Innis "camp" (McLuhan, 1982: 176).
McLuhan and Innis had much in common. Both were committed social critics, committed to the belief that a more refined understanding of the nature of social and cultural formations would permit a more refined understanding of social and political problems. Both believed that a more refined understanding would lead to solutions. Both were profoundly concerned with the role of the media in affecting social and political relations. Both were deeply suspicious of the unquestioning acceptance of the claims of science and technology. Both saw the need for a substantive critique of the institutions of science and technology.
But there were important differences, and these differences were to have significant consequences for McLuhan's later work. These differences are most evident in the "analysis" of Innis's work. For Innis, the media were "agents" in the broad sense of the term, that is, forces that act upon the world, creating situations, changing people's perspectives, changing what people think and feel. They were not, in other words, the passive vehicles for conveying information. Innis believed that the analyst's task was to uncover the nature of the "agency" of the particular medium under investigation, and to make this agency explicit. This was the "ideological analysis" of the media.
For McLuhan, however, the media were not "agents," in the sense of actively shaping events. They were "technologies" in a strict sense of the term, that is, passive vehicles that "extend" or "reproduce" the central human activity of communication. McLuhan believed that the analyst's task was to uncover the nature of the "technology" of the particular medium under investigation, and to make this "technology" explicit. This was the "technological analysis" of the media.
Furthermore, Innis believed that the "ideological analysis" of the media was the more important, since he saw the media as powerful social and political agencies, capable of creating situations and affecting people's perspectives and feelings. McLuhan, on the other hand, believed that the "technological analysis" of the media was the more important, since he saw the media as broadly "technological" agencies, that is, as passive vehicles that "extend" or "reproduce" the central human activity of communication.
"Innis's theory is a theory of the _ideological_ effects of media. I believe it is more profitable to begin with a theory of the _technological_ effects of media, as this is the basis of any understanding of the ideological effects" (McLuhan, 1977: 59, my italics).
"The shift in emphasis from Ideological to Technological analysis of the media is important. It is a shift from a study of the _effects_ of the media to a study of the _nature_ of the media. It is in this aspect that we can see Marshall McLuhan's contribution to communication theory" (Williams and Spiro, 1965: 21).
It is, of course, not uncommon for "schools" of thought to disagree on the relative importance of the cognitive and the practical, or on the relative importance of the "ideological" and the "technological" in understanding the media. But it is not so common for two thinkers to agree to disagree so publicly and in such a fundamental way. It is not merely that McLuhan and Innis disagree. It is that they disagree so publicly, and in such a fundamental way, that they seem to speak as if from different worlds.
McLuhan was to be the most influential of Innis's students. He was to develop and extend the "technological analysis" of the media into a vastly more comprehensive and general theory of the nature of technology. A TYPE OF STRUCTURALISM THAT POSITS OBJECTIVE CULTURAL FORMS AS THE MAIN SUBJECTS OF ANALYSIS. KEYWORDS: SOCIAL STRUCTURE, SOCIAL INSTITUTION, SOCIAL PROCESS, SOCIAL FORMS, SOCIAL RELATION.
Structural functionalism is a perspective in sociology and other social sciences that examines the functions of the entities of a society. This perspective arose from the work of Emile Durkheim, who was especially interested in how social order is possible and maintained. In addition to Durkheim, Talcott Parsons and Robert K. Merton played important roles in the development of structural functionalism.
Structural functionalism is the dominant perspective in sociology, though some scholars are turning to more critical perspectives. Structural functionalism explains social phenomena by comparing the social system to a machine. Each social system has certain basic functional components (known as functional prerequisites) that work together to maintain the system's stability. If there is a problem with one of the components, the whole society might be threatened. The theory is based on the belief that all societies are structured and that all social systems have a purpose, which is to fulfill social needs.
In many ways, structural functionalism seems to be the opposite of the conflict perspective. It does not see society as consisting of groups that are struggling for power. Instead, it sees society as made of interconnected parts that work together to maintain the stability of the whole. The structural functionalist approach examines the function of the parts in society rather than the distribution of power within the society. Structural functionalists do not examine social inequality, but instead examine how social inequality is maintained by society.
The term structural functionalism was first used by Talcott Parsons in his 1937 book, The Structure of Social Action . However, it was Emile Durkheim who had developed this approach in his work on social solidarity and social structure. Durkheim was the founder of the "school of French sociology" and argued that society is a distinct, separate entity, and that it has a life of its own. His most famous work is The Division of Labor in Society (1893). Durkheim's structural functionalism has been criticized for its over-emphasis on social order and its neglect of social conflict. However, it is still considered the foundation of modern sociology.

The first signs of Meyerbeer breaking with the Italian traditions in which he had trained are in Il crociato in Egitto . Amongs

the original ideas, there is the staging of the opera in a single set (acts 1 and 2 in a room of the Castle of Borsa; act 3 in the hall of the Castle of the Knights of St. John; act 4 in the church), a choice that recalls the work of Gluck, and in the choice of the Egyptian setting, a new choice at the time.
As the story goes, in 1824, Meyerbeer travelled to Egypt and Syria, and it was there that he conceived the idea for his new opera. He later wrote that he had been inspired by the "oriental music and their instruments, as well as by the legends and the oriental fables that he had heard or read". In the work, Meyerbeer intended to express the "colour and spirit of the East". The score is filled with melodies based on popular and folkloric themes, especially in the ensembles, where traditional dances are evoked, while the arias are usually based on the tonalities of the modes.
As with most of Meyerbeer's works, the music for Il crociato in Egitto is in typical Italian style, with its melodic writing, its clear-cut and expressive vocal lines, and its harmonic structure based on the modulation of the modes.
The libretto is by the poet Giacomo Antonio Piroli de' Rossi, who was also the librettist of several of Donizetti's early operas. It is based on the poem L'Égypte sous les croisés by the French writer Charles-Simon Favart.
The opera was commissioned by the Paris Opéra, where it was premiered on 7 October 1825. This was the first of the so-called "Meyerbeerian operas" to be performed in Paris, as the composer's name had attracted the interest of the French public. The opera was a great success and was performed 57 times that season, a very high number for the time. The opera was staged in London in 1826 and in New York in 1835.
The opera had a second performance in Paris two years later, on 26 December 1827, in the composer's presence. The performance was a disaster: the music was criticised as being "vulgar" and "unsuitable for Paris". Meyerbeer himself had to take on the responsibility of the failure and resigned from the directorship of the Opéra. It was not until 1853 that the opera was performed again in Paris, this time in an abridged version. The opera was never performed again in its original version.
The opera was revived in 1869 in London at Her Majesty's Theatre (with the role of Elcia sung by the famous soprano Adelina Patti). The opera was also revived in Paris in 1880. In 1896, it was revived in London at the Royal Opera House, Covent Garden.
The opera was revived in New York in 1950, performed by the New York City Opera. The opera was also performed in 1955 and 1956 in Buenos Aires by the Teatro Colón.
The opera was finally performed again in its original version at the Opéra-Comique in Paris in 1988, as part of the cycle "Les rendez-vous de Meyerbeer". There have also been performances in Chicago, Seattle, Concertgebouw Amsterdam, and Tokyo, among other places.
The opera was staged in Munich in 1999 as part of the series "Meyerbeer in München", with the direction of Gianluca Martinelli and costumes by Eike D. Schmidt.

The Secret of Monkey Island sold well and received positive reviews from critics . Hartley , Patricia , and Kirk Lesser of Drag

onsfoot stated that the game's non-linear storyline was a difficult thing to achieve in 1990 , but that it was well-executed in The Secret of Monkey Island .

### Acclaim

The game received an average rating of 9.2 out of 10, based on 11 reviews, by the review aggregator GameRankings .

### Legacy

In 1991, Computer Gaming World named The Secret of Monkey Island the best game of the year. In 1992, it won the Computer Gaming World's "Role-Playing Game of the Year" award. In 1994, the magazine's readers voted the game the second-best adventure game of all time, behind Zork: The Great Underground Empire . In 1996, PC Gamer US named it the 15th best game ever. In 1998, the magazine named it the 55th best game ever. The game was also ranked the 8th top adventure game of all time by PC Gamer UK in 1998, and the 64th best game of all time by PC Gamer US in 1999. In 2004, Adventure Gamers ranked the game 3rd on their list of the "Top 100 Adventure Games". In 2007, IGN ranked it 2nd in its "Top 25 Most Influential Adventure Games of All Time" list. In 2014, GamesRadar+ named the game an Honorable Mention in its list of "The 100 Greatest Video Games of All Time". In 2016, the game was inducted into GameSpot's "Greatest Games of All Time" list. In 2017, Polygon ranked the game 2nd on its "50 best adventure games of all time" list. In 2021, the game was ranked 11th in Nintendo Power 's list of the "200 greatest Nintendo games of all time".

The game's dialogue system is considered to be one of the most influential in computer gaming. The game's non-linear storyline is also considered to have been highly influential. The game's use of a 2D-style graphic and the characters' use of real-world accents have both been noted for their influence on the adventure game genre.

ideos.org website, and a worldwide protest movement, known as Operation Chanology. It is the name given to the protest movement enacted by members of the Internet community Anonymous in response to the Church of Scientology's attempts to suppress critical material posted online.
Operation Chanology began on 10 February 2008. This date is significant in that it is the 82nd anniversary of the birth of Scientology's founder, L. Ron Hubbard. It is also the 50th anniversary of the Church's creation.
 Project Chanology's mission is to "take down the Church of Scientology in retaliation for their harassment of the Internet community".
In the weeks following the launch, Chanology protests were held in 110 cities, with 20,000 protesters attending.
The Church of Scientology responded to the protests by removing the articles from the Wikipedia article regarding the website, and subsequently banning users from posting any further criticisms of Scientology on the Internet, including Wikipedia article editors.
These actions were met with protests from other Wikipedians and members of the Anonymous community. The Church of Scientology has since withdrawn the block.
Academics have linked Scientology's harassment efforts against critics to the pre-existing imageboard community.
 Project Chanology is an Internet phenomenon which has been covered by mainstream media.

## Background

The Church of Scientology fears criticism of its beliefs and practices. It has been described as "one of the most litigious organizations in history", and has been accused of using the courts to silence critics. It has been described as a "cult" and a "dangerous organization" by psychiatrists, and has been the subject of a number of government inquiries.

In 2005, the Church of Scientology bought the domain name 'xenu.net', a site previously owned by a person known as Aaron Saxton. Saxton had used the site to criticise Scientology. The Church of Scientology filed a complaint with the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) to prevent the 'xenu.net' domain from being used for criticism. The WIPO panel ruled in favour of the Church of Scientology.

The Church of Scientology has also taken legal action against an individual who used the Internet to broadcast a video of a Scientology service. The Church of Scientology sent a cease and desist letter to the individual, threatening legal action. The letter stated that "It is in your interest to remove this video from the internet immediately". The Church of Scientology also sent a cease and desist letter to the website hosting the video. The website, YouTube, removed the video without comment.

In 2006, the Church of Scientology took legal action to stop the publication of two books by a journalist, Paulette Cooper. The Church filed a number of lawsuits against Cooper, and also attempted to place Cooper under psychiatric care.

In January 2008, the Church of Scientology filed a number of lawsuits against the 'WhyWeProtest.net' website, which criticises the Church of Scientology.

Cognates of the name " Allāh " exist in other Semitic languages , including Hebrew and Aramaic . The corresponding Aramaic form

is אלהא .[ original research? ] The name is cognate with the Hebrew El , which is also used by the Samaritans as a name for God and is preserved as a given name in modern Israeli Hebrew.
The Islamic prophet Muhammad is said[ by whom? ] to have been illiterate, and the Quran is traditionally believed to have been revealed to him in the original Arabic language. As a result, the name " Allah " is the standard term for God in the Quran and is thus the term used by Muslims in their daily lives. The Quran states[ where? ] that God is known by many names, and uses a variety of names and titles for God in its text, including Allah in the case of the Arabic language.
Some Muslims believe that the word Allah should not be used by non-Muslims. This does not extend to the use of the word "Allah" by non-Muslims in Malay, the national language of Malaysia and Brunei, where it is the only word for "God" in the native language.
Islamic scholars have differed in their views on the permissibility of translations of the Quran. In recent times, some Islamic groups such as the Muslim Association of Britain have encouraged the use of the word "Allah" for God in English-language translations of the Quran.

Aerith Gainsborough (エアリス・ゲインズブール, Earisu Gainzuburu?) is a fictional character in the video game Final Fantasy VII and its sequels, as well as a major character in the prequel manga and film. She is a young woman who lives in the town of Nibelheim, and is the daughter of the town's leader, Barret Wallace.

Aerith has received a mostly positive reception. She is widely regarded as one of the most important characters in the series. In 2008, she was ranked the 18th top Final Fantasy character of all time by GameSpy. IGN ranked her the 12th best video game character of 2007, and 6th best video game character of 2013. Aerith won the 2019 Webby Award for Best Social Video, as well as the 2020 Webby Award for Best in Games for her appearance in a Cinematic Universe trailer.

## Appearances

### Final Fantasy VII

Aerith is a shy, quiet young woman who lives in the town of Nibelheim. Her father is the town's chief, a position he inherited from his father, and while Aerith looks forward to the day when she will assume that role, she also looks forward to a life away from the town. Aerith was born with latent magical abilities, and when she was a child, her mother was killed by an unknown assailant. Aerith is initially hostile to Cloud Strife, the main character in Final Fantasy VII. Over time, however, Aerith becomes more open and friendly to Cloud and his friends, and this friendship is a major plot point in the game. Aerith has the ability to cast Haste and Cure magic, and she has the highest Magic Defense stat among the party members. Aerith's love for Cloud is the driving force behind most of the game, and it is hinted that Aerith may have had a crush on Cloud since childhood.

### Other media

Aerith appears as a supporting character in the game's sequel, Final Fantasy VII: Advent Children. She has an important role in the 2005 prequel film Final Fantasy VII: Advent Children, where she is seen working as a waitress in the diner "Avalanche". She also plays a role in the 2006 prequel manga Before Crisis: Final Fantasy VII, and in the 2016 mobile game Final Fantasy VII: Mobius Final Fantasy.

## Reception

Aerith has received a mostly positive reception. She is widely regarded as one of the most important characters in the series. In 2008, she was ranked the 18th top Final Fantasy character of all time by GameSpy. IGN ranked her the 12th best video game character of 2007, and 6th best video game character of 2013. Aerith won the 2019 Webby Award for Best Social Video, as well as the 2020 Webby Award for Best in Games for her appearance in a Cinematic Universe trailer.

It has been estimated that average @-@ sized bacteria contain about 2 million proteins per cell ( e.g. E. coli and Staphylococc

ous aureus). This amount, about 20% of the total DNA, makes up 10% of the total weight of the cell. This protein mass is the equivalent of 50-100 million proteins per gram of bacterial cells.
 Protein synthesis in bacteria is a complex process and involves an assembly of many RNA and protein complexes. The main components of the cell which are involved in protein synthesis are the ribosome, the T-RNA, the mRNA, the tRNA synthetases, the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR), the CRP and the transcriptional apparatus. These components are not always found in the same quantities and the role of each one of them may be different in different bacteria.
 The ribosome is the key component of the translation apparatus in bacteria. It is a large complex composed of 70S for E. coli and 80S for mammals. It is composed of two subunits: a large and a small subunit.
 The large subunit is composed of two domains, one is a signature sequence and the other is a universal ribosomal binding site. The small subunit is composed of 16S rRNA.
 Often the ribosome is associated with the tRNA molecules (tRNA-ribosome complex) and is often referred to as a translational complex.
 The function of the tRNA is to bind to its cognate aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase (aaRS) during the translation process. The aaRS are able to recognize the specific anticodon sequence of the tRNA and in addition to form a specific complex with the tRNA, it also catalyzes the charging of the tRNA with its cognate amino acid. This step is known as aminoacylation and is followed by the association of the tRNA with the ribosome.
 In E. coli, the 70S ribosome is associated with 50-100 tRNA molecules and it is estimated that only 1% of them are associated with aaRS.
 The tRNA molecules in E. coli are 70 nucleotides long and are classified into 4 groups according to their secondary structures (i.e. cloverleaf, stem and bulge, hairpin and bulge-bridge-loop).
 The tRNAs can also be classified into two groups according to their internal arrangements of the anticodon and amino acid binding sites. The first group is the cloverleaf type and the second is the stem and bulge type. The cloverleaf type has an extension of five nucleotides at the 3' end of the anticodon sequence. The stem and bulge type is composed of a stem and a bulge at the 3' end of the anticodon sequence. The stem and bulge type are more abundant in E. coli.
 T-RNA molecules are the smallest and most abundant transfer RNA in bacteria. In E. coli, the 70S ribosome is associated with 50-100 tRNA molecules and it is estimated that only 1% of them are associated with aaRS.

The telescope has served as a centerpiece of science and technology for over three centuries, in a process of discovery and invention that has made our world smaller, more familiar, and more predictable.  A telescope's lens can enlarge an object—a flower, a skyscraper, a galaxy—and in so doing, reveal to the naked eye what the eye alone cannot see.  A telescope is a visualization device.  It enlarges the world, which we can then understand and control.
The invention of the telescope has been attributed to three men: the Dutch eyeglass maker Hans Lippershey in 1608, the Italian Jesuit mathematician and astronomer Galileo Galilei in 1609, and the Englishman Thomas Harriot in 1609.  The Italians believe that Galileo discovered the telescope and that he deserves the credit for its invention.  The English claim that the Englishman Thomas Harriot invented it.  Both ideas are false.  The telescope was invented in Holland, by a Dutch eyeglass maker named Hans Lippershey.  He made telescopes for the Dutch government and sold them to other nations.  The Dutch ambassador to England, who brought the telescope to England, was the one who gave Galileo the first telescope, and it was light enough to be carried around.  Galileo gave the telescope to the English astronomer Thomas Harriot and showed him how to use it.  Harriot, therefore, is credited with the invention of the telescope, at least in England.  Harriot is also credited with the first astronomical discoveries made with the telescope—the discovery of Jupiter's four largest moons.
Harriot's telescope was made of two lenses, one convex and one concave.  It was used with an eye that was held very close to the lenses to bring objects into focus.  Harriot's telescope magnified objects by a factor of three.  The telescope of Galileo Galilei, however, was of the same type as that made by Hans Lippershey, and in 1609 it was used to make discoveries that changed the world.
In 1609, Galileo Galilei was in Padua, where he had been studying medicine.  He heard that a telescope had been brought to Venice by a Dutchman and that it was being used by the Venetian doge, Marino Grimani, to see events in the city.  Galileo knew the Dutchman, and he made a regular practice of visiting him.  When Galileo told the Dutchman that he would like to have the telescope, the Dutchman was happy to give it to him.  Galileo received the telescope on 25 August 1609.  He took it to Venice, and on 7 September 1609 he observed the moon.  He found that the telescope allowed him to observe details on the edge of the moon that he could not see with the naked eye.
The telescope, which magnified objects by a factor of three, revealed to Galileo that the moon was not smooth, but had mountains and valleys, just like the earth.  He also observed that the moon had craters, and that the craters were not flat, but had raised rims.  He also observed that the moon had dark areas, which he called _seas_.  The discovery that the moon had mountains and craters changed our view of the heavens.  It was a discovery that was to have a profound influence on our thinking about the moon and our thinking about the earth.
During the next eight years, Galileo made many other discoveries with his telescope.  He observed the sun, the stars, and the planets.  He observed that the sun had craters, and he observed that the planet Jupiter had four moons.  He also observed Venus and the phases of Venus.  He observed that Venus was a planet, and he observed that the phases of Venus were similar to the phases of the moon.

## Construction

The Gneisenau was laid down on 15 June 1935 at the Deutsche Werke in Kiel and launched on 31 May 1936. She was commissioned into the Kriegsmarine on 15 January 1938 and was given the pennant number Z-2.

## Early career

The Gneisenau was commissioned into the Kriegsmarine on 15 January 1938 and in June 1939 she was assigned to destroyer squadron (Schutzstaffel) 2 ( Destroyer Squadron 2 ) along with the Leipzig. In September 1939 the squadron was assigned to the 2nd Destroyer Flotilla (2. Zerstörerflottille) and in November the Gneisenau and the Leipzig were assigned to the 24th Destroyer Flotilla (24. Zerstörerflottille) as part of the 2nd Destroyer Flotilla.

She was part of the German naval task force that attacked the Norwegian port of Narvik on 9 April 1940. The protective escort of the German ships was provided by the heavy cruisers Admiral Hipper, Admiral Scheer and the light cruiser Köln. The Gneisenau was part of the destroyer force that attacked and sank the Royal Navy destroyers Acasta and Ardent on the outer defensive minefields near the port. The Gneisenau was hit by a torpedo fired from the British destroyer Glowworm and the Gneisenau was severely damaged. Three crewmen were killed and 37 wounded. 

The Gneisenau was under repair in Kiel from April to August 1940. It was then transferred to the 1st Destroyer Flotilla (1. Zerstörerflottille) and participated in Operation Weserübung, the invasion of Norway, on 8 and 9 April 1940. She participated in the subsequent occupation of Denmark on 9 April.

On 29 April 1940 the Gneisenau and the destroyers of her squadron (the Hans Lody, Karl Galster and the Wilhelm Heidkamp) were ordered on a sweep through the Skagerrak to intercept an expected British convoy. The French destroyer Maillé-Brézé was encountered and destroyed.

On 26 July 1940 the Gneisenau was involved in the sinking of the British destroyer Afridi off the coast of Norway. On 27 July the Gneisenau and the destroyers of her squadron (the Hans Lody, Karl Galster and the Wilhelm Heidkamp) were ordered on a sweep through the Skagerrak to intercept an expected British convoy. The British destroyer HMS Ashanti was encountered and sunk.

The club adopted 'Dover Athletic' as its name in 1920, and became a founder member of the Kent League in 1921. In 1924, the club moved to its first permanent home, the Goldstone Ground, in the town centre. The ground did not have any floodlights, and the club moved to its current home, the Crabble Athletic Ground , in 1933.
The club was elected to the Isthmian League in 1968, and reached the final of the FA Trophy in the 1972–73 season, losing 1–0 to Conference champions Northwich Victoria . The club spent five seasons in the Southern League from 1976 to 1981, before returning to the Isthmian League.
In 2007, the club was taken over by former England and Aston Villa forward Darren Patterson. The club was placed into administration in June 2010, with the club in 12th place in the Conference National . The administrators were able to save the club from liquidation, with the club being relegated to the Conference South for the 2010–11 season.

### Reign

Main article: Leinster dynasty

After the death of his father in 1064 , Diarmait became King of Leinster .

In 1067 , Diarmait was killed in the Battle of Bladon Hill near Cahir on the River Suir in County Tipperary , but survived .

In 1068 , Diarmait married Ælfflæd , daughter of King Edward the Confessor of England as part of a deal to unite the English and Irish people .

According to the Annals of Tigernach , in 1070 , Diarmait died after a long illness. 

### Death

After Diarmait's death , Ælfflæd returned to England , and Diarmait was buried in the Church of St. Peter at Glendalough in County Wicklow .

the chaos, Sikhs were particularly vulnerable to attack, and the Punjab's wealthiest families were forced to abandon their land and property and flee to India, leaving behind their villages and small businesses. The Punjab's Muslims, who had been much better prepared for independence, were not so badly hit.
The transfer of land was completed in 1955. The following year, a new prime minister, Lal Bahadur Shastri, drafted a law through the Indian parliament that made it virtually impossible for refugees to reclaim their property.
Amalak Singh was one of those who was not deterred. He was born in the village of Basak, in the present-day Indian state of Punjab, on 20 April 1921, the son of a Sikh chieftain named Kartar Singh. In 1947, Amalak and his family were living in the village, the descendant of a line of village rulers, and Amalak was the latest in the succession of the family to inherit the title of _Majitha ._
Like all Punjabi village rulers, Amalak had his own land. He owned three hundred acres. But he also owned the land of the surrounding villages—the fields of his tenants and the lands of his tenants' tenants. Together, all this land was worth millions of rupees, and the profits from it were enough to support a family of eight.
Amalak was one of the few Indians who did not panic when India and Pakistan were created. He was confident that Pakistan would remain a secular state, and that if it did not, he could always flee to India. He knew that he would be able to make a fresh start in India, and that he would be able to claim compensation for his losses. He had his family pack up the jewellery and the silverware, and all their other possessions, and loaded them on his vehicles. He had his servants board the vehicles as well. He was travelling with 150 people in all.
On the morning of 14 August, Amalak Singh was sitting in his car, waiting for the rest of his possessions to be loaded. As he was sitting there, a gun suddenly appeared in his face.
'Put your hands up,' the gunman said.
Amalak did as he was told. The gunman could see that he was a Sikh, and he knew that Sikhs did not wear turbans.
'Why you don't wear a turban?' asked the gunman.
'We don't have to wear them,' replied Amalak.

Amalak took off his shoes.

Amalak did as he was told.

Proteins ( / ˈproʊˌtiːnz / or / ˈproʊti.ᵻnz / ) are large biomolecules , or macromolecules , consisting of one or more long cha

in molecules . Proteins perform a vast array of functions within cells. In living organisms , proteins are often conjugated to molecules such as saccharides , lipids , and nucleic acids [2] to form complex proteins . Many proteins are enzymes that catalyze biochemical reactions . Proteins are also important in cell signaling , immune responses , cell adhesion , and the cell cycle . In contrast to the inorganic crystals that are salts , proteins are organic (carbon based) macromolecules that are linear polymers of α-amino acids joined together by peptide bonds between the carboxyl and amino groups of adjacent amino acids. The sequence of amino acids in a protein is defined by the sequence of bases in the genes encoding them . In the gene, these bases are translated into a sequence of amino acids in a process called protein synthesis . Proteins are synthesized on ribosomes , which link amino acids in a specific order to make a polymer. The two main classes of polypeptides are fibrous proteins and globular proteins. Fibrous proteins form fibrous structures such as hair and collagen . Globular proteins include many enzymes such as trypsin and are often soluble in water . Proteins are composed of long chains of amino acids joined by peptide bonds between the carboxyl and amino groups of adjacent amino acid residues. Amino acids having a free amino group are called amino acids . Amino acids having a free carboxyl group are called carboxylic acids . The amino group is a primary alcohol in which the hydroxyl group is attached to the nitrogen atom . The carboxyl group is a carboxylic acid in which the hydroxyl group is attached to the carbon atom. Amino acids having a side chain attached to the alpha carbon atom are called aromatic amino acids .
Amino acids (from ɑmino aϭϭϮϯ / ʕ ɑ ˈ m iː n oʊ ˈ æ m iː n oʊ / ( listen ); Arabic : أمينو‎) are organic compounds containing a basic amino group (—NH 2 ), an acidic carboxyl group (—COOH) , and a side chain (R group)  . They are organic compounds made up of carbon , hydrogen , oxygen , and nitrogen . The term amino acid was first used in 1806 by chemist Pierre-Jean Robiquet .
Amino acids are used in the biosynthesis of proteins and peptides . They are also used in the biosynthesis of nonprotein molecules, such as NAD + and heme . Amino acids are the building blocks of protein, which make up the tissues and organs of all organisms. The 20 different amino acids that are used by living organisms can be classified in many ways. One classification is based on the substituents on the alpha carbon atom. This results in two categories, aromatic and nonaromatic. Over the years since European settlement Waterfall Gully has suffered from both bushfires and flooding . The gully was severely

damaged in the 1934 bushfires and again in the 1983 bushfires.
 A metal gate was installed at the start of the walking track to prevent vehicles from driving into the gully.
In 1870, soon after the settlement of Adelaide, the Adelaide Botanic Garden was established on the west side of the River Torrens. The botanical gardens were enlarged to include a range of hills known as the Adelaide Hills, which has been the centre of many of Adelaide's outdoor leisure activities ever since.
The Victorian era saw a boom in domestic tourism and in the early 1880s the government began to encourage visitors to the Adelaide Hills with the construction of the Picnic Point Railway line (1881). The Picnic Point Railway line was extended to the Botanic Park in 1883, and in 1884 the Adelaide Hills was surveyed and subdivided.
The Adelaide Botanic Garden continued to expand, and in 1889 it was joined to the Botanic Park by the completion of the Waterfall Gully Road.
Waterfall Gully Road was closed on 26 February 1953, and in 1954 the Conservation Board of South Australia purchased the land. The area was declared a national park in 1967 and renamed Waterfall Gully Reserve.
The 1983 bushfires destroyed a large amount of vegetation in Waterfall Gully Reserve, and in 1985 the Reserve was closed to the public.
The reserve was reopened in 1989 after a major rehabilitation program. The 1990s have seen further development in the reserve with the construction of boardwalks and trails, and the building of a new information centre.
The park is named after the Waterfall Gully Road which was built in 1889 to link the Botanic Gardens with the Adelaide Hills. In 1889 the road was named after a waterfall which was reportedly outside the gate of the manse of St Paul's Church in Stirling Street, Norwood. The waterfall was a popular picnic spot and a source of drinking water for horses. The waterfall is now described as having been a trickle of water which disappeared with the clearing of vegetation.
The waterfall was not given the name of Waterfall Gully, until the 1884 survey of the Adelaide Hills. The name was given to the gully because it resembled a waterfall.
In 1994 the South Australian government's Advisory Conservation Council recommended the reserve be renamed "Waterfall Gully Nature Park". The name change has not been adopted by the state government.
On December 7 , 2006 , Headquarters Marine Corps released a message stating that 2nd Battalion 9th Marines would be reactivated

, and would be assigned to 2nd Marine Division as part of the 2nd Marine Expeditionary Brigade, the Marines' ground combat element in the II Marine Expeditionary Force (II MEF). 2nd Bn 9th Marines was first activated on July 1, 1940 as part of the 2nd Marine Division. The battalion was originally composed of two companies, HQ & Service Company and Weapons Company. The battalion was assigned to Marine Barracks, Quantico, Virginia. The battalion was re-designated as the 2nd Separate Battalion on December 1, 1940, and was then re-designated as 2nd Battalion, 1st Marines on January 1, 1941. The battalion was then assigned to the 1st Marine Regiment.

On August 11, 1941, the battalion was re-designated as 2nd Battalion, 9th Marines and was assigned to the 9th Marine Regiment.

### First World War

The battalion landed at Cape Gloucester, New Britain, on December 26, 1943 and took part in the Battle of Cape Gloucester between December 26, 1943 and January 7, 1944. In the early morning of January 7, 1944, the battalion landed on Pavuvu Island in the Russell Islands of the Solomon Islands. The battalion then took part in the Battle of Cape Gloucester (1944) between January 24, 1944 and February 18, 1944. The battalion fought in the Battle of Peleliu (1944) between September 15, 1944 and November 27, 1944. The battalion was then declared non-operational on January 31, 1945.

### Korean War

The battalion was reactivated at Camp Pendleton on October 1, 1951 and was assigned to the 2nd Marine Division. The battalion then took part in the Battle of Inchon between September 15, 1950 and September 20, 1950. The battalion was then re-designated as the 2nd Amphibious Tractor Battalion and was assigned to the 1st Marine Division.

### Vietnam War

The battalion was re-designated as the 2nd Marine Regiment on November 1, 1955 and was assigned to the 2nd Marine Division. The battalion was then re-designated as the 2nd Light Armored Infantry Battalion on February 1, 1962. On July 1, 1968, the battalion was re-designated as the 2nd Tank Battalion. The battalion was then re-designated as the 2nd Light Armored Infantry Battalion on November 1, 1974.

### Post Vietnam War

The battalion was re-designated as the 2nd Light Armored Reconnaissance Battalion on February 1, 1994. On September 11, 2003, the battalion was re-designated as the 2nd Light Armored Reconnaissance Battalion (LAR).

In 2005, the battalion was deployed to northern Iraq. The battalion was attached to Regimental Combat Team 1.

The kill-and-cover attack is usually employed by a male Noisy miner trying to drive away a potential rival. Some of these attacks have been observed to be successful. However, many attacks are not, and the intruder may remain in the territory.

The kill-and-cover attack can be seen in a wide range of other animals, including lions and primates.

The common starling has about a dozen subspecies breeding in open habitats across its native range in temperate Europe and west

Asia. The most widely distributed of these is the subspecies _S. p. stellatus_ (Starlings of Europe, Middle Asia, and North Africa), which breeds from Ireland and Scandinavia east to Siberia, with a population in the Caucasus and one on the Arabian Peninsula. In the far north, populations from the Tundra zone in the Arctic circle to the taiga zone in Siberia are likely to have a single clone born of one pair of birds. In the lowlands, however, more numerous clones may be present and intermingled.
Every September, European starlings begin their extensive wanderings. They migrate south to the Mediterranean littoral and Africa, where they winter in large flocks. During the northward spring migration they generally travel in small flocks. This dispersal produces a high degree of genetic diversity in the wintering birds, but after birds have paired and settled, the populations become more genetically homogeneous, as pairs and their offspring remain in the same territory. In the summer, the European starling population in Britain and western Europe is about 50 million birds, of which 40 percent are the descendants of one pair.
The starling has been introduced to the United States, where it is now common in the east and middle states. There is also a population on the Hawaiian island of Maui.
* _Stellar's Jay_
_Sitta_ _stellaris_
The Stellar's Jay is a bird of the Pacific Coast forests of the western United States and Mexico. It breeds in the mountains of the southernmost Cascade Range in northwestern California and southern Oregon, as far south as Baja California. It also breeds in the Sierra Madre Occidental in Mexico, and in the Sierra Madre del Sur in the states of Oaxaca and Guerrero. It is the only jay in North America that has a black and yellow crest, and it is about one-quarter larger than the Black-capped Chickadee.
The Stellar's Jay has a few relatives in the New World that are also black and yellow. These include the Black-backed Jay ( _Cyanocorax_ _sternopterus_ ), found in central and South America, and the Black-cheeked Jay ( _Cyanocorax_ _nigricollis_ ), found only in Brazil. In the Old World, these colors are characteristic of the Eurasian Crested Jay ( _Garrulus_ _lidthi_ ), which is found in southern Europe and Asia Minor.
In southern Mexico, the Stellar's Jay is known as the _zacatecas_ or _chacatecas_ , which means "chatterer." The name _zacatecas_ was first used by the author Washington Irving in the 1830s. The name Chacatecas may have originated with the Aztecs, who used the name to refer to the bird that is now known as the Black-headed Grosbeak ( _Pheucticus_ _bairdi_ ).
In 1937, William Starr (1872–1938) reported that the Taos Indians of New Mexico called the Stellar's Jay the _cheche_ , which means "messenger bird." This is also the name used by the Klamath Indians of Oregon. In 1938, Starr said that he believed the _cheche_ and _chacatecas_ names were derived from the bird's call.

"Plunketts Creek is an 8.4-mile-long (13.5 km) tributary of the Susquehanna River in York County in Pennsylvania in the United States.
The creek flows through northern York County to the Susquehanna at Dallastown.
The creek's headwaters are at 40°11′37″N 76°50′18″W (40.193700°N 76.838333°W) in southern Dover Township. The creek flows west to the borough of Dallastown, where it turns south and joins the Susquehanna River at 40°05′59″N 76°53′01″W (40.099722°N 76.883611°W), less than 3 miles (5 km) upstream of the mouth of the Susquehanna's North Branch at Wrightsville.
Plunketts Creek drains the western portions of Dallastown, Lower Chanceford Township, and Dover Township.
Plunketts Creek is dammed at the southern end of the Dallastown borough to form a reservoir. The reservoir provides drinking water to the borough of Dallastown. The reservoir's dam is 100 feet (30 m) high."

White Dog was written by Edward Bunker, who was also the film's fight choreographer. A long-time friend of the director, Bunker had written the screenplay for Mean Streets, and had also written his own screenplays The Animal Factory and Straight Time, both of which were directed by John Boorman. Bunker would later write the screenplay for Boorman's 1987 film The Tiger's Tail. In addition to writing the script for White Dog, Bunker also participated in the film's promotion by writing a column in the Los Angeles Times and by serving as an adviser on the soundtrack album.

Film producer Dino De Laurentiis had been interested in making a film about the issue for some time. When he met Bunker to discuss the idea, Bunker pitched a film about a black man who takes a white dog and trains it to attack black people. De Laurentiis liked the idea and had Bunker write a script. Further inspiration for Bunker's script came from the death of a black woman who was mauled by a dog without provocation. Bunker recalled, "I made a lot of sketches of the dog, and I remember I had this one sketch where it's in the middle of [a black neighborhood] and it's running down the street with its head held high. I thought, 'That's a great shot!' And I had this other sketch of the dog in a white neighborhood, and it's in the middle of the street. It's very passive, you see it's just sitting there, and there's a house next to it and people are leaving their windows open and they're all coming out to pet the dog. This is a great metaphor for a black man in this society. He's walking down the street and everyone's giving him the finger and yelling at him but if he just stops and sits, they all want to pet him."
