John of Brienne ( c . 1170 – 27 March 1237 ) , also known as John I , was King of Jerusalem from 1210 to 1225 and Latin Emperor

(Emperor of Constantinople ) from 1225 to 1237 . He was a son of Raymond II , Count of Tripoli , and his wife Plaisance .

## Early life

John was the second of the five sons of Raymond II , Count of Tripoli, and his wife Plaisance . He was born in 1170. Raymond II was a younger brother of Raymond III , Count of Tripoli, and of William I , Count of Jaffa and Ascalon .

He was a younger brother of Bohemond IV, Count of Tripoli, and of Raymond III, Count of Tripoli.

## Crusade

John was 18 years old when he joined the Fourth Crusade in 1188. After the sack of Constantinople , he was treasurer of the Latin Empire , but he was removed from his post in 1201 by his uncle, the regent of the Latin Empire, Bohemond IV of Antioch .

In 1202 John went on the Fifth Crusade as a member of the imperial party. In Egypt he was taken prisoner by the Ayyubids and sold to the Mongols, who in turn sold him to the Khwarezmian Empire of Central Asia . He was captured in 1203 or 1204 and remained in captivity for eight years, probably until 1212. He was a prisoner in Samarkand or Bukhara . John received a ransom of 100,000 dinars from his brother Raymond-Roupen.

## King of Jerusalem

John was a younger brother of John of Ibelin , who was regent for his nephews, and his brother Bohemond IV, who had died in 1205. John was chosen as regent by the knights of the kingdom in 1210, after the death of his nephew, Aimery I , King of Jerusalem.

## Emperor of Constantinople

John of Brienne ruled in the Latin Empire of Constantinople as the Emperor of Constantinople from 1225 to 1237. He was chosen by the barons of Outremer, after the death of Frederick II, Holy Roman Emperor .

## Marriages and children

John of Brienne married, before 1202, Constance (died 1243), daughter of Henry I , Count of Champagne .

John and Constance had two sons and at least one daughter: 

* John of Brienne, Lord of Sidon and Beirut
* Philip of Nablus (died c. 1220)
* Alice of Brienne (died 1244), married in 1225 to Theobald I , Lord of Cysnes .

John of Brienne married, secondly, before 1227, Isabella, daughter of Andrew II of Hungary and Jutta of Hungary (died after 1241). They had two sons:

* Frederick (died 21 April 1246)
* Bohemond of Antioch (died 1233)

John of Brienne and Isabella had a daughter:

* Isabella (died after 1259), married in 1234 to Hugh III , Count of St-Pol .

John of Brienne married, thirdly, before 1242, Margaret de Beaulieu. They had four daughters:

* Margaret (died after 1244), married in 1242 to John of Valois, Count of Traves .
* Isabella (died after 1259)
* Constance (died after 1266), married in 1251 to Ralph I , Count of Vermandois and Valois .
* Joanna (died 1303/04), Abbess of Aix-la-Chapelle between 1258 and 1264.

John of Brienne married, fourthly, before 1253, Alice of Ibelin. They had no children.

John of Brienne married, fifthly, in 1254, Isabella of Villehardouin (died 1269), daughter of Isabella of Courtenay and Walter II of Villehardouin . They had no children.

## Content

The song is about a narrator's memories of his childhood in Tennessee. It begins with a memory of the narrator and his younger brother (named Danny) sitting on a car hood and listening to the radio. The narrator is in love with a girl named Mary Ann, and he is telling his brother about it. The song then switches to the present, and the narrator is driving down the road with his girlfriend (who is named Hannah) and talking about his memories of Tennessee. The narrator is telling Hannah that he is a changed man, and he is not the same person that he was when he was growing up in Tennessee.

## Critical reception

Publisher Deborah Evans Price of Billboard wrote that "McGraw has [written] a terrific ballad in which he shares his memories of growing up in Tennessee." She also noted that the song's "showcase" of vocals and instrumentation "is one of those recordings that makes you stop what you're doing and listen." Price also wrote that "it's one of the strongest songs on Everywhere and will have country radio playing it for a while."

Cortland County is located in the south-central portion of the state of New York . It is part of the Upstate New York region of the state . It is bordered by Tompkins and Seneca counties to the north, Cayuga County to the east, Onondaga County to the south, and Tioga County to the west.
Cortland County was created on March 30, 1788, from part of Onondaga County . The county was named for Richard H. Cortlandt, a public official in Albany during the American Revolution , who was a signer of the Articles of Association in 1774 and a delegate to the United States Constitutional Convention in 1787.
With an area of 790 square miles (2,050 km2), Cortland County is the 50th largest county in New York .
Cortland County is part of New York's 24th congressional district, which is held by Republican Tom Reed .
According to the U.S. Census Bureau, the county has a total area of 790 square miles (2,050 km2), of which 789 square miles (2,040 km2) is land and 0.6 square miles (1.6 km2) (0.08%) is water.
Cortland County is a largely rural county with a few exceptions. The northern and eastern portions of the county are sparsely populated and are made up of hilly terrain. The southern and western portions of the county are mostly low-lying and populated and are much more flat, with a few exceptions.
The northern and eastern portions are part of the Catskill Mountains.
The southern and western portions are part of the Great Appalachian Valley . This valley is dominated by the Susquehanna River and its tributaries, such as the Chenango and Tioughnioga rivers. The lower Susquehanna Valley is the most populated area of Cortland County.
The North Country National Scenic Trail , a 4,600-mile (7,400 km) trail that runs from New York to North Dakota, runs through the county and passes through the towns of Cortland, Willet, and Preble.

The key , in all games , starting with FIBA 's amendments to its rules in 2010 ( to be first implemented after the 2010 FIBA Wo

men's Basketball World Championship ) are:
1. Eliminating the 24 second shot clock .
2. Eliminating the three-point line ( the three-point line is still used in the WNBA ) .
3. Eliminating the five-second rule , and all other rules regarding the backcourt violation , and instead requiring that the ball be released after 8 seconds after it is awarded to the offense.
4. Eliminating the 10-second backcourt rule .
5. Eliminating the 10-second rule on the play after a made basket and the 24-second rule on the playing time after a basket .
6. Eliminating the one and one free throw technique for two free throws , and always requiring the two free throws to be shot in succession.
7. Eliminating the " out-of-bounds" rule ( the ball is played after the team that is awarded possession of the ball has control of the ball ) .
8. Eliminating the " foul and free throw" rule , and instead requiring that both fouls be called on the same player .
9. Eliminating the " double technical" rule , and instead requiring that both technical fouls be called on the same player .
10. Eliminating the " technical foul" rule , and instead requiring that all technical fouls be called on the same team .
As has been the case since 2006 , the FIBA Basketball World Cup , which is held every four years, is the premier FIBA competition for both men and women.

The 2005 Atlantic hurricane season was the most active Atlantic hurricane season on record, and the fourth costliest Atlantic hurricane season on record in terms of damage. The season officially began on June 1, 2005, and lasted until November 30, 2005. These dates conventionally delimit the period of each year when most tropical cyclones form in the Atlantic basin. During the season a total of twenty-eight tropical storms formed, of which sixteen became hurricanes, seven of which reached major hurricane status.  Winds in excess of 74 mph (119 km/h) occurred on two occasions. The season officially ended on November 30, 2005. However, the final tropical cyclone of the season, Tropical Storm Zeta, dissipated on January 6, 2006, becoming the latest tropical cyclone on record to form in the Atlantic basin.
The 2006 Atlantic hurricane season was the least active Atlantic hurricane season in 27 years, with only seven named storms forming, of which three became hurricanes and two became major hurricanes. The season officially began on June 1, 2006, and lasted until November 30, 2006. These dates conventionally delimit the period of each year when most tropical cyclones form in the Atlantic basin. During the season, twenty tropical storms formed, of which eight became hurricanes, four of which reached major hurricane status. Winds in excess of 74 mph (119 km/h) occurred on four occasions. The season officially ended on November 30, although the final tropical storm of the season, Tropical Storm Olga, dissipated on December 4, 2006.

Boreas remained on escort duty in the Eastern Atlantic until she arrived in Alexandria , Egypt on 11 November after escorting a

convoy from Gibraltar to Malta.

### Arctic convoy escort

On 16 November 1942 the destroyer left Alexandria for a voyage to the United Kingdom via the Suez Canal and the Red Sea, via the Indian Ocean and the Cape of Good Hope. Boreas arrived at her new base on 19 December.

On 25 March 1943 Boreas was ordered to join the sloop HMS Wells for escort duties in the North Atlantic. The destroyer was part of the escort for Convoy PQ 18. On 9 May, Whiteside, in command of a single destroyer, was ordered to take over the convoy from the corvettes and the destroyer HMS Offa. He was ordered to take the convoy through the night and to exercise great caution. At 10:10 pm his radar detected an air raid and he ordered the convoy to scatter. The destroyer HMS Achates and Offa were ordered to continue the voyage to Iceland, while Whiteside's Boreas, the corvettes and the merchant ships dispersed.

HMS Boreas and the corvettes were later ordered to return to Iceland and to wait for the convoy to rendezvous with the destroyer HMS Obedient, which had been sent to assist the convoy. At 2:00 am on 10 May, Whiteside's destroyer Boreas and the corvettes encountered the convoy. Boreas took the convoy in tow, while Whiteside awaited the arrival of Obedient. At about 6:00 am, Boreas was attacked by a German bomber. Whiteside was killed and the destroyer Boreas was set on fire. Obedient arrived and took the convoy to Reykjavík, Iceland. Boreas was towed into Akureyri, Iceland, where she was declared a total loss.

It seems that the kakapo – like many of New Zealand 's bird species – has evolved to occupy an ecological niche normally filled

by mammals.
This bird is large and flightless, having lost its wings and the ability to fly. It is nocturnal, and it feeds on fruit. It has large eyes, which are heavily pigmented to protect them from the glare of the daytime sky. It is also large-brained, and according to biologists, it has a very high ratio of brain to body size. It is covered in a thick layer of feathers, which is virtually indistinguishable from fur. It is also very strong, with the males possessing a large, sturdy beak that they use to fight with. And the kakapo has no natural predators.
Kakapos are found only in the southern-most parts of New Zealand's South Island, in the Fiordland National Park and Stewart Island , and the Chatham Islands off the east coast of New Zealand . But they were once more widespread. In prehistoric times, they lived in the hills and forests of what is now the North Island, near the coast. They were also spread across the South Island. It is estimated that by the time European settlement of New Zealand began, in the early nineteenth century, there were 100,000 kakapos living on the islands. But they were hunted, and after 1850 they were extinct on mainland New Zealand. In the late nineteenth century, a small population was discovered on Stewart Island, and their numbers have been steadily increasing since then.
Kakapos are also unique because, of all the birds in the world, they are the only ones that have a penis bone, called a baculum. It is a hollow tube of bone that is located between the legs, and it is almost 3 centimeters long. The baculum is actually a leftover from when the kakapo was a dinosaur.
To understand why kakapos have a baculum, it is helpful to know something about male mammals. A baculum is not common among mammals, but it is found in a variety of species, including the kangaroo, the elephant, the horse, the deer, and the rhinoceros. It is also found in some species of fish, including the bull shark. In these animals, the baculum is used for mating purposes. It is inserted into the female during mating – just as a penis is in mammals.
In male birds, the baculum is used to fight off other males during mating. The kakapo and other species with a baculum – called _penis bones_ – are all endemic to New Zealand, which means that they are found nowhere else in the world.
Kakapos used to be found in the mainland of New Zealand, and they probably were the most common species of bird there. But they have been extinct there since the nineteenth century, and it is not known what happened to them.

On the same day, the storm turned northwest, then north, and made landfall near the border of Texas and Louisiana on August 26 .

## Early life

Born in Hastings, Hawke's Bay, New Zealand, on 27 June 1922, to parents John Charles and Florence Elizabeth, aged 18 when he enlisted on 15 June 1940, having attended Hastings High School.

## World War II

Served with the Royal New Zealand Navy (RNZN) as a stoker between 15 June 1940 and 15 February 1946, including the following:

* RNZNVRA Seaman. Appointed 15 June 1940, serving with HMNZS Achilles until 15 February 1942.
* RNZNVR Able Seaman. Appointed 15 February 1942, serving with HMS St George until 15 February 1946.
* RNZNVR Radio Operator. Appointed 15 February 1942, serving with HMNZS Leander until 15 February 1946.
* RNZNVR Petty Officer. Appointed 15 February 1946.

## Post World War II

Between 15 February 1946 and 22 May 1946, he served with the RNZNVR as a radioman for the shore to ship skeds in Wellington, Hamilton, Napier, and Auckland.

## Work in New Zealand

Between 22 May 1946 and 30 April 1962, he held the following positions with the New Zealand Government:

* 22 May 1946 to 9 July 1948, Radio Operator for the shore to ship skeds from ZBP 8LK, Wellington.
* 9 July 1948 to 31 December 1951, Radio Operator for the shore to ship skeds from ZBP 8LK, Auckland.
* 1 January 1952 to 30 April 1962, Radio Operator for the shore to ship skeds from ZBP 8LK, Hamilton.

## Travelling

He travelled to Tahiti in June 1962, and to Hawaii in January 1963.

## Personal life

On 16 January 1965, he married Dorothy May Waberga in Hamilton. He died in Auckland on 11 October 1978.

The steamboat _St. Peter_ , commanded by Captain Henry M. Rice, arrived at St. Peters (now St. Paul) on the upper Mississippi in the summer of 1820. The boat had been carrying goods for the United States government.  At that time, the St. Croix River, which divided the British and American territories, was still in litigation, and the boundary issues were far from resolved.
Rice anchored his boat on the Minnesota shore just below the mouth of the St. Croix River. He had heard of the Falls of St. Anthony and wanted to see them. He wanted to buy furs from the Sioux, and he wanted to pack his boat up the St. Croix River to the headwaters, which he believed to be the source of the river. The name St. Croix comes from the French words _croix_ , cross, and _sainte_ , saint. In the early days, the river was called the _Riviere de Ste. Croix_.  The name was given to it by the French explorers, Sieur de la Vérendrye, who named it for the mission established there by the French Jesuits.
Captain Rice had the boat unloaded and sent part of it up the river to the headwaters. He explored the area with the Sioux Indians and hired a guide named John B. Kidd. Captain Rice and Kidd went 100 miles up the St. Croix River to Lake St. Croix, where they found the headwaters of the river to be in the neighborhood of the present city of Stillwater.
On their return down the river, Captain Rice met the _St. Peter_ near the present site of the city of St. Paul. The Sioux Indians had traded the furs they had captured from the Ojibwa Indians to the North West Company for European goods. Rice was impressed with the area and was anxious to return and establish trade there.  He wanted to establish a trading post and a settlement.

He had brought the first cargo of goods to be carried to the new settlement. He made a number of trips to the area back and forth. He laid out the grounds of Fort Snelling to the northwest of St. Paul.  He named the area for his grandfather, Colonel Josiah Snelling, who had been a Revolutionary officer and had later served as governor of the Maine Territory.
In 1823, another steamboat, the _Warren_ , commanded by Captain William A. Crosby, arrived at St. Peters, and Captain Rice engaged him to carry goods for the North West Company to the settlement. The same year, Captain Rice left St. Louis on another trip and carried the first cargo of goods to be sent to the settlement. During the next few years, several other steamboats carried goods up the river.

The next year, 1825, he began constructing a fort or trading post on the river just below the falls. In 1930 the Meteorological Office no longer used the Cooke telescope , and agreed to donate it to the university if they would

install it on the roof of the Old Chemistry building. The donation was made, and the instrument was moved to its present site.

### The 'Cooke Telescope', 1857

The 'Cooke Telescope' as seen from the Chemistry Building roof

In 1857 the University obtained a Cooke telescope, the first of its type in Australia. It was a remarkable instrument, the most advanced of its time in the world. It had a lens which could be adjusted to focus on objects at different distances and it was capable of magnifying objects up to 3000 times.

The Cooke Telescope was used by Isaac Roberts, a prominent English astronomer, who used it to discover 29 new nebulae. The Cooke Telescope was the first in the southern hemisphere to be used to study the heavens. It was the only instrument of its kind in the Southern Hemisphere until 1898, when the University obtained another Cooke Telescope.

The Cooke Telescope was housed in the Old Chemistry building from 1857 until 1927, when it was moved to the south-eastern corner of the Chemistry building. It remained there until 1940, when a new Cooke Telescope was installed in the department of Physics. In 1948 the original Cooke Telescope was moved to its present site, where it was installed on a telescoping mast that could be lowered when the weather was unsuitable for viewing.

The original Cooke telescope was removed from the site in 1987, and is now on display in the Australian National Maritime Museum, Darling Harbour.

### The 'Lord Tennyson Telescope', 1898

The 'Lord Tennyson Telescope' in its original 1898 position

The second Cooke Telescope was donated to the university by Lord Tennyson, the poet Laureate, in 1898. It was placed in the Old Chemistry building, in a room specially constructed to house it.

The telescope was removed from the site in 1957, and is now housed in the Sir William Lyons Observatory on the Mount Stromlo Observatory site.

### The 'Lord Tennyson Telescope', 1995

The 'Lord Tennyson Telescope' in its present site

When the Institute of Astronomy was expanded and moved to the Mount Stromlo site in 1986, the University donated the Lord Tennyson Telescope to the Australian National University, which placed it on a concrete platform on the roof of the Chemistry building, in a position similar to the one it had occupied in the Old Chemistry building. It is now used to study the faint objects the Lord Tennyson Telescope was used to study in 1898.

Charles Eaton , OBE , AFC ( 21 December 1895 – 12 November 1979 ) was a senior officer and aviator in the Royal Australian Air

Force (RAAF) .
Eaton joined the Royal Australian Air Force on 11 July 1919 with the rank of Pilot Officer, and was promoted to Flight Lieutenant in 1924 and Squadron Leader in 1935.
During World War II he served in the Middle East, Australia and New Guinea. He was appointed Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in 1946, and Air Commodore in 1950.
Eaton died in 1979.
Eaton was born in 1895 in St Albans, England, the son of William and Caroline Eaton .
The family migrated to Australia when Charles was five years old.
Eaton was educated at St Albans State School and Melbourne High School , graduating in 1914.
Eaton began work as a clerk in the Victorian Railways in 1914.
In 1915 Eaton enlisted in the Australian Imperial Force (AIF) as a private in the 18th Australian Infantry Battalion . He served in Egypt and Gallipoli and was wounded twice .
On 11 July 1919, Eaton joined the Royal Australian Air Force on the day it was created.
He was promoted to Pilot Officer in 1920, and Flight Lieutenant in 1924.
In 1925 Eaton was posted to the 2 Squadron (later 3 Squadron) as Squadron Leader. He returned to England in 1926 and attended the Central Flying School at RAF Upavon .
On his return to Australia he was appointed Officer Commanding, 7 Squadron , and became an exchange pilot with the Royal Air Force in 1929.
In 1930 Eaton was appointed Officer Commanding, 2 Squadron .
Eaton was promoted to Squadron Leader on 1 March 1935.
Eaton attended the Imperial Defence College, London, in 1936.
In 1939 Eaton was appointed the Chief of Staff to the Chief of Air Staff , Sir Charles Burnett .
During World War II Eaton served with the Middle East Command and later in Australia and New Guinea .
In 1941 Eaton was appointed Officer Commanding, 1 Fighter Wing. In 1942 he was promoted to Group Captain and took command of No. 243 Group.
In late 1942 Eaton was appointed Deputy Chief of Air Staff , Australian Military Forces (later, Royal Australian Air Force), and was promoted to Air Commodore in 1943.
In 1945 Eaton was appointed Commandant, RAAF College (later, RAAF Base Point Cook).
After the war he attended the Imperial Defence College, London, in 1946.
On 4 April 1946, Eaton was appointed Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE). He was promoted to Acting Air Vice-Marshal in 1949 and Air Vice-Marshal in 1950.
Eaton was appointed Chief of Staff at Headquarters, Air Force in 1951 and was promoted to Air Marshal in 1953.
In 1955 he was appointed Deputy Chief of Air Staff, Royal Australian Air Force.
Charles Eaton died in 1979 in Melbourne, Victoria.
The Charles Eaton Memorial Trophy is awarded each year to the top pilot in the RAAF Air Commanders Course.

"Hero" is a song by American recording artist Mariah Carey. It was written and produced by Carey and Walter Afanasieff for her fourth studio album, Daydream (1995). The song is an uptempo love song in which Carey sings of a "hero" for whom she has feelings. Since its release, "Hero" has received critical acclaim and it was nominated for Best Female Pop Vocal Performance at the 38th Annual Grammy Awards. It was released as the album's third and final single on September 12, 1995.
The song reached number one on the US Billboard Hot 100 for two weeks, becoming Carey's seventh number-one single on the chart. It also topped the charts in Australia, Canada, Finland, Ireland, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom. "Hero" was certified platinum by the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) for shipments of a million copies in the US. "Hero" was nominated for three Grammy Awards, including Record of the Year and Song of the Year . A live version of the song was included on the live album MTV Unplugged (1992).
Critical reception to "Hero" was generally positive. The song has been included in several lists of the greatest songs of all time. Nick Levine of Digital Spy ranked it at number 13 on his list of the 25 best songs of the 1990s, while Robert Copsey of Digital Spy ranked it at number 10 on his list of the 20 best Mariah songs .
A music video was released for the song. It was directed by Carey and was shot at the 72nd Street Boat Basin in New York City.
"Hero" was met with generally positive reviews from music critics. Robert Copsey of Digital Spy gave the song a five-star rating out of five, commenting, "It's easy to see why 'Hero' was such a big hit. It's an undoubtedly uplifting song - and that's without even considering the gospel-inspired back-up vocals and the song's inspirational lyrics. It's a reflection of her own strength of character - and it's a testament to her own inner hero, who triumphed over the tragic death of her beloved father." Nick Levine of Digital Spy gave the song a ten out of ten rating, calling it "the definitive Mariah song" and adding, "A bona fide 90s classic, 'Hero' was the sound of Mariah Carey at her most confident, self-assured and ambitious, while retaining enough of her pop roots to make her an easy-listening star." He ranked the song at number 13 on his list of the 25 best songs of the 1990s. Simon Price of The Independent called the song "devastating" and wrote that it's "one of the most moving pop songs you will ever hear". In 2007, Kitty Empire of The Guardian ranked "Hero" at number 10 on her list of the 100 best songs of the decade.

The first subfossil bird remains on Réunion were found in 1974 , and assigned to a stork , Ciconia sp . The remains were found

400 m above sea level in a marshy area in the Bois de la Table. The specimen consisted of a humerus and tibiotarsus, which were at least 20 cm long. The specimen was classified as a crane , because the humerus did not have a distinct keel (anterior process) and the proximal end of the humerus and the distal end of the tibiotarsus were not fused to the same bone. The description of the crane indicated that it was a species of the subgenus Balearica (now considered a separate genus, Balearica ), because the keel was not distinct and the humerus was almost two-thirds of the length of the tibiotarsus. A similar fossil crane was described from Mauritius , and it was later found that the two species were identical. The fossil crane is presumed to have been a migrant, because it was found in a natural area, and it was small enough to have been able to fly across the Indian Ocean. The fossil specimen could not be assigned to a subspecies, but it was estimated to be about 10 cm (3.9 in) larger than the largest living crane, the sarus crane , and the second largest crane, the common crane .
During a survey of Réunion for fossil birds in 1979, a humerus was found in a caves . The humerus was of a bird about the size of a crow , and it could not be assigned to a subspecies. The humerus was identified as a crane, but this was considered doubtful because the humerus had a distinct keel and the proximal end of the humerus was fused to the distal end of the tibiotarsus. When the fossil was later described in detail, it was determined that the specimen was a crane, but it could not be assigned to a subspecies.
In 1982, a humerus was found in the Bois de la Table , and it was identified as a crane. The humerus was larger than the humerus found in 1979 and it was estimated to be about 20 cm (7.9 in) longer than the humerus of the crane found in Mauritius .
During a survey of Réunion for fossil birds in 1984, a tibiotarsus was found in the Bois de la Table . The tibiotarsus was about 16 cm (6.3 in) long. The specimen was identified as a crane, but it was not assigned to a subspecies. The fossilized tibiotarsus was much longer than tibiotarsus of living cranes, and it was estimated to be about 20 cm (7.9 in) longer than the tibiotarsus of the crane found in Mauritius .
In 1986, a new species of crane was described from Réunion. The crane was found in the Bois de la Table , and it was described as a subfossil crane. The humerus and tibiotarsus were at least 20 cm (7.9 in) long, and they were not fused together. The humerus had a distinct keel and the proximal end of the humerus was fused to the distal end of the tibiotarsus. The crane was identified as a member of the genus Balearica (subgenus Balearica), and it was named Balearica reunionensis. The name reunionensis is based on the type locality, Réunion. The new species was considered to be a subspecies of the Mauritius crane because the two species were similar in size. The specimen described in 1986 had a keel that was not distinct and the humerus was about 2 cm (0.79 in) longer than the tibiotarsus , and it was estimated to be about 10 cm (3.9 in) larger than the largest living crane, the sarus crane .
In 1998, a new fossil crane was described from Réunion. The crane was described as a subfossil crane, and it was identified as a member of the genus Balearica (subgenus Balearica), and it was named Balearica reunionensis reunionensis. The name reunionensis is based on the type locality, Réunion. The new species was considered to be a subspecies of the Mauritius crane because the two species were similar in size. Mycena galericulata is saprobic , and grows on decaying hardwood and softwood sticks , chips , logs , and stumps . It can also

be found on soil or moss . It is found throughout the year in the Pacific Northwest .
M. galericulata is a small, white, bell-shaped gill mushroom that is usually found growing in clusters on the ground in forests. The cap is 1-2 centimetres (0.4-0.8 in) broad. The stem is 4-8 millimetres (0.16-0.31 in) long and 1-1.5 millimetres (0.04-0.06 in) thick.
The gills are white, with a whitish to brownish edge. The spore print is white .
M. galericulata has a distinctive odour, reported to smell like horse manure and/or old cheese.

The first published description of a case of leukemia in medical literature dates to 1827 , when French physician Alfred @-@ Ar

loing wrote about the case of a 21-year-old man who had been suffering from fever, headaches, and progressive anemia for more than a year. A bone marrow biopsy showed no abnormalities, and @-@ Arloing concluded that the patient had "a chronic anemia due to an infiltration of the bone marrow by small round cells." As with so many cases of leukemia that followed, @-@ Arloing's patient died before @-@ Arloing was able to publish his findings.
In the years following @-@ Arloing's report, more and more cases of leukemia were described, and it became increasingly clear that the disease was not just a chronic anemia. The term "leukemia" was derived from the Greek word leukos, meaning "white," and by the early twentieth century most physicians had identified the disease as a cancer of the blood. Leukemia was now considered a disease that could be diagnosed, and it was also recognized that the disease varied in terms of its characteristics. Some patients had a chronic form of the disease, and some had an acute form, and some had a combination of the two. Even within the acute form of the disease, there were numerous subtypes that varied in terms of the rate at which the cancerous cells were reproducing, and the degree to which the leukocytes—the white cells that fight infections—had been overwhelmed by the cancerous cells.
The study of the disease became more sophisticated during the first half of the twentieth century, and by 1949 scientists had identified more than twenty different subtypes of leukemia. Some of the subtypes were more aggressive than others, and the patients suffering from these more aggressive forms of leukemia had a much lower survival rate than patients with milder forms of the disease. These subtypes were also divided according to the type of cancerous cell most commonly found in the blood.
In 1960 two American physicians, @-@ Dale @-@ Lattimer and @-@ James @-@ Hamilton, Jr., proposed that the twenty-odd subtypes of leukemia could be organized into two broad categories, one of which they called "myeloid" and the other of which they called "lymphoid." According to @-@ Lattimer and @-@ Hamilton, the myeloid and lymphoid categories of leukemia were caused by two different types of leukemia cells. Myeloid leukemia cells were characterized by having granules in the cell nucleus, while lymphoid leukemia cells were characterized by having small nucleoli in the cell nucleus.
The myeloid and lymphoid categories were, in essence, two different diseases, and not all patients diagnosed with leukemia had myeloid or lymphoid cells in their blood. Therefore, leukemia was no longer seen as a single disease, but rather as a family of related diseases. This change in the way leukemia was viewed led to a new classification system that included three subcategories of myeloid leukemia and eight subcategories of lymphoid leukemia.

When observed under the electron microscope , the nucleolus can be seen to consist of three distinguishable regions : the inner

dense fibrillar center, the outer dense granular region, and the granular zone. The outer granular region is composed of an array of concentric rings of granules that are clearly distinguishable from the fibrils in the inner nucleolus.
The fibrils in the nucleolus , like those in the nucleoplasm , are composed of a protein-lipid complex. They are either straight or curved. The curved fibrils are less common than the straight ones.
The nucleolus is a distinctive feature of the nucleus of a cell. Although the nucleus is the largest organelle in the cell, the nucleolus is much smaller, usually occupying less than 5 percent of the entire nucleus.
The nucleolus is unstable during cell division. During mitosis , the nucleolus is broken up into fragments that are distributed throughout the cytoplasm. It reappears during interphase after cell division.

The prognosis is worse in those with larger burns , those who are older , and those who are females . The presence of a smoke i

leum also predicts a worse prognosis [ 49 ].
The aim of this study was to evaluate the prognostic value of the initial CT scans in patients with severe burns. The hypothesis is that burns receiving a higher MASSA score have a worse prognosis. The initial assessment of burn severity is important as treatment is based on this initial assessment. This is essential for the appropriate management of fluid resuscitation, wound care, and the administration of analgesia to avoid complications [ 68 , 69 ].
A retrospective study was conducted on all the patients admitted to the Burn Unit of a tertiary Hospital in Newcastle, Australia, between 2002 and 2012. The study was approved by the Newcastle and Hunter Medical Research Institute Human Research Ethics Committee, and all patients gave written informed consent. Data were collected from the patient’s medical records.
The demographic data, burn size, and initial and follow-up CT scans were collected for all patients. The patients’ age at the time of admission was recorded, and the body surface area (BSA) burned was calculated from the total body surface area (TBSA) burned. The TBSA was calculated by measuring the surface area of the burns from the top of the head down to the soles of the feet and from the back to the anterior chest wall. The BSA was calculated by the ratio of the total area burnt divided by the total body surface area [ 70 ]. The patients’ height and weight were measured at presentation, and the body mass index (BMI) was calculated. The BMI is the ratio of weight (kg) over height (m 2 ).
CT images were obtained at presentation and on the 4th and 10th days after admission to the Burn Unit. CT scans were performed with multidetector CT (MDCT) scanners (General Electric, Milwaukee, WI, USA; Siemens, Erlangen, Germany; and Philips, Best, The Netherlands) using the following protocol: 120 kVp, 120 mA, 1.25 mm collimation, and 0.625 mm layer thickness.
The CT scans were examined by an experienced radiologist. The CT scans were assessed for the presence of smoke ileum (SI), abdominal and visceral burns, pulmonary and cardiac burns, and burns to the chest wall, face, and neck. The presence of these burns was recorded, and the number of burns and the size of each burn was noted. The presence and the size of each burn was recorded in cm 2 .
MASSA was calculated according to the formula [ 71 ]: MASSA = 4.42 × BSA + 3.64 × (height 1.83). Height and weight were measured in centimeters and kilograms, respectively.
The patients were assessed for complications on the 4th and 10th days after admission and classified according to the following criteria: sepsis was defined as systemic signs of infection in a patient with a positive blood culture, and sepsis complicated by multiorgan failure was defined as the presence of sepsis and a new organ failure in two or more organs, including the respiratory system, the heart, the kidneys, and/or the liver [ 72 ].
Patients were classified into two groups: the survivors and the nonsurvivors. The survivors were defined as those who survived beyond 90 days after admission to the Burn Unit. The nonsurvivors were defined as those who died within the first 90 days after admission. The presence of complications was recorded for both groups.

In the early 1970s, the study of fossil skeletons of Iguanodon came to be recognized as key to the reconstruction of dinosaurian anatomy, especially posture. Iguanodon was one of the first dinosaurs to be recognized as a biped, and remains one of the best known and most extensively studied.
The first reconstruction of Iguanodon was based on the skeleton of "I. bernissartensis," the type species of Iguanodon, with an easily identifiable and remarkably complete skeleton recovered from the Bernissart quarry in Belgium. This skeleton is now in the Brussels Museum of Natural Science, and the reconstruction of Iguanodon was made by the museum's restorer, Louis Dollo, in 1880. This reconstruction was the first to be published in the scientific literature, in the Belgian journal _L'Année Scientifique_ in 1881 (Dollo 1881), and it served as the basis for many further reconstructions, including the famous model of Iguanodon in the London Natural History Museum. (Fossils of Iguanodon are almost completely restricted to Europe, so it was one of the first dinosaurs to be studied and understood in Western Europe.) The reconstruction of the skeleton of _I. bernissartensis_ , and the detailed knowledge of the morphology of the skeleton that Dollo and others made, was soon followed by the first reconstructions of Iguanodon posture. These reconstructions were based on the "I. anglicus" skeleton from Tilgate Forest, near Crawley, which was discovered in the 1870s and is now in the Natural History Museum in London. The reconstruction of the posture of _I. anglicus_ was made in 1885 by the English anatomist Henry Parker, using the skeleton in London (Parker 1885).
Henry Parker (1855–1935), anatomist and paleontologist, was born in London, the son of a barrister and solicitor. He was educated at University College London, where he obtained a first class degree in anatomy in 1878. He was appointed Assistant Anatomist at the Natural History Museum in 1879, and became Assistant Curator in 1885. He was appointed Professor of Morphology at University College London in 1892, a chair he held until 1928. He is remembered today for his studies of the anatomy and fossil remains of the large extinct reptiles known as pterosaurs, and for his studies of the postural reconstructions of dinosaurs.

From about 1826 Alkan began to appear as a piano soloist in leading Parisian salons , including those of the Princesse de la Mo

querie , the Princess de la Tour d'Auvergne , the Duchesse d'Havré , and the Duchesse d'Orléans . More than a decade later, in 1839, he gave a series of concerts at the Salle Herz .
During his lifetime Alkan was known as the "Paganini of the Piano" for his dazzling virtuosity. The son of a Polish Jew with family connections to the Frankfurt am Main Jewish community, Alkan was born in Paris in 1813, where he studied piano with Henri Herz. It was with Herz that Alkan made his debut at the age of eight. As a teenager, he played at a number of salons, including those of the Princesse de la Moquerie, the Princess de la Tour d'Auvergne, the Duchesse d'Havré, and the Duchesse d'Orléans. In 1839 Alkan gave a series of concerts at the Salle Herz. In 1841 he became the sub-organist and teacher of organ at the Sainte-Clotilde in Paris, a position he held until his death in 1888.
Alkan had a lifelong interest in Jewish history. This interest is reflected in his setting of Psalm 114, "When Israel went out of Egypt" (1860), his three-movement suite _Hebrew Melodies_ (1872), and his _Israeli Melodies_ (ca. 1882), all of which were published by Schirmer. His setting of Psalm 114, "When Israel went out of Egypt," was probably written between 1849 and 1852. The piece was published in 1860 in the _Art Journal_ , and later that year in New York by the firm of Edward Marx (plate 51).
Alkan's setting of Psalm 114 is a one-movement, five-stanza setting of the poem. The poem is in the form of a bicentennial commemoration, counting the years of the Exodus from Egypt to the time of David. The first stanza, which is the one that is sung in synagogue, celebrates the covenant that God made with Israel upon their liberation from Egyptian bondage. The second stanza describes the joy of the Israelites as they depart from Egypt. The third stanza describes the Exodus in terms of the sun rising and the moon setting in the wake of the Israelites' departure, which leads to the fourth and fifth stanzas, which describe the wonders of nature that accompanied the Exodus. The poem is a reminder that the liberation of the Jews from Egyptian bondage was not just a one-time event, but a covenant between God and the Jewish people.
Alkan's setting is a virtuosic display of all forms of piano technique, including the use of the pedals. The piece begins by suggesting the rolling of the sea and the upheaval of the earth, using large chords and a continuous motion. Alkan then suggests the rising of the sun, and the moon being obscured. The sunrise suggests the rising of the right-hand melody, which is accompanied by a "soldierly" bass that sounds like a snare drum. The effect of rising sun is made even more dramatic by the use of the pedals to create the illusion of a shining sun. At the beginning of the First World War , Black Prince was one of the four armoured cruisers serving in the 1st Cruiser Squadro

n, under the command of Rear-Admiral (later Admiral of the Fleet) David Beatty. Beaty was one of the most senior and respected officers in the Royal Navy. He was a keen advocate of the new 'all big gun' armoured cruisers. As a result, he was given command of the first squadron of armoured cruisers in 1908 and was appointed to the Board of Control for the Construction of the Dreadnought (1905–06).1 He was known for his aggressive and daring tactics, for example, in the Battle of Jutland (1916), and was one of the few naval commanders to be promoted to the rank of Admiral of the Fleet during the war.
Black Prince was one of the first armoured cruisers built for the Royal Navy and was very much a product of the end of the nineteenth century. Armoured cruisers were a new concept in warships and exemplified the new 'all big gun' approach to naval warfare. They were bigger, and generally faster, than the older protected cruisers and were armed with large guns. The name 'armoured cruiser' was coined by the French, who had built the first of this new type of warship. They had a heavy main armament of guns and an armoured belt to protect the vulnerable mid-ship section. The British were quick to recognise the potential of this new design and soon produced their own version. A Royal Commission on the Defence of the United Kingdom (1889) had recommended that a number of new armoured cruisers be built. The first of these, Imperieuse, was launched in 1892 and was followed by Abercorn in 1894.
The Royal Navy then embarked on a programme to build a number of armoured cruisers and the first ship of the new type, Black Prince, was launched in 1897. The name was well chosen to commemorate the famous medieval prince of Wales who led the English Army to victory at the Battle of Poitiers (1356). Thus, Black Prince was the first modern warship to be named after this famous prince. There was a great deal of public interest in the new ship and a number of her launching ceremonies were attended by the Prince of Wales.
Black Prince was 141 feet long and 22 feet wide. She was designed to carry a crew of 350 men and was armed with four 9.2-inch guns and twelve 6-inch guns. She was fitted with a 24-foot tall funnel, which gave her a very distinctive profile. The ship was built by Armstrong in Elswick and the keel was laid down on 21 June 1896. She was launched on 26 April 1897 and was completed by 10 October 1899.
Black Prince was a very fast ship, capable of 21 knots. Her main armament consisted of four 9.2-inch guns and she was also armed with twelve 6-inch guns. These were mounted in twin turrets, one forward and one aft. The guns had a very short barrel, which made them highly accurate and they fired a shell that weighed 136 pounds (62 kg). Black Prince was very heavily armoured to defend against the newer ships that had appeared on the scene. The belt of armour ran the whole length of the ship and was 7 inches thick. The side armour plates were 4.5 inches thick, while the armour plates below the waterline were 2.5 inches thick.121

On January 3 , 2014 , LiSA held a sold @-@ out solo concert at the Nippon Budokan . Her fifth single " Rising Hope " , which is

the theme song for the film " Ace Attorney " , was released on January 29, 2014 .

## Overview

### "Rising Hope"

"Rising Hope" was written by LiSA and composed by Tomoya Ozawa , who also composed LiSA's single "Day by Day" and "Senritsu". It is the theme song for the 14th film in the Ace Attorney series, Ace Attorney: Dai Gyakuten Saiban .

On March 16, 2013, LiSA announced in her blog that she will be performing the theme song for the film, Ace Attorney: Dai Gyakuten Saiban . It was confirmed that the song would be titled "Rising Hope" and would be released in January 2014.

### Release

The single was released in two editions: regular and limited. The limited edition included a DVD containing the music video for "Rising Hope", a documentary of LiSA's recording of the song, and a talk show. "Rising Hope" was used as the ending theme song for the film.

## Reception

### Chart performance

"Rising Hope" debuted at number 7 on the Oricon Weekly Singles Chart, with 13,829 copies sold in its first week. It charted for eleven weeks and has sold 43,771 copies.

Choral singing became increasingly popular in 19th @-@ century Wales , principally owing to the rise of the eisteddfod as a sym

posium for the dissemination of cultural and religious ideas. However, by the end of the century, there was a growing awareness that the older, traditional Welsh singing styles were being replaced by styles imported from England, which, although more in keeping with the tastes of the Victorian middle classes, were also less rooted in a Welsh tradition.
Consequently, 1890 saw the formation of the Cynghanedd Society (Cymdeithas Cynghanedd) at the National Eisteddfod in Caernarfon. The Society was founded to promote the use of cynghanedd or polyrhythms—a form of verse-melody that was being increasingly replaced by monorhythmic singing in Wales. The Society did not last long, but the idea of archiving and preserving Welsh folk music was taken up by the Welsh Folk-Song Society, which was founded four years later.
The Society's first president was the bard Evan James , a musician and composer, who was also a member of the Cynghanedd Society. In 1895, it was decided that the Society should hold a Welsh Musical Congress, the first of which was held at the Cymmrodorion Club in London the following year, with the aim of gaining public support for the preservation of Welsh folk music.
The Congress was attended by many eminent performers and experts in Welsh music, as well as by the Welsh folk-lore collector and musicologist, John Ceiriog Hughes , who was a member of the Society's committee. By 1902, the Society had become the Welsh Folk-Song Society (Cymdeithas y Canu Di-Gwladol Cymreig), and in 1930 the name was changed to Cymdeithas y Canu y Cylch (The Welsh National Choral Society).
The Society's original aim was to collect and preserve the Welsh folk-songs and songs that were in danger of being lost, and to disseminate them in Wales. However, the Society also played an important role in the development of the Welsh choral tradition in the 20th century.
In 1902, the Society published its first collection of Welsh folk-songs. This was followed by a second collection in 1921. By the end of the century, the Society had published more than 20 other collections, as well as a journal, _Canu_ (Song), and a number of books, including a book of Welsh hymns and the first edition of the classic Welsh hymnal, _Glan Rhondda_.
The Society also supported the establishment of the Welsh National Choral Union in 1927, and the Welsh Choral Union in 1936. These organisations were formed in response to the growing popularity of choral singing in Wales. The Society was also instrumental in the establishment of the Welsh Choral Union in 1935, which was responsible for the publication of a number of the Society's publications.
The Society is currently celebrating its centenary year, and is planning a number of events to mark the occasion, including a concert and a conference.

ieged island of Quang Tri, the responsibility for which had fallen to the People's Army of Vietnam. Fantastic stories were circulated about the American forces in the A Shau Valley. The 25th Infantry Division was said to have as many as seven divisions and to be deploying two battalion-sized airborne units. The American Army was said to be receiving huge quantities of vastly superior equipment and even chemical weapons.
However, no matter how powerful the American forces in the A Shau Valley may have been, this information was completely irrelevant to the situation in Quang Tri. Indeed, the Communist leadership in Hanoi regarded the American forces as little better than a screen that protected the Fourteenth Army from interference in the operations for the liberation of Quang Tri. To the Communists in Hanoi, the A Shau Valley was a means to reach the Ho Chi Minh Trail.
In Hanoi, the situation was equally desperate. The People's Army of Vietnam had been stalled at the outskirts of Hue for more than two weeks. Only 100 miles south of Hanoi, Hue was the capital of South Vietnam's central region. It was a city steeped in history and legend, and one of the oldest in the country.
It had been the home of the former Vietnamese emperors, who ruled the country from the fifteenth to the twentieth century. The city contained the tombs and mausoleums of some ninety-two emperors, including the tomb of Emperor Tu Do, who had ruled from 1802 to 1840. Hue's history was even older than that of Vietnam itself. It had been the capital of Vietnam for more than a thousand years, since 1009 A.D., when the emperor Ly Thai To had established a new dynasty, the Ly.
During the French period, Hue had been the site of a number of important battles between the French and the Vietnamese, including the Battle of Hue 1859, which marked the beginning of the end of Vietnamese independence. Hue had been the site of one of the most famous uprisings against the French, the 1930 events known as the Incident of Hue. In 1945, following the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor, the Viet Minh had proclaimed the Declaration of Independence in Hue, at the Citadel.
The French had always regarded the city of Hue as the symbol of national resistance. For the Communists, Hue was a symbol of American imperialism and a harbinger of the future, for it was in Hue that the Americans were now to be defeated.
With the fall of the city, the Americans would be defeated in Vietnam. It was for this reason that the Americans were encamped on the outskirts of Hue, defending the city, which was under siege by the Ninth Division of the People's Army of Vietnam. The assault on Hue had begun on January 18, 1968.
The city was surrounded by fortified trenches and a minefield, which the Ninth Division, supported by the Thirty-first and Seventh Divisions, had dug in the days before the attack. The mines and trenches were a hindrance to the attackers, as they had been to the defenders.
The 325th Division, the Communist division responsible for the attack, had been ordered to capture the city. The 325th Division was the smallest of the three divisions defending the A Shau Valley, and the most lightly armed. It had been the first to arrive in the A Shau Valley, in December 1967, and it had not been reinforced.
The 325th Division had been ordered to make a diversionary attack on the A Shau Valley, in order to draw the American forces away from the city of Hue. The 325th Division attacked the city, on January 18, 1968.
The attack began at 7:00 A.M. The attackers were in command of a large force of tanks and artillery, which the Communists had captured from the Republic of Vietnam.
The Americans had been warned of the attack. The South Vietnamese Joint General Staff had informed the Americans of the date and the time of the attack, and the Americans had placed a heavy force of tanks and artillery in the area. The Americans had also flown an air evacuation force to the area, which had been standing by, waiting for the attack.

### Events

In the morning, the German and Ottoman force were moving through Pine forest. Chauvel directed 11th Light Horse Regiment, 15th Light Horse Regiment and 3rd Light Horse Brigade to attack the Pine forest.

At 12.15 pm, the British and Empire force attacked the German and Ottoman force. In the attack, the 12th Light Horse Regiment and 11th Light Horse Regiment captured the Pine forest. The 15th Light Horse Regiment and 11th Light Horse Regiment were then in pursuit of the German and Ottoman force.

The German and Ottoman force reached Digla and then turned towards Beersheba.

## Aftermath

The Allied Official History noted the Battle of Katia and the Battle of the Pine Forest as "the last attempt of the enemy to force a passage through the hills and 22 miles of desert at the northern base of the Judean Hills, before the approach of the end of the rainy season, and the consequent hardening of the desert ground."

Both attacks were planned for December 11, but the 17th Brigade attack was called off due to heavy rain and mud. The 18th Brigade attack was successful, however, and the 18th Brigade captured the Bocchetta Pass.

20 years earlier, when the Somali government hired an East German company, Schleifring, to build a factory and housing development for the Ministry of Defence .

In 1990, as the Somali government began to crumble, and the country descended into chaos, the factory was abandoned and the housing development became home to thousands of Somalis.
By the time Al-Shabaab took control of Mogadishu in 2006, the Salaam Estate had grown to become the largest slum in the city. With the arrival of the insurgents, the estate was inevitably drawn into the conflict.
The Salaam Estate is a small bubble in the vastness of Somalia's capital, and it is one of the few places in Mogadishu where life appears to be normal. On weekends, men and women relax under palm trees and in the shade of a mosque. Children play football or stroll the dusty streets. They do not worry about Al-Shabaab or the daily violence that has become an integral part of life in Mogadishu.

In 2009, I visited the estate with a local journalist I had met while working on a documentary about Mogadishu's crime syndicates. We befriended a family who had been living in the Salaam Estate for more than 20 years. This family were the first of the residents to open up to us about the insurgents' presence in the slum.
The 1990s were a different time. During this period, Somalia was under the control of two warlords who had taken over the country: Ali Mahdi Mohamed and Gen. Mohamed Farah Aidid. The warlords were bitter rivals, and they spent much of their time fighting each other.

Leigh became pregnant in 1956 and withdrew from the production of Coward 's comedy South Sea Bubble . The day after her final p

antomime performance as Cinderella in 1957, she married actor Peter Hall in a civil ceremony at the register office in Westminster. She simultaneously withdrew from the playwright's comedy The Family Way , which she had been due to direct and star in. The couple announced she was pregnant in September. The first of their four children was born in 1958. She and Hall went on to direct plays together, including Peter Shaffer 's Black Comedy (1965).
Leigh's first post-pantomime role was in 1957 as Jean Harris in the film adaptation of Coward's Private Lives , opposite Peter Hall as Elyot Chase. The same year she appeared in three more films: The Naked Truth , a spy comedy with Rex Harrison and Tony Curtis; A Woman of Mystery opposite Robert Morley and Peter Finch; and The Man Who Knew Too Much , with James Stewart and Doris Day. She was reunited on screen with Stewart in The Man Who Knew Too Much in 1956.Her name was incorrectly spelled as "Julie Leigh" in the opening credits of A Woman of Mystery.
Leigh next appeared in the 1958 film The Bridge on the River Kwai , playing a Japanese hostess named "Katya", in which she appeared in a topless and then nude scene. Her nude scenes were cut from the film for several years, but were later restored in the director's cut released in 1992. The film won numerous awards and Leigh later said that "it was the role that made me famous."
In 1960, she began a relationship with actor Warren Beatty, and the following year they starred together in the film All Fall Down , a film about a dysfunctional family. It was released in the UK as The Family Fall and in the US as Home Before Dark. The film was not a commercial success, and some critics in the US felt that Leigh had been miscast. However, the film received some positive reviews and Beatty was praised for his performance. The same year, she starred in the comedy What a Way to Go! , a film about a woman who marries a millionaire, then a poor man and then a millionaire again. The film was released to mixed reviews but was a box office success, and the year after it was released, Leigh was voted the second most popular star in the UK polls, behind Elizabeth Taylor.
Leigh was cast in the 1961 film The Children's Hour , opposite Audrey Hepburn, Shirley MacLaine and James Garner, based on the play by Lillian Hellman. Her role was that of a woman falsely accused of being lesbian after she becomes romantically involved with her best friend's teenage son and reputations are destroyed. The film was a critical and commercial success and Leigh was praised for her role, with the New York Times calling her "a radiant Julie". The same year, she starred opposite Henry Fonda and Shirley MacLaine in the film What a Way to Go! , a black comedy in which she played a woman who marries a millionaire, then a poor man and then a millionaire again.
Leigh was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 1988, becoming the first actress to receive the honour.
In 2001, the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences awarded Leigh with an Honorary Award for her contribution to the film industry. She had previously been nominated for an Academy Award for Best Actress for her performance in The Roman Spring of Mrs. Stone (1961).
In 2010, she was voted number 10 on Empire magazine's "The Top 100 Movie Stars of All Time" list.
Leigh died on 11 December 2017, aged 90.

The Soviet authorities sought to remove all trace of the Polish history of the area now under their control . The name " Poland

" was replaced by "Belarus." When this was not possible, Polish names were changed: for example, the Polish name of a village was altered to a Slavicized version. When this was also not possible, the village was renamed and its former inhabitants were evicted from their homes. In some cases the villages were renamed in a derogatory manner. For example, Zubrowsk was renamed Farforowsk, meaning "cow shit," and Kedzierzyn was renamed Kedzierzyn-Kozle, where "kozle" means "goat's horn." In other cases the old Polish names were erased and shortened, for example, Zubrowsk was renamed "Zubrovo" and Kedzierzyn was renamed "Kedzierzyn." The Polish names of the villages were also rarely translated into Belarusian.
As the Soviet Union fell into chaos, some of the forced relocations were reversed by the Belarusian authorities. But the majority of the Polish villages had already been wiped off the map.
 In the 1990s, the Polish government enacted a law under which a special fund was established to provide financial assistance to the inhabitants of the "lost villages" in order to help them restore their homes. At the same time, Poland took steps to recognize the Polish nationality of the inhabitants of these villages. In 1992, Poland provided free Polish citizenship to the inhabitants of the "lost villages" who wished to become Polish citizens. The citizenship law was applied retroactively for the period beginning in 1950, when the relocation of the Poles began, and ending in 1991. At the same time, the Polish authorities reinstated the names of the villages as they had been prior to the relocation.
 Some Polish and Belarusian historians argue that the relocation was not the result of a Soviet policy of ethnic cleansing but rather was an accidental and unplanned side effect of Soviet agricultural reforms. They claim that the relocation was the result of the Soviet government's effort to collectivize agriculture, and that the Soviet government did not seek to remove the Polish population from the area.

George Johnston (1818–1891), was born in Dumfries , Scotland , and his parents separated when he was an infant . He and his mother moved to Carlisle , where he spent his childhood.
His mother, Janet Johnston (née Routh) was the niece of the Edinburgh printer and publisher John Ballantyne (1774–1821) and so was well connected in literary and publishing circles in the Scottish capital. George was educated at Carlisle Grammar School and was apprenticed to a cabinet maker in 1836.
When he was twenty-two, Johnston moved to Edinburgh and found work as a salesman for John Ballantyne and Co. He was able to use his connections to get a job as chief proofreader at the publisher's and was later promoted to editor of their newspaper The Scotsman .
In 1844 Johnston began his own weekly newspaper, The Northern Ensign , which he converted into a monthly in 1847. He was a member of the Edinburgh Literary Club , a club of writers and publishers who met regularly with Walter Scott as the president. The most prominent member of the club was James Clerk Maxwell, the physicist and mathematician.
At this time, Johnston was also the librarian of the Royal Institution of Great Britain . He was elected to the Royal Society of Edinburgh in 1848 and was an antiquarian and a member of the Spalding Club .
George Johnston died of a stroke on 11 January 1891. He is buried in the Grange Cemetery in Edinburgh in an unmarked grave.
Johnston's eldest daughter, Helen Johnston, became a successful novelist.

The defenders held the walls of the city of Ascalon, but the vanguard of the Christian army was surrounded and forced to surrender—except for one man: a knight called Foulques of Nantes. Having been a prisoner in the Muslim lands before, he had a higher tolerance for their brutality than his companions. He was able to escape—and he did so on a donkey. Those following him fled, and the fate of the city became sealed.
The Crusaders were able to fight their way out of their encirclement and into Ascalon, a triumph hailed as a miracle and one of the most important events in the history of the Crusades. The defeat of Foulques would have crushed the spirit of the Crusaders. It is a story that has been told, in many versions, for over 900 years.
The man who had escaped was Raymond IV of Toulouse, also known as Raymond of Saint-Gilles, a nobleman from the region around Toulouse in the south of France. The Crusades were a series of campaigns launched by the Christian church to take back the Holy Land and liberate Jerusalem from Muslim rule. They were a religious movement, and for many of the participants religion and war were inextricably linked. When the first Crusade was launched in 1095, its objectives were to seize Muslim-held Jerusalem and the surrounding area, to stop the advance of the Muslim armies into Europe, and to make the Holy Land a safe place for Christian pilgrims. It was expected to be an easy victory. The Crusaders believed they had the support of God, almost as if they were fulfilling a divine plan, and they were confident that their cause would be seen as just.
The first Crusade was launched in 1095, the year after the death of Pope Urban II, who had first suggested it. Urban was encouraged by the agreement of the Eastern Emperor, Alexius I Comnenus, that Christian armies would be allowed to cross Byzantine territory on their way to the Holy Land, and he hoped that the Crusaders would be able to establish a stronghold in the region that would be a permanent bulwark against the Saracens.
The Pope's speech at the Council of Clermont on November 27, 1095, is one of the most famous speeches in church history, and the event has often been hailed as the beginning of the Crusades. Urban was preaching to a huge crowd, and he used the occasion to call for the liberation of the Holy Land. The speech was written and delivered in Latin, and the translation was one that would be understood by his audience.

The Woodward case is the first ever successful punitive damages verdict against an airline for $200 million.
The plaintiff, David Woodward, a passenger aboard Comair Flight 3272, was seriously injured when the jet airplane that he was flying in crashed shortly after take-off from the Lexington, Kentucky Blue Grass Airport. The aircraft, a twin-engine regional jet owned by Comair, crashed after the pilot's attempted to abort the take-off. The jet touched down for a moment and then was airborne again, but then struck a utility pole, another plane and finally a car. The plane eventually crashed and caught fire.
The day of the crash, David Woodward and his wife, were heading to Phoenix, Arizona for a vacation. They had been delayed overnight because of mechanical problems, which added to the stress of the day. They were forced to wait five hours in the plane before take-off. Despite the already stressful situation, the pilot, Donnie R. Bland, abruptly announced that he had to abort the take-off. He did not give any explanation, and he did not tell the passengers what the emergency was.
Airline pilots are not trained to abort take-offs in the aircraft that they fly, and the Comair jet has a history of such emergencies. The pilots have been trained to abort take-offs only in one particular type of aircraft.
The pilot, who had been drinking, quickly applied the brakes. The jet made contact with the runway, then the air, the utility pole, another plane and finally the car. The pilots did not evacuate the plane. Instead, they ran from the plane.

Nieświedź is located approximately 20 kilometres south-east of Łódź , in the Łódź Voivodeship .
The first mention of the village of Nieświedź dates back to the year 1335. It was then a royal village, owned by the knights of the Nieświedź coat of arms. The village was then referred to as "Neswiedcze". In the 15th century, the village was owned by the Tęczyński and Jezierski families. In 1548, it was sold to the Duchy of Opole , and in 1580 it passed to the Potocki family. In 1606, Nieświedź received the town charter .
On 1 September 1620, during the Polish-Swedish War (1620–21), the battle of Nieświedź was fought here. The Swedish army was defeated by the Polish army commanded by Hetman Stanisław Koniecpolski.
In 1702, Nieświedź became a private property of the Wiśniowiecki family. In 1722, Prince Bogusław Stanisław Wiśniowiecki handed it over to his brother, Hetman Stanislaw August Poniatowski . The latter was the father of the last king of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, Stanisław August Poniatowski .
Nieświedź is home to several monuments. The most prominent is the Renaissance manor house of the Wiśniowiecki family. Its construction was completed in 1552. Subsequently, a park was established in the manor's surroundings. In the 18th century, the manor was considerably modified. It was later owned by the Krasiński family. In 1931, the manor house was acquired by the Polish state. In 1933, the building was converted into a sanatorium. In 1953, it was converted into a sanatorium for children. In 1976, the building was reconstructed and adapted for the needs of the medical centre.
The manor house is located in the centre of the village. It is a three-storey building with a half-basement. The building is surrounded by a moat. It is painted in red and white. On the facade, the building bears a commemorative plaque with the coat of arms of the Wiśniowiecki family.
In front of the manor house is a statue of Prince Bogusław Stanisław Wiśniowiecki.

first of these was USS _Tucker_ , authorized in the 1913 naval appropriation bill and authorizing $ 1,520,000 for its construction in the fiscal year 1914. The final cost, however, was $ 1,597,669 , placing _Tucker_ in a category of its own.
 The vessel's keel was laid down on 17 August 1914 by the New York Shipbuilding Corporation of Camden, New Jersey and was launched on 12 September 1915. The ship was commissioned on 13 March 1916, Lieutenant Commander Cyrus B. McLauchlin in command.
 USS _Tucker_ had an interesting career. She was assigned to the Yangtze Patrol in 1917 and was stationed at Shanghai, China. After the outbreak of war with Germany, Captain C. B. McLauchlin of the _Tucker_ was assigned to the command of the United States Naval forces on the Yangtze River .
 The _Tucker_ was relieved and returned to the Atlantic Fleet in 1918. After the Armistice, she was based at Philadelphia, Pennsylvania in 1919–1920, and then spent the next six years operating on the East Coast and in the West Indies. In 1965 , Braathens SAFE placed an order for three Boeing 737 @-@ 200s , costing a total ofNOK 100 million . They were intended

to be used for short-haul services , since the company had a policy of not operating jet services on routes of less than 500 km . However , they were soon put to more extensive use , including on longer routes .

In the fall of 1970 , Braathens ordered two more -200s , part of a larger order for six 737-200s and six 737-100s . The -200s were to be delivered in 1972 , but the 100 series were delivered in 1970 . The -200s were redesigned with an increased capacity of 66 seats .

On October 19, 1972, Braathens SAFE received its first 737-200 , tail number LN-BAM , which was the first 737-200 to be delivered to a European operator . Braathens also received LN-BAN (c/n 20103/2079) and LN-BAP (c/n 20105/2081).

## Design

737-200 on display at the Norwegian Aviation Museum

The 737-200 was lengthened from the 737-100 by 4.9 m (16 ft), adding two overwing exits and five rows of seats. The gross weight was 71,500 kg (157,618 lb), and the MTOW was 75,500 kg (166,500 lb).

The first 737-200 (F-WWAA) was delivered to Air Inter on January 27, 1967. The 737-200 entered regular service with United Airlines on February 26, 1967. The first 737-200 to be delivered to a European operator (Braathens SAFE) was LN-BAM (1972).

Boeing marketed a shortened version of the 737-200 as the 737-200C, with capacity for 64 passengers, for cargo use. The first 737-200C (N90664) was delivered to Northwest Airlines on July 21, 1971. Northwest ordered 12 in total, but only one was delivered before they cancelled the order.

Boeing also offered the 737-200 as a stretched version of the 737-100, with the same capacity as the 737-200C, for cargo use. The first of two 737-200Cs (N90663) was delivered to United Airlines on July 24, 1971.

UPDATE 1-U.S. Supreme Court blocks Texas abortion law, ruling in 5-4 vote
* Ruling prevents Texas from enforcing abortion law
* Conservative judge Neil Gorsuch joins liberals
* Texas abortion law may have nationwide implications
(Updates with additional details, comments, markets)
By Lawrence Hurley and Jan Wolfe
WASHINGTON, May 29 (Reuters) - The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday blocked Texas from enforcing a law banning most abortions after a federal appeals court ruled that the Republican-backed law placed an "undue burden" on women seeking the procedure.
The court voted 5-4 to grant a preliminary injunction requested by abortion providers, with Neil Gorsuch, President Donald Trump's nominee, joining the court's four liberal justices in the majority.
Gorsuch, who was confirmed in April, is the court's newest member.
The court's decision, which was unsigned, said the abortion providers were likely to succeed on the merits of their challenge to the law.
A challenge to the law had been brought by the U.S. Justice Department on behalf of clinics that perform abortions, and the case was before the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, based in New Orleans, which ruled 2-1 that the law imposed an "undue burden" on abortion access in the state.
The state has said it will appeal the 5th Circuit's decision to the Supreme Court.
"The court's order is temporary and does not decide the merits of the case. We are confident that the 5th Circuit's decision will be affirmed," said John Seago, director of Texas Right to Life.
Texas Governor Greg Abbott, a Republican who signed the law in 2017, criticized the court's decision, saying the abortion providers had "chosen to ignore the rule of law" and that the law "will save countless innocent life."
"I will continue to work to protect innocent life and make Texas the safest state in the nation for the unborn," he said.
The providers challenging the law, the Whole Woman's Health and the Center for Reproductive Rights, said in a joint statement: "We will continue to fight to ensure that all women have access to the full range of abortion care they need."
The court has a 5-4 conservative majority, including Gorsuch.
The Fifth Circuit's decision was the latest in a string of setbacks for the Texas law, known as House Bill 2, which women's rights advocates have dubbed the "heartbeat bill" because it bans abortions after a fetal heartbeat can be detected.
The law bans abortions at about six weeks of pregnancy, before many women know they are pregnant. The Supreme Court has said states cannot ban abortion before viability, typically around 24 weeks of pregnancy.
The 5th Circuit's ruling on Tuesday came after its full court had reheard the case in an attempt to break a 5-5 tie.
Trump's nominee to replace Justice Antonin Scalia, who died in February 2016, blocked the lower-court ruling from taking effect while the Supreme Court considers the case.
Trump has appointed two Supreme Court justices, including Gorsuch.
In 2016, the Supreme Court struck down a Texas law that required doctors performing abortions to have hospital admitting privileges. The court said the law placed an "undue burden" on a woman's right to obtain an abortion.
The Texas law was also in part designed to make it more difficult for abortion providers to operate. Doctors who perform abortions must have admitting privileges at nearby hospitals in case of an emergency. The law also bans most abortions after 20 weeks of pregnancy and requires clinics to meet hospital-like standards for outpatient surgery.

The anniversary of the landings , 25 April , has since 1916 been recognised in Australia and New Zealand as Anzac Day , now one

of the most significant national occasions in both countries. The first formal commemorative observance of Anzac Day was in Sydney in 1916, and was followed by commemorative services in Melbourne and other parts of Australia and New Zealand. The service in Sydney was held on 25 April 1916, the first anniversary of the landings at Gallipoli. In 1917 the service was held on 30 April (the day of the landing) at the Sydney Town Hall, and in 1918 the service was held at the Royal Australian Naval Hospital. In 1919 the service was held at the Sydney Opera House. This was followed by services at other venues in Sydney. In 1923 the first national Anzac Day service was held in Canberra. From 1927 the service was held at the Australian War Memorial .
 Between 1914 and 1918 Australia had a population of just over five million people. Of these, 417,000 enlisted in the Australian Imperial Force (AIF), of whom 339,000 served overseas. The AIF enlisted 37,000 New Zealanders, of whom 16,000 served overseas. Some 60,000 diggers (as the AIF soldiers were known) were killed or died of wounds. Of the more than 300,000 Australians who served, about one in five was wounded.
 In the First World War and the Second World War , the Empire of Japan and the United States of America joined forces with the British Commonwealth. For Australians, however, the First World War was the first time they had fought and died to defend the British Empire. It was the first time they had been involved in a conflict in which their country was at war with another great power, the German Empire. It was the first time Australians had fought on foreign soil.
Anzac Day has been observed since 1916 and is one of Australia's most important national occasions. In the First World War , 60,000 Australians were killed and another 156,000 were wounded.
The First World War had a profound effect on the Australian nation, turning it from a distant outpost of the British Empire into a nation with a distinctive identity. Anzac Day, the commemoration of the landing at Gallipoli and of the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps (ANZAC) in general, is the most important national occasion in both Australia and New Zealand. In 1978 Anzac Day was declared a national public holiday in New Zealand.
Australians remember the Anzac Day landing at Gallipoli as the beginning of the nation. Anzac Day is commemorated in Australia and New Zealand on 25 April to honour those who served and died in war and on active service for their country.
Anzac Day commemorations began in Australia and New Zealand on 25 April 1916, the first anniversary of the landing of Australian and New Zealand troops at Gallipoli.
The Gallipoli landings in 1915 were the first major action of the First World War for Australia and New Zealand. The ANZAC forces suffered heavy casualties and the Gallipoli campaign failed. Nevertheless, the experience of the campaign became a defining moment for the newly independent nations.
The Gallipoli campaign is remembered in Australia and New Zealand on 25 April as Anzac Day .
