" Rosemary 's Baby " was mainly filmed on September 11 , 2007 , while Fisher 's scenes were filmed the next day on September 12

.
The main storyline of the film revolves around Rosemary Woodhouse ( Mia Farrow ), a young, pregnant woman who moves into a new apartment with her husband, Guy ( John Cassavetes ). The building's elderly neighbors, Roman and Minnie Castevet ( Ralph Bellamy and Angela Lansbury ), befriend the couple and invite them to a dinner party at their home. At the party, Rosemary meets a drugged-up woman who calls herself Laura ( Ann Sothern ). Rosemary and Guy suspect that Laura is not her real name, but are unable to get any information out of her.
After the party, Guy tells Rosemary that he had sex with Laura and they both get drunk. The next morning, Guy is missing, and Rosemary is told that he has gone to work. She realizes that Guy has hidden the fact that he is an actor from her.
The Castevets invite Rosemary and Guy to a wedding in Rome where they meet Dr. Sapirstein ( William Prince ), a Roman Catholic priest who tries to convince Rosemary to give birth to a child in the hospital. Guy is unable to convince Rosemary to go along with the doctor's plan because she is worried that the hospital's staff may harm her unborn child.
Back home, the Castevets suggest that Guy get a job as a stagehand at a local theater, and he tells Rosemary that he has done so. Guy and Rosemary begin to suspect that the Castevets are trying to control their unborn child, and they decide to leave their apartment.
In the meantime, Laura returns to Rosemary and tells her that she is not her real name. Rosemary tells Guy that she is pregnant and that she has been having nightmares about a monster that is trying to take her child. The Castevets try to dissuade Rosemary from leaving their apartment, and Guy is killed when Rosemary falls down the stairs. Rosemary then gives birth to a demonic child, and she is taken to a mental hospital, where she is told that she is suffering from postpartum psychosis.
In the final scene, Rosemary returns home, and she realizes that the monster is her husband, Guy. He tells her that he has been dead all along and that he is her child.
" Rosemary 's Baby " was nominated for nine Academy Awards, including Best Picture, Best Director, Best Actor, and Best Original Screenplay. It won three Oscars, including Best Actress for Farrow.
The film was also nominated for two Golden Globes, including Best Motion Picture - Drama and Best Actress - Drama for Farrow.

The Reds were the NL champions in 1961 , and with the addition of Sisler , Dave Hillman , and Moe Drabowsky to ensure stability

at short , second , and the bullpen , they were a strong favorite to repeat. Sisler returned to the field in 1962 after an injury the previous year had ended his 1961 season early. He also had a breakthrough year at the plate, leading the team in runs (106) and hits (182) and finishing second in doubles (32) and batting average (.322).
 The Reds had an easy time of it in the first round against the Phillies , taking all four games . The Dodgers and Giants split the first round games , with Los Angeles taking two at home and San Francisco winning two at home. The Reds were at home for the first three games , with the Dodgers visiting Crosley Field for the final two . The Reds won the first two games , and were defeated in the third and fourth. With the series tied at two games apiece , the stage was set for a potential deciding Game 5 .
 Game 5 was a pitching duel between Bob Purkey and Sandy Koufax , with the Dodgers getting the 2–1 decision. The Dodgers were able to do so by aggressively running on Purkey . The Giants made an all-out effort to beat the Reds in Game 1 , but were defeated 3–0. They won the next two games at home before losing the final two in Los Angeles . The Dodgers won the series , 4 games to 3.
 Los Angeles beat the Yankees in the 1963 World Series , winning 4 games to 3. The Reds finished in third place in the NL in 1963 , and failed to make the playoffs in 1964 and 1965 . They finished in third place again in 1966 , and were fourth in 1967 and 1968 .
The Reds had the first pick in the 1967 amateur draft, and Hank Aaron's son made his MLB debut for the Reds in 1970. Pete Rose , considered by many to be the greatest hitter in National League history, joined the team in 1968 and played for the Reds until 1984.

The noisy miner does not use a stereotyped courtship display ; displays can involve ' driving ' where the male jumps or flies a

metre or so in front of the female, ' chasing ' where the male chases the female, or ' diving ' where the male flies to the ground and rolls over. They are also known to carry food to their mate.
 Breeding males defend a territory against all intruding males and females, even those that are not their mates. The territory is often defended from the ground or from a branch, and the display of aggression is quite impressive. The male often dive-bombs the intruder, often with a scattering of droppings (usually yellow, from the crop).
 The courtship feeding may be necessary to build up the female's energy reserves for copulation, and they may be necessary for the male to attract a female. The noisy miner also feeds its young (for a while) and may be a major source of nutrition for its brood.
 Males defend their territories from within, and the display of aggression is quite impressive. They may also defend the territory as a pair.
 These birds prefer to nest in dense forest. They are common in the top of tall trees, and they often excavate a nest hole in a tree, occasionally using a cavity previously made by another species. The nest is 20 to 30 cm deep; the hole may be 10 cm wide and 20 cm deep. The nest is lined with soft material (such as grass or hair) and the clutch usually contains four eggs.
The noisy miner is socially monogamous, with a pair-bond lasting for life.
 This parrot is common to abundant in eastern and southeastern Australia, from the top of the Northern Territory to the coast of Victoria. It has also been introduced to other areas, including southwestern Western Australia.
 The noisy miner is considered a major pest in many parts of eastern Australia, in particular in parks and gardens. It is considered to be a major pest in urban areas, and is responsible for an estimated 90% of all bird damage to fruit trees.
The noisy miner often attacks the nest of other parrots and birds, including those of the Australian raven, the sulphur-crested cockatoo, the little corella, the white-plumed honeyeater, the red wattlebird and the eastern spinebill. It also eats insects and other invertebrates, and is an important disperser of seeds (although the extent to which it does this is debated).
The noisy miner is a medium-sized parrot, measuring 16–20 cm long. It is predominantly green, with a yellow forehead and crown, a red face, and yellow underparts. The female is slightly duller in colour than the male.
 The species was formerly known as the Australian ringneck. Its scientific name, _Manorina melanocephala_ , comes from the ancient Greek words _manos_ (hand or palm) and _ōron_ (crest), and the Latin words _melanos_ (black) and _cephala_ (head).
 The noisy miner was first collected by Captain James Cook in 1770, and first described by the French naturalist Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon, in 1780; the noisy miner was one of several birds he described from Cook's voyage.
 The noisy miner is said to have been first seen in the 1830s in Sydney, and is generally considered to have been introduced deliberately around that time. It is now widespread and endemic in at least some regions of southeastern Australia. It is common in the top of tall trees, and also excavates nest holes in trees.
The noisy miner is a common bird, with a total population estimated at 50 million individuals.

The building was inaugurated on 30 March 1991 , in the presence of Josip Manolić, the President of the Republic of Croatia , and the Mayor of Zagreb, Ivo Šušak.
The 750 m2 space is divided into two levels. The exhibition space is on the ground floor , with a 300 m2 space. The floor above is used for storage and conservation.

The renovation of the building was started in 1999 , with the support of the Ministry of Culture, and was finished in March 2001 .

The Museum of Contemporary Arts in Zagreb is a place of dialogue between artists and their audience, a place of exchange and communication. The museum organises workshops for children and young people, and also teachers and the general public, and hosts lectures, discussions, symposia, concerts and other events.
The Museum of Contemporary Arts has a collection of Croatian art of the 20th century . It organises and presents exhibitions, lectures, symposia and other events. It also supports contemporary art in Croatia by issuing a bi-annual publication, _Art and Culture_ , and organising a biennial of Croatian contemporary art.
The museum is open from Tuesday to Sunday from 10 am until 6 pm . Admission is free.

Sadleir notes how Walpole 's considerable income enabled him to indulge not only his love of art and of old books and manuscrip

st but also his love of travel. He was a leading figure in the Society of Dilettanti, founded by his friend Richard Payne Knight, and was a friend of Richard Payne Knight and John Sackville Tufton, Earl of Thanet, whom he accompanied to Italy.2 It was a love that had its roots in the Grand Tour, a common rite of passage for aspiring aristocrates in the eighteenth century. Walpole himself had been to Italy, and he was evidently shrewd enough not to dissipate too much of his inheritance on travel, but he was sufficiently adventurous to undertake a second, much larger tour of Europe and the Near East in the late 1740s.
The details of Walpole's travels are not well known, but there is no doubt that he was in Paris in the winter of 1748/49. It is probable that he was present when the Scottish Enlightenment was at its most cosmopolitan. David Hume, despite the objections of his father, was in Paris at the time, as were William Robertson, Adam Smith, John Home (the future author of Douglas), and William Smellie.22 It was in Paris that Walpole became acquainted with the Italian writer Goldoni, who had fled from Venice, where he had been incarcerated in the asylum for the insane. Walpole had a particular interest in 'mad men' and madness, and he was himself a collector of madmen's writings.
The extent to which Walpole was familiar with the work of David Hume has not been well documented. When he left England for the second time in 1790, he took with him two volumes of Hume's _History of England_ , and he seems to have been a reader of Hume's _Essays and Treatises on Several Subjects_ , although neither of these works were listed in his library catalogue. In 1796, when the _Edinburgh Review_ was founded, Walpole wrote to the editor, William Wilkie, to complain that the new journal was not giving Hume sufficient attention. He suggested a special article on Hume's life and works, but Wilkie told him that there was insufficient space to accommodate such an article in the current issue.26 In 1817, Walpole's biographer, Horace Walpole, wrote to John Gibson Lockhart, the editor of the _Quarterly Review_ , who had recently published the first volume of the _History of England_. Lockhart was keen to draw attention to the fact that his Hume was the first edition published in Great Britain, and he asked Horace Walpole whether he knew whether Hume had been acclaimed in France. Horace Walpole thought he did not. 'I think it very likely that the works of Hume have been very little known in France,' he wrote. He then proceeded to give a detailed account of Hume's visit to France in 1749, which he had been told about by a Frenchman, M. Héron, who had been present at the time. He was told that the author of the _Essays_ had been so irritated by the ill-treatment he had encountered at the hands of the English that he had become something of a hypochondriac. Horace Walpole was impressed by Hume's 'working hard' in France, but he did not, interestingly, see anything that might have been construed as literary: 'Hume was so much persecuted by the English that he was obliged to work hard to live and the works he produced in France were not of a literary nature.'28 Whether or not the works he produced in France were of a literary nature, it seems that Hume was not entirely neglected in France, and that he was at least known by Walpole during the 1790s.

《 日の丸劇場 》 , he began the new series in Kodansha's Monthly Afternoon magazine in 2012. This is the first series to be digitally published on Crunchyroll .
 The series is described as a "sports comedy" that follows the daily activities of a high school student named Hibari Katsushika as he trains to become a professional sumo wrestler.
A show was produced and aired in 2014.
A 12-episode anime television series adaptation by Studio Deen aired between October and December 2014. The series' opening theme is " Sake, Hana, Takara " ( 酒・花・宝 ) , performed by Tomohisa Yamashita and the ending theme is " Gotta Go Faster " ( ギターモード ) by Kana Nishino .
Hibari, a short and stocky boy, has always enjoyed sumo, and so he makes his way to the sumo gym. He is welcomed into the gym with open arms by the coach, and he begins his training. He is unable to do squats, and when he tries to do sit-ups, he ends up hitting his head against the wall. No matter how hard he tries, he is unable to bulk up no matter how hard he tries. He does not have the height to be a top-notch sumo wrestler, and he is not as skinny as a professional sumo wrestler either. He decides to try his hand at lightweight sumo, a type of sumo that is played with very lightweight wrestlers and only lasts for about 3 minutes. Hibari is told that the best way to train is to watch sumo matches on TV. At the same time, he is told to join the sumo club at school, where the other students are all very strong. He continues to try his best, but he can't seem to get stronger. He decides to take a day off from training and walks around the streets of Tokyo, and ends up at a hotel where he ends up being mistaken with a professional sumo wrestler. The professional wrestler tells him to go to the bathroom, but Hibari ends up getting lost in the toilets.
The professional wrestler's manager, Anri-san ( アンリさん ) , is frustrated because Hibari is unable to find the bathroom, and she ends up getting into a fight with the hotel owner. The owner ends up beating Hibari up, and Anri-san decides to take Hibari back to her apartment. Hibari ends up staying the night there, but is unable to wake up the next morning. After waking up, Hibari has lost all of his weight, and ends up being less than 50kg! Anri-san decides to take Hibari back to the gym, but ends up meeting the hot springs club manager, Karin. Karin is a boy-loving girl, and Anri-san becomes jealous of her. After meeting with Karin, Anri-san is unable to get Hibari back to the gym, and ends up making him a manager of her cosplay club. Hibari is forced to take the job, because he is unable to pay for the grand sum of 300 yen.
Hibari is put in charge of the club, and is unable to make any sense of the club rules. He ends up being unable to earn any money, and ends up being unable to pay for the club expenses. He is able to get the attention of another cosplay club, but ends up losing his first cosplay competition. Hibari ends up becoming depressed, but after taking a bath, he is told by Anri-san that he looks exactly like a sumo wrestler. After being told this, Hibari decides to go back to the sumo gym.
The series is published in English by Cambridge University Press . It is also published in German as Sumowrestler Hibari .

Torres started playing football as a goalkeeper , the position his brother played in . When he was seven years old , however ,

Torres' older brother was transferred to another team , and Torres switched to the forward position. Torres's father was a football player , and was captain of his team in the 1970s , and his father instilled in him a love of the game. Torres is also a member of the FIFA 100 .
Torres was included in the Spanish squad for the 2002 FIFA World Cup . During a training session at the base of the squad in Cologne , he was involved in a collision with German goalkeeper Oliver Kahn . Torres was knocked unconscious and was taken to hospital , where he received stitches to his head . In the same session , forwards Raúl and Ronaldo were injured . Torres made his World Cup debut in the opening match against Cameroon . At the age of 19 years and 31 days , he was the youngest player in the squad. He became the youngest player to score for Spain in a World Cup match , and was the youngest player to score in a World Cup quarterfinal match .
Torres scored his first goal for Spain in a 3–0 friendly win against Luxembourg on 26 March 2003 . He became the youngest player to score for Spain in a competitive match , and was also the youngest player to score in the qualifying stages of the European Championship . On 19 November 2003 , Torres scored his first international hat-trick in a 5–1 friendly win against Hungary . In the 2004 European Championship , Torres was the youngest player to play in the finals . He scored in the group stage match against Greece to become the youngest player to score in the European Championship . He also became the youngest player to score for Spain in two European Championship matches . Torres scored a total of three goals in the tournament .
In 2008 , Torres was picked in Vicente del Bosque's first squad for the European Championship . He scored in the 3–2 group stage win against Russia , which was his sixth goal in six European Championship appearances . Despite this , Spain failed to progress past the group stage.
After the World Cup in 2006 , Torres was expected to leave Liverpool for Real Madrid . However , he was sold to Chelsea on 31 July 2007 for £50 million . It was reported that he had agreed a £170,000-a-week contract with the club, which would make him the world's highest paid player . He scored 24 goals in his first season with Chelsea , which won him the Golden Boot as the league's top-scorer. This was the first time in the Premier League that a player had scored more than 20 goals in their first season . He also became the first player to score in the Premier League, FA Cup , League Cup and the UEFA Champions League in the same season .
In the 2009–10 season , he scored 22 goals in all competitions , including a brace against Wigan in the League Cup final . Torres was the Premier League's top goalscorer for the 2009–10 season with 24 goals . He was also voted Player of the Year in Spain.
Torres was a member of the Chelsea squad that won the 2010 FA Cup and the 2010 League Cup . Torres scored his first goal of the season in the second leg of the 2010 League Cup Final against Portsmouth on 27 February 2010 . He scored his first Premier League goal of the season on 12 March 2010 against Bolton Wanderers , and scored his first European goal of the season against Maribor in the UEFA Champions League on 16 March 2010.
On 26 March 2010 , Torres scored his first goals of the 2010–11 season in a 4–1 win over West Bromwich Albion . He scored the first goal of the return leg of the Champions League quarter-final against inter Milan on 7 April 2010 . Wheeler's excavations included a Roman fort at Verulamium and a Roman ditch at Silchester, as well as the Roman cities of Pompeii and Herculaneum .

The 2014 Atlantic hurricane season was an average season in terms of both the accumulated cyclone energy (ACE) and the number of tropical storms and hurricanes. The season officially began on June 1, 2014, and ended on November 30, 2014. The first tropical cyclone, Tropical Storm Arthur, developed on June 18 and the last, Hurricane Andy, dissipated on November 6. The first tropical depression, Tropical Depression One, formed on July 18, while the final one, Tropical Depression Twenty-Eight, dissipated on November 4.
The season was notably active in the northwestern Caribbean Sea, the Gulf of Mexico and in Central America, as eight tropical cyclones formed in those basins. In particular, five of the six tropical cyclones that formed in the Gulf of Mexico strengthened to hurricane status, including Hurricane Arthur, which was the earliest formation of a Category 1 hurricane on record in the basin. In addition, the formation of Hurricane Dolly early in the season resulted in heavy rainfall and flooding in the Yucatán Peninsula and Central America, causing two deaths in Mexico. Hurricane Edouard also caused heavy rainfall and flooding in Central America, killing eight people. Hurricane Humberto became the first storm of the season to make landfall in Mexico, striking the Yucatán Peninsula; it later caused heavy damage in Honduras, with ten deaths reported. Hurricane Isaias also brought heavy rainfall and flooding to Central America, causing six deaths in Nicaragua.
The season produced a total of twelve tropical storms, eight of which strengthened into hurricanes. It produced one major hurricane, with winds exceeding 111 mph (178 km/h). Two tropical cyclones made landfall along the Mexican coast, with both Humberto and Isaias making landfall on the Yucatán Peninsula. The season is considered above normal by the National Hurricane Center (NHC), as the average is twelve named storms, six hurricanes, and two major hurricanes. According to Phil Klotzbach of Colorado State University, there were six times in the past century where the season reached 10 tropical cyclones with at least one tropical cyclone making landfall in Mexico.
Cancellation of the season is based on a total of 140 years of data, with the season starting on June 1 and ending on November 30.
Eight tropical cyclones formed within the Caribbean Sea, the Atlantic, and the Gulf of Mexico. Five of these became hurricanes.
TD One was the first tropical depression of the season. It formed on July 18, 2014, after a tropical wave affected Hispaniola and Puerto Rico. The depression drifted northward and stalled over the waters between the Florida Keys and Cuba. It then entered the Gulf of Mexico and strengthened into a tropical storm. The storm made landfall on July 20 in central Florida, near the town of Hernando Beach. It produced wind gusts of 50 mph (80 km/h) and rainfall of up to 13.1 in (330 mm), resulting in 24,000 homes being without power. Because of the storm, the Red Cross had to cancel 100 blood drives and 45 Red Cross centers were closed due to flooding.
Hurricane Arthur formed on July 1, as a tropical wave moved into the central Caribbean Sea. The wave organized into a tropical depression on July 3, which then strengthened into a tropical storm on the next day. Arthur then gradually intensified, reaching its peak intensity with 105 mph (165 km/h) and a minimum pressure of 969 mbar (28.6 inHg). Arthur made landfall just north of Cape Hatteras, North Carolina with 80 mph (130 km/h) and a minimum pressure of 961 mbar (28.4 inHg). The storm then moved inland and weakened, dissipating on July 5. The storm caused eighteen tornadoes, most of which occurred in North Carolina. In total, the storm produced $200 million in damage.

'satirical novel' (p. 18). The same is true of Clive James's review , where he describes it as a 'satire' (p. 18). In an interview she did with the BBC , Lessing said The Good Terrorist was 'a satire on the terrorists' (Lessing, 'Writers Meet . . .'). These designations are all misleading, in the sense that they suggest that The Good Terrorist is a parody of terrorism. It is not. To call it a satire is to misunderstand what a satire is.
The term satire comes from the Latin word saturus, meaning 'sated'. A satire is a work of fiction, often a poem or play, that is a critical, sometimes mocking, analysis of the failings of an individual or a group of people. In a satire, the author attacks what he or she considers to be the failings of a person or group of people. The author exaggerates the failings in order to make his or her point more strongly. For example, the satirical poem 'The Walrus and the Carpenter', by Lewis Carroll , attacks Victorian society for being foolish and self-indulgent, with particular reference to the way in which the upper classes, the rich, eat too much and then complain about their overweight. In this poem, the characters are exaggerations of human foibles in order to make the poet's point.
A satire ridicules its subject. That is the difference between a satire and a parody. The Good Terrorist is a parody of terrorism. A parody makes fun of a person or group of people by imitating their behaviour or mannerisms. For example, the television programme 'Monty Python's Flying Circus' was a parody of the serious television programmes of the 1960s. It was a comedic imitation of the BBC's serious programming. The Good Terrorist is a parody of terrorism. It is not a satire.
A satire points up the flaws in the object of its ridicule. In the case of The Good Terrorist, Lessing is pointing up the flaws in terrorism. In the book, the main character, a young man called Riad, becomes involved with a group of terrorists. He is persuaded to join them and to take part in a terrorist act. He believes that they are fighting for a just cause, to free the Palestinians from Israeli rule, but he soon realizes that the terrorists are self-serving. The group is manipulating the situation to suit themselves, and they are cruel and ruthless in their treatment of the Palestinians. Riad eventually decides to leave the group. The book ends with his death.
In a satire, the author is usually pointing out the faults of the hero or heroine. In The Good Terrorist, the author is pointing out the faults of the terrorists. It is not a satire.
This is the first of several parodies by Lessing of the terrorists, and it is, perhaps, the best.

After the end of the war in April , Atlanta was decommissioned in Philadelphia on 21 June 1865 and placed in reserve at League

Island , New York .
On 15 November 1869 , in compliance with the Third Naval Act , Atlanta was sold to C. W. Folsom , who renamed her Comet .
Secretary of the Navy Gideon Welles reported to Congress on 20 December 1869 that Comet had been sold to Folsom for $68,250, which was less than the contract price of $80,000.
The vessel was transferred to New York and was delivered to Folsom on 6 January 1870.
On 21 January 1870, Comet was chartered to John C. Stannard , who commissioned her as a training ship for his new company.
On 18 April 1870, she was designated as a training ship for the US Navy .
On 8 July 1871, she was transferred to the US Navy for conversion to a receiving ship at the Naval Yard at New York.
Comet underwent a three-year refit, and was recommissioned at New York on 20 April 1874 under the command of Capt. John H. Stevens.
Personnel aboard the ship included two midshipmen and 27 men.
The ship's force included two petty officers, six seamen, and 16 landsmen, and she had a crew of 39 men.
The ship was assigned to the Receiving Ship Division of the United States Naval Academy at Annapolis, Maryland .
On 1 September 1875, she was ordered to Annapolis, Maryland, for duty as a receiving ship and training ship in the United States Naval Academy at Annapolis, Maryland, and she remained there until 1883.
On 30 March 1883, she was reclassified as a receiving ship and in commission at the Naval Academy, in Annapolis, Maryland.
On 14 May 1883, Comet underwent conversion to a receiving ship at the Washington Navy Yard in Washington, D.C. and was recommissioned on 20 August 1883 for service as a receiving ship at the Naval Academy, and she continued to serve in that capacity until 1893.
On 14 June 1893, Comet was placed out of commission at the Naval Academy and sold on 19 July 1893 to M. W. Chapman.
The ship served as a training ship for the United States Lifesaving Service.
In 1902, the ship was sold to G.W. Porter .
After 22 years of service, the vessel was sold in 1902 to the U.S. Life-Saving Service for use as a training vessel.
At some point in the 1900s, she was sold to the state of New Jersey as a training ship.
In 1906, the ship was purchased by the state of New Jersey and renamed Mermaid .
She was sunk as an artificial reef in 1991.
On 17 July 1991, Comet was designated as an artificial reef off the coast of Seaside Park, New Jersey .
The ship was placed on the bottom of the ocean off of Seaside Park, New Jersey, in 1991 as an artificial reef .
After the ship was sunk, divers could dive to the bottom of the ocean to discover the remains of Comet.
Since 30 November 1991, the wreck of Comet rests in 100 feet (30 m) of water, 3.5 miles (5.6 km) off the coast of Seaside Park, New Jersey, in 10 fathoms of water.
The ship is now a popular dive site for divers, and the ship's remains are protected by the New Jersey Artificial Reef Program .
The ship is listed on the National Register of Historic Places .

## History

### Royal Navy service

HMS Hostile was laid down on 27 February 1935 by Scotts Shipbuilding & Engineering Company at Greenock , Scotland and launched on 24 May 1935. She was commissioned on 28 October 1936 under the command of Lieutenant Commander G. C. F. Maitland and was assigned to the 1st Destroyer Flotilla of the Home Fleet. She was used on trials as well as training.

### Second World War

During the Second World War Hostile was part of the 3rd Destroyer Flotilla in the Dover Patrol operating in the English Channel. She took part in the Dunkirk evacuation in May 1940. The ship was part of the Harwich Force under the command of Rear Admiral John Tovey.

In 1941 Captain Eric G. N. Urie took command of Hostile and she was appointed flagship of the 3rd Destroyer Flotilla. She was part of the British squadron that intercepted the German battleship Scharnhorst in the North Atlantic on 26 December 1943 , during which the ship suffered bomb damage.

Captain John Ramsay took over command of Hostile from Urie on 11 March 1944 and she was part of the Home Fleet when she was damaged by a mine on 12 March 1944 in the Cromarty Firth.

Hostile was placed in reserve in 1945 and was sold to be broken up for scrap on 27 May 1946 . She was scrapped by Ward and Goldie at Beverley , Yorkshire  .

The International Olympic Committee ( IOC ) is an organisation based in Lausanne, Switzerland, created by Pierre de Coubertin and Demetrius Vikelas on 23 June 1894. Its mission is to promote Olympism throughout the world and to preserve Olympism in its Olympic form.
The IOC organises the modern Olympic Games, and also works to strengthen the Olympic Movement. The IOC is funded primarily through television rights sales, marketing partnerships, sponsorship, and licensing agreements. In the lead-up to the 2020 Summer Olympics, the IOC had revenues of over US$1 billion. Its president is Thomas Bach.
IOC members or IOC delegates are elected by the 140-member IOC Session, in which each National Olympic Committee ( NOC) has one vote. Each IOC member represents approximately 25 million people on average. The IOC Session meets once every year, with additional meetings as required. The IOC has a permanent headquarters at the IOC House in Lausanne, Switzerland.
The IOC is the direct successor of the International Olympic Committee for Amateur Sports (French: Comité International Olympique d'Amateur Sport), which was founded on 23 June 1894. It was renamed on 24 July 1905 to its present name.

Rio de Janeiro (português brasileiro) ou Rio de Janeiro (português europeu) (About this sound listen (help·info)) is the second-most populous municipality in Brazil and the sixth-most populous in the Americas. The city's name was given by the Portuguese to mean "January River," an allusion to the month of their first arrival (in January 1502) in the area which at the time is called Grão-Pará, in Portuguese meaning Great December. It is located in the southeastern part of the Brazilian coast on Guanabara (a few kilometres inland from the Atlantic Ocean) Bay. It is the capital of the State of Rio de Janeiro, and the center of the metropolitan area of Rio de Janeiro, the second largest metropolitan area and third largest urban agglomeration in the Americas.
The city was the host of the 2016 Summer Olympics, and the 2016 Summer Paralympics.
Rio de Janeiro ranks 30th in the 2014 Innovation Cities Index, making it one of the 30 most innovative cities in the world. It was also ranked the third-most-livable city in Brazil.

Deadly Class is an American comic book series created by Rick Remender (writer) and Wes Craig (artist), published by Image Comics. The series is set in 1987 and follows the story of a disillusioned teenager recruited into a covert assassination academy.
The first issue of the series was published in January 2014. It received a positive reception and was optioned for adaptation by Sony Pictures.
In 1987, a group of students, known as the "kids", are recruited by a secret society, known as Kings Dominion, to attend King's Dominion, an elite assassination academy. The students are trained in various martial arts and combat techniques, and are told that they will be given their first mission upon graduation.
The series follows the story of one of the students, Marcus Lopez, a disillusioned teenager who is recruited into the academy. Marcus is a skateboarder who has been expelled from his previous school and is struggling to find his place in the world. He is taken under the wing of Saya Kuroki, a Japanese student who has been attending the academy for several years.
As the series progresses, Marcus becomes increasingly involved in the world of assassination and falls in love with a fellow student, Maria Salazar, who is also training to become an assassin. However, Marcus begins to question the morality of the work he is doing and starts to rebel against the system.
The series also follows the story of Saya Kuroki, who has been attending the academy for several years and is considered to be one of the best students. She is a skilled assassin and has been raised to believe that her work is justified. However, she begins to question her own beliefs and starts to rebel against the system.
The series also features several other characters, including the headmaster of the academy, the mysterious Mr. Miyagi, and the rival students, who are all training to become assassins.
The series is set in the late 1980s, and the characters are dressed in the fashion of the era. The artwork is gritty and realistic, and the storyline is dark and violent.
The series received a positive reception from critics, who praised the artwork, the storyline, and the character development. It has been described as "a new take on the superhero genre", and "a mix of John Wick and The Breakfast Club".

Translocation of noisy miners is unlikely to be a solution to their overabundance in remnant habitats . In a Victorian study wh

ipscarers (permanent exclosures) were much more effective at reducing bird populations than were translocation .
Our analysis of the factors affecting the success of translocation and whipscarering suggests that the success of these methods is highly dependent on the way they are implemented in practice. We believe that the factors affecting translocation are inter-related, rather than being independent of one another, and that differences in their implementation between projects lead to the observed variation in their success rates.
Therefore, future studies of translocations and restoration plantings should include rigorous documentation of the methods used and consider whether these methods are being implemented as intended, as a first step towards establishing best practice for each method.

The series was filmed and recorded on a scale large enough to be viewed in cinemas, and also broadcast on television. The Tracy brothers' technologically advanced headquarters, Thunderbird 1 through Thunderbird 5 , are monitored from a nearby island. From this location, the Tracy brothers and their colleague Lady Penelope and her butler, Parker, coordinate their rescue missions.
The series featured many of Gerry Anderson's signature  live-action model sequences  with special effects by Derek Meddings. Some episodes have been lost, and only a few episodes survive in their entirety. The series was followed by the 1966 feature film Thunderbirds Are Go .
Thunderbirds is set in the 2060s. The world has become more technologically advanced, resulting in a greater dependence on traveling by air. In the series, the world's transportation is controlled by a multinational organisation called International Rescue. The organisation employs the Tracy brothers, each piloting one of the organization's vast fleet of Thunderbird craft, and based in an underwater headquarters, International Rescue Island.
The organisation is led by ex-astronaut Jeff Tracy, under the supervision of Lady Penelope Creighton-Ward and her butler, Parker. International Rescue frequently rescues people who are in danger after disasters in the world, including those caused by the organisation itself.
The set of Thunderbirds is in the studio of Century 21 Productions, where it is known as the Thunderbirds/Space: 1999 set. The set is primarily used for the production of the 1999 television series Space: 1999.
The set is 80 feet (24 m) long by 40 feet (12 m) wide and 30 feet (9.1 m) high. The landing bays of the Thunderbird craft are 30 feet (9.1 m) wide and 15 feet (4.6 m) high with the walls of the bay being 5 feet (1.5 m) thick. Along the back wall of the set are the two 18 ft (5.5 m) high transmitter towers and one 7 ft (2.1 m) high and the 40 ft (12 m) high control tower. The control tower has a 12 ft (3.7 m) diameter computer disc operating room and three 10 ft (3 m) diameter computer disc rooms.
The interior of the control tower consists of a 6 ft (1.8 m) diameter lounge area and four 4 ft (1.2 m) diameter computer disc rooms. For the exterior of the control tower, the 30 ft (9.1 m) high walls of the first floor and the 16 ft (4.9 m) high walls of the second floor are actually the ceiling of the 26 ft (7.9 m) high first floor. The control tower's interior is 26 ft (7.9 m) high and 20 ft (6.1 m) wide.
The Thunderbirds series was created by Gerry Anderson and Sylvia Anderson. It was produced by the Andersons and Reg Hill, and was distributed by Lew Grade's ITC Entertainment.
The series followed a similar format to the Anderson shows which preceded it, including the use of marionettes and supermarionation, live actors, and models. As early as March 1911 , Madero 's representatives met in New York with Díaz 's finance minister , José Yves Limantour , and th

irteen businessmen to negotiate the terms for Madero's inauguration: the two principal points of contention were Madero's demand to have his own cabinet and his insistence that Díaz agree to be barred from running for reelection. After this meeting Limantour described the negotiations as "fruitless." On May 16, Madero issued his Plan de San Luis , declaring his intention to run for president himself. García Barragán , who was in New York at the time, wrote to Madero warning against an independent candidacy, and Madero's brother Pedro also opposed such a move, but Madero insisted that he run. Díaz was so sure that Madero would not carry out his threat that he wasted no time planning for his reelection, and even in May it looked as if San Luis Potosí was going to be the scene of a "Madero-Díaz" showdown.
In the end, however, Madero backed away from his intention to run, and the negotiations resumed in June. Díaz had already declared himself a candidate on May 24, and the two sides were able to come to a compromise. Díaz agreed to accept the results of the election and to renounce the presidency if he lost, and Madero promised to accept Díaz's cabinet appointments. The final agreement was signed on July 21, and the full text was released to the public on July 25. Under its terms Díaz would remain in office until the end of his term in 1916, when he would be succeeded by Madero, who would then serve until 1920. The Díaz regime would be responsible for the electoral process in the 1912 elections, and the Díaz regime would not be permitted to interfere in the election of the 1913 local and state governments in the republic.
 The 1912 elections took place on March 10. The official results gave Díaz 86 percent of the votes cast, and Díaz's closest rival, Adolfo de la Huerta, garnered only 97,000 votes, far less than the 100,000 or more he had expected to get in a three-way race. As was to be expected, there were no problematic regions, and the Díaz regime used the government press to tout the results. The opposition also had no trouble obtaining the results, and the Díaz regime's refusal to make the tally sheets available to the opposition was well reported in the opposition press.
 There were, in fact, some in the Díaz regime who were concerned about the lack of a clear outcome. On the same day that the vote totals were released, the U.S. ambassador to Mexico, Henry Lane Wilson, told the president, Porfirio Díaz, that he was "greatly disturbed" about the election and that he expected the opposition to be "disconcerted" by it, to which Díaz responded that he was confident that the opposition would not act against the results, although a few days later Díaz expressed concern that the opposition might provoke violence.
The opposition expressed its discontent by holding a large demonstration in Mexico City on March 22. They were protesting the decision to allow Díaz to run for reelection, and they were also protesting the lack of a clear outcome in the election. The demonstration was organized and led by Francisco I. Madero, but it was peaceful and it did not challenge the election, although the Díaz regime saw it as an attack on the government. The press on both sides expressed concern that the Díaz regime would use the demonstration as a pretext to crack down on the opposition.
In fact, the Díaz regime did crack down on the opposition, although it was unclear whether the decision to crack down had been made before or after the demonstration. The crackdown took the form of a series of raids on opposition newspapers and opposition meeting places, and the government arrested some prominent opposition figures. One of the opposition newspapers, _La Libertad_ , was closed, and another, _La Verdad_ , was suspended. The government also initiated legal proceedings against the opposition newspapers, and on April 16 the government charged the editors of _El Porvenir_ with libel for a poem that they had published in the newspaper.
The government's crackdown on the opposition was clearly in response to the opposition's demonstration, but the results of the elections were clearly a factor as well. The Díaz regime was determined to cling to power, and it was not going to allow a serious challenge from the opposition.

In a 1946 paper published in the Folklore journal , John H. Evans recorded the existence of a local folk belief that a battle w

aged in the area of Salisbury was won by the Saxons by the simple expedient of placing a rooster on the side of the hill occupied by the Danes and letting it crow. The first word of the battle cry, "Cocka," was enough to send the Danes into retreat.
A similar story was reported by George F. Blackburn in 1925 in his book _Salisbury: A Pictorial Guide to the City of Salisbury and the History of Salisbury_. The author states that the tradition is "a little vague" but the "legend" is that "the Danes were frightened away when a cock crowed."
Some years earlier, in 1918, the _Salisbury Times_ published a letter from a local resident, George Wood, who wrote:
I have been told that the Danes were frightened of a cock, and that the people of Salisbury found out how to frighten them away. A cock was kept in a box, and when the fight was going on, the box was taken up the hill, and, when the Dane saw the cock, he was so frightened that he ran away.
While this story is a localized one, it is interesting in that it comes at the end of the twelfth century. This is the time when cock fighting – a sport that was popular throughout the Dark Ages – was banned in England. It is also interesting that the story should involve the Danes in particular, for this was the era when the Danes launched their raids on England and the period of the "Dark Ages" when towns, villages and cities were systematically ravaged.
In 1926, a newspaper report from the _Bath Times_ was published in the _Salisbury Times_. The reporter, Herbert G. Morgan, wrote:
A tradition that dates from the time of the Danes, when they were defeated in one of the many wars with the Saxons for the possession of England, has been handed down from generation to generation in the family of Mr. James Hipwell of New Road.
The tradition says that the Saxons, with the assistance of a cock, defeated the Danes, who were a mighty army of thirty thousand, on a hill in the neighborhood of Salisbury.
The Danes had possession of the hill and were determined not to give it up, and they were looking forward to a long siege and plenty of fighting; but the Saxons, with the aid of the cock, placed him in a cage on the hill and, when the Danes found out what was happening to them, they ran away in the greatest haste and joined their army of thirty thousand men – "to the other side."
The Times report continues by stating that the cock was killed because it had become too familiar to the Danes and they would have been able to recognize it had it been released.
The tradition is, however, not only found in Salisbury. In Wiltshire, there is a tradition which differs in significant details but tells of how the Danes were enchanted by the clucking of a hedgehog.

the Millennium Park. The 11-year-old fountain has been expanded in 2019 to an additional 16,000 square feet (1,500 m 2 ) of space. The fountain was closed in September 2015 for renovation. Its reopening was delayed several times, and the fountain reopened on May 26, 2018.
The fountain is divided into two parts: a waterfall and a reflecting pool. The waterfall is a 50-foot (15 m) tall, four-sided glass and steel tapestry that has two sets of water jets that shoot water upwards. The water jets are illuminated from behind, and are visible from the street side. They shoot water up to the top of the fountain, where it cascades down the front of the waterfall. The water jets shoot water in a variety of patterns, including a horizontal square, a diagonal diamond, a vertical rectangle, and a cross. The water jets are 20 feet (6.1 m) wide at the base and 10 feet (3.0 m) wide at the top. The reflecting pool is located in front of the waterfall and has a 15-foot (4.6 m) high wall on its left side and behind that is a 20-foot (6.1 m) high wall on the right side. The reflecting pool is capable of holding 100,000 U.S. gallons (40,000 L) of water.
The waterfall is illuminated at night, with the lights shining on it from the street side. The fountain is also illuminated from behind, with the lights shining on the water jets from the inside of the fountain. The reflecting pool is illuminated at night, the lights shining through the water.
Sound artist Steve Reich created a sound composition for the fountain. The composition, called "Double Sextet", is played in the reflecting pool. Reich's composition is not a continuous composition, but rather consists of a series of loops that play in succession.  The loops are played for five to six minutes, then repeated. The loops alternate between two different compositions; one composition consists of sounds that are similar to the sounds made by the water jets, and the other composition consists of sounds that are similar to the sounds made by the water jets that are echoed by the reflecting pool. Reich's composition was first played in 2008, and is played every day between 3:00 p.m. and 9:00 p.m.

After the Second World War , aircraft were increasingly used for passenger transport.
The first aircraft carried a pilot and a passenger . The crew member acted as navigator and flight engineer . The flights were short, usually lasting less than 2 hours . In 1927, the first scheduled services were introduced . The first airline to make a profit was Imperial Airways in 1929 .
The first flights were made in the 1910s by the Wright brothers , who piloted a small plane . The first flight of a heavier-than-air aircraft by a woman is attributed to Raymonde de Laroche. In 1926, the first scheduled airline was established in the UK, Aircraft Transport and Travel ( A.T.T. ).
By the 1940s, there were 20,000 scheduled departures each day.  After World War II, jet aircraft were introduced. The Boeing 707 and the Douglas DC-8 were the first aircraft to enable jet service to become profitable.
In the 1970s, the introduction of the Boeing 747 enabled the first regular long-haul flights to be introduced. Other advances in aircraft design, such as the supersonic Concorde, were developed for passenger service.
Regulations in the UK aim to ensure the safety of passengers and crew.  The Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) is the UK's aviation regulator.  The European Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) regulates aircraft design and manufacturing in the European Union .
Globally, airlines are regulated by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO).  In the UK, the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) is the government body responsible for regulating airline safety.  The Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) investigates any accidents or incidents involving aircraft.
Airports are licensed by the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) .  London Heathrow Airport and London Gatwick Airport are the busiest in the UK, handling 73.4 million passengers in 2017.  London Gatwick Airport is the second busiest airport in the UK and the busiest single-runway airport in the world.
The airline industry is one of the world's largest industries.  It carried about 3.5 billion passengers in 2016 and generated revenue of over $800 billion .  In 2017, there were 6.9 million commercial aircraft flights .  The airline industry is dominated by a few large companies.
The largest airline in the world by scheduled revenue passenger-kilometers flown is American Airlines .  The largest airline in the world by total number of passengers carried is the China Southern Airlines, a state-owned airline.
Airlines for America (A4A), formerly known as the Air Transport Association (ATA), is an airline industry trade association based in Washington, D.C. It is the largest industry association in the United States. Its members include 15 of the largest U.S.-based airlines  and their affiliates. It advocates on behalf of its members on legislative and regulatory issues while providing a forum for its members to share ideas and discuss issues.
Airlines in the United States are regulated by the Federal Aviation Administration ( FA A) . The FAA is responsible for the safety of civil aviation, including setting minimum training, licensing, and operational standards for all participants. The airlines are also subject to a variety of other federal regulations.
The airline industry is a highly competitive industry. The airline business is dominated by a few large companies. The " Big Four " airlines in the United States are American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, United Airlines, and Southwest Airlines .

agnar Søderlind , and David C. Sames . Creutz provided a supply of stacks of _The_ _Freeman_ and _The_ _American_ _Scholar_ , the two publications he had founded in New York . He also provided a gift of $10,000 to support the Wisconsin literary series.
Creutz's financial support extended to the university library, which he had renovated and enlarged in 1928. He had also provided funds to build a library in the new English building, which was named the Creutz Memorial Library. He frequently contributed to the salaries of librarians.

Creutz was a member of the First Congregational Church in Madison , and served as president of the board of trustees. He was a member of the State Historical Society of Wisconsin , and president of the Wisconsin Club of New York. He was a member of the Wisconsin State Historical Society and of the Wisconsin Club of Chicago. He was a member of Lambda Chi Alpha , a fraternity.
Creutz was married on June 23, 1925, to Elizabeth McLean of Madison . They had no children. He died on December 15, 1931, in Madison.
Creutz's papers are in the Wisconsin Historical Society Archives, Madison.

Two secular small chests with carved whalebone panels and metal fittings illustrate some aspects of the Scottish arts . The Egl

inton chest (Fig. 1) is made of oak and dates from the late sixteenth century. It is of a superficially simple form, with a rectangular body and a hinged lid. The chest is carved with floral motifs in low relief, and the carving is emphasised by the use of darker wood for the ground pattern. Scottish chests have a tradition of carved panels, but the convention is that these would be carved only on the exterior surfaces.
The panel on the lid of the Eglinton chest is monochrome; the whalebone of the panel has been cut away to reveal the darker oak ground. The panel has a central motif of a peacock surrounded by a border of complex foliage and scrolling vine-like elements, which are repeated on the lid of the chest. The panel is further elaborated by carving in low relief, which includes the foliage and vine-like elements, and by a series of incisions of small dots in the ground. The use of whalebone in the panel draws attention to the technique of carving, and the repetition of the central motif in the border emphasises the importance of the central image. This combination of carving and low relief, and of conventional and unusual techniques, is characteristic of Scottish carving of the late sixteenth century.
The other example is an eighteenth-century chest made for the Duke of Argyll. It has a rectangular body with a hinged lid, and is made of oak (Fig. 2). The chest is carved with a central panel of whalebone in low relief. The whalebone is divided into sections by a series of incisions, across which the artist has marked the sections by cutting out a diamond pattern. The upper section is carved with a stylised peacock, while the lower section is decorated with an elaborate foliage motif. On either side of the panel are slender columns of entwined foliage, with a figure in each. The use of entwined foliage and peacocks is characteristic of Scottish carving of the early seventeenth century. The carving on this chest is detailed to a level of refinement unusual for the period, and the whalebone panel is a particularly elegant use of the material.
The use of whalebone in carved panels is not unique to Scotland. It appears in carved chests of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries in England, Holland and France. The carved chests of the sixteenth century have a similar style of decoration to those of Scotland, but are not as refined. For example, the carved chest from the collection of the Duke of Buccleuch (Fig. 3) has a rectangular body with a hinged lid. The exterior carving is of foliage and scrolling, and the use of whalebone is limited to a single panel of vine-like elements in low relief above the foliage. The use of whalebone is not as extensive as in the Scottish examples, and the carving is less refined.
The Dutch chest in the Victoria and Albert Museum (Fig. 4) has a rectangular body and a hinged lid, and is carved with floral motifs, including stylised peacocks. The use of whalebone is limited to a single panel, in which a series of incisions indicates the outline of the designs. The use of whalebone and the decoration of the chest are less elaborate than in the Scottish examples, and the carving is not as refined.
The carved chest in the Musée de l'Homme in Paris (Fig. 5) is made of oak and dates from the late seventeenth century. It has a rectangular body and a hinged lid. The use of whalebone is limited to a single panel, and the carving is less refined than in the Scottish examples.

Addressing the sediment problem in the Mississippi River system has been a focus of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) for more than 60 years. @-@ The USACE is responsible for assisting in the evaluation, planning, and construction of the Mississippi River system for navigation and flood control. @-@ In 1965, Congress authorized the USACE to study the feasibility of dredging the lower Mississippi River. @-@ The reports of the first two studies, the 1967 Feasibility Report on the Lower Mississippi River and the 1971 Study on the Mississippi River Dredge Material Disposal Problem, recommended that dredging of the lower Mississippi River should be combined with an overall ecosystem restoration program. @-@ The 1971 report also recommended that a comprehensive study be conducted to assess the feasibility of projects and identify a long-term program to restore the Mississippi River system. @-@ The resulting 1975 Feasibility Report for Comprehensive Restoration of the Mississippi River System (Feasibility Study) recommended a two-phase program. Phase I consisted of dredging and disposing of sediment in a manner that maintained navigation and prevented flooding while improving water quality and habitat. @-@ Phase II consisted of a rehabilitation program to restore sediment transport into the Gulf of Mexico. @-@ The Feasibility Study was the first comprehensive study to address the entire Mississippi River system, including the tributaries. @-@ After the Feasibility Study was completed, Congress approved the Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Program, which included the USACE's Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan, in 1992. @-@ The Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan recommended a program to address sediment deposition in the Ten Thousand Islands, the Florida Keys, and the Everglades estuaries. @-@ The 1996 National Water Quality Initiative and the 1998 Water Resources Development Act directed the USACE to study the feasibility of ecosystem restoration projects throughout the Mississippi River system under the authority of Section 701 of the Water Resources Development Act of 1986. @-@ The USACE conducted an additional feasibility study, the 2000 Feasibility Report for Comprehensive Ecosystem Restoration of the Mississippi River System (2000 Feasibility Study), which was completed in 2000. The 2000 Feasibility Study recommended a program to address sediment deposition in the Gulf of Mexico and the continued operation and maintenance of existing sedimentation control structures. @-@ The 2000 Feasibility Study recommended the use of existing projects and identified 123 projects that could be used to implement the program. @-@ The program would require $20.6 billion to address a projected cost of $13.2 billion to restore sediment transport. @-@ In addition, the program would require $7.4 billion to address a projected cost of $4.2 billion to operate and maintain existing projects. @-@ The 2000 Feasibility Study recommended that the program be implemented over periods ranging from 19 years to 33 years. @-@ The USACE revised the program and its costs in 2004 and 2007 in response to new information and changes in the funding environment. @-@ The 2007 Feasibility Study was completed in 2008 and recommended that the program be implemented over 14 years. @-@ The total cost of the program was estimated to be $11.3 billion to address a projected cost of $6.1 billion to restore sediment transport and $5.1 billion to operate and maintain existing projects. @-@ The 2007 Feasibility Study recommended that the program be implemented in phases. Electronic Arts rebranded Flight Combat as Jane 's Attack Squadron , to fit with the Jane 's Information Group license that the

game was based upon at the time. The game received a sequel two years later, Jane's Attack Squadron 2 .

## Gameplay

The game is a flight simulator, which allows the player to pilot a variety of fighter jets and attack helicopters. The player can fly solo or cooperatively, and can choose to fly the United States Navy's F-14 Tomcat, the British Royal Navy's Sea Harrier, the French Navy's Super Étendard, or the Japanese Navy's Mitsubishi F-1. The player will be tasked with completing various missions, including air-to-air combat, bombing runs, and escorting ground forces.

## Plot

During the height of the Cold War, the Soviet Navy has deployed a missile platform off the coast of Spain. NATO has launched a strike force to destroy the Soviet platform, but the missile launches before the strike force can reach its target, destroying several NATO warships. In response, NATO launches a retaliatory strike on the Soviet platform. The Soviet Navy is unable to defend the platform, and it is destroyed. The Soviet Union wastes no time in launching a nuclear strike on NATO, but the missile is intercepted by a NATO fighter. The Soviet Union declares war on the United States, and World War III is underway.

The effects of antimony and its compounds on human and environmental health differ widely . The massive antimony metal does not

occur in nature but is a by-product of mining and smelting of antimony-bearing minerals . Antimony compounds, particularly antimony trioxide, are used in the production of flame retardants, pigments, semiconductor materials, and pharmaceuticals . Antimony metal and its compounds are frequently found in indoor air during smoldering house fires. Antimony trioxide is found in consumer products such as paints, plastics, and pesticides as well as in toys and cosmetics . Antimony trioxide is typically used in antimony-containing flame retardants . Major routes of human exposure to antimony are via inhalation and dermal contact [8,9].
 Inhalation exposure to antimony trioxide has been associated with pulmonary effects and hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HP), and dermal exposure has been associated with skin irritation, allergic contact dermatitis, and photosensitivity [10–14].
 Antimony trioxide and other antimony compounds have been found in the air near smelting operations and in soils at disposal areas . Antimony trioxide has been found in indoor air during smoldering house fires . A study of the levels of antimony in air, dust, and soil in antimony-containing flame-retardant-treated upholstered furniture, carpets, and floor coverings found that antimony was present in all three environments .
 Antimony trioxide is a known human carcinogen . Increased rates of lung cancer and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease have been reported in populations exposed to antimony trioxide . Data from a prospective study of 8939 Chinese cadmium-smelter workers showed that the risk of lung cancer increased with increasing cumulative exposure to antimony . Increased rates of non-Hodgkin's lymphoma have been reported in populations exposed to antimony trioxide .
 Antimony trioxide is a reproductive and developmental toxicant in animal studies . Antimony trioxide has been shown to disrupt thyroid hormone and sex hormone levels in laboratory animals .
 Antimony trioxide is a known mutagen in tests with bacteria and mouse lymphoma cells, and it is a known tumor promoter .
 Antimony trioxide is in wide use in many consumer products, and its use in such products is increasing . The European Union has banned antimony trioxide in some products, and the United States Environmental Protection Agency has proposed a ban on antimony trioxide in children's pajamas .
 In 2007, the California Environmental Protection Agency Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment (OEHHA) received a petition requesting that antimony trioxide be listed under the Safe Drinking Water and Toxic Enforcement Act of 1986 (Proposition 65)  because it is a chemical known to cause cancer. OEHHA had previously determined that antimony trioxide was not a reproductive toxicant and therefore did not require listing under Proposition 65.
 In the present study, we reviewed the toxicity of antimony trioxide, including data on its effects on human health and on the environment. For this review, we searched PubMed, the ToxLine database, the ToxRef database, and the Toxline Toxics Review database. We also searched the Internet for unpublished information. We obtained additional data by contacting the technical information section of the Antimony Industry Council (Washington, D.C.). In addition, we reviewed all relevant information in the OEHHA files.

Finkelstein has written of his Jewish parents ' experiences during World War II . His mother , Maryla Husyt , grew up in Warsaw

, Poland and was a survivor of the Warsaw Ghetto and the death camps of Auschwitz and Bergen-Belsen . She met her husband , Gershon Finkelstein , while they were both interned in Bergen-Belsen. Finkelstein was the only member of his family to survive the war.
 Born in 1937 , he grew up in Woollahra , New South Wales. After leaving school , he studied law at the University of Sydney and worked as a solicitor with the law firm Mallesons Stephen Jaques in Sydney for 10 years. He has also worked in the management of private companies and as a consultant to the New South Wales state government on privatisation and other matters.
 Finkelstein has been active in the Jewish community and was a former president of the Executive Council of Australian Jewry. In 2007 , he was appointed to the board of the Holocaust Memorial Centre in Sydney .
 In 2007 , Finkelstein was appointed by the then Minister for Immigration and Citizenship , Senator Amanda Vanstone , to the position of Special Envoy for Humanitarian Programs. In 2009 , he was appointed to the position of Special Envoy on Asylum Seekers by the current Minister for Immigration and Citizenship , Senator Chris Evans .
 He is a member of the Council for the Advancement of Arab-British Understanding .
 Finkelstein has been a member of the Australian Human Rights Commission , the Australian Council for Civil Liberties and the Advisory Board of the Australian Jewish Democratic Society .
 He has written on a variety of legal and public policy issues , including foreign policy and the Middle East .
 He has also edited the Australian Jewish Democratic Society's journal , Hesed .
 Finkelstein is married to the journalist and editor of _The Australian_ , Rosemary Searle , and has two sons , Raphael and Jacob .

Woodhouse was born in Beverley and raised in Driffield . His father , Bernard Woodhouse , died at the age of 51 after he had a

heart attack while playing football with Woodhouse's brother, Dennis. Woodhouse was brought up in a rugby league family and played for Driffield and Bridlington . He played for Yorkshire Schoolboys in 1935 and 1936.
 Woodhouse made his début for Yorkshire against Surrey on 6 June 1938 at Bramall Lane , Sheffield . He scored a fifty in the match and took five wickets. Yorkshire won by 194 runs.
 Woodhouse played in all of Yorkshire's Championship matches in 1938 and in 1939. He was a member of the Yorkshire team which won the County Championship in 1938.
 Woodhouse joined the Royal Air Force during the Second World War. He served in North Africa and was involved in the Allied invasion of Sicily in 1943.
 Woodhouse played for Yorkshire again in 1946. He was chosen to take Yorkshire's opening bowling spot and played in the Championship against Lancashire. In his second match for Yorkshire he took eight wickets for 151 against Derbyshire. After the war he played all of Yorkshire's matches in 1947 and 1948.
 Woodhouse played for Yorkshire until 1952. He played in 141 first-class matches for Yorkshire. He took 462 wickets. Woodhouse took all ten wickets in an innings on two occasions.
 Woodhouse played for Yorkshire against Cambridge University in 1949. He took five wickets in the match.
 Woodhouse died in Leeds in 1972.
 Woodhouse played club cricket for Ecclesall at Sheffield.
 Woodhouse played for Yorkshire against Cheshire and Leicestershire.
 Woodhouse's wife, Joan , was a member of the Women's Institute in Lofthouse .
 Woodhouse played for Yorkshire against the touring Australians in 1938. He played in all of the County Championship matches against the tourists and took nine wickets.
 Woodhouse played for Yorkshire against the touring South Africans in 1947. He played all of the County Championship matches against the visiting team.
 Woodhouse played for Yorkshire against the touring West Indians in 1952. He played in three of the County Championship matches against the tourists and took three wickets.
 Woodhouse took five wickets in an innings on six occasions.
 Woodhouse was awarded the MBE in 1946.

## Plot

Raj(Prabhu Deva) is a young man who is forced to be a smuggler by his father in order to pay off his debts to a ruthless local goon, Sadhu Mehta (S. Thyagarajan). He meets Mehta's daughter Asha (Vasundhara Das), who at first refuses to marry him but later agrees to do so. Meanwhile, Raj is blackmailed by Mehta to kill an innocent man. After Raj refuses to kill the man, Mehta orders his henchmen to kidnap Asha. Raj pays Mehta's henchmen and they let Asha go. Raj decides to take revenge on Mehta and his henchmen and kills them one by one. He finally gets rid of Mehta and his men by killing them in a way that is reminiscent of the death of the ten commandments of Moses.

 Carey started writing songs for her next album in June 2005 , before she started recording the album . She went to the Bahamas and spent a lot of time on the beach .  In July 2006 , Carey released the single " We Belong Together ", which is the first single from her seventh studio album . The song became a worldwide hit , reaching number one in over ten countries worldwide , including the United States , UK . The song became the longest running number one single ever in the history of the Billboard Hot 100 and became the number one single in the US for 14 weeks , second longest single to spend that long at number one ever . In October 2006 , Carey released her seventh studio album , The Emancipation of Mimi , which had previously been titled The Emancipation of Mariah Carey . The song was also the best selling single of 2005 in Ireland , selling over 350,000 copies . " We Belong Together " was also the best selling single of 2006 in Australia , selling over 350,000 copies . " We Belong Together " is the best selling single of the 2000s decade in the United States .

A 2006 molecular phylogenetic study of different regional populations of A. muscaria by mycologist József Geml and colleagues f

alsified the classical classification of A. muscaria into two species. This study found that the geographical distribution of the wild mushroom correlates with the haplotype distribution, which implies that A. muscaria as a species is not homogeneous.

## Taxonomy

The generic name Amanita was coined by Christiaan Hendrik Persoon in 1796. The specific epithet muscaria is Latin for musk.

Several other species are frequently referred to as Amanita muscaria, but are not members of the Amanita muscaria species complex. Some of these species are:

* Amanita lactea
* Amanita pantherina
* Amanita phalloides
* Amanita rubescens

## History and cultural significance

The use of A. muscaria is recorded in the Arctic, Siberia, and parts of North America from at least 10,000 years ago, the same time period in which the ancestors of Native Americans were first arriving. The Sámi people of northern Europe use it as a traditional recreational drug.

### Central and Eastern Europe

The Sámi people of northern Europe use it as a traditional recreational drug.

Amanita muscaria has long been used recreationally by people in Europe and Asia, particularly in the Russian Arctic and Siberia. The mushroom was once commonly used in Siberia and elsewhere in the Russian Empire.

The spores of A. muscaria were found in 19th century graves in the Caucasus, indicating that they were used as a drug.

### The Balkans

Amanita muscaria has been used in the Balkans for centuries to induce, facilitate, and maintain trance states for the purpose of divination and the performance of shamanic rituals.

### China

Amanita muscaria (simplified Chinese: 鹿茸; traditional Chinese: 鹿茸; pinyin: lùróng; Wade–Giles: lu-lung), called "Buddist mushroom" (佛丹菇; fodan gū) or "Tsangkang" (湯康; tāngkāng, 湯仙; tāngxiān), has been used in China for centuries to induce, facilitate, and maintain trance states for the purpose of divination and the performance of shamanic rituals.

### South America

Amanita muscaria is also used in South America as a hallucinogenic mushroom in Indigenous rituals.

### North America

The use of A. muscaria is recorded in the Arctic, Siberia, and parts of North America from at least 10,000 years ago, the same time period in which the ancestors of Native Americans were first arriving.

### The Pacific Northwest

This mushroom is not indigenous to the Pacific Northwest, though it has been found growing in the region.

### North Africa

Amanita muscaria is used in Tunisia, which is the only North African country that has a research department devoted to the study of Saami shamanism.

### Culture

In the late 18th century, A. muscaria was introduced to Europe by the botanist Augustin Pyramus de Candolle, who reportedly found it growing in North America. The first mention of A. muscaria in English can be found in an 1833 book by Irish botanist and physician William Curtis:

Amanita muscaria, a species that does not occur in England, has been introduced and cultivated in Britain, and is said to be of a stronger kind than the species of the same genus growing spontaneously in the country.

As a recreational drug, A. muscaria has been used among Russians, Sámi, and other Siberian peoples for centuries.

### Legal status

Amanita muscaria is listed as a Schedule I drug in the United States.

### Religious significance

The Church of Our Lady of Light, an offshoot of the Church of Scientology, has incorporated A. muscaria into its rituals.

## Gameplay

Jade Raymond, producer of Assassin's Creed, has said that the game includes an open world, a game mechanic that the team had considered in the past. The game takes place in a "hybrid 2D – 3D" setting, where the player can walk around, explore and perform missions in a 2D world, but can also move into a 3D world for combat and stealth, and can switch between the two at will. The game's open world is navigated on foot or by horse.

The game's protagonist, Altaïr Ibn-La'Ahad, is an assassin who kills targets by stabbing them with a hidden blade or by strangling them. The game's combat system is based on the Batman: Arkham Asylum series, where combat scenes are seen from a third-person perspective. Altaïr can also use a variety of weapons, including hidden blades, swords, throwing knives, axes and crossbows, and can dodge enemy attacks. The player can also perform a counterattack by pressing a button at the right time. For example, the player can counter an enemy's attack by slashing the enemy with a sword, and can counter a thrown weapon by throwing it back. The game also has a stealth mechanic, where the player can take down enemies silently by strangling them, stabbing them, or using a smoke bomb to distract them.

The game features an experience system, which rewards the player for completing tasks and challenges by giving them points. These points can be used to upgrade the player character by using them to buy weapons, items or armour. The game takes place in Jerusalem, Acre and Masyaf, and includes missions and side quests. When completing a mission, the player is rewarded with experience points, money and an artifact. The player can also complete side-quests by killing a target or by helping a citizen. The player can also ride a horse throughout the game, and can ride into battle and in the open world.

## Development

Assassin's Creed is primarily developed by Ubisoft Montreal with contributions from Ubisoft's other studios including Ubisoft Annecy, Ubisoft Singapore, Ubisoft Bucharest, Ubisoft Montpellier, Ubisoft Shanghai, Ubisoft Toronto and Ubisoft Kyiv. The project was led by Jade Raymond, who had previously worked on the Splinter Cell series, and was the executive producer for the game. The project was led by Peter Leclercq, who had previously worked on the PC game Steerpike. Serge Hascoët, who was the art director on Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory, and Yannis Mallat, who was the art director on Splinter Cell: Double Agent, were the art directors for the game. The game's soundtrack was composed by Jesper Kyd.

The game originally focused on 2D – 3D mechanic and did not yet have open world ambitions. It was initially being developed for Microsoft Windows, Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3, and was to be released in 2007. Altaïr Ibn-La'Ahad was originally the main character of the game, but was replaced by Ezio Auditore da Firenze. Bédard coded 90% of the game's code himself before the game was handed over to the rest of the team to polish. When the game was released, it sold one million copies. The host spectrum of the Amylostereaceae comprises several , partially very different genera of Coniferae . A. chailletii usual

specie of the genus Anisoloma is a representative of the family Amylostereaceae. The well-known coniferous tree was pointed out as a new tree of the family Amylostereaceae by Antoine Magnin and Marcel Thiriet in 1946.
The typical species of the genus Anisoloma are found in the Tropics and subtropical regions of the world. They are trees of the humid and wet forests of the lowlands, which can reach on the ground heights of up to 30 meters. The wood is not used for forestry and gardening.
The roundish and ovoid, angled cones are formed in the higher situated branches and have a diameter of 1-2 cm. The cones are brownish and have a conical or pyramidal form.
Bringing into relation the appearance of the wood with the genus name of Anisoloma, it is assumed that the wood has a sweet smelling, anisol-like smell.
The Amylostereaceae are characterized by a branching system in which the branches are all growing in one direction, i.e. they are monopodial. The leaves of most species are in fascicles, which are formed in pairs. The leaves are spiny, with a long, spine-like, stiff tip.
The leaves are aromatic and the aroma is described as anisol-like. The name Anisoloma is composed by the Greek words Anisos, which means aromatic, and loma, which means tip.
The seeds are hard and covered with a thick shell. The seed of the Amylostereaceae are dispersed mainly by the wind and also by animals.
The family Amylostereaceae is placed in the order Coniferae. The family includes 17 genera with 132 species.
The most important species of the family Amylostereaceae are the species of the genus Anisoloma. Other genera are Amylostereum, Borderea, Dacrycarpus, Dacrydium and Pseudotaxus.
