The new commander of the US Military Assistance Command , Vietnam ( MACV ) , General Creighton W. Abrams , recommended to Presi

dent Lyndon Johnson that the mission of the US Armed Forces should be limited to:
1. Training the South Vietnamese Army and supporting it in combat.
2. Increasing the number of US advisers in South Vietnam to 40,000, in order to produce a "sustained effort" in the country.
3. Providing "minor defensive support" to South Vietnam, but not to engage in major combat operations.
4. "Rejecting the concept that the U.S. Armed Forces in South Vietnam should have the mission of preventing the enemy from winning the war in South Vietnam."
Lyndon Johnson, in a conversation with his Secretary of Defense, Robert McNamara, rejected the idea of a 40,000-man adviser commitment, but concurred with the other recommendations.
 This was the beginning of what the US media called the "credibility gap."
#  **1. THE PUBLIC IS BARELY AWARE OF THE VICIOUSNESS AND FEROCITY OF THE VIETNAM WAR.**
There was a vast discrepancy between the public's perception of the war and its actuality. As the number of Americans killed in Vietnam increased, the government's propaganda campaign intensified.
The public's perception of the war was based on the news of the day, which was fed them by the media. The media, in turn, were influenced by the government's propaganda. As the media were pro-government, they hardly reported the realities of the war. (See the Media section in Appendix II.)
The media used the same slogans as the politicians. They used the word "pacification," a word that suggested that the war was won or being won.
The term "pacification" was first used by the US government in 1965, when the Secretary of Defense, Robert McNamara, reported to Congress that it was the basis of the US military strategy in Vietnam. After the Tet offensive of 1968, the media used the term as well—a fact that was corroborated by the _New York Times_ , which reported that "pacification" was "the government's new slogan."
The media, however, misrepresented the facts. In a 1969 poll, more than half of the respondents believed that the United States was winning the war.
In 1971, the _New York Times_ reported that the public was "more apt to believe that the United States is winning the war in Vietnam than that it is losing."
And in 1972, NBC, the most popular television network in the United States, referred to the war as a "successful war in Vietnam."
The public was misled.
#  **2. MOST OF THE AMERICANS KILLED IN VIETNAM DID NOT GET KILLED IN COMBAT.**
Most of the American casualties did not die in combat.
More than 47,000 Americans were killed in Vietnam and the war in Indochina (Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia). Of these, 23,258 died in combat and about 12,250 died of "other" causes, such as in helicopter crashes, accidents, and illnesses (many of which were related to combat).
The remainder of the casualties died from accidents, illnesses, and suicides.
Most of the American casualties were from accidents, illnesses, and suicides.

Hinduism and the Ethics of War
The Hindu tradition is very much concerned with the ethics of war. The Bhagavad-Gita is perhaps the most famous philosophical text dealing with the subject of war. It arises in the form of a dialogue between the warrior Arjuna and Krishna, an avatar of Vishnu, who serves as his charioteer. On the battlefield, Arjuna bewails the fact that he has to kill his kith and kin, and he seeks Krishna’s guidance on how he should proceed. Krishna replies that it is the duty of the warrior to fight for the dharma of the state, and that one who does not do so is unworthy of being called a warrior. Arjuna asks Krishna to explain the nature of dharma. Krishna replies that dharma is what is conducive to the maintenance of the natural order. In this natural order, there are two sides, the good and the bad, against which war can be conducted. He illustrates this with the example of the struggle between the herbivores and the carnivores. The carnivores, the lions and wolves, have to kill the herbivores, the deer and the sheep, to survive. The herbivores have no option but to fight back. There is no dharma in the herbivores’ fighting back, but there is dharma in the carnivores’ killing the herbivores, because this is what sustains the natural order. Arjuna, who has been emboldened by this discussion, goes on to defeat the armies of his enemies.
The Bhagavad-Gita has been understood to have a lot to say about the ethics of war. It is often claimed that it is opposed to the use of military force. A number of scholars have claimed that the text is a pacifist work. Some of these scholars have even argued that the text is opposed to the use of all violence, including the use of force by the state. This is based on the author’s acceptance of a particular reading of the text, according to which the text is opposed to the use of all force except in the case of self-defense. This reading is, however, based on a very selective reading of the text.
It is true that the Bhagavad-Gita can be interpreted as opposing the use of force in the context of war. But this is not because the text is opposed to the use of force; it is because the text is opposed to violent war. This latter position is, in fact, in accordance with the text itself. The text is not opposed to the use of force in all contexts. Rather, it is opposed to violent war.
A number of scholars have argued that the Bhagavad-Gita is opposed to the use of all forms of violence, including the use of force by the state. This is based on the author’s acceptance of a particular reading of the text, according to which the text is opposed to the use of all force except in the case of self-defense. This reading is, however, based on a very selective reading of the text.

## History

In 1839, the city of Galveston was incorporated by the Texas Congress, and named after General Bernardo de Galvez, a Spanish colonial governor of Louisiana. Galveston was designated as the county seat of the newly formed Galveston County, and the city limits expanded to include the entire island. The port, with its natural deep-water harbor, quickly emerged as the largest in Texas, and soon attracted numerous businesses.

By 1860, Galveston had grown to be the fourth largest city in Texas, with 9,788 residents. With the outbreak of the American Civil War in 1861, Confederate forces seized the city and made it the base of operations for the Confederacy's western blockade-running operations. Galveston was subject to a long and costly siege by Union forces until the end of the war. When the war ended, Galveston became a port for trade with France and the United Kingdom.

In 1900, Galveston became a center of commerce and industry, with over 37,000 residents and a port that was the third-largest in the United States. The city had become a center of commerce and industry, with over 37,000 residents and a port that was the third-largest in the United States.

-lenticular form , although the areo-lenticular form is not as common as in A. mirabilis .

## Distribution

This species is found in the Wet Tropics region of Queensland Australia, in wet sclerophyll forests at elevations of 200 to 700 m ( 660 @.@ 2300 @.@ 2300 ft ).

## Ecology

Astraeus pteridis has a symbiotic relationship with the orchid Gastrodia pteridis , also known as the Swamp Coral Orchid . The orchid is found growing above the mushroom , which grows out of the orchid's stem .

**IT WAS RAINING** today, drizzling, wet, cool.
Sometimes the weather in California is just like the weather in Philadelphia. Like now.
I ran my fingers through my hair, trying to make it stop dripping on my face. My running clothes were soaked. I was barely wearing any makeup, and I didn't have time to deal with that right now. I'd have to take a shower as soon as I got home.
I was still running, still headed east, when I saw the large truck coming up behind me. I guessed it was a garbage truck. I hoped it was a garbage truck. What I didn't want was a car coming up quickly behind me on the shoulder.
I heard a woman scream.
I looked back.
The woman was lying in the grass along the side of the road. She was holding her head in her hands.
_It's just a car,_ I told myself. _It's not a weapon._
It was a car, all right, and it was coming fast.
The woman screamed again, and I knew the car would hit her. I dove off the road and into the grass, just as the car came past me.
I lay there, my heart pounding. I heard the car slow down, then stop. I looked toward the sound of the engine, but I couldn't see anything.
The woman was still screaming.
I crawled back to her side. "Are you all right?" I asked. I could tell she was shaking all over.
"Oh, my God," she said, holding her head again. "I'm so sorry."
"Do you need an ambulance?"
"No, no." She shook her head. "Just get me out of here. I need to get out of here."
She tried to stand, but she had a bad gash above her eye, and it was bleeding. She was also still holding her head, and I could tell she was in a lot of pain.
"I can take you to a doctor," I said.
"No, no, no. Just get me out of here."
I brought out my cell phone. "Let me call for an ambulance," I said.
"No. Please."
I looked at her. She was crying now. "Why don't you sit here while I walk to the store down the road and get you a couple of bandages?"
She shook her head. "No. I can't do that."
"Okay, I won't."
"Thank you."
I walked back to the road, reached in my pocket, but had no cell phone. I turned around. "I don't have a cell phone," I said. "I just ran into the woods to get away from that car. It was going to hit me."
"Oh, my God," she said, wiping her eyes. "I'm so sorry."
"I know. I'm sorry, too."
"My husband is going to kill me."
"I'm sure he won't."
"He'll kill me."
"No, he won't."
"I promised him I wouldn't run in the woods. I promised him. But I did anyway."
She was still holding her head.
"I'll be right back," I said.
I ran to the store. It was a small place called the Bread and Jam—a great name for a place in California—where you could buy bread and jam, that was for sure. They also sold bread and a lot of other stuff.
I came back with two Band-Aids, and she put them on her head.
"I can't believe this," she said. "I can't believe this."
I didn't say anything. I was thinking about the car, and I was thinking about the woman's husband. I was wondering if he would really kill her.
"I'll be right back," I said, and ran to the store again.

From 1858 to 1865 Busch chiefly worked for the Fliegenden Blätter and the Münchener Bilderbogen . The period from 1866 to 1884

was a time of intense artistic activity. In 1866 he began the series of drawings and woodcuts of the life of Christ in the Münchener Bilderbogen and later in the Fliegenden Blätter , together with Adolph Born, who died in 1868. In 1870 Busch published a collection of his drawings of the Biblical stories, Das Leben Jesu , and later the same year the book Bilder aus dem Leben Jesu . During these years he also continued to work on the Münchener Bilderbogen .
From 1884 to 1891 Busch worked as an illustrator for the weekly magazine Jugend . In 1891 he began to illustrate the works of Charles Dickens, which he continued until his death.
On 19 June 1898, Busch died in Munich and was buried in the Alter Südfriedhof .

Recognising his stature within the archaeological establishment , the government appointed Wheeler as the British representativ

eto the French Institut de France in 1924.  This was an extraordinary appointment. The Institut de France was the most prestigious scientific body in Europe, and Wheeler was the first British archaeologist to be honoured in this way. To the French, he was a 'doyen of British archaeology' and the 'father of British prehistory'.  Wheeler was a member of the Conseil de l'Institut de France and was appointed a Chevalier de la Légion d'Honneur, the highest French award for service to France.
 In 1929 Wheeler was appointed director of the Royal Ontario Museum in Toronto. This was the first time a British archaeologist had been appointed to direct an American museum. A few months before his arrival in North America, Wheeler had been given the Freedom of the City of London. At a ceremony held on 20 May 1929, the Lord Mayor of London, Sir John B. Snell, presented Wheeler with a gold medal on behalf of the Corporation of London.  The City of London had awarded Wheeler the honour 'in recognition of his valuable researches in the field of archaeology'. In his speech, the Lord Mayor referred to Wheeler as a 'great archaeologist' and a 'leader and pioneer in the field of prehistoric research'.  The Freedom of the City of London was one of the highest honours that could be bestowed on a British subject.
 Wheeler was profoundly honoured by these appointments and awards, and he spent the rest of his life as a beloved and respected figure in the world of archaeology. His achievements are too numerous to list in full. He contributed to the early development of archaeological science and made some significant discoveries himself. He inspired a new generation of British and American archaeologists that included Sir Mortimer Wheeler, Ian Richmond, Sir Stuart Piggott, Alison Richard, Erich von Daniken, David Rohl and Nicholas Saunders. However, Wheeler's contribution to the history of archaeology is not limited to his own achievements. He also inspired a group of British and American scholars to produce a series of books and articles that eventually transformed the way in which the ancient world was perceived.
This book is the first comprehensive biography of Wheeler in nearly seventy years. It was written by a British archaeologist, Professor Sir Barry Cunliffe, who has spent more than forty years at the forefront of prehistoric archaeology in Europe and Britain, and who is now the emeritus professor of European archaeology at the University of Oxford and a fellow of All Souls College. As the founder of the European Journal of Archaeology and the editor-in-chief of the _Oxford Encyclopaedia of Archaeology in the Classical,_ _Oriental, and Medieval Worlds_ , Sir Barry Cunliffe is one of the most influential scholars of all time.  He has a unique perspective on the development of archaeology in the twentieth century, and his understanding of Wheeler's legacy is unparalleled.
The book is divided into four parts. Part I explores Wheeler's early life and career. This includes his schooling, his first archaeological excavations, his time as an undergraduate and as a graduate student at Cambridge University, and his appointment to the British Museum. Part II covers Wheeler's time at the University of Pennsylvania, including his excavations in the Middle East. Part III explores his life and work in academic institutions – the British School at Rome, the British Museum, the University of Toronto, and the University of Pennsylvania again. Part IV deals with the later chapters of Wheeler's life and includes the introduction of the chronological scale, his involvement with the British Museum, the creation of the Institute of Archaeology, and his service to the University of Pennsylvania.
There are a number of reasons for writing this book. First, there is a need in the general public for more information about Wheeler, and about the history of archaeology in the twentieth century. In a recent survey, members of the general public ranked archaeology as the second-most interesting subject, after art, but the public knows nothing about the history of the subject. The public trusts academic institutions to maintain their knowledge of the past, yet these institutions have failed in this respect.
Second, there is a need for a comprehensive biography of Wheeler. Many biographies and autobiographical works exist, but none of these deals with the entirety of Wheeler's career.

The Alabama Crimson Tide football team is a college football program representing the University of Alabama in the sport of American football. The team is currently coached by Nick Saban and plays their home games at BryantDennyStadium in Tuscaloosa, Alabama. Alabama competes in the Football Bowl Subdivision (FBS) of the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) and the Western Division of the Southeastern Conference (SEC). Alabama has won 25 overall national championships, including 13 under coach Paul "Bear" Bryant and two under coach Gene Stallings. The Tide has won 14 national championships recognized by the NCAA and two recognized by other organizations. The 2009 and 2012 teams were recognized as national champions by the Associated Press (AP).

land did not retell his life in an orderly sequence , but instead provided a series of vignettes in no particular order , with narratives that sometimes reached back to his boyhood , and other times skipped ahead to recent times . Kitsunetsuki ( Japanese : 狐憑き , 狐付き ) , also written kitsune @-@ tsuki , literally means " the state of being possessed by a fo

x ". Kitsune-tsuki can refer to a Native American belief in ghosts and to a Japanese belief in foxes. There are a number of differences between Native American kitsunetsuki and Japanese kitsunetsuki, but both share some commonalities. [1] [2] Kitsunetsuki can also refer to the belief that humans are being possessed by the spirits of foxes who can use the humans for their own purposes. [1]

Native American belief [ edit ]
Native American belief [ edit ]
In Native American belief, foxes are believed to be the spirits of children who were not allowed to grow up, or who were separated from their parents and died. [3] [4] Kitsunetsuki is a phenomenon that has been reported in the United States, Canada, and Mexico. [1] [5] [6] Some Native American tribes have stories of kitsunetsuki, but the phenomenon is not widespread. [3] [7]
Stories of kitsunetsuki in the United States [ edit ]
Stories of kitsunetsuki in the United States are rare and usually involve Native Americans. [1] [7] [8] In a 1977 study, researchers found that “more than half of the persons interviewed had heard stories of ‘fox spirits’ or ‘fox ghosts’ possessing humans … ,” [9] and that “many of the accounts seem to be a mixture of myth and fact. [7] According to researchers, “these stories … are more likely to be found in … more remote areas.” [1] [10]
Stories of kitsunetsuki in Canada [ edit ]
Stories of kitsunetsuki in Canada are rare. [1] [11] According to researchers, the phenomenon “is most likely to occur among the Plains Indians. [1] [12] However, there has been one non-Native American case in Canada. [13] In 1976, a man named Leon was killed in a hunting accident. After his funeral, a few days after his death, his wife, Louise, began to behave strangely. She would disappear for hours at a time during the day and would return home late at night. One day, she called her son, Tom, and told him that she was going to her father’s house to visit. When Tom went to look for her, he found that she had gone to her mother’s house. Tom’s mother, Mary, was also acting strangely. She would “sit in her room smoking cigarettes and drinking whiskey,” and “would not allow anyone to enter the room.” [14]
Stories of kitsunetsuki in Mexico [ edit ]
Stories of kitsunetsuki in Mexico are rare. [1] In 1998, a woman named Maria was visited by a man named Rafael, who claimed to be her husband’s brother. Rafael asked Maria to take him to her husband’s house, but Maria refused. When Maria’s husband returned home, he found that Maria had “decided to move to Mexico City and was leaving with Rafael.” [15] The next day, Maria’s husband and Rafael argued, and Rafael left. When Maria’s husband went out to look for Rafael, he found that Rafael was dead. [16]
Japanese belief [ edit ]
Foxes in Japanese Mythology [ edit ]
In Japanese mythology, foxes are not always depicted as cunning and deceitful. Some stories portray them as compassionate and helpful to humans. For example, in one story, a fox saves a man’s life by bringing him food. [17]
Foxes in Japanese Folklore [ edit ]
Foxes are often portrayed as cunning and deceitful in Japanese folklore. [18] In one story, a fox tricks a monk into giving it a pearl. Doris Lessing 's interest in politics began in the 1940s while she was living in Southern Rhodesia ( now Zimbabwe ) . She was a

member of the Southern Rhodesian Communist Party and involved in the trade union movement. She continued to be politically active after the party was banned in 1954, and in 1962 she moved to England.
Lessing began writing novels in the early 1950s but did not publish until _Grasses of Parnassus_ appeared in 1949. Her breakthrough came in 1958 with _The Grass Is Singing_ (1950), which established her reputation as a serious novelist. She published the first volume of her five-volume _Children of Violence_ sequence in 1959. The sequence was completed in 1969 with _The Habit of Loving_.
Lessing's social criticism was based on a feminist analysis of race and class. In the 1960s she became increasingly critical of colonialism and capitalism. In 1968 she visited Czechoslovakia to observe the Prague Spring and in 1971 went to Chile to observe the socialist government of Salvador Allende . In 1970 she published _A Proved_ , a collection of essays on Marxism and literature, and in 1974 _The Sweetest Dream_ , a collection of short stories. The following year she published _The Golden Notebook_ , which was a milestone in the history of women's writing in England. She used it to combine her political analysis with the feminist analysis of the difference between male and female experience.
In 1987 Lessing published _The Good Terrorist_ , a collection of essays which reflected her views on terrorism and insurrection. In the early 1990s she published _The Fifth Child_ , about a woman who takes care of an African child. The novel was the first of her books to be set in England. In 1992 she published _The Island Under the Earth_ , a novel about the Mayan civilization, and _Under My Skin_ , a collection of autobiographical essays. _The Grandmothers_ was published in 1993 and _Balkan Holiday_ in 1994.
In 2000 Lessing published _The Golden Notebook_ (2000) in a revised version. The new version of the novel was heavily criticized by feminists because Lessing had altered the sequence and political orientation of the novel. In 2001 Lessing's autobiography _Under My Skin_ was published in the United States and in 2002 she published _This Was the Old Chief's Country_ , a novel about the Mayan civilization. She won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 2007.
Lessing's novels are distinguished by their vigorous critical style and their retelling of the history of European imperialism and colonialism.

The film was loosely styled after Akira Kurosawa 's 1954 film Seven Samurai , and drew heavily from the conventions of Westerns

. The title refers to a classic Western character: the " lone gunman ", the lone gunfighter who rides into town to face the outlaws, who are often referred to as " bad men ". The film is also known for its long-range shootouts, in which the hero is forced to shoot accurately from long distances while being shot at by the villain.
In the film, a tough-talking, quick-drawing gunslinger named John Mason is hired by a town leader to protect the town from a gang of outlaws called the Wild Bunch. The story begins with the outlaws attacking and robbing a train, killing the passengers and railroad workers. After the robbery, the gang leader, Pike Bishop, and his gang are pursued by a posse of lawmen. However, when the lawmen set a fire to cover their retreat, they mistakenly kill a woman and child. Pike becomes furious and turns back to kill them, but is too late. He then orders his men to track down John Mason and kill him.
A local ranch owner, Mabry, hires John, and the two men make a deal. John will protect the town in exchange for Mabry's daughter, Rachel, as his wife. John takes a dislike to Pike, who is also in love with Rachel. John remains in town to protect the town while Pike meets with Rachel, and they have a brief affair. After Pike leaves, Rachel tells John the truth about her father. Mabry is actually a bootlegger, and he is using Rachel to help him smuggle whiskey into the town. John arranges for the townspeople to drink the whiskey, with the plan that they will become drunk, allowing the outlaw gang to enter the town and robbing it easily.
In the course of defending the town, John is wounded and Pike is killed. John and Rachel agree to leave town and live together, but Mabry shoots John in the back. Rachel then shoots him in the head, killing him. John reveals to Rachel that he had known Mabry was a bootlegger all along, and he had used the plan to kill both the outlaws and Mabry. The outlaws enter the town and kill Mabry, taking the townspeople's money.
The film was shot in Texas and New Mexico . In 1976, Westerns were not as popular as they had been in the 1950s and 1960s, and the film was not a box office success. A sequel titled Return of the Seven , which was an adaptation of the 1956 novel The Brave Cowboy, was filmed in 1966.
The film was originally released by Paramount Pictures. It was later re-released by MGM/UA Entertainment Co. in 1978, and again in 1981. It was also released on VHS by CBS/Fox Video in 1984 and 1985.
The film was released on DVD by MGM Home Entertainment on October 21, 2003. It was re-released by Paramount Home Entertainment on October 26, 2004.
The film was released on Blu-ray Disc by Paramount Home Entertainment on November 18, 2014.
The film was met with mixed reviews. Bosley Crowther of The New York Times called the film "a respectable entertainment", and said that Robert Ryan and Woody Strode "are the best things about the picture." In a review for Time Out, Philip French called the film a "long-range shootout between two gunfighters that's worth seeing for the outdoor location work alone."

The Archaeology of Ritual and Magic was reviewed by John Hutchings for the Folklore journal , the published arm of The Folklore

Society. In his review he argues that 'the book appears to be part of a growing interest in the archaeology of religion and ritual in the ancient world, which has been stimulated by the work of the likes of Daniel Miller and Lynne Hunt'. Hutchings praises the book for its 'easy style' and 'sense of humour' and for its 'intriguing and highly controversial thesis' that 'the use of magic in the ancient world was not widespread or commonplace'.
Hutchings's review was followed by a comment by Roger Beck, Professor of Anthropology at the University of Illinois. Beck is the author of many books on anthropology, including Ritual Dynamics: Transformations in Symbolic and Ritual Systems (1988), The Cosmology of Evolution: The Study of Representations of Time and the Cosmos in the World's Religions (1992), and Ritual Dynamics and the Anthropology of Religions (1997). He has also published numerous articles on ritual and religion.
In his comment he argues that 'The Archaeology of Ritual and Magic should be of interest to all archaeologists, both those who study ancient societies and those who study modern ones. The book provides a useful foundation for a discussion of the full range of ceremonial behavior and the relationship of that behavior to social and economic power in a number of ancient societies'.
The Archaeology of Ritual and Magic was reviewed by James Scott in the journal Anthropology Today . In his review Scott argues that '[d]espite some useful insights, Archaeology of Ritual and Magic suffers from poor organization, a tendency to overreach and over-simplify, and a lack of critical engagement with relevant literature. This volume should be of interest to undergraduates and beginning graduate students, but it is not a work that will be likely to be considered authoritative'.

Shanks argues that '[n]o one has undertaken the task so far, but Sutton's book is a good start. It is also defensible in that it is a book for non-specialists, making it a good introduction to the field'. Shanks praises the book for its 'good coverage of magical practices in the Greek world' and for its 'good coverage of the Roman world'.

t wasted no time in bringing in legislation to restrict the franchise to the 3 per cent who had a household income of 10 shillings a week. Gladstone, who was now an opposition leader, resumed active politics and, after a series of short-lived Tory ministries, led the Liberals to power in 1892.
23rd June 1900.
My dear Austin,
I am with regret forced to write you a formal letter, in answer to your last.
I do so because your letter has raised the question of your relationship with the Alliance.
I am not at all good at these sorts of things, but I feel that you are leaving me a little in the dark about what you are about.
I have been informed that you are advancing a motion in favour of the Alliance at the next meeting of the Social Democratic Federation. I have asked your comrade, Mr Tonkin, whether this is so. He has assured me that it is not, that Mr Hyndman has been present at no such meeting, and that you have been misinformed.
Now, if this is so, I think I should like to continue my friendly relations with you, and I think you should like to do the same.
If, on the other hand, it is true that you are advancing a motion, then I should feel that I must decline to go to your meetings in any case.
Another point: I think you are aware that the SD Federation is at present very much in a state of disorder, and that it is a matter of extreme difficulty to obtain any clear idea of what is going on there. There is a real danger that the Federation may cease to exist, and that the Alliance will then find itself without a single effective organisation within the workers movement. I know that you do not wish this to happen, and I think you would be the last to shrink from sacrificing your personal interests in the cause of the Alliance.
The Alliance is in a state of crisis and needs your help. The important thing now is that the Alliance should be a united organisation, and all the forces of the workers party should be concentrated within it. The Alliance is now a great deal more united than the SDF, and there is no reason why the Alliance should not continue to be united. The only thing that would be likely to endanger this unity would be failure to take advantage of every opportunity to bring the Social Democrats and the Marxists together.
I am quite aware that you have an intense dislike of the Social Democratic Federation, and that you feel we should have nothing to do with them. But I think that to refuse to work with them at a time like this would be to endanger the Alliance, and I hope that you will take a different view.
Yours sincerely,  
H.M. Hyndman
The letter had all the makings of a love letter.
The Alliance was a marriage of convenience between the Social Democrats and the Marxists. It had its origins in the doomed attempt by Hyndman's Social Democratic Federation to form an electoral alliance with Henry Labouchere's Irish National Federation. This had come about because the Irish National Federation had been for many years the largest Marxist organisation in Britain. But the two groups parted company with the coming of the Russian Revolution, and the Marxists established the Socialist Labour Party in 1905. The Social Democrats followed a year later, as a result of internal disputes within the Social Democratic Federation.
The Alliance was a purely tactical alliance, and was always intended to be temporary. For the moment, the Social Democratic Federation was in a state of complete collapse. There was no need to expend time and energy on a solution to that problem, when the immediate problem was the formation of a united Socialist Party in opposition to Gladstone. The Alliance was designed to be a temporary device for bringing the two Marxist groups together in the face of the Tory Government. The hope was that the Alliance would serve its limited purpose, and then be allowed to fold up and die. But the Alliance had gone on surviving long after the Tory Government had gone. The Social Democrats had never really abandoned the Alliance, and so had been in the uncomfortable position of having to take part in Alliance meetings while attacking the Marxists from the platform.
Hyndman had been working hard to try and bring the Social Democrats and Marxists together, but so far without success. He had been trying to persuade the Social Democrats to dissociate themselves from the SLP and to unite with the Marxists. The Social Democrats had so far refused, but Hyndman had succeeded in persuading them to agree to a meeting in the autumn of 1905

The Rangers became the first team to have their first All-Star representative since the team's inception in 1961, when pitcher Ferguson Jenkins was selected. In 1961, the Texas Rangers became the first team to have three representatives in the All-Star Game, with pitcher Hoyt Wilhelm and outfielder Ted Williams also selected  The Rangers and the Senators finished with the two worst records in the American League and tied the major league record for most losses in a season with 107  The Rangers' 107 losses broke the major league record of 106 losses set by the 1934 Boston Braves. The 107 losses were also an AL record, breaking the previous mark of 105 losses set by the Detroit Tigers in 1934.
 When the Rangers relocated to Arlington after the 1972 season, the Rangers became the first major league team to relocate to a new city since the Cleveland Indians moved to Milwaukee in 1953, before moving to Cleveland again in 1954  The Rangers recorded the first no hitter in the history of the Astrodome, on June 24, 1965, when Jim "Mudcat" Grant pitched a 3–0 five hit shutout against the New York Yankees  The Rangers also recorded the first triple play in the history of the Astrodome on May 5, 1966, when second baseman Bob Aspromonte caught a line drive by Detroit Tigers pinch hitter Angel Mangual in foul territory, tagged second baseman Billy Hoeft while he was attempting to advance to first, and tagged first baseman Jim Northrup while he was attempting to advance to second.
 The Rangers' 116 losses in 1973 broke the major league record for most losses in a season, which was set by the 1935 St. Louis Browns and the 1962 New York Mets with 112 losses each.

In 1996 , when Hamels was only seven years old , he was diagnosed with a brain tumor that was pressing on the trigeminal nerve . He underwent surgery to remove the tumor , which was in an inoperable location , and recovered completely .
Hamels began playing baseball at an early age . In 2005 , he attended the prestigious Woodrow Wilson High School in San Diego . He was a member of the varsity team for four years and was named first team all-state in his senior year . During his junior and senior years , Hamels was 27-1 with an 0.75 earned run average .
In 2006 , Hamels was selected by the Philadelphia Phillies in the first round of the Major League Baseball draft . He signed a contract with the Phillies on July 7 , 2006 .

Route 65 is a former state highway in the city of Newark , New Jersey . The route went for 4 @.@ 12 miles ( 6 @.@ 63 km ) along

the south side of the city , from a junction with U.S. Route 1 ( US 1 ) and Interstate 78 ( I-78 ) in the southwestern part of the city to an interchange with I-280 and U.S. Route 22 ( US 22 ) in the central part of the city.
Route 65 was first designated in 1940 as a state highway, connecting US 1 and NJ 62 in Newark. The route was paved, and work began on a four-lane expressway in 1958, but was canceled before it was completed. The remaining two-lane expressway was completed in 1960. The route was decommissioned in 1961 and replaced by parts of I-280 and US 22.
The entire route was in Essex County .

Fowler made 22 appearances for the England national team, scoring four goals. His first international goal came on 15 November 1993, in an 11–0 win over San Marino .
Fowler made his England debut in the 1993 European Under-18 Championship . He scored three goals in the tournament, including two in England's 3–0 victory over the Netherlands in the final . He also scored in the 5–0 victory over Germany in the semi-finals .
Fowler's first major tournament was the 1995 FIFA World Youth Championship , where he was the top goal scorer for England with four goals , including the equaliser in the 3–3 draw with Spain in the final .
Fowler's only appearance at a major tournament came in Euro 2000 , where he made two appearances as England were knocked out in the first round by Romania . He came on as a substitute in the 3–2 loss to Romania and was an unused substitute in the 2–1 defeat to Germany .
Fowler's final international appearance came in a friendly against Argentina on 15 November 2000 , where he was substituted at half-time in the 2–0 defeat .
Fowler made his Liverpool debut in a 1–0 defeat to Everton in the FA Charity Shield on 12 August 1993. He scored his first goal for Liverpool on 4 September 1993, in a 2–1 home win over Tottenham Hotspur .
Fowler's goal tally for Liverpool was low, scoring only 11 times in his first season, but he scored 12 times in the following season, and a further 10 goals in his third season, which included a hat-trick against Leeds United on 8 April 1995 .
Fowler's form dipped in the 1995–96 season , scoring only four times in 33 appearances . He scored his only goal of the 1996–97 season on 8 February 1997, in a 3–0 home win over Sheffield Wednesday .
Fowler found it difficult to establish himself in the Liverpool first team in the 1997–98 season , and manager Roy Evans made it clear that he would not be part of his plans for the following season . He scored four goals in 15 appearances in the 1997–98 season .
Fowler's final goal for Liverpool was a " wonder goal " against Manchester United on 27 May 1998, in a 2–1 defeat which meant Liverpool finished fourth in the league and qualified for the UEFA Cup .
Fowler was sold to Leeds United for £15 million on 20 May 1998 .
Fowler spent three years at Leeds, scoring 16 goals in 68 appearances . He scored his first goal for Leeds in a 2–0 home win over Bradford City on 17 September 1998 .
Fowler's first season at Leeds was also his first full season as a professional, and he scored 10 goals in 40 appearances as Leeds finished third in the Premier League .
Fowler's second season at Leeds was a disappointment, as a combination of a lack of form and injury meant he only played 12 times . He scored his only goal of the season in a 1–0 win over Southampton on 31 March 2000 .
Fowler's third and final season at Leeds was his most prolific. He scored 12 goals in 30 appearances as Leeds finished second in the league, before losing the play-off final to Bolton Wanderers .
In August 2003, Fowler returned to Liverpool on a free transfer . He made his comeback in a 2–1 defeat to Tottenham Hotspur at the start of the 2003–04 season . He scored his first goal for Liverpool on 1 November 2003, in a 1–1 draw with Charlton Athletic .
Fowler scored his second goal for Liverpool on 17 March 2004, in a 2–1 defeat to Chelsea . He scored his final goal for Liverpool on 22 May 2004, in a 3–1 defeat to Chelsea in the FA Cup final .

Krasnyi Kavkaz ( from Russian : " Красный Кавказ " - " Red Caucasus " ) was a cruiser of the Soviet Navy that began constructio

n in Germany in 1916, but was abandoned in 1917 due to the outbreak of World War I. The Soviet government purchased the ship at the end of the war, and towed her to Nikolayev in the Soviet Ukraine. She was renamed Krasnyi Kavkaz ( Red Caucasus ) and commissioned in 1922.
During her career, Krasnyi Kavkaz participated in the evacuation of Crimea, and the Russian Civil War. She was renamed to Novorossiysk in 1926, and served in Soviet naval bases in the Black Sea and the Mediterranean, as well as the Baltic Sea. She was sold to Romania in 1948, and renamed to Regele Carol I ( King Carol I ). She was scrapped in 1976 in Italy.
A model of the Krasnyi Kavkaz is on display at the Russian Museum of Ethnography in Saint Petersburg, Russia.
Krasnyi Kavkaz was laid down as the second ship of the Kronprinz sub-type of the König class of pre-dreadnought battleships, ordered by the German Imperial Navy on 6 December 1908. She was launched on 13 July 1912, and commissioned on 12 May 1915 into the German fleet.
She was the lead ship of the Kronprinz class, which was intended to be a follow-on to the preceding Kaiser class. Her keel was laid down on 6 December 1908, and she was launched on 13 July 1912. She was commissioned on 12 May 1915, after the start of World War I.
Krasnyi Kavkaz was moored at Kiel, ready for sea trials, when World War I began. She was taken in hand for conversion to a seaplane carrier, and her armament was removed. She was to have been renamed Gneisenau, and was to have had a crew of 377. She was not completed, and remained partially completed until 1917. When the Russian Revolution of 1917 began, Krasnyi Kavkaz was incomplete and her crew was reduced to 40 men. The Germans abandoned Krasnyi Kavkaz on 3 November 1917, and the Soviets raised her on 22 November.
The Krasnyi Kavkaz was under repair in Kiel by the Germans when the Revolution began. The Soviet Navy found it and raised it on 22 November 1917.
The Soviets sent a commission to Germany to inspect the ship. The Germans then agreed to sell the cruiser to the Soviets for 1.5 million gold marks. The first section of the poem is titled "A Song for Coming Forth by Day," and it expresses the poet's joy at being able to experience the world through her senses. "May your days be many and may your troubles be few" is a common saying in the South. The second section, "A Song for the Dusk," expresses the poet's joy in life and the beauty of the natural world. The Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) is the UK regulator for civil aviation, including general aviation. The CAA’s main role is to promote safety and efficiency in aviation, and to support the UK’s world leading position as a centre for aviation excellence. The CAA’s main functions are the safety regulation of aircrew, air traffic services, airports and airlines, and the provision of air navigation services.

The CAA has the responsibility for the safety of UK civil air operations, and represents the UK on European Union air safety matters. In this role it works closely with the European Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) and the European Commission.
The CAA’s duties are to protect the public, to promote safety and efficiency and to foster the development of international civil aviation.
The CAA issues certificates of airworthiness, registration and the UK Operator’s Licence, which are required for aircraft to operate in the UK.
The CAA manages the UK’s air traffic control (ATC) system and provides air traffic control services for UK-bound commercial airliners. It also manages the UK’s airspace, which it does by controlling the volume, height and speed of aircraft and their separation from each other. The CAA provides air traffic management (ATM) services for aircraft operating under the UK’s Instrument Flight Rules.
The CAA manages the UK’s civil airports, including Heathrow, Gatwick, Stansted, Luton, Manchester, Birmingham, Glasgow, Edinburgh, Prestwick and Southampton, and is responsible for deciding which airports can be used for certain types of aircraft.
The CAA also issues licences to fly certain small aircraft for experimental purposes, and manages the UK’s civil air traffic management (ATM) system.

Shortly afterwards, in 1920, Charles Rolls was killed when he crashed his aircraft near Bournemouth, the first fatal accident in the United Kingdom that was not caused by a military operation.
The first year-round passenger service in the United Kingdom was established by the Aircraft Dispatch Company in 1920, with a passenger train from London to Paris and back. However, the company went out of business within a year, and it was not until the formation of Aircraft Transport and Travel (A.T.T.) in 1921 that regular passenger flights began in the United Kingdom.
General aviation in the United Kingdom grew slowly but steadily in the following years. Corythosaurus / ˌkɒrᵻθoʊˈsɔːrəs / is a genus of hadrosaurid " duck @-@ billed " dinosaur from the Upper Cretaceous Period , abo

ard 76.51–75.5 million years ago , in what is now Alberta, Canada. The genus name is derived from the Greek words koru ( κόρυ ) , meaning "helmet ", and sauros ( σαυρος ) , meaning "lizard ". The type species is C. casuarius , from the Late Campanian Dinosaur Park Formation, first described by Lawrence Lambe in 1902.
The most distinctive characteristic of Corythosaurus is the crest on its head. The crest of Corythosaurus is one of the best known and most studied hadrosaurid features. It is the first hadrosaurid crest to have been discovered and described. Another distinctive feature of the genus is the presence of a horn on its nose. The skull of Corythosaurus is long and narrow, with large nostrils, and it has a toothless beak.
The first remains of Corythosaurus were discovered in 1912 by Lawrence Lambe. Lambe's find prompted the creation of the genus name, Corythosaurus, which was derived from the Greek words koru ( κόρυ ) , meaning "helmet ", and sauros ( σαυρος ) , meaning "lizard ". The type species is C. casuarius , from the Late Campanian Dinosaur Park Formation. The generic name was derived from the ancient Greeks' Corythus, a hare, and the Latin saurus, lizard. Lambe noted that ancient Greek writers such as Aristotle and Pliny implied that the crest of the Corythosaurus had a resemblance to the hare, while other writers compared it to the helmet of an ancient Greek warrior. The species name casuarius is Latin for the helmeted crest of the bird casuarius. The name Corythosaurus casuarius was published in 1913.
In 1950, Charles M. Sternberg suggested that the holotype of Corythosaurus be moved to the genus Edmontosaurus. In 1957, Sternberg and J.L. Ostrom noted that the holotype was referred in the original description to the species Edmontosaurus casuarius. They noted that Corythosaurus is a separate genus, and that the name Edmontosaurus casuarius is a nomen nudum , a name that is only a description and does not meet the requirements for a valid name. Sternberg and Ostrom treated the nomen nudum as a senior synonym of Corythosaurus casuarius.
Corythosaurus is a medium-sized hadrosaurid, with a length between 6.6 and 8.2 meters (22 and 27 feet). It is estimated to have weighed 1.2 – 2.5 tonnes (1.3 – 2.7 short tons). The skull is between 90 to 100 centimeters (35 to 39 inches) long, and the lower jaw is 58 centimeters (23 inches) long.
The crest of Corythosaurus is one of the best known and most studied hadrosaurid features. The crest is the most distinctive feature of the genus, and it is present in all Corythosaurus species. The crest of Corythosaurus is a double-pronged structure. It is composed of a large bony core that is conical in shape, and a thin keratinous sheath that is fused to the surface of the crest. Although the skull is usually articulated with the neck, the bony core is anatomically separated from the bones of the skull. The crest is located on the snout, and it is offset from the midline of the skull.
The crest of Corythosaurus is considered an advanced structure . It is the first hadrosaurid crest to be discovered and described, and the first bony crest to be identified among dinosaurs. The crest has been shown to act as a loudspeaker, producing a loud bell-like sound. It has been hypothesized that the crest is a nuptial structure, used in courtship displays. Many hadrosaurid species are known to have had crests, and some of them may have also been used for loud displays. The crests of Corythosaurus, Edmontosaurus, and Lambeosaurus are the most studied hadrosaurid crests.

The Carnation Revolution was the result of a combination of factors, including the marginalization of the main ruling political party (the National Union Democratic , or UDN ) and its inability to form a new government, the growing unrest of the Portuguese working class, and the impact of the end of colonialism in the Portuguese African territories. The negative consequences of the Estado Novo regime , the ongoing Portuguese Colonial War , and the political and economic crisis in Portugal itself also played a role in the revolution.

In such cases the grave itself is not dissected but merely the surrounding land around it may be searched for the grave goods.
This is the case at the church of St. Columba at Skara Brae in Orkney. The site was excavated by Sir Joseph Simpson in 1925 and he reported that in the vicinity of the church no graves were located, but that in the surrounding land he located more than 100 sites, some of which had been robbed and some not. In the robbed sites he reported that he found between 3 and 10 pieces of metalwork. He assumed that the grave goods were not left in the graves but were removed to the neighbourhood.
Simpson's conclusion was that the graves had not been robbed but that the grave goods had been removed, and that this was the reason they had not been found in the graves. However, the presence of grave goods in the surrounding land may be explained by the fact that the graves were robbed and the grave goods were left scattered around the graves and the surrounding land. The grave goods would have been buried in pits to a depth of some 15 centimetres and there may have been a covering of turf over them which would have prevented their discovery.

The leg-before-wicket rule has been changed several times. Initially, the umpire's decision was final, but the 1889 law book stated that an appeal to the umpires could be made, and that decision was final. In 1914, the fielding captain could now ask for a referral to the umpire's decision, and in 1922 the fielding captain's decision was final. The 1926 laws changed this, and the umpire's decision was final again.
In 1934, the word "ball" was added to the word "wicket", and the full term "leg before wicket" was adopted.
The 1999 laws of cricket changed the definition of leg-before wicket. The batsman was previously out if he was struck by a bowled ball that pitched outside the leg stump and had then, in that direction, passed or passed behind wicket. The revised definition stated that the ball had to have pitched outside leg stump and then hit the batsman in that direction or in the opposite direction, and the batsman was then out.

Alkan was born in Paris on 30 September 1813 to Jewish parents of Polish-Russian descent. His father, Schneur, was a respected merchant, and his mother, Fanny, was a musician who gave piano lessons. Alkan's father was a man of very modest means, and Alkan later recalled that he was not born in a palace, but in a modest apartment.
Alkan's father died when he was seven years old. His mother, who was a very religious woman, was left with two small children, one of whom was Alkan. Alkan's mother relied on the modest financial support of her brother, Bernhard Herz, to raise her two children. The children lived with their mother and her brother in his house, which was located at 6 Rue de la Chaussée-d'Antin in Paris.
Alkan's childhood in Paris was not happy. He had a difficult relationship with his mother, who was extremely strict and did not let him go out to play with other children. Alkan later recalled that his parents did not want him to become a musician, saying, " My father did not want me to be a musician. My mother did not want me to be a musician. Many Polish writers collaborated with the Soviets , writing pro @-@ Soviet propaganda . They included Jerzy Borejsza , Tadeusz

Boy-Żeleński , Antoni Słonimski , and Kazimierz Wierzyński .

The other famous Polish writer who had been deported to the gulag and then worked as a journalist in the Soviet Union was Witold Gombrowicz .

Soviet occupation of Poland (1939–1941) was the period when Soviet Union occupied and annexed a part of Second Polish Republic, which was later a part of the Soviet Union.

### Deportations

Even before the start of the war, thousands of Polish people were deported to the Soviet Union from territories occupied by the Soviet Union. Many of them were victims of Stalin's Great Purge of the 1930s. In 1940, under the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, the Soviet Union invaded and occupied Polish territories in eastern Poland. After the Soviet invasion, the Soviets started deportations of Polish citizens and massacres.

During the Soviet occupation, the Soviets arrested, sent to the Gulag, and deported to Siberia tens of thousands of Polish citizens. This included not only the members of the Polish government, but also civilians.

Those deported were often not only accused of being spies or saboteurs, but also members of the Polish underground resistance.

### Soviet propaganda

Main article: Soviet propaganda

During the occupation, the Soviet Union used Polish writers to write propaganda about Poland. In addition, the Soviets used Polish writers to write about the Soviet Union.

Those who wrote pro-Soviet propaganda included Jerzy Borejsza , Tadeusz Boy-Żeleński, Antoni Słonimski, and Kazimierz Wierzyński.

## Polish writers who collaborated with the Soviets

The Polish writers who collaborated with the Soviets included:

* Jerzy Borejsza (1905–1940)
* Tadeusz Boy-Żeleński (1874–1941)
* Antoni Słonimski (1895–1976)
* Kazimierz Wierzyński (1894–1969)

The largest find of Iguanodon remains to that date occurred on 28 February 1878 in a coal mine at Bernissart in Belgium , at a

35–40 m level. The coal seam was 2.4 m thick and lay 420 m below the surface. The quarry had been opened by J. Desclée & Cie and the site was excavated by a team of 12 miners, chiefly Jean-Nicholas Houzeau and Jules Poulain. The latter became familiar with the local geology, noting that the fossils were not derived from the underlying Rotliegend strata but were found in an alternation of water-lain sandstone and limestone strata that formed a 60 m thick unit above the coal. This was a marine environment and the fossils were found in lenses of mudstone that had been deposited in a shallow sea.
The quarry was worked up to a level of 26 m below the surface and yielded a total of 19 skeletons, 3 of which were in nearly perfect condition. The second skeleton was that of an adult male and its skull was 1.5 m long and 1.2 m wide. The quarry also produced 1100 bones from other individual skeletons. The fossils are now housed in the Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences in Brussels .
In 1879, the same quarry produced the skeleton of a 20–25 year old Iguanodon, which has been named I. bernissartensis. This specimen was larger than the other skeletons. The quarry was abandoned in 1880, because it had become too unstable as a result of a mining accident. The skeletons were reassembled in the Musée Royal de l'Afrique Centrale in Tervuren in 1884.
The Bernissart iguanodont is thought to have had a body length of 12 m, a height of 5 m and a weight of 9 tonnes.
The Bernissart specimens were exhibited at the Paris Universal Exhibition of 1889 and all the mounted skeletons are still on display, in the same position as they were when first displayed. The skeletons are now housed in the Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences in Brussels.
The Bernissart Iguanodon was the last of the iguanodonts to be discovered. Paleontology had to wait nearly 60 years for the discovery of the next major dinosaur fossil find, the remains of the hadrosaurid dinosaurs, Hadrosaurus and Iguanodon.

In 1820, Tennyson composed the poem Ulysses and sent it to his friend Christopher Wordsworth. Wordsworth criticized the poem, advising Tennyson, 'I do not think it will ever be published' (Hutchinson 1981: 23). Tennyson, however, was undeterred. In 1828, he published the poem in the second edition of Poems by Two Brothers, along with poems by his brother Charles. In 1833, the poem was published in a collection of Tennyson's poetry entitled Poems, Chiefly Lyrical, with a preface by Samuel Taylor Coleridge. Ulysses is a departure in style from Tennyson's conventional iambic pentameter. The poem is written in alexandrine verse, with two stresses per line, the second one falling on the syntactically significant word.

The poem's setting, the Iliad and Odyssey, and characters, Ulysses and Ajax, are all drawn from the ancient world. Tennyson expresses an interest in the ancient world in his journal, written in 1833, 'I like the ancient world: I am a sort of Epicurean, a Hellenist, if you like, and therefore I am glad that your Gymnasium is so full of busts of Greek and Roman heroes' (Bate 2002: 31). His most recent predecessor to draw on the ancient world had been Byron, whose Childe Harold's Pilgrimage (1812) was set in the Middle Ages, specifically in the time of the Crusades. Tennyson's poem has been described as the first modern appropriation of the character of Ulysses from ancient sources, and it offers a significant addition to the ancient sources Tennyson has used, among them Homer's Iliad and Odyssey.

Before the formation of Alice in Chains, then @-@ drummer Layne Staley landed his first gig as a vocalist when he auditioned to front the glam metal band Sleze.
Staley was also playing guitar in his first band, Lydia's Symphony of Dawn, at this time.
When Sleze broke up, Staley formed Alice N' Chains with guitarist Jerry Cantrell and bassist Mike Starr.
That band name was shortened to Alice in Chains, and the trio was soon joined by drummer Sean Kinney.
The band's first gig was at the Red Square nightclub in Seattle on October 19, 1987.
The band's first recorded material was a demo tape that was passed on to Columbia Records.
By this time, the band's line-up was completed with the addition of second guitarist, Greg Hetson, who had played with the Circle Jerks and Bad Religion.
The band was signed to Columbia Records in 1989.
Alice In Chains' debut album, Facelift, was released on August 21, 1990.
It reached #41 on the Billboard 200 but the band felt that it was not the right time to release the album.
By the time the album received proper promotion, the grunge scene had taken over and the band returned to their hometown of Seattle to regroup.
The album's first single, "We Die Young," was released as a single in 1991, but the band did not release a follow-up single until 1992.
"Man In The Box," the second single from Facelift, was released in July 1992 and reached #1 on the Billboard Mainstream Rock Tracks chart.
The song was also a #1 hit on the Modern Rock Tracks chart and #28 on the Billboard Hot 100.
The song was the band's first top 10 hit and was certified platinum by the RIAA.
The band's second album, Dirt, was released on March 19, 1992.
The album peaked at #4 on the Billboard 200 and was certified five-times platinum by the RIAA.
The album sold over 10 million copies in the U.S. and was certified 25-times platinum by the RIAA.

The song was also a #2 hit on the Modern Rock Tracks chart and #12 on the Billboard Hot 100.
The song was the band's second top 10 hit and was certified platinum by the RIAA.

The album peaked at #1 on the Billboard 200 and was certified 10-times platinum by the RIAA.

The song was also a #1 hit on the Modern Rock Tracks chart and #13 on the Billboard Hot 100.
The song was the band's third top 10 hit and was certified platinum by the RIAA.
The band's fourth album, Alice in Chains , was released on March 20, 1995.
The album peaked at #1 on the Billboard 200 and was certified 10-times platinum by the RIAA.
The album sold over 5 million copies in the U.S. and was certified ten-times platinum by the RIAA.

## Biography

Mitsuda was born in Kanagawa Prefecture , Japan on August 22, 1968. He studied music at the Conservatory of Music in Yokohama. He was inspired to become a musician after hearing John Williams ' music in the movie E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial , and later cited the music of Yoko Kanno as an influence on his work.

Mitsuda began his career working for several video game companies, including Nintendo , where he worked on the Game Boy games Kirby 's Dream Land ( 1992 ) and Kirby's Dream Land 2 ( 1995 ); Jaleco , where he worked on the Game Boy games Densetsu no Stafy ( 1993 ) and Densetsu no Stafy 2 ( 1994 ); and Square , where he worked on the Super Famicom games FINAL FANTASY V ( 1992 ) and FINAL FANTASY VI ( 1994 ).

They are also able to survive longer periods of drought because of their ability to eat leaves from a wide variety of trees, including leguminous species.
The oribi is solitary or in small groups. It prefers to graze on grasses at night, but may feed during the day if food is scarce. However, it is more likely to be seen at night because it is shy and more active at this time.
The oribi has a large range, which includes most of sub-Saharan Africa , except for North Africa, the Sahel and Zaire.
The oribi is a small antelope, approximately 100 centimetres (39 in) in length. Its coat is brown to reddish-brown in colour, with a darker pattern on the head. It has a white underside, with a tassel of white hairs on the end of its tail. It weighs between 30 and 40 kilograms (66 and 88 pounds).
The oribi reproduces all year round. In the rainy season, oribis are able to give birth to a single calf. In the dry season, they give birth to twins. Females do not have a fixed breeding period, but they will usually mate with the dominant bull in the area.
The gestation period is 230 – 240 days, and the calves are weaned after 120 days. They reach sexual maturity at 18 months.

The road , also known as Old Post Road , was incorporated in 1813 as the Elk and Christiana Turnpike in order to get more money

for the post road after the opening of the Wilmington and Newark Turnpike. 

The road was part of the Old Post Road and was later designated as U.S. Route 202 and U.S. Route 40. In the 1920s, the road was designated as the U.S. Route 13 corridor.

## Route description

The road begins at the intersection of U.S. Route 13 and U.S. Route 40 in Delaware and heads north through the capital city of Dover. It then crosses the Delaware River at the Delaware Memorial Bridge and enters New Jersey. The road continues through Camden and Trenton before entering Pennsylvania. The road runs through Morristown and Hackettstown before ending at U.S. Route 22 in Netcong. 

In Pennsylvania, the road is known as the White Horse Pike, a reference to the road's former name for the white horse painted on the Blue Ball Tavern in White Horse, New Jersey.

## History

The road was established in the 18th century as the main road north from Philadelphia to New York City. It was one of the earliest turnpikes in the United States and was commissioned by the Pennsylvania General Assembly in 1792. 

The road was part of the King's Highway, a colonial road that ran from New York City to Boston. The road was also part of the King's Highway, which was built by George Washington and Thomas Jefferson.

In the 19th century, the road was part of the stagecoach route from New York City to Boston.

In 1911, the road was paved from Philadelphia to New York City.

The 47th Royal Marine Commando was assigned to capture the small harbour at Port @-@ en @-@ Bessin , on the boundary with Omaha

Beach. On the morning of 6 June, 2nd Lt. R.J.W. Morgan and 30 of his men of the 47th RM Cdo crossed the river in a rubber raft and landed on the beach to the west of Principal Point. The force was then split into two units, 30 men under Morgan and the remainder under 2nd Lt. B.A.O. Fraser.
Morgan's group moved inland and captured a small hamlet. They then moved south-east to capture the small towns of Guéblange-lès-Dieuze and Guéblange-lès-Entzheim. Fraser's group captured a small hamlet and a farmhouse on the heights north-east of the hamlet. The two groups then returned to the harbour, which was held by a platoon of the 47th RM Cdo and a platoon of the 49th RM Cdo. The harbour was heavily shelled, but caused no casualties.

The theme of love is central to the novel . Bolívar had a reputation as a womanizer , and books have been written on his philan

- thropic, political, and military exploits. But none have delved into the intimate details of his life. His love affairs have been covered in the pages of tabloids and gossip maga- zines with titles like "Bolívar's Six Wives." He was a man who loved women and who was passionately loved in return. Many historians have written about his love affairs, but they have been less than accurate in their details. As an effort to set the record straight, this book exposes the intimate details of his love life, from the relationships that Bolívar enjoyed with his wives and mistresses to his dally- ing affairs with prostitutes and courtesans. It also includes a chapter on his relationship with his son, whose mother was one of his many mistresses.
Many years of research have gone into this work. The author has traveled to several countries throughout the Americas to verify his sources. For the first time in many years, the author has received access to Bolívar's private journals (written in Spanish), which include his accounts of his love affairs and the women he met and befriended during his lifetime.
 The author has also consulted with the descendants of Bolívar's mistresses and wives and has been given access to their personal journals and correspondence. These sources were very helpful in confirming some of the details in these pages and provided information that had been omitted by historians.

Between 1737 and 1742 , Richard Pococke , an English anthropologist , toured the Middle East and wrote of what he thought were

'the most remarkable ruins in the world' . These were the site of Baalbek , the 'ruins of Heliopolis', and 'the ruins of Petra'. In the next century,  'the most remarkable ruins in the world' were the 'ruins of Palmyra'. In the early 1960s, a major German archaeological team excavated at Palmyra and dug out the remains of an immense 7th-century   basilica . On the basis of this discovery, the late Sir Max Mallowan  , the distinguished British archaeologist, suggested that Palmyra could be linked to the widespread ,  'new' Christianity of the 4th century.
 The term 'new' Christianity was first used by such scholars as Otto Bauernfeind  , who argued that from the 3rd to the 5th century a new type of Christianity emerged that was not only influenced by the doctrines of the church fathers , but also by the philosophies of the 'pagans', and particularly by the Platonism of the Greco-Egyptian world. In the next century, a new wave of scholars took up Bauernfeind's model, including Hans Georg Gadamer  and Werner Jaeger  . Gadamer , in his important work _Truth and Method_ , argued that the Christianity of the 4th century was a cultural movement – a movement that was influenced by the Platonism of the Greco-Egyptian world and that sought to 'sublimate' and 'transfigure' the world.
 At the time Bauernfeind and Gadamer were writing, the Syrian city of Palmyra was 'discovered' and made a cultural attraction for the tourists visiting Lebanon. The new attraction was the Great Temple of Bel, to which a new name – the Temple of Baal  – was given. The 1960s excavations of the Great Temple of Bel did indeed reveal a basilica dating from the 4th century and was 'the most remarkable ruin in the world'. At the same time these excavations revealed a number of inscriptions on the walls of the basilica, which enabled scholars to piece together a history of the Great Temple. The inscriptions revealed that the temple was dedicated to the cult of Bel-Marduk. The first temple on the site was built during the Seleucid period, around 150 BC, and was dedicated to the cult of Bel-Marduk. This temple was destroyed by the Romans under the Emperor Septimius Severus, around 200 AD, and the temple was rebuilt by the emperor's son, Caracalla. This second temple was dedicated to the cult of Jupiter Heliopolitanus, as a result of the growing influence of the Roman religion. The temple was destroyed again by the invading Islamic armies in the 630s and 640s.
The Great Temple of Bel in Palmyra, Syria, as it appears today.

The temple was destroyed again by the Romans in the 3rd century AD. The temple was rebuilt by the emperor Caracalla in the 210s AD and was later damaged by earthquakes and by the invading Islamic armies in the 630s and 640s.

Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was composed of six constituent republics : Bosnia @-@ Herzegovina , Croatia , Macedon

-ia , Montenegro , Serbia , and Slovenia . It was a socialist country, and a federation divided into two parts: the central communist government and the local communist governments of the republics. The six republics were further divided into oblasts (provinces).
Besides the six republics, the SFRY also included two autonomous provinces: Kosovo and Vojvodina .
The Socialist Republic of Bosnia - Herzegovina (in Bosnian language: Socijalisticka Republika Bosna i Hercegovina, in Croatian language: Socijalistička Republika Bosna i Hercegovina, and in Serbian language: Socijalistička Republika Bosna i Hercegovina) was a constituent republic of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (SFRY).
It had an area of 51,197 km (about the size of Maryland) with a population of 4,330,000 (1991 census). Bosnia-Herzegovina was formed from the western regions of the former Ottoman Empire, and was given to the Kingdom of Serbia and the Kingdom of Croatia after World War I. It was occupied by Nazi Germany in April 1941 and annexed to the Independent State of Croatia. After the liberation from Nazi occupation in 1945, it was included in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.
Bosnia-Herzegovina was one of the six republics of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. It declared sovereignty and independence in 1991, and went on to experience a long-lasting civil war which finally ended in 1995 with the signing of the Dayton Peace Agreement in Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, just outside of Dayton, Ohio, USA. The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was established as a member of the UN and a member state of the Council of Europe.
The Socialist Republic of Croatia (in Croatian language: Socijalistička Republika Hrvatska) was a constituent republic of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (SFRY).
Croatia was formed as a Socialist republic in 1945. In 1991, Croatia declared independence from Yugoslavia and in 1992, it became a member of the United Nations and the Council of Europe.
The Socialist Republic of Macedonia (in Macedonian language: Социјалистичка Република Македонија, Socijalistička Republika Makedonija) was a constituent republic of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (SFRY).
It had an area of 25,713 km (about the size of West Virginia) with a population of 2,198,452 (1991 census). The republic was named after Macedonia, one of the four historical republics of the First Yugoslavia (Kingdom of Serbia, Kingdom of Montenegro, Kingdom of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs, and the Kingdom of Yugoslavia).
The Socialist Republic of Montenegro (in Montenegrin language: Социјалистичка Република Црна Гора, Socijalistička Republika Crna Gora) was a constituent republic of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (SFRY).
It had an area of 13,810 km (about the size of Delaware) with a population of 760,000 (1991 census). Montenegro was formed in 1945 from territories of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. In 1991, Montenegro declared independence from Yugoslavia and formed a federal state called the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

Otter and Staunch both fell rapidly behind Boadicea , while Africaine pulled far ahead . By 18 : 20 , lookouts on Africaine cou

riered the news to the other vessels, who promptly shortened sail and began closing the distance to the sinking ship. Aframis and Tangerine were closest to Africaine when the order came down to fire their guns; the first shots were fired at 1 8 : 25 .
The situation was rapidly becoming critical. Africaine and Otter were close enough to be in danger of running into each other, and Africaine was not yet close enough to the sinking ship to pick up survivors. One of the two ships that had been nearest to Africaine, however, was about to go to her aid. 50 A short time later, Tangerine, which had been commanded by Captain John F. D. Sweeting, came up to Africaine 's port quarter and took over the task of rescue, while Africaine turned away and headed for the bay.
Africaine 's captain, Commander Barkley, had to keep his ship close to the wind to drive her towards the bay, and this meant that the ship was still at anchor when the first of the survivors from Boadicea were hauled aboard.
It was not until 18 : 45 that Africaine and Tangerine could begin to take aboard survivors from Boadicea . On the way in, the ships had to pass Otter and Staunch. Both ships had still been close enough to the sinking ship to get an accurate bearing on the survivors who were in the water, and both ships had been ordered to pick up the survivors from the water. Staunch never made it to the survivors. 51 At 18 : 45, she was struck by a large wave that smashed her onto the coral reef and sank her within four minutes. 52 Otter was a different story.
She had taken her time making her entry into the bay, and had picked up survivors from Boadicea only after Africaine and Tangerine had made good progress towards the bay. Otter was also able to rescue more of the Boadicea 's survivors than Africaine. The rescue operation in the bay continued for a little over two hours, until 20 : 25. During this time, Otter and Africaine had taken aboard 95 survivors and had left 126 in the water. 53 Africaine 's log for the evening of 11 August recorded that 31 of the 126 survivors left in the water had been picked up by Tangerine. 54 Tangerine 's log, however, recorded that she had taken aboard 90 survivors and had left 110 in the water. 55 In addition, Otter 's log recorded that she had left 78 in the water. 56 Otter and Africaine had both picked up survivors from Boadicea , but Otter picked up more.
The reason for this was that Otter remained in the bay until 20 : 20, after which she left Africaine behind and continued out to sea to pick up survivors from Otter. When Otter had finished her search, however, Africaine was still searching in the bay. 57 Otter had left Africaine behind because Africaine had been ordered to stand off shore and wait for the other vessels that had been ordered to go out to sea to pick up survivors from Otter. The existing harbour regulations were not set up to cope with a situation in which there were survivors in the water and ships were trying to pick up the survivors, and the problem would soon be worsened by the fact that Africaine 's rescue operation in the bay was taking longer than the ships' captains had anticipated.

Devin Garrett Townsend (born May 5, 1972) is a Canadian musician, songwriter, and producer. He was the founder, songwriter, vocalist and guitarist in extreme metal band Strapping Young Lad from 1994 to 2007, and has since continued as a solo artist. He has released a number of solo albums, including four under the Devin Townsend Project name, in addition to other albums under the name Devin.
Townsend has also contributed to the music of numerous other bands, including the Canadian metal band Annihilator, the British extreme metal band GWAR, the Canadian heavy metal band Nevermore, and the Canadian alternative rock band The Smashing Pumpkins. His music has been featured in video games such as Saints Row, Guitar Hero III, and Skate 2, and in the film 300. He has also written and starred in the animated short film Devin Townsend Presents: Ziltoid the Omniscient.
Townsend has been lauded by music critics for his musicianship, as well as his social media presence and dedication to interacting with his fanbase.
Townsend was born in New Westminster, British Columbia, to an American father and a Dutch mother. His father was a military man who worked for the United States Air Force during the Vietnam War.
Townsend grew up in Calgary, Alberta. As a child, Townsend was diagnosed with Tourette syndrome, an involuntary neurological disorder which includes symptoms such as tics and involuntary noises. Although Townsend's tics have been controlled by medication, his Tourette syndrome led to him being bullied and teased as a child, which he says led to him developing a low self-esteem and a desire to rebel against his parents. Townsend's father was a Jehovah's Witness, and as a result, Townsend was raised in the religion.
Townsend's first musical exposure was listening to music that his father had brought back from the United States. His father would listen to music such as Led Zeppelin and Kansas in the car, and Townsend's mother would listen to a lot of country music. Townsend learned to play the piano and took lessons from an early age. His mother eventually bought him an electric guitar and Townsend would experiment with different genres, including heavy metal. Townsend has cited Slayer and Metallica as his earliest influences. Townsend also listened to bands such as Black Sabbath, Judas Priest, Iron Maiden and Rush. Townsend began playing in bands at the age of 12, and by the age of 15, Townsend had dropped out of high school and moved to Vancouver, British Columbia to pursue a musical career.
The name Ziltoid is a combination of Devin Townsend's middle name, Zil, and the word "zodiac".
Townsend's first band, called Casualties of Cool, released two demos. In 1992, Townsend joined the progressive metal band Annihilator on lead vocals and rhythm guitar. Townsend was a member of the band for five years, contributing to the albums Set the World on Fire (1993), King of the Kill (1994) and Refresh the Demon (1996). Townsend was also the bassist and backing vocalist for the Canadian metal band Wild Dogs.
In 1994, Townsend formed the band Strapping Young Lad. Townsend wrote all the material for the band and was the only constant member. Townsend had worked with former members of the band, including former members of Annihilator, while he was in Annihilator.
Townsend released his first solo album, Heavy as a Really Heavy Thing, under the name Devin Townsend in 1995. Heavy as a Really Heavy Thing was released to positive reviews. During the era of log floating , logjams sometimes occurred when logs struck an obstacle . Log rafts floating down the West Bra

zos had been known to run aground on submerged mud flats, where the river bottom was covered with a slushy mud that could trap logs. Logjams could also occur on channels that had insufficient water flow to carry the logs downstream.
Logjams have also been known to occur on the San Marcos River, where stagnant water sometimes causes logs to settle to the bottom and form a dam. When too many logs are trapped in one area, the water level rises and the dam is breached.
The IH 35 bridge over the river at San Marcos was known to be particularly prone to logjams. Many of the capsized logs from the 1982 logjam were driven by the river current onto the bridge, where they dammed the roadway and caused a major traffic jam.
