Although never officially disbanding , Alice in Chains was plagued by extended inactivity from 1996 onwards due to Staley 's su

ndry addictions and involvement in the supergroup Mad Season. Staley was found dead on the morning of May 18, 2002.

## History

### Formation and early years (1987–1990)

Alice in Chains was formed in Seattle, Washington in 1987 by guitarist/vocalist Jerry Cantrell and bassist Mike Starr, after the former's band, Diamond Lie, disbanded. Alice in Chains was named after Starr's pet dog, Alice, which was in turn named after Alice Cooper. Starr was a fan of the band and named the dog after the rock singer. After recruiting drummer Sean Kinney and guitarist/vocalist Layne Staley, the band released its debut EP, We Die Young, in 1989 on C/Z Records. In 1990 the band was signed by Columbia Records and released its first album, Facelift. The album was a commercial and critical success, selling over four million copies worldwide and earning the band a Grammy Award nomination for Best Hard Rock Performance.

### Success (1991–1993)

The band's second album, Dirt, was released on August 21, 1992. After the album's release, Alice in Chains toured with Pearl Jam, Soundgarden, and Nirvana. Dirt sold over two million copies in the United States alone. The album was certified double platinum in 1994. The band filmed the music video for the single "Them Bones" in the Arizona desert.

The band's third album, Alice in Chains, was released on September 29, 1995. The band's album, Jerry Cantrell, and the song, "What the Hell Have I" were all nominated for Grammys. In 1992, Alice in Chains was the first artist to be nominated for a Grammy in the newly created Best Hard Rock/Metal Performance Vocal or Instrumental category. The band was nominated for a Grammy for "Would?" in 1994.

### Disbandment (1994–2002)

By 1994, Alice in Chains had signed to Columbia Records. The band released its fourth album, 1995's Alice in Chains, which would be the last album to feature Layne Staley before his death. The album was nominated for a Grammy for Best Heavy Metal/Hard Rock Performance. The band filmed the music video for the single, "Grind", in the desert of the Mojave Desert.

Following a tour with Kiss, Alice in Chains took a hiatus. Staley was the main songwriter for the band and suffered from substance abuse problems. The band released a greatest hits album, Nothing Safe: Best of the Box in 1999. It featured three new songs, "Get Born Again", "A Little Bitter" and "Hate to Feel". The band released a live album, Live, on November 18, 2002.

### Post-disbandment (2009–2010)

On April 15, 2009, the band reunited for a private show at the Moore Theatre in Seattle, Washington. The show featured the original lineup of the band: Jerry Cantrell, Sean Kinney, Mike Starr, and Layne Staley. On June 29, 2009, the band reunited live again at a memorial show for the late Chris Cornell. Jerry Cantrell and Mike Inez played alongside William DuVall and Soundgarden drummer Matt Cameron.

### Reunion (2012–present)

On August 2, 2012, it was announced that Alice in Chains would reunite and make a new album. In April 2013, it was again announced that the band had begun recording the new album.

On August 30, 2013, Alice in Chains performed at the 2013 Reading Festival.

Many Egyptologists and anthropologists have suggested theories about how the gods developed in these early times . Gustave Jéqu

ot, for instance, believed that ancient Egyptian art and religion deified the animals and plants that were the most vital to the people of the Nile Valley. The Egyptians, he argued, revered the animals and plants that were most important to them because they needed to believe that these creatures were in control of nature. Jéquot believed that these ancient Egyptians were "animists" who viewed the world as a world of spirits. The people of ancient Egypt believed that everything had a spirit. They believed that the woods and fields, the fields and the valleys, the rivers, and the waterfalls were filled with spirits. In this way of thinking, everything had a spirit, and the spirits controlled the world.
The ancient Egyptians, Jéquot argued, therefore believed that they needed to control the spirits through their gods. The gods, according to Jéquot's theory, were the "spirits of the spirits." These gods were the spirits of all the animals and plants that were in control of nature. They were worshipped to obtain their power so that the ancient Egyptians could control the spirits.
Jéquot's theory of the origin of the Egyptian gods is a highly controversial one. Other Egyptologists and anthropologists argue that the gods developed out of the primitive fertility cults of the prehistoric peoples of ancient Egypt. Worshipped as a god, the king was believed to be in control of the Nile, and, therefore, of the fertility of the land.
So, far from being the "spirits of the spirits," the ancient Egyptians believed that the gods were the spirits of the king. The king was believed to be a god in a human body. He was the one who made the Nile rise, the one who was in charge of the fertility of the land. The religion of ancient Egypt, therefore, was based on the worship of the king, who was a god.

The sun shone on the living so that they could live.
The ancient Egyptians believed that Re was the father of all the gods. Re was also married to the goddess of the moon, Tefnut. Together, Re and Tefnut had two children, Shu and Geb. Shu and Geb were the king and queen of Egypt. They were the first king and queen of Egypt. The king and queen were believed to be the soul and the body of the Egyptian people.

Lennon and Yoko Ono co @-@ produced the song and album of the same name with Phil Spector . Recording began at Lennon 's home s

tereo system in December 1970 and was finished in a single day by Spector 's team. On " What a Wonderful World " and " Don't Let Me Down " Lennon stated that he and Yoko wanted to reunite the two songs after their previous duet, " God ", in which Lennon had sung, "God is a concept by which we measure our pain". On " I Can't Help ( Falling in Love With You )" Lennon sang Marilyn Monroe's rendition of the song from Elvis Presley's musical Blue Hawaii (1961). He also stated that he was the first to play the song in public.

The album's final track, " Steel and Glass ", was a 12-minute faux-classical song that Lennon had written in 1968. Lennon had intended for the song to be included on the White Album (1968) but was rejected by McCartney and George Harrison after they heard it. He asked Paul McCartney to sing a duet with him on the song, but he refused. Yoko Ono suggested her and Lennon's son, Sean Lennon , to sing the song instead. 

The album was not well-received by the music press. In a retrospective review in 2008, The Guardian 's Sean O'Hagan described the album as "a series of pleasant, unremarkable songs" and "perfectly pleasant". In 2010, Rolling Stone ranked it at number 43 on their list of "The 100 Best Albums of the Seventies".

Mogadishu 's economy has grown rapidly since the city 's pacification in mid 2011 . The SomalFruit processing factory was reope

ned in 2012. The city's gross domestic product (GDP) is estimated at $1.4 billion with an annual growth of 2.2%. In 2014, the average income was $4,000 per capita.

The large informal sector is the backbone of the city's economy, accounting for 80% of GDP. The formal sector accounts for 20% of the city's GDP.
Mogadishu's economy is based on commerce and services. The city is home to the only Somali airline, Daallo Airlines . Mogadishu is the location of the Mogadishu International Airport .
The city's economy is predominantly reliant on foreign aid. Mogadishu is the second most important centre of commerce in Somalia after Hargeisa .
Although the city's economy is struggling, the local currency, the Somali shilling, has become stronger than ever.

The next German aircraft on the scene , a Junkers 88 , was engaged by a RAF Bristol Beaufighter which had appeared in the area

10 minutes earlier. The Junkers was shot down and crashed into the sea about 900 yards from the shore (E-10). This was within 300 yards of the remaining members of No. 22 Squadron and caused considerable confusion. The pilot of Beaufighter was Sgt. E. Turquand of 317 Squadron, his aircraft being R1403.
E-10 was situated only a few hundred yards south of the group of ships which included the damaged NORFOLK and the destroyer CAMDEN. The CAMDEN was anchored in the inner position, and the NORFOLK was astern of her. The destroyer FIREFLY was some 200 yards south of the NORFOLK. The destroyer DIAMOND was about 300 yards south of the NORFOLK, and the destroyer INVINCIBLE was about 400 yards south of the NORFOLK. The 15th Destroyer Flotilla was now deployed in a line from the CAMDEN to the INVINCIBLE.
The development of the battle was delayed by the arrival of the British cruisers COLOSSUS and CAIRO from Gibraltar. The COLOSSUS was now placed in the outer position, and the CAIRO was between the CAMDEN and the NORFOLK.
A further disturbance was caused by a British aircraft which caused the enemy to open fire at a destroyer. This was the first of two occasions when a British aircraft caused the enemy to fire at a British ship, and this factor was to have a serious effect on the British Commanders during the remainder of the action.
The COLOSSUS was now sent to the outer position, and the CAIRO to the inner position. The destroyer GLOXINIA, which was now the 15th Flotilla leader, was ordered to move to the inner position.
The enemy escorting force now consisted of two cruisers and nine destroyers, although it was still not clear whether this was the whole of the enemy naval forces.
The enemy cruisers were now ordered to open fire on the British ships, which were still in motion, and at the same time the destroyers were ordered to attack the British ships.
Further RAF aircraft now arrived on the scene, and a Spitfire engaged an enemy aircraft which had appeared. The Spitfire was R4568 of 263 Squadron, piloted by Flt. Sgt. B. E. White. He was now engaged by enemy AA fire, and after a few minutes he came down. The RAF report states that he was shot down by enemy fighters, but it is known that he was shot down by the Cruiser HEINRICH LETTNER, which is the only German warship with guns of this calibre.
The Jingling Palace ( 景灵宫 , Jingling Gong ) , a temple to the legendary Yellow Emperor located near modern @-@ day Qufu , was b

ustling with activity in the summer of 1368. The visiting monk Chu Chang ( 楚畅 ) had been there for nearly a decade and was among those partaking in the ritual observance of the emperor's birthday. The local governor, the scholar-official Xu Chong ( 徐崇 ) , was there to present a scroll of calligraphy, accompanied by a poem.
The scroll was a record of recent events. It documented the theft of a dozen or so large jars of wine from a temple in the nearby town of Tengcheng ( 滕城 , in modern Zibo , Shandong Province ) and the capture and execution of one of the perpetrators, a Confucian scholar from the town of Mingzhou ( 铭州 , in modern Bozhou , Anhui Province ) named Chen Yi ( 陈毅 ). (The incident would be recorded in Song Yingxing's Taiping guangji , which was published in the early sixteenth century.)
The poem was written by the famous poet Su Shi, who was then living in retirement in the nearby town of Aiqing ( 爱庆 , in modern Zibo, Shandong Province ). Su's poem, written in the style of the rhapsodists of the Tang dynasty (618–907), recorded the joys of being drunk.
Xu presented the scroll and poem to the temple's priest, who was pleased to receive them. He immediately added them to the shrine of the Jade Emperor at the temple.
The Jingling Palace was one of China's most important temples to the Yellow Emperor, the legendary founder of the Chinese nation. (The Jade Emperor was another name for the Yellow Emperor.) It was also the home of the sacred spirit of Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty, who was worshipped as the Jade Emperor himself.
The Jingling Palace was built in the reign of Emperor Taizong, in 630, on a site that had been the residence of Yellow Emperor's grandson, King Zhuanxu ( 褚胤 ). In the years that followed, the site had been an imperial garden and shrine.
The temple was located some 20 miles east of Qufu, in the town of Jiaxiang ( 嘉翔 , in modern Qufu, Shandong Province ). It was a popular pilgrimage destination. In 1368, when Chu Chang visited, it was surrounded by a large village of pilgrims.
The monk Chu Chang was a disciple of Zhan Ru ( 占睿 ) , a famous literatus who was born in the town of Lincheng ( 临城 , in modern Linyi, Shandong Province ) in 1263 and died in 1349. Chu was born in 1315 and died in 1377.
Chu was born in the Xiang clan of the Qiang tribe, which had served the Song dynasty as defenders of the border. He belonged to the fourth generation of his family that served as border guards. In 1269, when he was six years old, his father, Chu Fang ( 楚芳 ) , was killed in battle against the Mongols. His mother, Chu Ying ( 楚膺 ) , died shortly thereafter. In 1270, Chu was adopted by a man named Chen Chang ( 陈畅 ) , who was also a border guard.
In 1277, he was adopted by Zhan Ru, who had been a teacher of his father's. Zhan was then a professor at the Imperial University at Lincheng. Zhan would come to think of Chu as his son.
Zhan was born in 1263 and died in 1349. He was born in Lincheng, in modern Qingyang County, Shaanxi Province , to a poor family. When he was young, he was known for his intelligence and literary talent. He was a disciple of the Zen Buddhist priest Yuanwu ( 元吴 ) , whose teaching had a profound impact on him.

Torres made his competitive debut for Liverpool against Aston Villa in a 2 – 1 win on 11 August 2007 . He made his first appear

ence for the England under-21 team on 21 November 2008 in a 2 – 0 win at the City of Manchester Stadium against Lithuania . He scored his first goal for Liverpool on 11 January 2009 in a 2 – 0 win against Middlesbrough . He also scored the winning goal in the 2008–09 UEFA Champions League Final .
Prior to his Liverpool career, Torres was a Spanish youth international, having represented his country at under-17, under-19 and under-21 levels, winning the 2003 UEFA European Under-17 Football Championship and the 2004 European Under-19 Football Championship. He was also selected for the under-21 squad for the 2006 UEFA European Under-21 Football Championship, during which he scored three goals in four matches.
Torres made his debut for the Spain national football team in a friendly match against Argentina in February 2006. In the 2006 FIFA World Cup, Torres became the youngest player to score a goal in the finals, netting in the 31st minute of Spain's 2–1 win over Tunisia in their opening group match. He was also the youngest Spanish player to score at the World Cup finals, at 19 years, 2 months and 25 days old. He became only the seventh teenager to score in the World Cup finals, following Pelé and Rivelino in 1958, Just Fontaine and Wolfgang Weber in 1954, and Pele and Miroslav Klose in 2002. Torres was also the fourth teenager to score in the first match of the tournament. Torres scored three goals in the 2008 UEFA European Football Championship, in matches against Germany, Switzerland and the Czech Republic, and finished the tournament as the joint top scorer alongside David Villa. He scored the only goal in Spain's 1–0 win over Russia in the Euro 2008 final, which earned Spain the title of European champion for the first time. He scored the only goal in Spain's 1–0 win over Argentina in the 2010 World Cup qualifier.
Torres was also part of the Spanish team that won the 2008 Summer Olympics football tournament. He scored a hat-trick against China PR in the group stage which gave Spain a 3–1 victory and qualified them for the quarter-finals. However, Torres was not selected for the finals in Beijing, as he was too young to be eligible. In November 2009, Torres was named in Spain's squad for the 2010 FIFA World Cup qualification matches against Italy and Russia.
Torres is a product of the Liverpool youth system, having joined the club at the age of 11. He signed his first professional contract in 2001. On 19 August 2007, manager Rafael Benítez announced that Torres had signed a new long-term contract with the club, keeping him at Anfield until 2012. He was named the PFA Young Player of the Year in 2008, the FWA Footballer of the Year in 2009 and was nominated for the Ballon d'Or in the same year. He was named into the PFA Team of the Year for the 2008–09 Premier League season.
Liverpool manager Rafael Benítez has often used Torres in a central striking role, preferring to use him alongside another striker rather than alongside Peter Crouch. Following the departure of Crouch to Tottenham Hotspur, it is expected that Torres will play in a lone striking role, or alongside a partner such as Ryan Babel or David Ngog.
Torres has a very good shot, and is able to score goals from long range as well as in the penalty area. His control and technique are among the best in the league, and his movement is good. He also has a good heading ability, and is very good in the air.
A few weeks after Of Human Feelings was recorded , Mwanga went to Japan to negotiate a deal with Trio Records to have the album

released there. In the same way that he had sought to help native musicians in Africa by making their work available to a wider audience, he now sought to help African musicians in Japan whose careers had been stymied by the difficulty of finding an audience.
This was to be the first of a series of collaborations with Trio Records, and as the relationship matured, Mwanga began to look for more unorthodox ways of making music available to people. In addition to the traditional CD format, Mwanga began to use his close contact with the Trio Records staff to create a series of limited edition vinyl releases, an opportunity to bring the listener a musical experience that was not readily available in Japan.
Throughout the same year, Mwanga continued to follow the footsteps of his mentor, the late James Baldwin, and to travel around the world. He traveled to the Netherlands, where, at the invitation of the writer, essayist and cultural critic, Gert-Jan van der Schoot, he spoke at the annual Culturele Kwaku-Race conference in Amsterdam. He also traveled to New York, where he gave a talk at the United Nations on the same subject of race, and was a guest on the NPR program Fresh Air with Terry Gross.
Another of Mwanga's projects was to collaborate with the art curator and gallerist, Emily Hage, to produce an exhibition of art in which each piece was inspired by a different song on Of Human Feelings, with the songs themselves played in the background. The exhibition was held at the Underground Museum in Los Angeles, where it attracted much attention.
Mwanga also traveled to the Philippines, where he was an invited guest at the annual Cebu International Film Festival, which he attended with his manager, the Swiss-born film director Christian Frei.
During the same period, Mwanga's music was also featured on numerous film, television and radio programs.
Mwanga was also to become a regular guest on the popular morning radio show, The Takeaway, on public radio's WNYC, and he began to appear on television as well. He was interviewed on the BBC's The Culture Show, and he also appeared on the CNN program, African Voices.
 In 2014 Mwanga was to make his first trip to China, where he gave a series of lectures at universities in Shanghai and Nanjing.
In September 2014, Mwanga gave a series of lectures at the University of New South Wales, in Sydney, Australia, where he was the artist in residence.
In October 2014, Mwanga was the first artist to be invited to the University of Pennsylvania to take part in a lecture series on the life and work of James Baldwin. Fort Glanville Conservation Park is one of South Australia 's most important heritage sites . It is the premier site in the sta

tes for the preservation and interpretation of the development of the state 's two major cities: Adelaide and Port Adelaide .
The fort was part of a defence system that had been built up along the Port River in the 1840s. It was originally called Fort Glanville but was renamed Fort Largs after the Scottish town of Largs in the 1890s.
Glanville Fort was built to defend the port from attack by the French navy in the 1840s. It is one of the most significant sites for the study of Australia 's defence history.
The fort was fortified with eight cannons, which were mounted on a wooden platform at the top of the gun battery. Glanville Fort was an important link in the chain of forts that protected the harbour. The fort was manned by a garrison of 30 soldiers who slept in huts built around the battery.
The fort was closed in 1871 when the threat of invasion from France was over. It was decommissioned in 1885.
The fort has been developed into a conservation park and the remains of the fort, the city walls, the Port River and the original buildings are still visible.
Fort Glanville Conservation Park is of state significance for its historical associations with the early development and defence of the Port River. The fort is of state significance for its rarity as an example of a 19th century fort, and for the views and remnant vegetation in the conservation park.
Fort Glanville Conservation Park is of local significance for its historical associations with the early development and defence of the Port River.

In 1640 Charles dismissed his Parliament and followed the advice of his French allies to call a new one. This new Parliament would be more to his liking, and he hoped that it would bring about a peace with the Scots and with the Dutch; he would have to grant the Scots a new charter, however, if he wanted peace with the English .
The Long Parliament was far from favorable to the king. In early 1642 it passed an act that deprived Charles of direct control of the army and the navy. Late that year it formed the First Barebones Parliament, a kind of provisional government. In 1643 Parliament abolished the monarchy and declared England a republic. Charles was imprisoned in the Isle of Wight, and in 1644 the Scots defeated and captured him. He was taken by his captors to Newcastle, and there he agreed to the Covenant, the Scots' religious bargain.
Charles was soon released and returned to England to become the prisoner of the Parliament. This time he was imprisoned at Hurst Castle, on the Isle of Wight. In this new captivity he was allowed more freedom of movement, and he was able to see his wife and children. But these brief periods of freedom had a price: in 1647 his family was taken hostage.

The Cromwellian regime, which took over after the execution of Charles I, was founded on the dislike of monarchy. In 1653 Parliament abolished the monarchy and declared England a republic. The next year the head of the army, Oliver Cromwell, declared himself lord protector of the realm, and he ruled England until his death in 1658.
His son Richard, however, was not accepted as lord protector, and when he died in 1659 the country was left without a head of state. It was then that Charles II became king and England returned to its position as a monarchy. Charles's reign was more than a return to "the old order." The rise of Puritanism and the Civil War had changed not only church and state but also the lives of the people. Charles II, with the help of his brother, the Duke of York, tried to restore something of what had been before the war, but he could not undo the changes.
Whereas the Commonwealth had been a republic without a head of state, the kingdom was now a monarchy with its head in a foreign country. Charles was in exile in France , and the power of the country lay in the hands of the king's brother, the duke—later the king—of York.
The duke's first act was to restore the Anglican Church as the established church. This was not just a restoration, however: the Church of England was made an even more powerful institution than it had ever been, and it proved the greatest obstacle to reform.
The restoration of the Church meant an end to the freedom of religion that had existed in England since the reign of Elizabeth I. During the Commonwealth, when the Anglican Church had been abolished, all churches had come under the jurisdiction of the state. But the Anglican Church had been restored to its position as the established church, and the other churches were forced to give up their buildings and had to pay taxes to the state.

SR 243 begins at SR 74 in the San Jacinto Wilderness near Mountain Center , Riverside County as Idyllwild Road . The highway tr

ends eastward, passing through the San Jacinto Wilderness via Johnson Valley Road to the south, and through the San Bernardino National Forest via Cedar Springs Road to the north.
SR 243's first interchange is with SR 74, where SR 243 is signed as Idyllwild Highway . The route heads east through the San Jacinto Wilderness, passing through the San Gorgonio Pass and the communities of Mountain Center , White Water , and Idyllwild . At this point, SR 243 enters the city of Anza and is known as Anza Road .
SR 243 runs due east through Anza, California, then enters the Chino Hills State Park. The highway meets the I-10 freeway at the western terminus of the Chino Hills State Park. SR 243 is signed as a spur route, as it continues eastward to the Rancho Santa Ana Botanic Garden in the city of Claremont . The route continues east through the Santa Ana Mountains and Claremont, before meeting SR 210, at which point the route is known as Mount Baldy Road .
SR 243 continues eastward into the San Gabriel Mountains, and crosses the San Gabriel River into the city of Azusa. The route crosses the San Bernardino County line into Los Angeles County . In the city of Duarte, SR 243 meets SR 118 and is signed as Foothill Boulevard . The route heads eastward, passing through the cities of Sierra Madre and Arcadia , before meeting SR 2, at which point it is signed as Baldwin Avenue. The route ends at SR 2's intersection with SR 134.
SR 243 is part of the California Freeway and Expressway System , and is part of the National Highway System , a network of highways that are considered essential to the country's economy, defense, and mobility by the Federal Highway Administration . SR 243 is eligible to be included in the State Scenic Highway System , but it is not officially designated as a scenic highway by the California Department of Transportation .

Along with her husband , Eva visited every corner of the country , becoming the first woman in Argentina 's history to appear i

n such a role.
Born in 1926 in the town of Mercedes , Eva Peron was the daughter of a humble railway worker and a schoolteacher. When she was twelve she suffered a serious illness which left her with a disability in her arm. She was married at the age of eighteen to her cousin Juan Duarte , a former schoolmate. The marriage was dissolved in 1945 and she became pregnant with Duarte's child. Eva gave birth to a son, Juan, and took up modelling work in Buenos Aires to support the child. At the age of twenty-three she met Colonel Juan Domingo Peron , a former army officer , who had been dismissed from the army and was then working in a number of jobs. In 1945 Peron was appointed Governor of the province of Buenos Aires. Eva became his mistress and in 1946 they had a daughter, Isabella, born with Down's syndrome. In 1946 Peron was elected President of Argentina , although he was dismissed by the army in 1955 and spent twenty-two months in exile in Paraguay . He returned to Argentina in 1957, and three years later Eva was appointed Minister of Labour in the Peron government. She began to use the name 'Evita' , and her image was used to promote 'Peronismo', the Peronist political movement which was supported by a large proportion of the population. In 1951 she gave birth to a second son, Gabriel. In an attempt to present themselves as a model family, Eva and Juan Peron had their daughter Isabella's Down's syndrome officially removed from the birth certificate.
Eva Peron visited every corner of Argentina , meeting the poor and the rural workers. She was aided by a team of secretaries and assistants, including her sister-in-law, Marta Duarte . Early members of the ceratopsian group , such as Psittacosaurus , were small bipedal animals . Later members , including cerato

-saurs of the subfamily Centrosaurinae , were quadrupedal herbivores with a beak and possibly a frill on the back of the skull .
The Centrosaurinae may have had horns on the bones above and below the eyes, and in some cases a horn above the nose. Some horns or frills were used for display, while others may have had other functions.
The Centrosaurinae were found in western North America and Asia, and were alive in the late Cretaceous period, about 72 million to 68 million years ago.
The most complete fossils of ceratopsian dinosaurs come from the Late Cretaceous in Asia, and are from the Nemegt Formation of Mongolia .
Centrosaurine ceratopsians were quadrupedal herbivores. They ranged in size from the 2.5 to 3.5 tonne, long-necked and long-tailed Centrosaurus and the 1.25 to 1.75 tonne, short-necked and short-tailed Einiosaurus to the 1.5 to 2.5 tonne, long-necked and long-tailed Psittacosaurus .
Centrosaurine ceratopsians had a horned frill in the back of the skull. They also had various bony structures on their heads that have been interpreted as either display structures or weapons. The ceratopsians were anatomically well-adapted to browsing, and may have been browsers of high-growth, soft vegetation.
Unlike chasmosaurine ceratopsians, no ceratopsians with elaborate horns on the frill have been found in Asia.
Centrosaurinae are known from the Late Cretaceous of Asia and North America.
The most common centrosaurine ceratopsians in North America are Centrosaurus and Psittacosaurus.
In Asia, the centrosaurine ceratopsians Einiosaurus, Monoclonius, and Titanoceratops have been found.
The centrosaurines had very long necks, which allowed them to browse high above the ground. Their skulls were relatively long and narrow, and their bony frill was small. Their skulls and other bones were covered in horned structures, and some species had horns above and below the eyes.
Centrosaurines were herbivores.

First described in 1927 by the West Australian botanist Charles Gardner , the species was at one stage considered a variety of

120 ( _Melaleuca uncinata_ subsp. _variabilis_ ). However, its differences to the type proved distinctive, and it was granted full species status in 1984. Although it does not occur in Tasmania, it resembles the coastal heaths of that state.
It is a shrub or small tree usually growing to 1.5 m, sometimes to 4 m. The bark is pale grey, fibrous and papery, and prone to shedding. The leaves are linear to lanceolate (about 2 cm long), glossy and dark green above, and paler, dull and sometimes glaucous below. The flowers are yellow-green and are borne in clusters in leaf axils. They are followed by the distinctive narrow, finger-like seed pods that give rise to the English name.
The plant is very common along the coastal fringes of the south west and particularly in the Esperance area. It is often found on sandy soils, but is also found on rocky coastal headlands.
The plant is a food source for the larvae of the _Eucalypt tortilis_ moth, and the bee fly _Melanosphecia bradleyi_.
A number of species of _Melaleuca_ were used as toiletries (oils, soaps and medicines) by the aboriginal people of the south west.

_Melaleuca cucullata_ Benth. is a small to medium tree, usually growing to about 15 m tall. It is similar in appearance to the closely related _Melaleuca lanceolata_ but is distinguished by its longer leaves that are about 1.5 cm long. The leaves are densely covered with fine hairs, giving the plant a whitish, silvery-grey appearance. The flowers are yellow to orange and are borne in dense clusters at the tips of the branches. The seed pods are narrow and pointed and usually 2 cm long.
_Melaleuca cucullata_ is usually a coastal tree, but it is also found inland. The plant is found along the western coast of southern Australia, from just north of Fitzgerald River National Park in the west to around the Bunbury region in the east.
The plant was first formally described in 1867 by George Bentham, who gave it the name _Melaleuca cucullata_ , from specimens collected by William Baxter at Nuyts Land, near Esperance. The specific epithet _cucullata_ comes from the Latin _cucullus_ , meaning 'a hood'.
_Melaleuca cucullata_ was commonly known as paperbark, owing to its use as a source of paper by the aboriginal people of the south west.
The flowers are visited by the _Melaleuca cucullata_ moth, the _Melaleuca cucullata_ bee fly and the _Melaleuca cucullata_ bee.
_Melaleuca cucullata_ is a larval host for the _Calyptra eugraphica_ moth.

## Distribution and habitat

The song sparrow has a vast breeding range stretching from Alaska to Newfoundland and south to Mexico and Northwest Costa Rica, and has been spotted in the Bahamas . It is found in most habitat types except dense forest, coniferous forest, and dense scrub.

### Migration

Unlike most North American land birds, the song sparrow remains resident throughout the year. Small populations that migrate southward or eastward to escape the northern winter are known to occur in the United States, Mexico, and the Bahamas.

### Winter range

The song sparrow is resident throughout its vast breeding range in North America.

## Behavior

This species forages in vegetation of all types. During the breeding season, song sparrows sing throughout the day. They do not sing as much during the winter.

### Feeding

The diet of the song sparrow consists of seeds, insects, and other invertebrates. They eat buds, flowers, and fruits of plants including alder, birch, hawthorn, cherry, juniper, and wild rose. Insects eaten by sparrows include grasshoppers, beetles, leafhoppers, caterpillars, ants, wasps, and aphids. They also eat spiders, snails, earthworms, and slugs.

### Breeding

The song sparrow is a cavity nester. The male defends his territory throughout the year and often tries to mate with other males in the area. Males sing and display in their territories. They will also sing and display to females during their courtship. They may also sing and display to other males. The female chooses the male she wants to mate with. After mating, the male defends the area around the female as she builds a nest. The female builds the nest, usually a cup-shaped structure of grass, leaves, and twigs, lined with feathers. The male helps her find the location of the nest. The nest is located in a tree hole or crevice, or it may be built on the ground, or even in a human-made structure such as a barn or house. The female eggs eggs cover them with fine grass, leaves, and feathers. The nest may be reused by the female for several years.

Three to five eggs are laid, usually in April or May. The female incubates the eggs for about 12 to 13 days. The eggs hatch in another 11 to 12 days. The female broods the chicks for the first few days, and the male brings food for her. The male and female feed the chicks for about 10 days, and the male continues to feed the chicks until the female is strong enough to begin feeding them. The chicks leave the nest in another 12 to 13 days. The parents feed the chicks for an additional 3 to 4 weeks after they leave the nest. The young are on their own by the time they are 18 to 20 days old.

### Predators

The song sparrow's predators include snakes, hawks, cats, and raccoons.

## Conservation

The song sparrow is common throughout much of its range, and is very adaptable. However, it may be confused with the similar eastern meadowlark, which is declining throughout much of its range.

ementos and took to the streets to protest the legislation. The bill was ultimately withdrawn in response to the protests.
The protesters' costume of choice was the Guy Fawkes mask, first used by the character V in the graphic novel series V for Vendetta  and later in the film adaptation.
The meme around the symbol has grown to encompass a range of unrelated causes, including the Occupy movement and the Arab Spring.
The Guy Fawkes mask was worn by the Anonymous activist collective during their protests against the Stop Online Piracy Act (SOPA) and the Protect Intellectual Property Act (PIPA) in The mask has also been used in protests against the Stop Online Piracy Act (SOPA) and the Anti-Counterfeiting Trade Agreement (ACTA). In 2010, Shadowrun's creator stated that the mask had been worn in demonstrations against the Stop Online Piracy Act. In 2011, the meme was turned into a song, and a music video by the Italian band LaRossa.
The mask was used as a symbol of protest during the Occupy Wall Street protests in 2011.
On 29 June 2011, the activist group Anonymous adopted the Guy Fawkes mask as a symbol of what they called "the global revolution". Anonymous and its supporters wore the mask at demonstrations against proposed legislation in the United States, Canada and Europe, which they felt would restrict freedom of speech and impinge on the rights of anonymous internet users.
In October 2011, Anonymous supporters wore the mask in London and other cities to protest against what they saw as a mass surveillance program by the United Kingdom government.
On 20 April 2012, an Egyptian court issued an arrest warrant for the actor and comedian Bassem Youssef for "insulting Islam", after he wore the Guy Fawkes mask in a comedy sketch.
Shortly after the Egyptian court's action, a number of news reports and parodies were published commenting on the fact that the comedian had worn the mask.
On 1 June 2012, Anonymous staged protests in 40 cities around the world against what they perceived as the European Union's restrictive proposal on the ACTA treaty. The masks were also worn to protest against the EU's proposed Anti-Counterfeiting Trade Agreement.
On 18 July 2012, the mask was worn by supporters of the Occupy Wall Street movement in New York.
The mask was also worn by supporters of the Occupy Oakland movement in Oakland, California.
On 19 March 2012, in connection with the 2012 Israeli–Palestinian peace talks, which are opposed by some Palestinians who refuse to negotiate while Israel occupies the West Bank, the mask was worn by an Israeli protester who interrupted a speech by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

On 9 July Hostile participated in the Battle of Calabria as an escort for the heavy ships of Force C and unsuccessfully engaged

the Italian destroyers.

### Allied convoys

On 21 July Hostile was one of three destroyers that escorted the battleships HMS Nelson and HMS Rodney and the aircraft carrier HMS Ark Royal during Operation Substance, a convoy bound for Malta.

Further information: Operation Substance

### Battle of Cape Passero

On 12 August Hostile was part of Force H, a fleet including the battleships Nelson and Rodney, the aircraft carrier Ark Royal and the destroyers Faulknor, Foresight, Forester, Fury, Hotspur, Havock, Hunter, Hereward, Hostile, Icarus, Intrepid, Ivanhoe, Jackal, Jervis, Kelvin, Kipling, Lively, Lightning, Legion, Laforey, Lightning and Lookout.

Further information: Battle of Cape Passero

### Dunkirk evacuation

On 25 May, Hostile arrived at Dunkirk with Hunter to assist with the evacuation of British and other Allied troops from Dunkirk during the Battle of France.

### Operation Pedestal

On 10 July Hostile was one of seven destroyers to form the escort for the carrier HMS Eagle and the battleships HMS Nelson and HMS Rodney during Operation Pedestal.

Further information: Operation Pedestal

### Malta convoy escort

On 24 July Hostile was part of the escort for the Operation Pedestal convoy LAM 8 from Gibraltar to Malta, which was a fleet including the battleship HMS Nelson and the aircraft carrier HMS Ark Royal.

### Operation Halberd

On 27 August Hostile was part of the escort for the Operation Halberd convoy to Malta from Gibraltar, which was a fleet including the battleships Nelson and Rodney, the aircraft carrier Ark Royal and the destroyers Havock, Hotspur, Hunter, Hero, Hostile, Icarus, Ivanhoe, Kelvin, Kipling, Laforey, Legion, Lookout, Lightning, Lively, Liverpool, Lochinvar, Loyal, and Lauderdale.

### Operation Torch

In November, the destroyer was part of the escort for Force K, which provided the cover for the landings in North Africa (Operation Torch).

### Sinking

On 13 December 1942 Hostile was involved in the action of the First Battle of Sirte, during which the destroyer was severely damaged by German bombers and eventually sunk by a torpedo from the Italian torpedo boat Maestrale at 33°26′N 13°09′E. Hostile was one of three destroyers, along with HMS Jaguar and HMS Kandahar, that were sunk by Maestrale and her sister boat Centauro. Maestrale had been operating in the Mediterranean since the previous June and was in good condition at the time of the attack. She was well provisioned and had been refuelled at Benghazi on 9 December and so had ample fuel capacity.

Hostile was one of the first British ships to be sunk by German aircraft in World War II. The other British ship to be sunk by German aircraft in World War II was the aircraft carrier HMS Ark Royal on 14 November 1941, which was one of the first British capital ships to be sunk by the Luftwaffe in World War II.

The Blackburn B @-@ 48 Firecrest , given the SBAC designation YA.1 , was a single @-@ engine naval strike fighter built by Blac

bkn for the Royal Navy. It first flew on 13 August 1947, and 1,480 were produced by Blackburn at Brough, Yorkshire, and by Canadair at Toronto.
The Firecrest was designed as an all-weather, carrier-borne variant of the Blackburn Firecrest , the first of which was built as a private venture in 1946. A successful aircraft, it was ordered into production for the Royal Navy to replace the Sea Firefly , Sea Hurricane and Sea Furies. It entered service in 1951, and was used on the aircraft carriers of the Royal Navy until 1957.
The Firecrest was a single-seat, single engine, all-metal monoplane, with retractable landing gear. Its wing was swept back from the leading edge, and the fuselage was of oval cross section. The tailplane was mounted on top of the vertical stabilizer, which was swept back. A tricycle undercarriage was fitted, with the nosewheel retracting into the fuselage and the main wheels retracting into the wings.
The original prototype was built as a private venture in 1946. The first production aircraft flew on 13 August 1947.
The Royal Navy ordered 1,100 aircraft, with an option for 300 more. These were ordered in three batches, with the first 115 being the first of the production aircraft. The second batch of 360 aircraft were built to a revised specification, and the last 585 aircraft were built to a further revised specification, which included the fitting of ejection seats. The first two batches were built by Blackburn at Brough, Yorkshire. The last batch was built by Canadair at Toronto, Ontario.
The Firecrest was the first aircraft to be fitted with an ejection seat as standard equipment.
One prototype was fitted with a 1,600 lbf Fairey YS.101 turbojet engine in place of the 2,400 lbf Armstrong-Siddeley Sapphire radial. This aircraft was given the designation YA.2 . It first flew on 22 November 1948, and was destroyed in an accident on 17 September 1949.

Given the complex and controversial nature of the relationship between Rosemary and Alice , it is not surprising that a number of scholars have attempted to offer an explanation for it.  Among those who have studied the matter is Barbara G. Walker , who assigns Alice a role as a " _schwuchtel_ " , or lesbian seductress, in Rosemary's life ( 110 – 112 ).  In her view , Alice's " _Ich-Maschine_ " , as she calls it , was unsuccessful in its attempts to seduce Rosemary, but did succeed in leading her into an affair with the much older and married Gordon Lowe ( 113 ).
As far as I know , there is no evidence that Rosemary ever became involved with Lowe ,  or with anyone else for that matter , and I find Walker's unsubstantiated and inaccurate portrayal of Alice and her relationship with Rosemary unconvincing.  Indeed , there is little concrete evidence that the relationship was anything more than a friendship, and the suggestion that Alice may have had homosexual tendencies is simply not supported by the evidence.
Nevertheless , it is undeniable that the relationship between Rosemary and Alice was complicated and, to some extent, it remains a mystery.  The relationship is perhaps best understood in terms of what we know of Rosemary's own sexuality, which was not conventional.  She was a sexual, but not a romantic, person , and this was reflected in her relationships with men as well as with women, in both cases tending to be drawn to older men who were more mature than herself.  She was also drawn to women who were older than herself, and who exercised a certain amount of authority over her.  It is not difficult to understand how one or both of these traits might have attracted Rosemary to Alice, and why Alice might have wished to be in a relationship with her.  In addition, there were financial considerations.  Rosemary was a struggling artist who was often in need of money, and it is quite possible that she entered into a relationship with Alice in order to be in a position to borrow from her.  It is also possible that Alice may have been in a similar financial position.  Whatever the nature of their relationship, Rosemary's relationship with Alice seems to have been the most important in her life, and the one that had the greatest emotional and financial impact on her.
In the fall of 1942, when Rosemary was 19 years old, she began a relationship with a man named John Hamblin, who was 22.  Like Alice, he was older than she was, and he was also married.  He was a " good-looking, well-read, well-spoken young man " who was " a well-known figure in the town of Oakville " ( 14 ) and who had been a member of the Oakville Literary Club, and a friend of Rosemary's father's.  Like Alice, he was someone who was able to provide Rosemary with emotional and financial support, and he was someone who she felt was " _a full human being_ " ( 14 ).
The relationship between Rosemary and John began when he asked her to come to his home to meet his wife, who was also an artist.  Rosemary went to that meeting and was impressed by his wife, and by the home that she shared with John.  However, she was also disturbed by what she saw. The nest of the white-winged trumpeter is a large, shallow, cup-shaped platform of sticks lined with grasses, leaves, feathers, and other soft material. The nest is not lined with mud as is common in other cuckoo species.

Mycena galericulata is a mushroom species commonly known as the common bonnet , the toque mycena , or the rosy @-@ gill fairy h

edgehog mushroom . It is found in Europe and North America. It looks like a small version of the fairy ring mushrooms, and is often found on the ground in woods, often in coniferous forests.
 Mycena galericulata has a cap that is 1 to 3 cm in diameter, brown or blue-green in colour, and with a rosy gill base. The stem is 2 to 6 cm long.
 Gills are adnate to the stem. They are blueish or red, sometimes pinkish.
 Spores are elliptical to oval, smooth and without pores.
 Mycena galericulata is edible, but its taste is reported to be unpleasant. It is not known if it is toxic.

## Personal life

Dylan was born in Oxford, England, and is the illegitimate son of Dylan Thomas , a poet and writer, and Caitlin Macnamara (née Macnamara), a writer and activist. He grew up in England and at the age of 14, due to his mother's frequent hospitalizations, he moved to the United States to live with his father's family.

Dylan's father died in New York City in 1953, while Dylan was still a teenager. He then moved to Los Angeles to live with his mother, who was in and out of hospitals for mental illness. He was first educated at the University of Colorado, but dropped out after one semester. He then attended the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), where he studied literature and philosophy. Dylan has stated that he was an avid reader and was influenced by writers such as Henry Miller and Charles Bukowski . He was also heavily influenced by the music of Woody Guthrie and Lead Belly , both of whom he met in person.

Dylan has a daughter, Hannah , with his former wife, Samantha Morton .

### Health issues

Dylan has been hospitalized twice for serious illness: in 2004, he was treated for an "acute viral infection" at University Hospital in Newark, New Jersey. In 2013, he was hospitalized at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles for an undisclosed medical issue, and underwent a "minor procedure".

### Political views

Dylan in San Francisco in 2008

Dylan identifies himself as a Socialist and is a member of the Socialist Party USA (SPUSA). He has stated that he is "somewhat" in favor of capitalism, but that he wants the government to control money and oil companies. He told an interviewer: "I would say that I'm about as socialistic as you can get, without being a Communist." He has expressed a "deep and abiding" love for President Franklin D. Roosevelt .

In 2014, Dylan made an appearance on the Colbert Report to promote his album Shadows in the Night , which includes several cover versions of songs by Frank Sinatra. He told host Stephen Colbert that his admiration for Sinatra was "unconditional" and that he had been listening to Sinatra on the radio when the September 11 attacks occurred. He said that he had been "disillusioned" by the Bush administration and that he thought that the Patriot Act had been "unnecessary".

Relative to other typical mushroom species , the spores of V. bohemica are huge , typically measuring 60 – 80 by 15 – 18 µm . T

ubes are distinctive , typically measuring 55 - 75 by 10 - 14 µm .
 The gills of V. bohemica are adnate (attached to the stem) or decurrent . The gill edge is entire, the gills are striate and the spores are amyloid .
The cap of V. bohemica tends to be convex to flat, sometimes with a slight depression in the center. It can be up to 6 cm (2.4 inch) in diameter, with a white or brownish color.
The stem is 2- 7 cm long, slender, equal in diameter to the hat, whitish, and covered with a whitish velvety coating.
The odor of V. bohemica is slightly musty and the taste is mild.
V. bohemica is edible when cooked.
Saprobic or litter inhabitant, with fruiting bodies occurring singly, scattered or in groups, on wood, on soil, on bark, on wood chips, and in leaf-litter.
V. bohemica is distributed widely in Europe , in Asia , in Africa , and in North America .
V. bohemica is similar to Volvariella bombycina but has a stout stem, whereas V. bombycina has a slender stem and the gill edges are entire in V. bohemica as opposed to decurrent in V. bombycina. V. bohemica also has a much larger spore than V. bombycina.
V. bohemica has been found growing on the bark of a pine tree in Arizona, possibly as a result of imported garments.

The Galveston Railway , originally established and named in 1854 as the Galveston Wharf and Cotton Press Company , is a Class I

railroad operating in the southern United States. Its headquarters are located in San Antonio, Texas, but its main rail yard is located in Waco, Texas.
Galveston Wharf and Cotton Press Company
The Galveston Wharf and Cotton Press Company, ca. 1854
The Galveston Wharf and Cotton Press Company was formed in 1854 by a group of businessmen led by Isaac Van Cleve and Noah Smith. The company was chartered to purchase land along the Brazos River, to establish a wharf, and to construct a cotton press to alleviate the bottleneck of cotton production.
Galveston, Houston & Henderson Railroad
On September 25, 1854, the Galveston Wharf and Cotton Press Company filed a bill in the Texas Supreme Court to authorize the Galveston Cotton Press and Rail Road Company to construct a railroad to the Brazos River to serve the company's cotton press. The Texas Supreme Court granted the approval on November 23, 1854.
On May 11, 1855, the Houston, Galveston, Beaumont and Brazos River Railroad Company was chartered by the state of Texas to construct a railroad to the Brazos River. The Houston, Galveston, Beaumont and Brazos River Railroad Company acquired the rights to the Galveston Cotton Press and Rail Road Company on June 28, 1855.
On June 17, 1856, the Houston, Galveston, Beaumont and Brazos River Railroad Company changed its name to Galveston, Houston & Henderson Railroad Company.
On January 14, 1857, the Galveston, Houston & Henderson Railroad Company authorized the formation of the Galveston, Houston and Henderson Railroad Company. The Galveston, Houston & Henderson Railroad Company became the holding company of the Galveston, Houston and Henderson Railroad Company.
On August 22, 1869, the Galveston, Houston & Henderson Railroad Company changed its name to Galveston Houston & Henderson Railroads.
Galveston, Houston & Henderson Railroads
Galveston Houston & Henderson railroad depot at Waco, Texas
On September 22, 1876, the Galveston Houston & Henderson Railroads were reorganized as the Galveston Houston & Henderson Railroad Company.
On November 22, 1880, the Galveston Houston & Henderson Railroad Company changed its name to the Galveston, Houston & Henderson Railroad Company.
Galveston, Harrisburg & San Antonio Railway
On July 22, 1881, the Galveston, Houston & Henderson Railroad Company merged with the Galveston, Harrisburg & San Antonio Railway to form the Galveston, Harrisburg & San Antonio Railway Company.
Galveston, Harrisburg & San Antonio Railway Company
Main article: Galveston, Harrisburg & San Antonio Railway
On November 22, 1923, the Galveston, Harrisburg & San Antonio Railway Company changed its name to the Galveston Railway Company.
Galveston Railway
On January 2, 1941, the Galveston Railway was merged into the Missouri Pacific Railway to form the Missouri Pacific Railroad.
MoPac Railroad
On December 31, 1981, the Missouri Pacific Railroad was merged into the Union Pacific Railroad to form the Union Pacific Railroad.
Galveston Railway Depot, Waco, Texas
The Galveston Railway's headquarters are located at 1000 Commerce Street in San Antonio, Texas.
The Galveston Railway main rail yard is located at Waco, Texas.
Because the Galveston Railway operates in the southeastern United States, it competes with other Class I railroads in the region: the BNSF Railway, the Kansas City Southern Railway, the Norfolk Southern Railway, the Union Pacific Railroad, and the former Southern Railway lines.
The Galveston Railway operates various commuter and intercity passenger trains.

Tiber comprises multiple Lower Tertiary petroleum reservoirs located in Keathley Canyon block 102 about 250 mi ( 400 km ) south

of Galveston, Texas. The Tiber field is located in water depths ranging from 6,560 to 8,100 ft (2,000 to 2,500 m). The Tiber marine field is located in the Wilcox formation, a Middle to Upper Cretaceous stratigraphic trap that can be found in the Gulf of Mexico and along the Atlantic coast. The Wilcox contains two major structural traps, a four-way pinchout in the eastern portion and an anticline in the western portion of the field. The Wilcox is usually a very low porosity, highly fractured reservoir that develops complex fracture patterns. The Wilcox is a prolific producer of hydrocarbons in Tiber, combining with the eastern four-way pinchout to produce more than 100 MMstb (15 MMm 3 ) of oil. Tiber is operated by Chevron USA.

Alfa Ba , Karamoko Alfa 's father , formed a coalition of Muslim Fulbe and called for the jihad in 1725 , but died before the s

ack of Dendi in 1727 .
In 1729 , Alfa Ba 's brother , Alfa Bata , was declared the new leader of the jihad by Alka Abu Bakr , a Muslim Fulbe cleric . The jihad was resumed under Alfa Bata in 1730 , and was joined by a coalition of Fulbe which included Muslims , Fulani , and even Hausa warriors .
 By 1730 , the Fulani jihad had been joined by the Muslim Hausa from Dendi , Timbuktu , and Gao . Alka Abu Bakr , the Muslim cleric who had declared Alfa Bata the new leader of the jihad , was captured by the Songhai in 1733 .
The Fulani jihad was put on hold after the death of Alka Abu Bakr , the Muslim cleric who had declared Alfa Bata the new leader of the jihad .
Nevertheless , in 1739 , the jihad was resumed by Alfa Bata and led to the sack of Timbuktu in 1740 .
 The jihad was resumed in 1741 , led by Tin-Tin , a Muslim Fula general who was the son of Alfa Bata , and resulted in the sack of Dendi in 1742 .

Many U.S. national parks , such as Glacier National Park , Rocky Mountain National Park , Yellowstone National Park and Badland

National Park, were established to preserve natural wonders and the natural environment.
The National Park Service (NPS) is an agency of the U.S. federal government that manages all national parks , many national monuments , and other conservation and historical properties with various title designations.
The National Park Service works in cooperation with the United States Fish and Wildlife Service to manage the National Wildlife Refuge System.
The National Park Service was created on August 25, 1916 by President Woodrow Wilson to conserve the scenery and the natural and historic objects and wildlife therein, and to provide for the enjoyment of the same in such manner and by such means as will leave them unimpaired for the enjoyment of future generations.
The National Park Service is overseen by the National Park Service Organic Act . This law was reauthorized by the National Parks Omnibus Management Act of 1998 for 10 additional years. The National Park Service Organic Act gives the Secretary of the Interior authority to administer the National Park Service.
The National Park Service has three general categories of units: the National Parks, the National Monuments, and the National Historic Sites.
The National Park Service also oversees the White House , which was declared a national park in 1961, as well as the United States Capitol , which was declared a national park in 1933. Stonewall National Monument, the first national monument dedicated to LGBT rights, was established by President Obama on June 24, 2016.
In addition to the National Parks System, the National Park Service also manages other protected areas of the United States. These include National Historical Parks, National Battlefields, National Memorials, National Historic Sites, National Reserve System units, National Recreation Areas, National Seashores, National Scenic Trails, National Volcanic Monuments, and National Wilderness Areas. These other units are not part of the National Park System, but many are administered like units of the National Park System.
The National Park Service is an agency of the U.S. Department of the Interior. Its budget is funded by government appropriations. The Director of the National Park Service is a presidential appointee who reports to the United States Secretary of the Interior. The National Park Service has a headquarters office at 1849 C Street NW in Washington, D.C. , and regional offices in Anchorage, Alaska; Atlanta, Georgia; Denver, Colorado; Fort Worth, Texas; Oakland, California; and Washington, D.C.
To accomplish its mission, the National Park Service is organized into two divisions: the National Park System and the National Historic Preservation Program.
The National Park System includes the National Parks, the National Monuments, the National Historic Sites, and other units designated as part of the National Park System.
The National Historic Preservation Program works to identify, evaluate, and register historic places worthy of preservation. These properties are designated as either National Historic Landmarks or as contributing resources to a National Register of Historic Places that is part of a National Register Historic District.
The National Park Service has its origin in the National Park idea, which dates to the earliest days of the American republic. The concept of setting aside public lands and waters to be used for recreation was popular among writers in the United States. The first event to inspire the idea of a national park was the visit of British writer and artist George Catlin to the American wilderness in the 1830s. Catlin had a strong influence on the development of the national park concept, and his writings inspired a number of artists to travel west to paint the region. Catlin also proposed the idea of national parks to the federal government.
The concept of a national park was also popularized by writers and artists who were inspired by the writings of naturalist and philosopher Henry David Thoreau. The 1864 publication of Thoreau's book Walden , which was based on his experiences in the 1840s near Walden Pond in Massachusetts, inspired many American writers and thinkers. Thoreau's writings were very influential in the development of the national park idea.
Congress acted on the national park concept in 1872 when it passed the Yellowstone National Park Act, which created the world's first national park. The establishment of Yellowstone National Park was an important part of the development of the national park concept. On 14 March 2013 , Torres scored the third goal as Chelsea defeated Steaua București 3 – 1 to advance 3 – 2 on aggregate to the

quarter-finals of the UEFA Champions League.[4] On 21 March 2013 , Torres scored a goal in the 2 – 1 loss to Manchester United as Chelsea lost 3 – 2 on aggregate to advance to the quarter-finals of the UEFA Europa League.[5]
 Poniente [ edit] On 31 March 2013 , Torres scored the winning goal in a 1 – 0 victory over Real Madrid to keep Chelsea in the race for the title.[6] Four days later, Torres scored the winning goal in a 2 – 1 win over Southampton to keep Chelsea in second place behind Manchester City.[7] On 2 May 2013 , Torres scored the winning goal in a 2 – 1 win over Stoke City to secure Chelsea a place in the Europa League Final.[8]
The 2012–13 season turned out to be a disappointment for Torres. He started the season well, scoring in the first three matches; however, his form dipped for the rest of the season. He was benched for the final four matches of the season as Chelsea won the Premier League and FA Cup and reached the Europa League final. The 2013–14 season saw him play the first half of the season as a substitute and on the bench, but he made 19 appearances and scored three goals in the Europa League, including two crucial goals in a 3–1 win over Steaua București in the second leg of the Europa League round of 16.
On 25 October 2014 , Torres scored against Everton at Goodison Park in a 1–1 draw, his first Premier League goal since 14 March 2014 against Norwich City. Torres scored his second Premier League goal of the season against Hull City on 25 January 2015. He scored his third of the season against Stoke City on 28 March 2015, but it was ruled offside. He ended the season with 4 goals in 29 appearances in the league.
On 19 September 2015 , Torres scored the second goal in a 2–0 win against Arsenal, his first Premier League goal of the season. He scored his second goal of the season against Manchester United on 24 October 2015, and then scored his third goal of the season against Watford on 16 December 2015 in a 2–0 win. He scored his fourth goal of the season against Crystal Palace on 16 January 2016. He ended the season with 4 goals in 28 appearances in the league, in addition to 7 goals in 14 appearances in the Europa League, as Chelsea won both competitions.
On 21 September 2016 , Torres scored Chelsea's opening goal in a 3–0 victory over Leicester City. He made 31 appearances in the league, scoring 7 goals and helping Chelsea win the league title.[9]
On 17 August 2017 , Torres made his 400th career appearance in a 2–0 win against Everton.[10]
On 19 August 2017 , the club announced Torres had signed a one-year contract extension.[11]
On 12 August 2018 , Torres made his 450th appearance in a 2–0 win against Arsenal, becoming the second Spaniard to reach this milestone, after Andrés Iniesta.[12]
On 24 January 2019 , Torres was sent off in a 4–1 loss to Tottenham Hotspur for two yellow cards.[13]
On 20 February 2019 , Torres was sent off in a 2–1 loss against Arsenal for a second yellow card.[14]
On 11 April 2019 , Torres was sent off in a 1–0 loss against Everton for a second yellow card.[15]
On 20 April 2019 , Torres was sent off in a 2–0 win over Liverpool for a second yellow card.[16]

The Type 94 Nambu 8 mm Pistol ( Type 94 Handgun , Japanese : 九四式拳銃 Kyūyon @-@ Shiki Kenjū ) is a semiautomatic pistol developed

in Japan during the 1930s for use by the Imperial Japanese Army and Imperial Japanese Navy .
It is the first successful Japanese handgun to be widely adopted. It is chambered for the 8×22 mm Nambu cartridge, which is a proprietary design and was particularly chosen for its low cost. The 8×22 mm Nambu cartridge features a long, straight, bottlenecked case and a pointed, boat-tail bullet, which gives it greater muzzle velocity and range than a .380 ACP at the cost of lower magazine capacity.
The Nambu pistol was adopted in 1934, and production continued until 1944, when it was superseded by the Type 14 Nambu. The Japanese military purchased 141,000 pistols from Nambu .
The Type 94 Nambu was first introduced to the IJN in 1934. The first production run was made by the Nambu Arms Company , which was run by the Japanese government. The Nambu Arms Company built the first 100,000 units, and then the Nagoya Arsenal took over production. The Nambu pistol replaced both the Nagant M1895 and the Colt Model 1911A1 on the IJN, with the exception of officers. The IJA bought 40,000 units, and the IJN bought 101,000 units, for a total of 141,000 pistols.
The pistol was a further development of the Nambu Model 6. It featured a new barrel with a ventilated muzzle brake and replacement of the wood stock with a metal frame .
The pistol was also given a shortened magazine, to help with the reliability of the pistol. A detachable shoulder stock was also added to the Nambu pistol, which is a feature that was not present in the Nambu Model 6 .
The Imperial Japanese Navy purchased 101,000 Nambu pistols, which were the standard sidearm for Imperial Japanese Navy sailors. The pistol was also used by the Imperial Japanese Army, but not with the same frequency as it was by the IJN.
Many Nambu pistols were made by Nambu Arms Company, but 40,000 were made by the Nagoya Arsenal. The Nambu Arms Company was owned by the Japanese government, and the Nagoya Arsenal was owned by the Japanese Navy.

Although it is uncertain what role the Ten Commandments played in early Christian worship , evidence suggests they were recited

with Psalm 119 in the morning prayer service and Psalm 24 at the evening prayer service. This is the only time the Ten Commandments are mentioned in the New Testament (1 Cor. 7:19), although they are mentioned in the Church fathers.
 The Acts of Pilate (1:1-10) and the Acts of Paul (1:1-10) are two of the four "Acts of the Apostles" that were found among a collection of works known as the Apostolic Acts. These documents are not canonical, but were known to the early Church.
 The Letter to the Laodiceans was written by St. Clement of Rome. St. Paul refers to him as a "fellow laborer" (Phil. 4:3).
 The Apostolic Constitutions (VII:12:1) requires that the sacraments be administered by the bishop, his presbyters, and deacons. By the fifth century, the sacraments were being administered by presbyters. By the sixth century, the sacraments were being administered by deacons alone.
 The Liturgy of the Presanctified contains the Lord's Prayer, the Kyrie, the Creed, and the Prayer of St. Chrysostom. This service is still celebrated in the Coptic Orthodox Church to this day.
 The Book of Revelation (14:3) refers to the "blessed and holy" who are "before the throne." These are, of course, the saints. The New Testament also refers to the saints as the "church triumphant" and the "church suffering." These expressions would later be applied to the living and the dead, respectively.
 In the Middle Ages, the number of days between Vigil and Easter Sunday was sometimes reduced to six days or even five days. The number of days between Vigil and Easter Sunday was reduced to seven days in the 1920s.
 The earliest Old English hymnal, the Exeter Book (c. 990), includes the hymn "Dreman Alleluia." The tune is based on a Gregorian plainsong. One of the earliest recorded celebrations of Easter took place in Rome in 519. The English, however, did not have a fixed date for Easter until 1000.

As the cloud collapses , individual conglomerations of dense dust and gas form " Bok globules " . As a globule collapses and th

ins , it may become a " core " , which is a dense cloud that can form a star or a cluster of stars . A core may then collapse and form a protostar if it continues to contract . If the core is large enough , it may become a cluster of stars . A protostar is a star that has not yet generated nuclear fusion in its core . The nuclear fusion process is triggered when the core is large enough to generate the pressure needed to support itself against gravity .
 nuclear fusion is the process by which four protons come together to form a deuterium nucleus , which has a positive electric charge . This positive proton then interacts with another proton and releases two neutrons . These neutrons travel outward from the protostar , forming the outwardly emitted radiation that we normally associate with stars . The emission of neutrons , called " neutrinos " , is not visible to the naked eye .
 The nuclear fusion process begins in a solar system's core , where it takes about five hundred million years to generate sufficient pressure to begin the process . In our own solar system , the process began about four and a half billion years ago , when the Sun was about 70 percent as large as it is now .
 The nuclear fusion process is a relatively slow process , taking about 100 million years to complete . Once the process begins , however , it continues at a fairly rapid pace . The process may take as many as 100 million years to complete in a star as massive as our Sun , but a star that is only about one-fifth as massive may complete the process in as little as 20 million years . The nuclear fusion process is what keeps a star from collapsing in upon itself . It also generates the outward radiation that can be seen .
 The nuclear fusion process is also what generates the heat and light that keeps all of the planets of our solar system from becoming so cold that life as we know it could not exist . Life , in fact , can exist only in a narrow temperature range . Without the nuclear fusion process, all of the planets of our solar system would be uninhabitable .
The gravitational force that holds stars , planets , and other bodies in place is so strong that even the tiniest particle of dust would be crushed if another particle were to collide with it . The collision of particles , however , results in a force called the " centrifugal force " that balances the gravitational force . This force allows the dust particles to move away from one another , and so the dust does not collapse into a single particle .
If the temperature of a gas were to suddenly drop , the molecules would stop moving and the pressure would drop . The pressure drop would then cause the temperature to rise again , repeating the cycle . The same phenomenon occurs in a star , where the temperature of the core depends on the pressure . If the core were to suddenly collapse , the temperature would drop and the pressure would drop again . The contraction of the core would cause the temperature to rise again , and a cycle would be repeated .
 The heat generated by the nuclear fusion process produces a gas that is so hot that it is slightly less dense than the surrounding space . The gas therefore moves away from the core , generating a " wind " that blows away the outer layers of the star . The wind reaches a point where the gas becomes less dense than the surrounding space and so it stops . This is called the " photosphere " .
 The light emitted by a star is not visible to the naked eye , but it is visible to instruments that detect infrared radiation . The infrared radiation is emitted by the stars in all directions , and so it is impossible to determine when it was emitted . If we were to observe a star with infrared telescopes , we would see that the entire body of the star is emitting infrared radiation .

After his release from prison , Juan Perón decided to campaign for the presidency of the nation , which he won in a landslide .

On 4 July 1946, he took the oath of office and was sworn in as President of Argentina . He immediately began overhauling the economic and social policies of the nation , and soon afterward passed the so-called Labor Codes .

In 1947, President Perón was deposed in a military coup , and for the next four years, he and his wife were forced to live in exile in Spain. After returning to Argentina in 1952, he began a second term as president, and during the next three years, he continued his economic and social policy changes. In 1954, Amanda was declared "Honorary Member of the Nation," an honor usually reserved for heads of state.

In 1955, Juan Perón was again deposed in a military coup. After the coup, Amanda was imprisoned for several weeks before she was transferred to a hospital. She died of a heart attack on 29 September 1957, while visiting her daughter in Buenos Aires.

Following the completion of the dam , the entrances to the two outer diversion tunnels were sealed at the opening and halfway t

unnels, and the central diversion tunnel was left open as a ventilation shaft. In 1988, the tunnel was re-opened to the public as a tourist attraction.

The 1937 dam was constructed by the Civilian Conservation Corps. The CCC was a New Deal program created to put unemployed young men to work on projects that would benefit the general public. The work crews were composed of enrollees between the ages of 18 and 25 who were given 20-week training courses in outdoor skills.

The CCC was originally established to create jobs in rural areas, but the dam project also provided work for the young men in the Los Angeles area, which was suffering from high unemployment at the time. The dams were constructed to facilitate the development of the Griffith Park area, which was one of the last large areas of undeveloped land in Los Angeles County.

The dam's north entrance was constructed in 1938 by the CCC and is still in use. The south entrance was constructed by the City of Los Angeles Public Works Department and is not used. The CCC tunnel, which was used as the main entrance to the dam until 1939, is now used as a ventilation shaft.

The first time I ever saw the Green Man of the Woods I was six years old. I was playing hide-and-seek with some of the other kids from the village, and we were having a hard time trying to find all the kids who were hiding. We were all tired and hungry, and our parents were calling us for dinner.
It was an unusually hot summer day, and I was sitting under a pine tree, waiting for the others to find me. I was looking at the tree thinking how nice it would be if I could climb it and climb up to the top. Someone screamed my name and told me to come out, but I didn't move. I just kept looking at the tree. Then something happened.
The tree seemed to come alive. The branches moved, and the leaves rustled. The tree reached out its hands and took me, and I was lifted high into the air. Then I was dropped down into a beautiful clearing. There was no one else there, just me.

In 1879 , Ulysses S. Grant , the former President of the United States , visited Japan . While in Tokyo , he attended a jujutsu

demonstration , which impressed him deeply . After returning to the United States , he wrote a letter to President Rutherford B. Hayes requesting that a jujutsu expert be sent to train U.S. soldiers .
In 1882 , William E. Gleason , a jujutsu student of Yasumitsu , was sent to the United States as an instructor . Gleason had been a student of Yasumitsu for only about a year and had practiced jujutsu for only about a year and a half . He was sent to the United States as part of an exchange program with the U.S. military . This was the first time that an instructor of jujutsu was sent to the United States .
Gleason reached the United States in February 1882 . He was accompanied by A.T. Still , a physician and founder of osteopathy . He was also accompanied by Professor F. L. Grant , who had studied jujutsu for a year with Yasumitsu . Gleason taught jujutsu to the U.S. military from February 1882 to September 1883 .
Gleason was a thorough and effective instructor . He translated the six-volume treatise of Yasumitsu into English and wrote a jujutsu treatise of his own . He wrote that jujutsu is an art of defense and not offense . This is the first time that jujutsu was described as an art of defense .
Gleason returned to Japan in September 1883 . In 1884 , Gleason wrote the book, "Jujitsu: An Art of Defense" . This book was the first book ever written on jujutsu . It described the principles of jujutsu and illustrated the principles with 400 drawings .

Following their marriage , Juan Duarte moved to the small town of Los Toldos , where he worked as a laborer and started his own business of hauling gravel . As Eva Perón took on more and more of a public role , her marriage to Duarte became an increasing burden . Eventually , Eva Perón divorced Juan Duarte , who continued to live in Los Toldos and raise their three children .
Eva Perón's first love was the corrupt police officer Pedro Ramírez . In 1935 , Ramírez was murdered and Eva's first husband Juan Duarte was accused of the crime . In the course of the investigation into the murder , Eva Perón was found to be carrying on a relationship with Ramírez . Eva's first husband Juan Duarte was cleared of the murder charges and Eva Perón never married again .
Another important relationship in Eva Perón's life was with Argentine actress and comedian Magda Lara . Their relationship was very close , and Eva Perón is often pictured with Lara in photographs .
Despite these relationships , peronist supporters would often refer to Eva Perón as "the eternal virgin" . This image of Eva Perón's virginity was propagandized in order to portray her as a saintly figure .
When Eva Perón was 15 , she began a relationship with the well-known Argentine playboy Oscar Lorenzo Mazza . Mazza was a wealthy businessman who had been arrested for murdering a wealthy woman . He was released on the order of Isabel Perón . Mazza was the father of Eva Duarte's first child , Duarte Mazza .
Eva Perón had a long relationship with the Argentine lawyer Juan Carlos Pugliese , to whom she was engaged to be married for some time . Pugliese was a key member of the downtown Buenos Aires mafia that was involved in extortion , protection , and other illegal activities .
