The 1947 UN Partition Plan in late November 1947 designated Haifa as part of the proposed Jewish state . Arab protests over tha

eparation of the city from the rest of Palestine led to the 1948 Arab-Israeli War, which ended with the city under Israeli control.
The city interior is divided into two areas: the religious quarter and the secular quarter. The religious quarter is located on Mount Carmel and includes the Tikotin Museum of Japanese Art, the Carmelite Monastery, the Stella Maris Monastery, the Baha'i Gardens and World Center, the Hasidic Shalom al Israel Synagogue, the Ades Synagogue, the Bnei David Synagogue, the Haifa Museum of Art, and the Haifa School for the Deaf. The secular quarter is located on the coastal plain and includes the Technion, the University of Haifa, the University of Haifa's Ophir Center for the Visual Arts, the Haifa Museum of Art, the Haifa Public Library, the Municipal Theater of Haifa, the Hecht Museum, and the National Maritime Museum.
Haifa has a temperate Mediterranean climate (Köppen climate classification: Csa). Summers are hot and dry with cool sea breezes. Winters are cool, rainy and cloudy. The average annual temperature is 20.3 °C (68.5 °F). Annual precipitation is 614 millimetres (24.2 in) and annual average relative humidity is 75%. The hottest month is August, with an average temperature of 24.8 °C (76.6 °F) and the coldest month is January, with an average temperature of 13.6 °C (56.5 °F).
Haifa has a broad economic base ranging from high tech and shipbuilding to light and medium industry. The city is home to the biggest maritime port (Haifa Port) in Israel, the country's main oil refinery and the country's primary tanker terminal. Haifa has the country's only natural gas processing terminal and is home to major companies in the fields of communications, finance, manufacturing, and food processing. The city was named a global city in 2010.
The city has a relatively well developed public transportation system. The city's buses are operated by Dan and Egged. The city's main bus terminal is located next to Haifa railway station, and is served by several long distance bus lines. The city's railway station is served by both the mixed-service rail line between Tel Aviv and Afula, and the electrified narrow gauge rail line between Haifa and Nahariya, which is a branch of the electrified standard gauge rail line between Haifa and Beersheba (not serving Haifa railway station).
The city's two ports, the general and the oil, are served by ferries from Jaffa and Ashdod.
Haifa is served by several hospitals and clinics. Haifa's largest hospital is Rambam Medical Center. Other hospitals in the city include the Ichilov Hospital and the Haifa Medical Center.

Both McLuhan and Innis assume the centrality of communication technology ; where they differ is in the principal kinds of effec

tive technology that have taken place. They see the emergence of electronic communication as the most general social effect. Innis saw the telegraph as the essential technology. McLuhan sees it as information technology.
For both McLuhan and Innis, the principal effect of new communication technology is a change in the structure of the society itself. This change is most evident in the way that communication is organized.
For Innis, the telegraph is the most significant new communication technology. The telegraph is a direct form of communication, whereas other technologies such as the newspaper interpose an intermediate layer of information. This layer is necessary because of the nature of the information it carries, but it is a source of confusion and misunderstanding. Innis sees the telegraph as a threat to the newspapers, because it allows direct access to information.
The newspaper, as a major factor in social communication, changes in a variety of ways. Newspapers become more numerous, more ambitious, and more expensive. Their larger size and enlarged circulations mean that they are more central to the life of a community. As newspapers become more ambitious, they must appeal to a larger audience and so become more general in tone. They lose their individual character, and so become more indistinguishable from one another. As newspapers expand their coverage, they lose the ability to concentrate on a particular subject.
Effective communication technology also changes the structures of society. Innis sees the telegraph as a source of social fragmentation. A telegraphic society is made up of a number of small communities, each with its own centers of communication. Each community has its own information centers. This creates a number of problems. The telegraph requires a great deal of manpower to operate, which takes people away from their productive work. Innis also sees the telegraph as a source of political fragmentation. The news that the telegraph carries brings together people in a small community. But the same news that brings people together also drives them apart. The telegraph is a source of social and political fragmentation.

It is a dopant in some types of glass in lasers and other optoelectronic devices . Europium oxide ( Eu2O3 ) is widely used as a

doping agent in transparent conductors, especially in the transparent conductive oxides (TCO) .

### Spectral absorption properties

Europium has a wide range of electronic energy levels, with many empty electron shells available for absorption of light at the free energy minimum. The wavelength absorbed is dependent on the particular oxidation state of europium, but is typically in the ultraviolet and visible range and is a function of the energy of the incident radiation.

* Eu(III): 280–320 nm
* Eu(II): 340–380 nm

### Spectral emission properties

Europium, as a singly ionised element, emits in the ultraviolet and visible region of the electromagnetic spectrum. The specific emission wavelength is a function of the particular oxidation state of europium.

* Eu(III): 490–510 nm
* Eu(II): 610–617 nm

When Europium is used in a laser, it is often in a compound with other elements, such as Erbium.

## Uses

### Optoelectronic devices

Europium is used as a dopant in some types of glass in lasers and other optoelectronic devices. Europium oxide (Eu2O3) is widely used as a doping agent in transparent conductors, especially in the transparent conductive oxides (TCO) such as zinc oxide and indium tin oxide.

### Phosphors

Europium is also used as a doping agent in phosphors. In particular, europium is a dopant of yttrium aluminium garnet (YAG) crystals, which are used in gas discharge lamps. The emission from Eu3+ in YAG is in the infrared region, and has the maximum at 614 nm.

### Medical

Europium oxide has been used as a fluoroscopic agent for barium enema. It is a commonly used injectable.

### Research

Europium is also used in nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy to enhance the signals from hydrogen and nitrogen nuclei.

Europium has been used as a dopant in the organic compound rubrene.

### Other applications

Europium is used in the manufacture of non-magnetic alloys with iron and nickel. It is used in the chemical industry in the production of ammonium salts and as a catalyst in the manufacture of nitric acid.

## Safety

Europium is a contributor to the rare earth effect.

Within a few decades of Christopher Columbus 's landing on the coast of what is now Venezuela in 1498 , South America had been

completely colonized by Spain. The Spanish  exploited the natives and their labor to build mining and agricultural  enterprises to produce food and minerals for Spain. Under  this system, South America was essentially a Spanish colony.
 By the end of the fifteenth century, most of the lands once  inhabited by the Aztec and Inca empires were Spanish territories.  The northern portion of Spanish America was called New  Castile, the southern portion New Andalusia, and these regions  bordering the Pacific Ocean were called New Extremadura.  The Spanish crown administered its American territories through  a series of viceroyalties (administrative regions) and audiencias  (judicial regions).
 These viceroyalties and audiencias were ruled by viceroys  and audiencia presidents, respectively. Viceroys and audiencia  presidents were appointed by the king and were responsible  for governing their territories.
 In 1713, Spain's central American territories, which included  Mexico, were separated from the viceroyalty of New Spain  (Mexico City), and a new viceroyalty, New Granada (Bogotá), was  established to govern northern South America. The viceroyalty of New  Granada encompassed much of present-day Colombia, Ecuador,  Panama, and Venezuela. By the mid-eighteenth century, the  Spanish crown had decided to form a single viceroyalty of New  Granada, which included all of the territories that had  previously been under New Castile, New Andalusia, and New  Extremadura.
 Spain's administration of its American territories was  frequently ineffective, particularly in the eighteenth  century. The Spanish crown appointed viceroys to rule most of  its territories, but few of these viceroys were qualified for  the task. Many of them were noblemen who had obtained  their positions as viceroys through the influence of friends  at court. These viceroys were distrusted by the people they  were supposed to govern, and the lack of qualified  viceroys led to unrest and rebellion in many of the colony's  major cities. In addition, Spanish revenues from its  American territories were inadequate for the maintenance of  the military, the church, and the state institutions.
 By the early nineteenth century, most of the Spanish  American colonies were in the control of local leaders who  administered the territories independently of the Spanish  crown. These leaders, many of whom were mestizo (of  mixed Spanish and Indian descent), dominated the  economies of their territories. They had access to vast  mineral deposits and, with the help of the Indians,  established large plantations to produce food and minerals.  They controlled the market for food, as well as the markets  for the products of their mines and plantations.
 The Spanish crown tried to enforce its control over its  colonies, but the lack of funds, the corruption of local  officials, and the power of the local leaders all contributed  to the failure of Spanish attempts to control its colonies.  The Spanish crown did not try to enforce its laws on  slavery in the colonies, which led to an increase in the  number of slaves, as well as an increase in the number of  slaves who ran away. The crown did not exert control over  the local merchants, who were able to trade freely.
 The Spanish crown had to pay large sums of money to  the French, British, and Dutch, who had forts on the Atlantic  coast, to ensure that these powerful countries would not  attack the Spanish colonies. In 1807, Napoleon's  troops entered Madrid and drove the royal court to the  Spanish-controlled islands of Cádiz. The Spanish crown  tried to keep its colonies independent, but it was  clear that all of its territories would be independent  within a short time.
 The viceroyalties and audiencias were abolished in 1810,  and the Spanish crown reverted to a system of direct  rule. rier air from the nearby mountain range restricted surface moisture which caused the system to struggle to maintain convection . On September 27 , the system was upgraded to Tropical Storm Norbert .

## Preparations

### Mexico

The government of Mexico issued a tropical storm warning for the entire coast of Baja California Sur. Governor Carlos Mendoza Davis declared a state of emergency for portions of the state. Governor Davis also called up the Mexican Navy to help evacuate locals along the coast.

### United States

The government of the United States issued a tropical storm watch for the Gulf of California coast from Isla Ángel de la Guarda to the southern tip of Isla Cedros.

## Storm effects

### Mexico

The Mexican government issued a tropical storm warning for the coast of Baja California Sur. A tropical storm warning was also issued for the coast of Sonora. The government of Baja California Sur issued a voluntary evacuation order for the entire coast of the state. As the depression moved ashore, 300 people were evacuated from San José del Cabo and the tourist area of San Lucas. 300 others were evacuated from Cabo Pulmo. 50 people were evacuated from El Triunfo. Two people were reported missing while fishing off the coast.

Numerous houses were destroyed in the town of San José del Cabo and in the neighboring village of Todos Santos. A woman was killed by a falling tree in Todos Santos. A woman was also killed by a falling tree in Cabo Pulmo. 2,478 people were evacuated in San José del Cabo, 135 in Cabo Pulmo, and 350 in Todos Santos. Debris from roofs and trees also damaged about 1,600 homes in San José del Cabo and another 3,000 homes in Cabo Pulmo. About 2,000 more houses were damaged in Todos Santos. At least 900 homes were damaged in the communities of La Ventana and El Triunfo.

In San José del Cabo, 2,000 people were left without electricity, while another 300 were left without electricity in Todos Santos.

Almost 30,000 people were left without electricity in San José del Cabo, 10,000 people were left without electricity in Todos Santos, and 5,000 people were left without electricity in Cabo Pulmo. The total cost of damage in San José del was estimated to be $24 million. The total cost of damage in Todos Santos was estimated to be $23 million.

### United States

The government of the United States issued a tropical storm warning for the coast of Sonora. The warning was later discontinued.

## Career

Woodhouse began his career with Hull City, where he made his début in the Football League Trophy in February 1997. He moved to Bradford City in 1998 where he made 16 appearances in the 1998–99 season, in which City were relegated to the Second Division. His three appearances in the 1999–2000 season would be the only appearances he made for Bradford in the Football League. From 2000 to 2004, Woodhouse spent time on loan at Halifax Town, where he made 71 appearances and scored 6 goals. On 27 December 2002, Woodhouse made his only appearance for Halifax in the Football League, in which he was replaced at half-time after suffering a concussion. Upon returning to Bradford, he was released by the club in February 2004. After a brief spell with Darlington, Woodhouse joined Barrow on loan, but was released from his contract before a move was finalised. He joined Gainsborough Trinity of the Conference North on 25 November 2004, and scored on his début against Boston United on 28 November. He made 33 appearances and scored 7 goals in the 2004–05 season.

In 2005, he joined Harrogate Town of the Conference North, where he stayed for a year and made 44 appearances, scoring 5 goals. He joined Doncaster Rovers in 2006, where he made 10 appearances in the 2006–07 season, scoring once. He joined Kidderminster Harriers in 2007, where he appeared 9 times. In 2008, he joined Boston United, where he made 14 appearances and scored 2 goals. In 2009, he joined Worksop Town after Boston United were relegated to the Conference North. He made 18 appearances in the 2009–10 season. In 2010, he joined Frickley Athletic, where he made 14 appearances in the 2010–11 season.

Anderson was involved in filmmaking at a young age and never really had an alternative plan to directing films . He made his fi

rst film, The Godsend , at age 21 and teamed up with his brother, Michael, to make the 1972 thriller The Nightcomers . He moved to Hollywood and directed his first big budget film, The Naked Prey , in 1966, and began working with producer Dino De Laurentiis. Ander-son made his second film on the continent, an adaptation of William Golding 's novel A Man for All Seasons . He made his third film, the Solomon Kane-inspired The Wilby Conspiracy , in his native England. Anderson moved to California and spent the next decade making a string of commercial and cult films: Hell Ride (1969), The Long Day's Dying (1970), The Immortal Story (1968), and The Night of the Generals (1967). He then collaborated with Dino De Laurentiis again to make his most commercially successful film, the 1985 sci-fi adventure Conan the Destroyer .
Anderson has had great success with his various collaborations with Anthony Burgess . He directed three of the author's novels: A Clockwork Orange (1971), The End of the World News (1975), and The Pianoplayers (1989). He has also directed The Assassination Bureau (1969), The Night of the Generals (1967), The Naked Prey (1965), and The Wilby Conspiracy (1975).  He has also directed films such as The Long Day's Dying (1968), The Immortal Story (1969), The Wilby Conspiracy (1975), and The Assassination Bureau (1969).
Anderson has received many awards, including the Grand Prix for Best Director at the 1975 Cannes Film Festival for The Assassination Bureau .

Mortimer Wheeler was born on 10 September 1890 in the city of Glasgow , Scotland . He was the first child of the journalist Rob

erson Wheeler and his wife Florence. Wheeler's father was a keen amateur archaeologist and a keen amateur photographer. In 1904, when Wheeler was fourteen, the family moved to London. Wheeler was educated at the Leys School and then he went to University College London. In 1907 he joined the Department of Ancient Monuments in the British Museum , where he worked as an Assistant Keeper (1910–28) and Keeper of the department (1928–47). He married Daphne Millar in 1912, whom he had met through his father.
In 1929, Wheeler began to combine his archaeological work with the study of prehistoric archaeology. In 1932 he was appointed to the Chair of Prehistoric Archaeology at University College London. In 1936 he was appointed Lecturer in Prehistoric Archaeology at Cambridge University , where he was appointed to the Chair of Prehistoric Archaeology in 1946. He was appointed a Knight Bachelor in 1938.
Wheeler was one of the first archaeologists in England to study prehistoric sites as if they were under modern conditions. He believed that the best way to study the past was through direct excavation. He established the first excavation unit for the University of Cambridge , which was known as the Prehistoric Excavation Unit (PEU). The first excavation that the PEU undertook was at the site of Old Sarum in 1934. In 1937, the PEU discovered a Neolithic long barrow at West Kennet Long Barrow . The PEU also took part in a 1937 excavation of the settlement at Star Carr, and conducted an excavation of the village at Grimes Graves in 1939.
In 1948 Wheeler was appointed Professor of Medieval Archaeology at the University of Cambridge , where he remained until his retirement in 1959.
Wheeler's best known excavations were at the Neolithic site of Stonehenge , which he began to excavate in 1920. He found that the site was much older than had been thought, and he suggested that the site consisted of three separate phases. He also suggested that the bluestones had come from Pembrokeshire, and the sarsens from the Marlborough Downs. Wheeler's second major excavation was at Silbury Hill . He was the first person to excavate the hill in 1937. He found that it was a mound of earth that had been brought to the site from surrounding areas (for example, Avebury). He also found evidence that a Neolithic long barrow had been built on top of this mound. He excavated the hill again in 1947, and in 1954 he found that the site had been built around 2,400 BC.
Wheeler also carried out excavations at the prehistoric site of Maiden Castle. He also carried out excavations at the Iron Age site of Old Sarum and the Bronze Age site of Barrow Clump. Wheeler also carried out excavations at the Roman settlement of Dorchester-on-Thames.
Wheeler wrote a number of books, including _Stonehenge_ (1934), _Megalithic Art_ (1941), _The Neolithic Sites of England_ (1952), _Prehistoric England_ (1957), and _Prehistoric Art in Europe_ (1964). He also wrote a number of articles for magazines such as _Antiquity_ , the _Man_ and the _Antiquaries Journal_.
Wheeler was appointed President of the Prehistoric Society in 1956. He was appointed a Fellow of the Society of Antiquaries of London in 1930. He was elected a Fellow of the British Academy in 1951. Wheeler was knighted in 1938 and was appointed an Honorary Fellow of the British Academy in 1959.
Wheeler died on 17 September 1976 in Cambridge, England .

The band first became involved with Sarajevo in 1993 on their Zoo TV Tour ; approached by aid worker Bill Carter about bringing

relief to the people of the besieged city then under attack by the Yugoslav army, U2 performed in a soccer stadium to an audience of 40,000 people. Simon Coveney, then a journalist with the _Irish Times_ , reported that they had "no request for a donation, no call for money, no plea for help. Just an emotional and political call for peace. Bono took off his jacket and, in his trademark camouflage combat trousers and sneakers, climbed on top of the stage. The crowd roared as the band launched into 'One', the song they had written about Sarajevo. When it finished, the crowd silenced and focused on Bono in his trademark trousers and sneakers, and he began to sing 'Sunday Bloody Sunday'."
The band were also the first to perform there after the war. In April 1997, they played a benefit concert for the building of a Youth Arts Centre in the city. The concert was filmed and broadcast on television, and was the first public performance by the band for four years.
In 2001, the band returned to the city with the Elevation Tour , playing a free concert in the abandoned soccer stadium to 60,000 people. Bono said that the audience had to be "the biggest, bravest and toughest in the world". The concert was filmed for release as _Elevation 2001: Live from Boston_ , and the band also performed "Miss Sarajevo" , an unreleased song by The Edge and Luciano Pavarotti.
Two years later, the band made their third trip to the city with the Vertigo Tour . In addition to the concert, the band filmed the documentary _Bono in Conversation with Edge_ , with Bono talking to the Edge about his writing and the creative process, and the Edge talking about his appreciation of U2's music.
In 2006, the band performed at a concert in Sarajevo in support of the One Campaign, during which Bono told the crowd that the city had "bled" for him. In 2011, the band played a concert in Sarajevo as part of their U2 360° Tour, with the band including the city on the first leg of the tour.
 On the Zoo TV Tour, the band performed two shows in Esters Park in Dublin.

Marlborough was 622 feet 9 inches ( 190 m ) long overall and had a beam of 90 ft ( 27 m ) and an average draught of 29 ft 6 in

( 8.99 m ). She had four funnels and a square stern. She was propelled by a pair of vertical triple-expansion steam engines, each driving a shaft, using steam provided by six coal-fired boilers. They produced a total of 10,000 indicated horsepower (7,500 kW) and gave a maximum speed of 20 knots ( 37 km/h; 23 mph ).

## Construction

The ship's keel was laid down at Yarrow's shipyard in London on 8 May 1886. She was launched on 21 October 1886 and completed on 25 July 1887.

## Wartime service

In 1906, Marlborough, under the command of Captain E. M. Thornton, was stationed in the South Atlantic. In 1907, she was in the Mediterranean.

In 1909, Marlborough was converted to a first-class cruiser. In 1910, she was placed in reserve.

## Disposal

Marlborough was stricken on 19 November 1912. She was sold to Thos. W. Ward for £11,500 on 5 July 1914. She was broken up by Thos. W. Ward at their yard in Grays, Essex.

Furtado said that with the release of her albums before Loose , she had wanted to prove herself as a musician and earn respect

from other artists and from fans. She explained that she did not want to be dismissed as a one-hit-wonder . She also said that she had been inspired to write the album's songs after she became an aunt and as a result of the September 11 attacks .

Furtado released the album's first single " Maneater " as the lead single on 20 September 2006 in Australia and on 17 October 2006 in the United States. The song peaked at number 13 on the US Billboard Hot 100 singles chart and at number 17 on the UK Singles Chart . The song "Say It Right" was released as the second single in March 2007. "Say It Right" peaked at number three on the US Billboard Hot 100, and number 11 on the UK Singles Chart. The album's third single " All Good Things (Come to an End)" was released in September 2007. The video for "All Good Things (Come to an End)" features Furtado in a variety of different outfits and locations, including a biker bar, a beach in Hawaii , and a nightclub.

### Title and packaging

The album's title comes from the phrase "the loose cannon", which is used to describe an unpredictable person. Furtado said that with her album Loose , she did not want to be categorized as a "loose" woman. She explained that the album's title is "a fun thing to say" and showed respect to her fans.

The CD booklet was designed by Furtado's friend and photographer, Max Vadukul. Furtado wrote her thoughts about the songs on a notecard and gave them to Vadukul. Vadukul then used the notecards to design the booklet.

### Musical style

The album's musical style was the subject of a great deal of speculation before the album's release. It has been described as pop, world music, dance-pop, R&B, electronic, hip hop and rock. According to Furtado, she wanted to make the album "different" from her previous albums.

## Critical reception

Professional ratings

Upon its release, Loose received generally positive reviews. At Metacritic, which assigns a normalized rating out of 100 to reviews from mainstream critics, the album received an average score of 66, which indicates "generally favorable reviews," based on 27 reviews.

Rolling Stone stated that "Furtado's become a master of the pop bounce, and her bouncy plus her social conscience equals a great pop album". AllMusic's Stephen Thomas Erlewine described Loose as "consciously eclectic". He praised Furtado as a "pop star who can sing, dance, and rap without sounding like an artifice". Entertainment Weekly wrote that Furtado "has made a career of blending various musical styles into cohesive, head-bopping pop", and that Loose "proves how adept she is at that". The Washington Post stated that "Furtado's efforts to broaden her sound always have been respectable, never boring".

Some critics, however, were more negative. The Times said of Loose that "the lyrics are pretty much the same - she's either bemoaning the plight of the poor, or mourning the loss of a lover". The Guardian said that the "highs are high but many of the lows are low" and that the album was "like a fairground ride with a few too many loops". Spin magazine noted that the album "doesn't quite live up to the promise of its title".

## Commercial performance

Loose debuted at number one on the Canadian Albums Chart , selling 71,000 copies in its first week. The album debuted at number two on the US Billboard 200 chart, selling 272,000 copies in its first week, becoming Furtado's second consecutive number-one album in the United States. The album has sold over two million copies in the United States, and over four million copies worldwide.

" Burns ' Heir " is the eighteenth episode of The Simpsons ' fifth season . It originally aired on the Fox network in the Unite

States on February 15, 1994 .
In this episode, Homer Simpson wins $ 20,000 in the lottery , but his money is taken by Fat Tony and his gang . Homer then decides to steal money from Springfield 's big businesses .  In 1993, Homer Simpson wins $ 20,000 in the lottery , and he uses the money to buy a new car, but Homer loses the car in a tragic accident involving Bart and Lisa Simpson . Homer decides to steal money from Springfield's big businesses, and he and Bart go on a crime spree . Chief Wiggum catches Homer and Bart, and Fat Tony and his gang members take them to a deserted island . While there, Homer gets his own money back, and he and the children escape . Fat Tony and his gang capture Bart again and leave him on the island . Homer, however, convinces Bart to help him defeat Fat Tony and his gang .

Meyerbeer 's immense wealth ( increased by the success of his operas ) and his continuing adherence to his Jewish religion set

him apart from the world of the aristocratic and established _' haute école'._ There was also a personal factor.  In 1857 he married Eugenie Désirée Delannoy, a young Parisian actress and _grande dame_ , who was to have a profound influence on his work. They had no children.  The marriage was quite remarkable in its equality.  There are no hints of friction in the letters.  Indeed, the relationship is very much that of husband and wife.  The _ménage_ lived in a large and sumptuous apartment in the rue du Faubourg-Saint-Honoré, Paris.  The atmosphere was warm and homely.  'The entire household is in good health and happy,' wrote Isabella in 1862.  Meyerbeer, however, was often away.  He was a regular visitor to Baden-Baden, where he built a villa and lived much of his life.  He was also in Italy and America.  The _ménage_ survived his death, and continued to live in the rue du Faubourg-Saint-Honoré.  Eugenie's last days were spent in a room in a  nursing home in the rue de la Glacière (see plate 1).
There is a lot of information on the subject of Meyerbeer's finances.  He was very wealthy, and the details of his income and expenditure have been preserved in the archives of the Meyerbeer family in Paris.  The information is held in a series of three volumes called _Les finances de Meyerbeer_ , which are in the Bibliothèque National, Paris.  They were published in 1877 by his executor, Édouard Maret, and are available for consultation.  _Les finances_ cover the period from 1831 to 1864.  The first volume contains the income and expenditure of the _ménage_ , the second the income and expenditure of Meyerbeer himself, and the third the income and expenditure of his musical works.  All the amounts are in francs, and the figures are in round figures.  The figures were converted into pounds sterling at the rate of one franc to one shilling.  The information in the _finances_ was supplied by the executor, and is therefore suspect.  For example, the figure for the income of Meyerbeer's works for 1860 is stated as 1,032,000 francs.  The income for the same year was 750,000 francs.  The 1860 figure is therefore 150,000 francs too high.  The total income in 1860 was 1,322,000 francs – the highest income of the whole period.  The 1860 figure for expenditure is given as 1,376,000 francs, which is correct.  The total expenditure for the whole period was 17,209,000 francs.  This was a large sum in the 1830s, but was dwarfed by the expenditure of Napoleon III.  His personal expenditure in 1860 was estimated at 50 million francs.  Meyerbeer was a great patron of the arts and architecture.  He spent large sums on collecting works of art and furnishing his home.  He also spent a lot on charities, including the Freemasons, the orphanage in Berlin, and the Fund to Help the Indigent.
 The figure of 14 million francs in the _finances_ is probably a rough estimate of the income from Meyerbeer's operas for the period.  The income from his operas was in any case a very small fraction of the total income, which was mostly from his investment income.  The investment income was so large that it is tempting to describe Meyerbeer as a money-lender.  But this is an exaggeration.  He did not in fact make his fortune from his investment income, but from his operas.  The money that his operas made for him was spent on investments.  In 1856 he was able to invest 2.5 million francs from a sale of shares in the Cologne-Mindener railway.  In 1860 he invested 4 million francs from the sale of the shares in the railway between St Gothard and Brenner.  The investments made him a large income, but not a fortune

On July 24 , the SS Pacificus encountered a storm with maximum sustained winds meeting the threshold of tropical storm status r

ated at 50 mph.

## Storm

The storm developed over the South China Sea on July 23 and began to track westwards. The storm reached peak wind speeds of 75 mph (120 km/h) on July 24 , persisting until the storm merged with a frontal system on July 25 . The storm was named by the JTWC as Tropical Storm 15W.

## Impact

Tropical Storm 15W never reached the Philippines. However, the storm's strong winds caused the SS Pacificus to sink. The Pacificus had a crew of 23 and 2000 tons of cargo on board. Of the 600 men on board, 255 were rescued, while 335 remained missing.

This case is about whether the Massachusetts Workers' Compensation Act (the WCA ) provides benefits to an employee injured at work even if the employee settles his or her liability to a third-party tortfeasor. The WCA provides an exclusive remedy for the employee's injuries-that is, if the employee is injured at work, he or she can only recover workers' compensation benefits under the WCA. The third-party tortfeasor, therefore, is not responsible to the employee for the employee's injuries. See G. L. c. 152, § 1.
The case before us involves the issue of whether a settlement agreement between the employee and the tortfeasor releases the employer from liability under the WCA. The employee settled with the tortfeasor, but the employer, unlike the tortfeasor, did not release the employee in the settlement. The employer claims, therefore, that it is not liable to the employee for the employee's injuries.
While we agree with the majority that the WCA provides an exclusive remedy, we conclude that the WCA does not require the employer to release its liability to the employee under the WCA. We therefore reverse the order of the Appellate Division and the judgment of the District Court.
 On June 25 , 2001 , the Appellate Division affirmed the decision of the District Court and determined that the employer was liable under the WCA. Id. The employer appealed to the Supreme Judicial Court, and we reserved and reported the case.

On August 4, the 10th Light Horse Brigade , under Brigadier-General H. E. Elliott , struck a tentative blow against the Ottoman defenders at Romani.  During this engagement, the 10th Light Horse Regiment had 259 casualties with 55 missing, and the 2nd Light Horse Regiment lost 169 casualties with 65 missing.  The 5th Light Horse Regiment had 185 casualties with 53 missing.  The 10th Light Horse Brigade had 437 casualties with 183 missing.

### Battle of Bir el Hassana (August 9)

Main article: Battle of Bir el Hassana

On August 9, the 5th Mounted Brigade , under Brigadier-General E. S. Morshead, reinforced the 3rd Light Horse Brigade and made a night march to Bir el Hassana, 12 kilometres (7.5 mi) north-east of Romani.  The 5th Mounted Brigade , along with the 3rd Light Horse Brigade , attacked and captured Bir el Hassana.  The Ottoman forces were driven off with 142 casualties.  The 5th Mounted Brigade suffered one killed and nine wounded.

The typhoon also moved over a region where the vertical wind shear was low and the relative humidity was high, which promoted strengthening. Townsend was born in Weston-super-Mare, Somerset, England. He had a brother and sister. Townsend's father was a professional saxophonist and his mother a pianist. He had a strict Catholic upbringing, and recalls being repulsed by the sight of a man wearing a dress, which he believed was a woman.

Townsend's first instrument was a tambourine at the age of four. He quickly moved on to the piano and then, at the age of nine, to the guitar. He was inspired by his father's record collection to listen to artists such as The Beatles, Jimi Hendrix and The Kinks, and he took up the guitar.

At the age of 11, Townsend formed his first band, The Detours, with his brother Paul, and their friend John 'Rhino' Edwards. The band was named after a local pub in their hometown of Weston-super-Mare. Townsend and his brother Paul were later joined by Ian Hill and John Deacon, making the original lineup of Judas Priest.

The need for phylogenetic studies on this group has been suggested (Schulze et al. 1993).
 In the present study, we used sequences of the internal transcribed spacer (ITS) and beta-tubulin from Amylostereum and Phanerochaete species to test the monophyly of these genera, to determine their phylogenetic relationships with other species, and to reconsider the taxonomic status of Amylostereum and Phanerochaete species.
 The isolates used in this study were identified on the basis of macroscopic and microscopic characteristics, and were deposited in the culture collection of the Forestry Research Institute at Ljubljana, Slovenia (FRL).
 The data used in this study were obtained from the isolates of P. chrysosporium and A. areolatum deposited at the FRL. These fungi have been previously used in taxonomic studies (Fischer et al. 1997, 2000). We also used sequences of ITS and beta-tubulin from P. chrysosporium ATCC 60600 (Schulze et al. 1993) and A. areolatum FRL 00901 (Fischer et al. 2000).
 The 5.8S, ITS1 and ITS2 regions of the nuclear ribosomal DNA were amplified by using the primers ITS1F (Gerry et al. 1990) and ITS4 (White et al. 1990), respectively. The beta-tubulin gene was amplified by using the primer pair Beta-3 (Fisher et al. 2001). The PCR products were sequenced using the ABI PRISM BigDye Terminator Cycle Sequencing Ready Reaction Kit (Applied Biosystems) and an ABI PRISM 310 Genetic Analyzer (Applied Biosystems). The sequencing of the internal transcribed spacers was performed with the primer pairs ITS1F and ITS4 (White et al. 1990).
 Homology searches were performed using the Basic Local Alignment Search Tool (BLAST) at the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) website (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/BLAST/).

The percentage of similarity between sequences was calculated using the ClustalW multiple sequence alignment program. ## Geography

The island has an area of 278.3 square miles (721 km²) of land and 10.4 square miles (27 km²) of water. It is 27 miles (43 km) long and between 3 and 8 miles (4.8 and 13 km) wide. The eastern end of Galveston Island is known as the East End .

### Climate

Galveston has a humid subtropical climate (Koppen Cfa) with a mean annual temperature of 70.9 °F (21.6 °C). Although there is no true winter season, the average daily low temperature can fall below 50 °F (10 °C) on 82 days per year, and fall below 40 °F (4 °C) on 24 nights per year. The record low temperature is 11 °F (−12 °C), last recorded on January 4, 1930.

The average annual precipitation is 48.9 in (1,242 mm), with the bulk of the rainfall occurring in May through September. The wettest month is June, with an average of 6.29 in (159 mm) of precipitation, and the driest month is January, with an average of 2.28 in (58 mm). Snow is rare, with an average of 0.1 in (0.25 cm) falling per year. The record snowfall is 1.0 in (2.5 cm), which fell on February 24, 1933.

The highest recorded temperature was 107 °F (42 °C) on July 1, 2011, and the lowest recorded temperature was 11 °F (−12 °C) on January 4, 1930.

## Demographics

According to the 2020 census, 50,180 people lived in Galveston. (The 2010 census population was 47,743.) The 2010 population was 57.7% White, 28.2% Black or African American, 0.7% American Indian and Alaska Native, 1.7% Asian, 0.1% Native Hawaiian and other Pacific Islander, 12.1% Some other race, and 5.5% two or more races. Hispanics or Latinos of any race were 25.2% of the population.

The Westminster Assembly of Divines was a council of theologians ( or " divines " ) and members of the English Parliament appointed in 1643 by Parliament to restructure the Church of England. The assembly is known for its work on the Westminster Confession of Faith and the Westminster Shorter Catechism , which are still used by Presbyterians today.
Nevertheless, the Assembly's work resulted in the Presbyterian form of church government being adopted in Scotland and Ireland, and the Congregational form in New England. The assembly is notable for its own internal disagreements.
The assembly was formed in 1643, following the start of the First English Civil War. It met in Westminster Hall in London until its dissolution in 1649. The assembly was made up of 121 commissioners from the Church of England and 22 commissioners from the Church of Scotland, together with 18 divines from New England. The assembly was presided over by William Laud (Archbishop of Canterbury), George Gillespie (Church of Scotland), and Thomas Goodwin (Church of England).
The assembly's work on the Westminster Confession of Faith was the culmination of a period of doctrinal dispute between the Scottish and English churches, which had begun in 1638 and was part of the wider political tensions of the period. The assembly's other chief work was the production of the Westminster Shorter Catechism, commissioned by the English Parliament as a "short" version of the Catechism that had been a mainstay of education in Scotland since 1642. The assembly's doctrinal standards and catechisms were intended to be authoritative for the Church of England, and they later became influential in American Presbyterianism, Congregationalism, and the Church of England.
The assembly was disbanded by the Rump Parliament in 1649, but the Westminster Confession of Faith and the Shorter Catechism remained important documents in the Presbyterian tradition. In 1662, the Westminster Confession was adopted by the Church of England as the Thirty-Nine Articles.

The noisy miner is one of four species in the genus Manorina in the large family of honeyeaters known as Meliphagidae , the oth

- ers being yellow-faced, grey-headed and red-bellied. They are small to medium-sized birds, usually 14 to 18 centimetres long with a wingspread of 25 to 27 centimetres. Their plumage is darker than that of the other three species, and they are also more robust.
Their range extends from the Kimberley region of Western Australia southwards through the tropics and sub-tropics of northern Australia to the East Coast of Queensland. They are also found in New Guinea and the Moluccas. The noisy miner was introduced to New Zealand in 1866, but is absent from the northern North Island.
The noisy miner has been recorded in large flocks of up to 400 birds, but most sightings are of 20 to 40 birds. They are usually found in trees near water, but can also be seen in open woodland, orchards, gardens and suburban areas.
Their loud, metallic 'chirp-chirp-chirp-chirp', which is often heard throughout the day, is the source of the common name. The miner's name comes from their eating habits. They are ferocious predators and will chase off other birds in search of food, both in trees and on the ground. They lay their eggs in holes in trees and other cavities such as old cattle troughs and will also use nest boxes.
Their nests are made of grass, straw fibres and feathers and lined with hair and fur. They lay 2 to 4 eggs and both parents share incubation duties.
The noisy miner is a highly social bird and will often mob or attack people if they enter their territory. This is a defence mechanism to protect their food source.
This species is classified as Least Concern on the New Zealand Threat Classification System.

number that is growing as the bugs are found in more of the southern United States.  It is the most commonly found species of the genus A. fragilis, reaching its northern limit at the southern fringe of the Great Lakes. It is parasitic on the larvae of several species of tiger and longhorn beetles, including the common green tiger beetle (Cicindela campestris) and the longhorned or stag beetle (Cicindela hybrida). The life cycle starts in the soil, where a female burrows into the ground to lay her eggs. She deposits them next to the larvae of a tiger beetle or longhorn beetle. The female then dies. The eggs hatch into nymphs. They seek out the larvae of a tiger or longhorn beetle. Once they find their prey, they penetrate the exoskeleton and enter the body cavity. The nymphs then develop into adults, which leave the prey larvae and move on to find another. They then seek out a host to lay their eggs.
A. fragilis is a small wasp, with a body length of about 6.5 millimetres (0.26 in). The coloration of the body varies with the species, but is usually a dull brown or gray, the thorax more yellowish than the abdomen. In some species the abdomen is black or dark blue.  The species has a slender body, with a long and slender abdomen. The abdomen is somewhat flattened, with the first two segments being longer and narrower than the last two. The head is small, with large eyes and short antennae.  The mouthparts are well developed and appear to be adapted for piercing and sucking.
The male is slightly smaller than the female. The abdomen is somewhat less flattened, with the first segment only slightly longer and narrower than the last. The female is also the more common of the two species.
The species is parasitic on the larvae of longhorn beetles and tiger beetles in the subfamily Cicindelinae, especially the genus Cicindela. They attack larvae of Cicindela campestris (green tiger beetle), Cicindela hybrida (stag beetle), and Cicindela scutellaris (copper tiger beetle).
The life cycle of A. fragilis is a little unusual for wasps. The females do not lay eggs as soon as they find a host. Instead, they burrow into the ground, at least 10 centimetres (4 in), and deposit their eggs. They then die. This is the first stage of the complete life cycle.
The eggs are laid next to the larvae of the tiger or longhorn beetle. The larvae hatch from the eggs and seek out the females as they move about. Once found, they penetrate the skin of the female and enter her body cavity.
The larvae then develop into the adult wasps. The adult wasps seek out other tiger beetle or longhorn beetle larvae. Once they find a host, they enter the body cavity and lay their eggs. They then leave the prey larvae and seek out a host to lay their eggs.
A. fragilis is capable of penetrating the skin of the larvae and entering their body cavity. It can also penetrate and enter the body cavity of adult tiger beetles.

## Plot

See also: List of Sholay characters

Thakur Baldev Singh, the Thakur of the village, is a tough and honest man who is opposed to dishonesty and injustice. He is served by his loyal and righteous son Veeru, and his ambitious and ruthless nephew, a police inspector by the name of Jai.

The Thakur is marked for death by Gabbar Singh, the local dacoit, as he had earlier put an end to Gabbar's brother. Gabbar Singh and his gang of dacoits are terrorising the village, with the Thakur's men protecting the villagers. The Thakur refuses to pay protection money to Gabbar Singh, who in retaliation murders his brother.

Jai and Veeru are sent by the police to capture Gabbar Singh, who has a reward of ₹1 lakh (US$1,300) on his head. Jai and Veeru pursue Gabbar Singh and his gang to a nearby hill, where Gabbar Singh has ordered his men to dig a well. Gabbar Singh and Veeru fight and Gabbar is wounded. Jai pursues Gabbar, who throws a knife at him. Gabbar Singh discovers that he is wounded and orders his men to help him return to his hideout. Jai and Veeru return to the village to find the Thakur's men dead.

Veeru and Jai return to the Thakur to tell him of the attack. The Thakur is shocked and prepares to leave for the village with Veeru and Jai. Gabbar Singh's men attack the Thakur's entourage and kidnap the Thakur. Gabbar Singh and his men return to their hideout. Veeru and Jai return to the village and inform the police. The police officers in the village are corrupt and do not help them. Veeru and Jai meet Basanti, a girl living in the village who has a crush on Jai. Basanti is asked by Veeru and Jai to cook a meal for them. She agrees, but takes a gun belonging to Veeru, which goes off and kills the Thakur's cook. Jai and Veeru realise that Gabbar Singh is hiding in the hill with the Thakur. Veeru and Jai decide to go to the hill to rescue the Thakur.

They take the Thakur's daughter-in-law, Radha, with them, along with a few guns and other ammunition. They head for the hill and meet Basanti, who is now carrying the gun and is reluctant to return it. They convince her to return the gun. They arrive at the hill and find the Thakur's son, Thakur's family members and the Thakur's men dead. Gabbar Singh and his men have killed everyone. Veeru and Jai kill Gabbar Singh and his men in a fierce fight. Veeru and Jai kill Gabbar Singh and his men, and set the entire hill on fire. Veeru and Jai rescue Thakur Baldev Singh and his family, and everyone is present at the funeral of the Thakur's son.

York mostly occupied the bottom half of the table before the turn of the year , and dropped as low as 23rd in September 2013 .

The club's form improved noticeably in the second half of the season, reaching 12th by the end of April. In the final table of the 2013–14 Premier League, they secured their highest placing since their relegation from the top flight in 2004, finishing in 10th position.
The 2014–15 season saw York again finish in 10th place in the Premier Division, and in 2015–16 they finished in the top three for the first time in their history, winning promotion to the National League for the first time.
York are the oldest and most successful of all the Yorkshire clubs and are one of the oldest clubs in England. They first played football at Knavesmire in 1877 and were one of the founders of the Northern League in 1892. They were elected to the Football League in 1929 and spent 51 years in the division, before being relegated in 1980. Their best league performance was in 1973–74 when they finished third in the old Second Division. After their relegation they spent a further 27 years in the Football Conference, before being relegated again in 2007. York were promoted to the Conference Premier in 2012, but were relegated again the following season. They returned to the National League in 2016.
York were formed in 1877 by a group of students at the York County School for Boys. The school was founded on 18 September 1873, but the students started playing football a year later. They played initially at the school playing field, but moved to the Knavesmire in 1876. They were admitted to the Northern League in 1892, where they won the title in the 1894–95 season, the first of their many successes. In 1897 they won the short-lived Yorkshire Senior Competition before becoming founder members of the Football League Third Division North in 1921.
The club's first season in the Football League was a success. York were runners-up to Manchester United, and were promoted to the Second Division a year later. However, they were relegated in 1929 with the lowest points total in the division's history. They remained in the division for 51 years, ending their spell in the Second Division as the second lowest scorers in its history.
York's first relegation came in 1970, but they remained in the Football League until 1980 when they were relegated to the Third Division following a 0–0 draw with Wrexham on the final day of the season. York finished in the top three in 2015–16, and were promoted to the National League for the first time in the club's history.

In the last decade, the diamond stingray (Dasyatis brevis) has been involved in a variety of fisheries in the Gulf of California , which has led to the increase in its abundance in artisanal fisheries. The purpose of this study is to determine the distribution of the population of the diamond stingray in artisanal fisheries, and to determine the relation- ships between its abundance and the catch of other species.
The specimens were collected by artisanal fishermen in 2010 and in 2011 in the Gulf of California, México. The specimens were identified to species level and size, sex, and state were recorded. The data were analyzed using the Generalized Linear Model with binomial error structure.
During the study, 995 specimens of diamond stingray were collected in the artisanal fishery of the Gulf of California. It was found that the abundance of the diamond stingray in artisanal fisheries is related to the catch of sharks and rays (p = 0.04) and to the size of the catch of the other species (p = 0.03).
Knowledge of the abundance of the diamond stingray in artisanal fisheries is important for the regulation of the artisanal fishery of large sharks and rays in the Gulf of California and for the sustainability of the fishery of these important resources.

He was a member of the household of King Henry I.  He was elected as Archbishop of York in 1091, and consecrated on 29 January 1100 by Anselm ,  Archbishop of Canterbury.  His influence as Archbishop was at the time limited, because the Archbishop's palatine powers over the diocese of York were restricted by the King.  He had to gain permission from the King to enter York.  He was deposed by the King on 20 May 1108, but was restored to his see in 1109.  He died on 21 May 1108.  He was buried at Westminster Abbey .  His remains were later transferred to Durham Cathedral . 

As an Archbishop, Gerard's actions were limited to his diocese; he was unable to exercise his functions elsewhere.  He was nevertheless, in this capacity, a leader of the church in England.  His election as Archbishop was the result of the influence of his uncle, Thomas Becket, who was then Chancellor of England.  He was appointed to the post of Chancellor of England by King Henry I in 1085.  His influence in this position was considerable.  In 1092, he was planned to be replaced by his brother, Robert FitzHerbert, but the King was dissuaded from this by Becket.  He resigned in 1095, being replaced by his brother.  He was known for his piety,  and was a friend of Pope Urban II .

The rhyme has traditionally been seen as a nonsense verse , particularly as the couple go up a hill to find water , which is of

course the very opposite of sense. The spelling of place names and the inclusion of people's names suggest that the verses were written in the 1740s. If this is so, they were written after the publication of the _Transactions of the Society for the Encouragement of Arts, Manufactures and Commerce_ , which contained a number of articles on the proposed building of the Grand Canal . In 1753, John Abernethy, the chairman of the canal committee, published an account of a voyage made in a boat along the Thames from Oxford to London. Thames water was described as being 'not only brackish, but bitter and fetid'. The Grand Canal was to be built to bring fresh water from the River Thames to the City of London.
 The rhyme itself is much older than the 1740s, having first been recorded in the English ballad 'The Old Juggler' (Child 6, Roud 551), in which the couple goes to the seaside and the wife goes to the seaside to drown herself. It is also found in the Scottish ballad 'The Twa Corbies' (Child 64, Roud 473, Laws P28(260)), in which the couple goes to the seaside to find water and the wife goes to the seaside to die.
 The rhyme also appears in 'The Water-Cop', a curious ballad with a Scottish or Irish provenance which describes the murder of a man who had been stolen away by water genii. The genii drowned the man in a well and buried him in the ground. The man's body was then discovered by a boy who took the body to his mother. The woman washed the body and treated it with an ointment which made the body waterproof. She then hid the body in the well. Later, the boy was caught by the genii and brought to the well. The genii drowned him and his remains were taken to the same well. The woman was then forced to bring the body to her mother who had a similar ointment to her own. The woman's mother, who had been visited by the genii, was able to revive the boy. 'The Water-Cop' is found in several sources, including in a collection of Scottish ballads published by James Hogg in 1822.

The ESS was created by Thomas Mitchell and a team from the Carnegie Mellon University .
Until then, building an expert system was a very tedious process. First you had to define and model the domain, the area of expertise. Then you had to program the knowledge base, the rules that made up what the expert knew about the domain. Finally, you had to implement the inference engine, the algorithm that made the rules come to life and actually answered questions.
The ESS, in contrast, was a way to implement a knowledge base and reasoning engine in a generic way. It decoupled the logic of building a knowledge base from the logic of implementing the reasoning engine. This meant that the first step had to be to define the rules of the domain - the knowledge base. Then the second step was to implement the inference engine, the module that makes the rules come to life.
In 1984 , Thomas Mitchell and his then colleague at CMU, Michael Brady , wrote a book about the ESS, _Expert Systems Foundations and Practice_.
The ESS was not the first expert system shell but it was the first one that was truly successful. It was one of the reasons that expert systems suddenly exploded in popularity in the early 1980s. Now anyone could build an expert system.

In animals , amino acids are obtained through the consumption of foods containing protein . Ingested proteins are then broken d

o w n into their constituent amino acids by digestive enzymes . The various amino acids are then absorbed into the bloodstream and transported to the liver , which synthesizes the amino acids that are not obtained through dietary sources.
The body uses amino acids to synthesize protein (the most important job for amino acids), but they also play an important role in a variety of other functions throughout the body. These functions include the synthesis of neurotransmitters, antibodies, enzymes, hormones, and cellular energy . In addition, amino acids are important in the regulation of the body's fluid balance .
A number of amino acids are also needed to maintain good health. Some of these amino acids are considered to be nonessential because the body can make them from others. Essential amino acids, on the other hand, are those which cannot be made by the body and must be obtained from the diet.
The essential amino acids are arginine , histidine , isoleucine , leucine , lysine , methionine , phenylalanine , threonine , tryptophan , and valine . The amino acid, cysteine, is sometimes considered to be an essential amino acid.
The amino acids arginine and histidine are both important for the growth and repair of tissues, the synthesis of proteins, and the production of immune cells. Isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, and threonine are involved in the synthesis of proteins and in the production of antibodies.
Cysteine is required for the synthesis of glutathione, an important antioxidant . Threonine, tryptophan, and valine are also involved in the production of antibodies and other immune cells .
A variety of amino acids are also important for the regulation of fluid balance. For example, arginine and cysteine help to increase the flow of urine . In addition, glutamate and aspartate help to increase the flow of urine and stimulate the release of other amino acids into the bloodstream.
The amount of each amino acid that is required to maintain proper bodily function varies. However, most experts agree that the body requires 11 to 12 grams of the essential amino acids and 1 to 1.5 grams of the nonessential amino acids each day.
Amino acids are found in the greatest number in animal sources of protein. For example, eggs, milk, and cheese are rich in the essential amino acids, while lean meat, fish, and poultry are rich in the nonessential amino acids. In addition, the amino acid, histidine, is found in high concentrations in legumes .
The body's need for amino acids can be met through a well-balanced diet which includes foods containing both animal and vegetable sources of protein.
Many people take amino acids in supplement form to meet the body's need for specific amino acids, or even to provide the body with all of the amino acids it needs. For example, many athletes take amino acid supplements to increase their energy and endurance. Other people take amino acid supplements to treat a variety of conditions.
Amino acids are generally well tolerated and are safe to take in supplement form. However, certain types of amino acids may interact with certain medications or have side effects. For this reason, it is important to consult a doctor before taking any supplements.

It was on 30 July that the travelling funeral party reached the town of Oakland , Illinois for the funeral with 10, 000 people in attendance , including the families of all of the victims.  The funeral was held at the Oakland Methodist Church and the coffins that had been taken from the lake were placed in the church at 9 a.m.  A procession to the Oakland Cemetery followed , with the hearse leading the way to the site of the burial.  A wreath was placed at the base of the harp on the cemetery monument and the caskets were placed in the graves.  The funeral was well attended and a short eulogy was given by the Rev. William F. B. Heintzelman.  In addition to the funeral , a memorial service was also held at the Oakland Methodist Church for the victims of the crash.  The memorial service was held on 27 August 1917.  A total of 1420 people attended and the Rev. Heintzelman delivered a eulogy before the church.  Also present was the Executive Secretary of the Pilgrim Fathers Society , George H. Barnes.  The passengers that were killed were buried in 36 graves , with the two graves that were unclaimed being later filled in by the families of the victims.  In total , the funeral cost $35,000 .  On 27 July 1917, the bodies of the dead were removed from the lake to the Illinois Central Railroad station at Peoria , Illinois for transportation to Oakland , Illinois.  The bodies were then taken to the Mortuary of the Patterson Funeral Home in Oakland.  The bodies were removed from the lake by a large crane that was positioned on shore at 4 p.m. on 26 July 1917.  This crane was able to reach down and grab the bodies under the water and then lift them to the surface.  The bodies were then transferred to an ambulance for transportation to Oakland.  The bodies were then stored at the Oakland Methodist Church for the funeral and the burial.

She felt that the episode "made a much stronger point" about the Federation's flaws when it showed the character of Dathon, who was "an idealist hiding in the midst of a messy, selfish, and corrupt society." She also felt that the episode set up the character of Captain Kirk as a "boorish, emotionally manipulative, and very human leader" and that the episode "showed how far Kirk's actions would go to protect the Enterprise and her crew".

George R. N. Wright concluded that the episode is "generally mediocre". He wrote that the performance by the actors is "reasonably good" and that the sets, costumes and special effects are "acceptable". He praised the episode's first half and the "encounter with the Capellans" but felt that the second half was "rather weak". He felt that the episode's main problem was that it was "very disjointed".

In 2016, SyFy Wire included "A Taste of Armageddon" on their list of "The 10 best Star Trek episodes that aren't on Netflix" and Zack Handlen reviewed the episode for The A.V. Club. He wrote that the episode "isn't great Star Trek, but it's a good reminder of the series' strengths", and that the episode "shows the series' willingness to play around with its format" and that the episode shows "an impressive vision of what Star Trek can be, when the show isn't afraid to put its characters in danger". He concluded that the episode was "a great example of how the show can do more than just explore the ship's tech and explore the unknown. It's a testament to how much the show can do with what it's given".

Several critics have focused on the theme of motherhood . In " Mothers and Daughters / Aging and Dying " , Claire Sprague wrote

that _The Trip to Bountiful_ "concentrates on the conflicts between a mother and a daughter: between the two in the past, and between the two in the present . . . the play focuses on the mother's desire to return to her past, and, at the same time, her daughter's desire to escape from it."  In "How to Kill a Mother," Linda Steiner wrote: "The mother's domesticity is the wellspring of her power, and this is what the daughter wants to escape. It is also what the daughter fears her mother is trying to escape."  Steiner also compared Hurd-Wood's Carrie Watts to the character of Martha in Edmund Wilson's _The Woman Who Had Two Navels and Tales of the Tropical Gothic_ , "a mother whose whole existence is reduced to the needs of her children . . . her days are filled with the care of her children . . . she is unconscious of her own nature, and consequently nothing but her children exist for her . . . Martha's story is one of progressive escape from her children, from her role, and from her self."  The theme of motherhood is further explored in Sprague's article, "Mothers and Daughters: Aging and Dying in the Theater," in which she discusses the psychoanalytic concept of mourning (which consists of a series of stages: denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance). She writes that in _The Trip to Bountiful_ , "The family conflict is a struggle between the daughter's desire to escape from her mother's domination and the mother's inability to let go of her domination. The conflict is not resolved, but the daughter is struggling to reach a stage of maturity and independence that will allow her to do so."  Sprague next discusses the character of Miss Thibideaux, who helps the mother and daughter come to terms with their relationship.

Senna and Ratzenberger were killed during the Grand Prix as a result of the latter's car hitting a concrete barrier while racing and Senna's car hitting Ratzenberger's car after it spun off the track.
The 1995 season was the first since 1970 without the death of a driver during a race. Ratzenberger's death was the first since Steve Thompson's at the 1975 British Grand Prix . The 1995 season is also the longest time since the 1965 season that every driver reached the end of a Grand Prix or retired from a race. The 1995 season was the first since 1979 that no driver was eliminated from a race due to an accident.
 The 1994 Indianapolis 500 was the 78th running of the Indianapolis 500 and the ninth annual Indianapolis 500 race sanctioned by the International Race of Champions (IROC). The event took place on May 30, 1994, at the Indianapolis Motor Speedway in Speedway, Indiana.
The race was won by Bobby Rahal, who started from second place, after Mario Andretti's engine failed while leading. The race was marked by a rare full-course caution on lap 90 when a blown engine on the car of Jimmy Vasser caused a massive oil leak.
The 1994 CART PPG Indy Car World Series season was the 19th season of the CART PPG Indy Car World Series. Mario Andretti won the series championship, the third of his career.
The 1994 season marked the beginning of the IndyCar Series's "unification" with the Indy Racing League, which began in 1996.
The 1994 IROC season was the second and final season of the International Race of Champions. The season consisted of 12 events ran between 14 February and 31 October. The final event was the IROC 12 Hours of Daytona, held at the Daytona International Speedway in Daytona Beach, Florida.
The 1994 season was originally scheduled to consist of 14 races, but the IROC race at the 1994 Indianapolis 500 was cancelled after the death of driver Paul Dana during practice for the race.
Arie Luyendyk won the championship, his second of three in IROC.
The 1994 Pendle Rally was the 13th running of the Pendle Rally, a motor racing event held in the United Kingdom. It was the seventh round of the 1994 British Rally Championship. The rally was based in Colne and ran in the Colne Valley, Burnley, Pendle, Clitheroe and Rossendale areas of Lancashire. The rally began on 25 June 1994 and finished on 26 June 1994.
The 1994 World Rally Championship season was the 22nd season of the FIA World Rally Championship. The season began on 21 January with the Monte Carlo Rally and ended on 20 November with the Rally Catalunya. The FIA World Rally Championship was won by Mitsubishi's Tommi Mäkinen.
The 1994 Australian Grand Prix was a Formula One motor race held on 20 March 1994 at Adelaide Street Circuit, Adelaide. It was the second race of the 1994 Formula One season.
The 1994 Australian Grand Prix was a Formula One motor race held on 20 March 1994 at Adelaide Street Circuit, Adelaide. It was the second race of the 1994 Formula One season. The race was held over 67 laps of the Adelaide Street Circuit and was won by Johnny Herbert of Tyrrell.
The 1994 Canadian Grand Prix was the third race of the 1994 Formula One season. It was held on 19 June 1994 at the Circuit Gilles Villeneuve in Montreal, Quebec, Canada.

Flooding damages on the Mississippi – Missouri river system were one of the primary reasons for which Congress passed the Flood

Control Act of 1928. In 1944, the Flood Control Act of 1944 authorized the Corps to construct a flood control project for the upper Mississippi River and its tributaries, including the Missouri River.
The project, named after the tributary, was authorized to be developed over a five-year period, with construction to begin in 1945 and be completed by 1950. The flood control works were to be planned and constructed by the Corps of Engineers, and included the construction of dams, levees, and floodway, in addition to a flood-control channel for navigation. The project was designed to provide a capacity of 100,000 cubic feet per second (2,800 m3/s) in all stages of the flood.
The project included the construction of 14 major dams, along with numerous smaller dams, levees, and floodways. The dams were to be built in five major river basins, known as the Oahe, Big Bend, Canton, Garrison, and Fort Randall Basins. The project also included the creation of Lake Oahe, a large reservoir on the Missouri River.
In 1947, the Congress authorized the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to develop the feasibility report for the project. Construction began in 1949, and the project was completed in 1967.
In total, the project cost $531 million, and was the largest flood control project in the United States. The project has been credited with reducing flood damage along the Missouri River by 94 percent.
The Missouri River Headwaters Project is a flood control project on the Missouri River in the United States. The project was authorized by the Flood Control Act of 1944 and was completed in 1978.
The project includes the construction of the Fort Peck Dam and Reservoir, which is the largest dam and reservoir in the United States by volume. The project also includes the Garrison Dam and Reservoir, which is the second largest dam and reservoir in the United States by volume, as well as the Fort Randall Dam and Reservoir, which is the third largest dam and reservoir in the United States by volume.
The project is operated and maintained by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers.
By August , Alabama had a combined 21 players on 12 different preseason award watch lists . These included both Mark Barron , M

VP of the BCS National Championship, and Dont'a Hightower , the defensive player of the game.
Several other awards had added Alabama players in recent days, including being the leading candidate for three of the four Lombardi Awards (Offensive Lineman, Defensive Lineman, and Linebacker).
Despite the accolades, Alabama was still a 12-point underdog in the game against the No. 1 LSU Tigers. The game was played in Tiger Stadium, in Baton Rouge, Louisiana. The game was broadcast nationally by CBS, with Brad Nessler calling the game alongside Gary Danielson and studio host Jamie Erdahl.
Both teams came out firing. LSU scored on its opening drive, and Alabama countered with a touchdown drive of its own. Neither team would score again for the rest of the first quarter.
On the first drive of the second quarter, LSU regained the lead with a touchdown. Alabama responded with a 77-yard touchdown pass from AJ McCarron to Amari Cooper, and a two-point conversion, to regain the lead. The Crimson Tide went for two on the next drive and failed, leaving the score at 21–14.
LSU got a field goal to make the score 21–17 at halftime.
LSU regained the lead in the third quarter with a touchdown, and went for two to make the score 29–21. Alabama again went for two and failed, leaving the score 29–21.
On the Alabama's first drive of the fourth quarter, McCarron threw an interception to LSU safety Eric Reid. LSU scored on the drive, but missed the extra point, leaving the score 29–27.
On the Crimson Tide's ensuing drive, McCarron threw another interception to LSU, this time to safety Craig Loston. LSU scored again on the drive, leaving the score 36–27.
Alabama's next drive resulted in a punt. LSU, on its first offensive play of the drive, committed a penalty that resulted in a 50-yard loss, taking the ball out of bounds. Alabama took over with excellent field position and was able to reach the LSU 26-yard line before turning the ball over on downs.
LSU punted and Alabama got a first down on its next drive. Alabama marched down the field and scored on a fake field goal to reach the score 36–33. Both teams went for two and failed on both attempts.
Alabama got a first down on its next drive, which was eventually followed by a punt. LSU's ensuing drive was a 12-play, 80-yard drive that took up more than 6 minutes of the fourth quarter. LSU kicked a field goal to make the score 42–33.
LSU's next drive was a 3-play, 25-yard drive that ended with an interception to give Alabama the ball back. Alabama had one last chance to win the game. On the first play of the drive, McCarron threw an interception to LSU safety Eric Reid. LSU would not attempt another offensive play in the game.
Despite the loss, Nick Saban became the first coach in college football history to win a national championship without dropping a game in the regular season. His record now stood at 2–0.
Alabama was selected to play in the 2012 BCS National Championship Game against Notre Dame and won the game 42–14.

The 1968 Republican National Convention was held from August 5 to 9 at the Miami Beach Convention Center in Miami Beach , Flori

- da .  It was held to nominate a Republican candidate for President of  the United States  and  Vice  President  of  the  United  States  in  the  election of 1968. 

The delegates voted for the nominees of Richard Nixon and Spiro Agnew. Nixon, the former Vice President of the United States, ran against Hubert Humphrey, the incumbent Vice President. Nixon won the presidency in the general election with over 60 percent of the popular vote.

## Republican Party platform

The 1968 Republican Party platform was adopted on August 5, 1968, at the Republican National Convention.

### Contents

The platform included the following planks:

* Commitment to the Constitution
* Opposition to the Civil Rights Act of 1964
* Increase in the military defense budget
* Opposition to the ongoing war in Vietnam
* Support for free speech and freedom of assembly
* Support for laws against organized crime and corruption
* Support for the Equal Rights Amendment
* Support for the construction of the Trans-Alaska Pipeline

## Conventions

### Presidential nominations

See also: Republican Party presidential primaries, 1968

As of late 1967, there were four major candidates for the Republican nomination: Governor Ronald Reagan of California, Senator Edward Brooke of Massachusetts, Governor Nelson Rockefeller of New York, and Governor John Lindsay of New York.

In January 1968, Rockefeller created the Committee for the Re-Election of the President. After his campaign failed to gain much momentum, Rockefeller dropped out of the race in March, and endorsed Nixon.

In a televised debate on April 22, 1968, Reagan, Brooke, and Lindsay all refused to endorse Nixon. This made Nixon the overwhelming front-runner.

#### Convention

The convention was held at the Miami Beach Convention Center in Miami Beach, Florida.

In camp , Caesar welcomes Marcus Junius Brutus , his unofficial stepson whose mother is Caesar 's lover , Servilia of the Junii

, and his close friend Gaius Cassius Longinus . Meanwhile, Octavius, Julius Caesar 's nephew and heir, is vacationing in Greece with his sister Octavia Minor and her husband Lucius Paulinus. Caesar's wife Calpurnia dreams that Caesar's statue weeps blood and fears he will be killed. Caesar dismisses her fears as superstition. Around the same time, Caesar's good friend and adopted son, Marcus Antonius , begins an affair with Cleopatra , the Queen of Egypt. Caesar tells the Senate of the conspiracy to murder him, but the senators are too cowardly to act on it.
Meanwhile, Cassius and Brutus have been plotting the assassination for years. Cassius believes that the Roman Republic has been replaced by an autocracy and wants to free the Roman people from Caesar's tyranny. Brutus has been influenced by his mother's beliefs, and he also believes Caesar's rule is making the Romans weak and soft. The two conspirators plan to kill Caesar on the Ides of March .
The assassination begins with Cassius, along with a group of senators and hired killers, successfully attacking Caesar as he enters the Senate. Caesar is dazed, but Brutus is able to finish him off. Brutus and Cassius believe the people will be pleased with the assassination and that they will support the republic. However, Brutus and Cassius banish Antony and Octavius, and the two young men decide to get revenge on Brutus and Cassius.
The two murderers flee to the Greek island of Pharos, where Cassius is killed by his own men. Antony and Octavius ally to achieve their primary goal of avenging Caesar and avenging themselves on Brutus, who they believe is responsible for Caesar's death. In the meantime, Brutus, however, has been living in isolation, mourning the loss of his friend, and refusing to accept responsibility for his actions.
 Octavius and Antony gather their troops and march on Rome, where Brutus and the remaining conspirators have retreated to the Capitol . At a crucial moment, Brutus's friend and lieutenant, Titinius , is killed by the enemy. Brutus orders the remaining conspirators to burn all their papers so that Antony and Octavius cannot expose their plans. Brutus then takes his own life. Antony and Octavius then declare a war on the assassins.
