In the early evening of 15 June , Webb began his next attempt by passing over the lower obstructions in the Wilmington River an

area known as 'the minefield'.

It was a cloudy evening and the moon was hidden behind the clouds. The sea was as smooth as a millpond and the water was as dark as ink. At 1845 the flotilla moved into position in line ahead.

### The attack

As soon as the flotilla was in line, the destroyers opened fire. At 1846, the destroyers opened fire on the fort. At 1856 the minesweepers opened fire on the fort. At 1858 the minesweepers opened fire on the fort with their 3-inch guns. Webb and the other minesweepers closed in on the target. At 1859 Webb approached the target at 4 knots.

At 1900 Webb crossed the line of obstructions in the river. Webb continued to fire until she reached the target at 1901. As she approached the target, the fort opened fire with its 16-inch guns. Webb continued to fire until 1902. As Webb approached the target, it began firing with its 6-inch guns. Webb dropped her torpedo. At 1903 Webb dropped her first depth charge and continued to drop depth charges until 1904. As Webb approached the target, it began firing with its 12-inch guns. Webb continued to fire until 1905. As Webb approached the target it began firing with its 4.7-inch guns. Webb continued to fire until 1906. As Webb approached the target it began firing with its 3-inch guns. Webb continued to fire until 1907. As Webb approached the target, it began firing with its 20 mm guns. Webb continued to fire until 1908. The gunfire continued for 90 seconds and then ceased.

During the attack, Webb continued to fire on the target. During the attack, Webb dropped eight depth charges. In addition, Webb and Tracy, which was following Webb, dropped four depth charges each. The flotilla then moved out of range of the fort. After the attack, Webb returned to the flotilla.

## Aftermath

Following her attack on Fort Sumter, Webb was assigned to the Coast Guard to patrol the coast of South Carolina.

On 18 June, the 18th Auxiliary Coast Guard District requested Webb to patrol the coasts of South Carolina. Webb was to patrol the waters off the southeast coast of South Carolina. Webb was to patrol the waters off the coasts from Cape Fear, North Carolina to the Savannah River, Georgia. The 18th Auxiliary Coast Guard District had jurisdiction over the waters off the southeast coast of South Carolina from Cape Fear to the Savannah River.

On 20 June, the 18th District patrol craft were ordered to patrol the waters off the southeast coast of South Carolina. The 18th District patrol craft were ordered to patrol from the Cape Fear River, North Carolina to the Savannah River, Georgia.

On 1 July, Webb returned to the 16th Naval District and was assigned to the 14th Naval District.

The SAS had a very short time in which to do this , they had to find a place very quickly to establish a base and they found it in a cave .
They dug a well , and built a kind of shelter.
One such shelter is still visible today , albeit in a bad state.
The SAS then moved further north and found a rocky outcrop on which to build a more substantial shelter , it is known as the "Iron Chest" , and is where they stayed until they were relieved by the commandos in September.
The Iron Chest shelter was built on the edge of a cliff .
This shelter was very basic and had no facilities other than a well and a thatched roof.
The one thing it did have was a telephone and a radio.
This shelter was also used as a marijuana growing facility until it was discovered and destroyed by the commandos.
The Commandos , MGB and Iron Chest .
The MGB was the base for the commandos who were to relieve the SAS .
The MGB came in to shore at Iron Chest .
One of the commandos was Lt Col Newman .
He and another commando , Lt Col Wylie , were landed on the island by the MGB and they set off to find the SAS.
They found the SAS and Newman took over command of the SAS and re-established the commandos HQ at Iron Chest .
During this time the commandos were evacuated from the island.
The SAS were then placed under command of the Indians and were relieved by the commandos.
The commandos left the island in September 1945 .
Koreans in the cave - the cave is believed to have been used as a base for smuggling marijuana.
During 1945 the Iron Chest shelter was used as a base by the Koreans.
This is the only evidence of this.
It is believed that they used the shelter to grow and sell marijuana.
The Koreans used the cave as a hideout and hide it from the Japanese.
It was also a place of business , for the Koreans.
The Japanese had a blockhouse built in 1944 on the coast .
This was used as a lookout post and to defend the area.
This was situated about 2 miles from the Iron Chest.
The Japanese also set up camp on the island and this was their home until they left in 1945.
The Japanese were not intended to be on the island , this was because they were at war with the Chinese and the Chinese had landed on the island and set up camp and the Japanese were reluctant to return to the island .
This was their camp site .
The Japanese left the island shortly before the commandos arrived.
They were so frightened that they left everything behind.
The Japanese left behind about 11 bicycles , 2,000 tins of food and 1,000 tins of water.
The tins of food and water were left in the camp , the bicycles and other items were left in the cave.
The Japanese left the island in May 1945.
During their occupation the Japanese were not very good at records and no one knows who they were , or what their job was on the island.
The commandos arrived on the island in late August 1945 and the SAS were pulled off the island to help with the invasion of Japan.
The commandos stayed on the island until September 1945.
The commandos left the island on September 18th 1945.
There was no ceremony to mark their departure , no guns were fired, no band played , it was just a quiet departure.

The 2010 Alabama Crimson Tide football team ( variously " Alabama " , " UA " , " Bama " or " The Tide " ) represented the University of Alabama in the 2010 NCAA Division I FBS football season. The Tide was led by third-year head coach Nick Saban and played their home games at Bryant–Denny Stadium in Tuscaloosa, Alabama. They are members of the Western Division of the Southeastern Conference (SEC). They finished the season 10–3 and were ranked #6 in the final AP Poll.
The Tide started the season ranked third in the nation. However, their first game against San Jose State was moved to the last day of August due to Hurricane Earl and the game was never played. Alabama opened the season with a decisive 34–7 victory over East Carolina. The Tide also defeated Tennessee, Ole Miss, LSU and Auburn. A loss to South Carolina ended any chance at a National Championship.
Alabama was invited to the 2011 Sugar Bowl, where they defeated Michigan State 49–7. The victory earned the Tide a number 6 finish in the AP Poll.

Most of the early writers were either lawyers or barristers . There were also a number of journalists , who later became writers .

### Partition and Independence

The partition of India was the first major event covered by the Indian writers . The partition led to a new wave of writers , who wrote about the traumatic experience of living in the new nation -state . The partition also gave rise to the Hindi film industry .

The Indian writers in English wrote about the post-colonial world . The partition led to a new wave of writers who wrote about the traumatic experience of living in the new nation-state.

### 1960s to 1980s

India's move to non-alignment and friendship with the Soviet Union, and its confrontation with China led to a number of writers, including pioneers like Manohar Malgonkar and B. K. S. Iyengar, who wrote of the " Third World " experience. The 1960s saw a new wave of writers - those who had been born in the first quarter of the 20th century - who wrote about the changing world .

In the 1970s and 1980s, there were writers who wrote about the new post-independence India . Many of the early writers and poets wrote about freedom , and the new writers wrote about modern India .

### 1990s onwards

The 1990s saw a rise in the number of writers from the Indian diaspora who wrote in English, including Salman Rushdie .

The 2000s saw a growth in the number of writers from India's poorer states , including those from the Dalit community .

In the 21st century, there has been a rise in the number of women writers .

Valve 's interest in the Defense of the Ancients property began when several veteran employees , including Team Fortress design

ers Tim Willits and Robb Waters , who wanted to create a game centered around multiplayer online battle arenas . The original DotA was a mod for Blizzard 's Warcraft III: Reign of Chaos and its expansion, The Frozen Throne. When the game reached a level of popularity outside of the modding community, Valve approached Blizzard with the intention of buying the rights to the mod, but the deal did not happen as Blizzard had not created it.

This article is about the video game series. For the first game in the series, see Defense of the Ancients.

In 2008, Valve decided to create its own MOBA in the DotA style after being impressed by the mod. The game was developed internally at Valve until 2014, when it was handed over to a team of Chinese developers and published by Valve. The first game in the series, Defense of the Ancients 2 (DotA 2), was released in July 2013, and is one of Valve's first games to be released outside of the Steam platform. The sequel, Dota Underlords , launched in 2020 as a mobile game.

## Games

#### Defense of the Ancients 2

Main article: Defense of the Ancients 2

The first game in the series, Defense of the Ancients 2 (DotA 2), is a multiplayer online battle arena (MOBA) game. DotA 2 was developed and published by Valve, with the game's development being led by IceFrog, the creator of DotA. The game is free-to-play and was released on July 9, 2013, for Microsoft Windows and OS X. It is one of Valve's first non-Steam games. The game was met with critical acclaim, being praised for its gameplay, accessibility, and improvements over Warcraft III: Reign of Chaos and The Frozen Throne's mod, Defense of the Ancients. The game has over 200 heroes, with new heroes being released regularly. DotA 2 also has a competitive scene, with multiple tournaments, such as the Defense of the Ancients 2 Championships (DOTA 2 Championships), The International (The International ), and the ESL One series being held annually.

#### Dota Underlords

Main article: Dota Underlords

Dota Underlords is a multiplayer online battle arena (MOBA) game and the second game in the series. It is a spin-off of DotA 2 with a different gameplay style from the original. Both games are developed and published by Valve, with the development being led by Steve Feak and IceFrog. Dota Underlords launched on January 23, 2020, for Android and iOS. The game features heroes from DotA 2. Dota Underlords is a standalone game and is not a DotA 2 mod. The game is free-to-play.

### Other media

In 2010, Valve released a promotional DotA 2 comic book called "DotA 2: Origins" as a prequel to DotA 2. The comic book was written by Valve employee Jeffrey Vaughn and was drawn by Jason Howard. The comic book was given away to attendees of PAX Prime 2010.

In 2020, Valve released a film based on DotA 2 called Free to Play.

### Future

Valve has stated they are "working on" a new Dota game, but did not provide any other information.

In Japan , kitsunetsuki was noted as a disease as early as the Heian period and remained a common diagnosis for mental illness

until the 19th century. In the 19th century , it was recognized as a symptom of mental illness.
The term kitsunetsuki is derived from the Japanese word for fox  (kitsune) and the suffix for sickness (tsuki). Kitsunetsuki is thought to have a similar etiology to lycanthropy (a disease that causes people to believe they are animals) or epilepsy . There are different types of kitsunetsuki, such as kitsune-gatana (a fox carrying a sword), kitsune-kabe (a fox with a painted-on face), kitsune-obake (a fox that has become a ghost), and kitsune-no-ihai (a fox burying its body).
Kitsunetsuki has traditionally been thought to affect children and the elderly, but can also affect adult men. In Japan, it is thought to be caused by the fox-spirit (kitsune) assuming the form of a human.
There are many stories of children who have been bitten by foxes and later experience disruptive behavior, including sleepwalking , nightmares, and talking to invisible friends. Japanese folklore states that foxes are capable of turning into men at night and that they are attracted to children.
In the 19th century, kitsunetsuki was considered a symptom of a mental illness. In modern times, the disease is not recognized as a diagnosis under the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders or the International Classification of Diseases .

Dylan is considered a seminal influence on several musical genres , especially folk rock , country rock and Christian rock . As

a songwriter , he has received several awards , including two Golden Globe Awards , an Academy Award (one of only seven recording artists to win an Academy Award and a Golden Globe Award for best original song tape) , ten Grammy Awards , and a Pulitzer Prize . In 2016, Dylan was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature , making him the first musician to receive the Nobel Prize .
 regard him as one of the key figures of the 1960s counterculture .
 Dylan's lyrics have received mixed critical reception throughout his career, although his influence as a songwriter is broad and deep, with his songs being recorded by more than 4,000 artists . Dylan has sold more than 100 million records , making him one of the best-selling artists of all time . He has also received numerous honors and awards, including a Golden Globe and Academy Award in 1970 for Best Original Song (for ' A Place in the Sun '), 10 Grammy Awards , and the Presidential Medal of Freedom . He was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1988, received the Prince of Asturias Award in 2007, and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2016.
Dylan's early work, as a folk singer and songwriter , made him one of the most influential musicians of the 1960s . His social and literary abstraction of his lyrics, combined with his own caustic humor and unconventional vocal and instrumental styles, set him apart from his folk contemporaries. Much of his most celebrated work dates from the 1960s, when, with fellow musicians, he pioneered the genres of folk rock and country rock and helped to popularize the genre of rock music .
Dylan's music has evolved throughout his career, and his recorded work incorporates elements of rock , pop , rock and roll , folk , blues , and country . Since 1994, there has been a resurgence in the popularity of Dylan's music, especially in the new folk revival . He has sold more than 100 million records worldwide and is often ranked as one of the greatest songwriters of all time. He has also released 35 studio albums, with worldwide sales of 120 million copies (11 of which have received gold and platinum status in the US alone). He has had 10 albums enter the Billboard 200 top 10, and in 2009 he was ranked No. 2 in the Rolling Stone list of the 100 Greatest Artists of All Time.
Dylan has been covered by other artists more than any other living songwriter. More than 4,000 artists have recorded one or more Dylan songs, and more than 100 of his songs have been recorded by over 2,000 artists.
In 1994, Dylan was awarded the Polar Music Prize for his exceptional contribution to contemporary music.
In 2006, Dylan was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom , the highest civilian award in the United States .

In 2016, Dylan was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature , the first time the award had been given to a musician.

On 30 December 1941 , after transferring responsibility for their defensive area to a Militia Light Horse machine gun regiment

20 km south of El Alamein, the 1st Armoured Division embarked on a 24-hour drive to the coast.  The division's vehicles proceeded in good order, but the trucks carrying the infantry and the artillery were delayed in the early morning of 31 December at the village of Tel el-Eisa. There, the 1st Armoured Division came under artillery fire from a German battery 10 km to the south. When they arrived at the coastal town of Matruh, the infantry and artillery were still strung out in the desert sand. By then, all of the division's tanks and guns had been shot out or immobilised.
The Germans had waited for the 1st Armoured Division to come to the coast, and they had been ready for them. The main force of the 90th Light Division had landed at Matruh on 29 December, and they were supported by elements of the Italian regiments Ariete and Trento. The Italian light tanks were no match for the British Matildas and Valentines, but the Germans had 150 tanks, including the modern Panzer IIIs and IVs and the Soviet-built T-34s. The Germans were also supported by 380 fighter-bombers, and they had a very clear plan of action. While the British and Indian 2nd Armoured Division was still at El Alamein, the Germans intended to strike and destroy the 1st Armoured Division on the coast. With the 2nd Armoured Division still on the western side of the Matruh position, the Germans intended to cut off the 1st Armoured Division at El Alamein.
The 1st Armoured Division was a formidable fighting force, but it was never intended to be capable of operating independently. It was created with the express purpose of forming up with the second armoured division, the 7th Armoured Division.  The plan was to use both divisions to form a mobile force capable of breaking out and advancing along the coast road to the Nile, and then to move east with the 7th Armoured to reinforce the Eighth Army at a time of great need and to block the German advance through the Western Desert.
The 1st Armoured Division was commanded by Lieutenant-General Michael O'Moore Creagh, the hero of the Great Escape from Hong Kong. His deputy was Major-General Sir John Harding, who had been appointed to the post of Chief of the Imperial General Staff only four days earlier. Colonel John Orr-Ewing commanded the infantry and artillery brigades, and Brigadier John Hunt led the armoured brigade. The 7th Armoured Division was commanded by Major-General Sir Alastair Willison. The 1st Armoured Division Artillery was organised in three field regiments and a medium regiment. On the one hand, there are feminists who believe that all sexuality is good and that it should not be limited by gender roles.

## History

MD 71 was designated on November 27, 1927 , when the Maryland State Roads Commission (MSRC) assigned numbers to state highways that were previously numbered by counties . MD 71 was assigned to a route between MD 61 and MD 123 (now MD 23) in Richland County .

MD 123 was rerouted to follow MD 61 to U.S. Route 40 (US 40; now MD 34) in 1930 . The following year , MD 71 was extended to its current eastern terminus at US 1 in Columbia . At this time, MD 71 was established as a 1.5-mile (2.4 km) connector highway between Columbia and Ellicott City along MD 91 (now MD 100) and MD 123 .

MD 71 was renumbered MD 111 in 1956 . MD 91 was extended to replace MD 71 and MD 111 . In 1999 , MD 91 was rerouted to follow MD 100 west to MD 100's former eastern terminus at US 29 (now MD 124). The former alignment of MD 91 was redesignated MD 71A and the old alignment of MD 71 was rerouted to follow MD 100 east to US 29 and MD 100 was extended west to US 29.

The format of the program is for the experts to analyse the items and reveal their value to the guests. The series has been produced by RDF Media and FremantleMedia since 1997. The original production company was Granada Television, which produced the programme for 12 years. The program is broadcast on BBC One , and is one of the most-watched television programs in the UK. The format has been adapted by other broadcasters and is currently produced in over 30 countries.

### Landfall

Cyclone Burevi at peak intensity, on December 3

On December 2, Burevi intensified into a strong cyclonic storm, with a maximum sustained wind speed of 65 km/h (40 mph). Later that day, the IMD stated the system would continue to intensify into a severe cyclonic storm in the next 12 hours. The JTWC also stated that Burevi was likely to intensify into a severe tropical storm, with peak winds of 75 km/h (45 mph). The storm continued to intensify, with the IMD upgrading Burevi to a severe cyclonic storm on December 3, and the JTWC upgrading Burevi to a category 1 hurricane, with peak winds of 120 km/h (75 mph). The next day on December 4, the IMD upgraded Burevi to a very severe cyclonic storm, as it continued to intensify. Later on the same day, the IMD stated that the cyclone had crossed the coast near Palk Bay at its peak intensity, and intensified into a severe cyclonic storm.

## Impact

### Sri Lanka

On December 3, the heavy rainfall caused by Burevi resulted in the collapse of a dam in a tea estate in the Badulla District of Sri Lanka, which affected 40 families. On December 4, a landslide occurred in Katharagama, killing one person and affecting 20 others.

### India

Cyclone Burevi was the first cyclone of the 2020–21 North Indian Ocean cyclone season to make landfall in India, as well as the first tropical cyclone to make landfall in Kerala since Cyclone Ockhi in 2017. Burevi was the first major cyclone to affect Kerala since Cyclone Thane in 2011. As a result of the tropical cyclone's landfall in Kerala, the Kerala State Disaster Management Authority (KSDMA) issued an alert for heavy rainfall and winds in the state. On November 30, the Kerala State Electricity Board (KSEB) announced that all of the state's 33 power grids were prepared for the cyclone. About 6,000 people were evacuated from low-lying areas in Thiruvananthapuram, Kollam, Pathanamthitta, Alappuzha, Kottayam and Ernakulam. On December 1, the Kerala government issued a red alert for low-lying areas of Alappuzha, Kollam, and Pathanamthitta. The Malabar Coast was placed under a high alert.

On December 2, the Kerala government issued a red alert for the coastal districts of Alappuzha, Kollam, Ernakulam, Thiruvananthapuram, and Kasaragod. The state government also ordered the evacuation of over one million people from low-lying areas. The Kerala police ordered the evacuation of 10,000 people from low-lying areas, and 20,000 people from hilly areas, in the Kollam district. On December 3, a portion of the NH 47 at Alappuzha was submerged due to the heavy rainfall, and the state government opened 150 relief camps in the state. The Indian Navy deployed 12 ships and two aircraft to help with rescue efforts. On December 4, the district collector of Kollam District, KS Sreekumar, stated that the cyclone had caused ₹2,500 crore (US$320 million) in damages to the state. The cyclone caused a total of ₹4,500 crore (US$580 million) in damages to the state.

In the earlier part of the 19th century the area which is today Minnesota was not recognized as a single entity . The Mississip

i River divided the territory into the Western and the Eastern Districts which were under the jurisdiction of the Superintendent of Indian Affairs for the District of Louisiana. The Indians living in the territory were under the jurisdiction of the United States Office of Indian Affairs for the district of Louisiana.
 In 1820 the "Missouri Territory" was formed, which comprised all the territory between the Mississippi River and the Rocky Mountains. In 1834 Minnesota was separated from the Missouri Territory and was organized as the Wisconsin Territory. In 1836 Minnesota was organized as a territory of the United States. In 1849 Minnesota was admitted into the Union as a state. Minnesota is the 32nd state of the Union.
The Chippewa Indians of Minnesota had been under the jurisdiction of the Office of Indian Affairs for the territory of Louisiana since 1801. Minnesota was not recognized as a separate territory until 1849. Chippewa Indians in Minnesota were under the jurisdiction of the Office of Indian Affairs for the district of Minnesota. All the Indians in Minnesota were placed under the jurisdiction of the Office of Indian Affairs for the district of Minnesota.
The Office of Indian Affairs (BIA) was established in 1824. It had jurisdiction over all Indian Affairs in the United States. The BIA was under the direction of the Secretary of the Interior. The Office of Indian Affairs for the district of Minnesota was under the direction of the Governor of Minnesota.
The records of the Office of Indian Affairs, the predecessor of the BIA, are in the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA). These include letters and other records relating to Indian Treaties. These records have been microfilmed by NARA as part of their Microopaque Program. The records of the Office of Indian Affairs, 1824 - 1881, include two rolls of microfilm published by NARA as M694. The rolls contain Letters and Other Records Relating to Indian Treaties. These include Treaty No. 3, between the United States and the Chippewa Indians, 1837. This treaty was signed by the Chippewa Indians on August 3, 1837, at Traverse des Sioux, Minnesota.
Digital Images of the original Treaty, with signatures, are included in roll M694, frames 130 - 136.
The images from the microfilm copy of the Treaty are included to show the original as signed by the officials representing the United States and the Chippewa Indians.
Description of the Collection and Contents
The Treaty contains nine articles. Article I of the Treaty states that the Chippewa Indians cede to the United States all their rights title, and interest in the territory ceded by the Treaty of 1825. Article II of the Treaty states that the Chippewa Indians cede to the United States all their rights title and interest in all lands lying East of the Mississippi River from the Red Cedar River to the Head of Lakes. Article III states that the United States shall pay the Chippewa Indians $20,000 within four years after the ratification of the treaty. Article IV of the Treaty states that each male Chippewa Indian living on the lands ceded by the Treaty of 1825 shall receive $8 annually in addition to the annuity provided for in Article III of the Treaty. Article V of the Treaty states that the United States will make provision for the education of the children of the Chippewa Indians. Article VI states that the United States will pay for the removal of the Chippewa Indians to the land ceded by the Treaty. Article VII states that the United States shall establish trading houses on the land ceded by the Treaty, to be occupied by traders of the United States, and that the proceeds of these trading houses shall be used to pay for the expenses of the United States in carrying out the provisions of the Treaty. Article VIII states that the United States will furnish the goods necessary to carry into effect the provisions of the Treaty. Article IX of the Treaty states that the Treaty shall be ratified by the President of the United States by and with the advice and consent of the Senate.
The digital images from the microfilm copy of the treaty are included in this presentation as received from NARA.
Signatures are included on the digital images to show the signatures of the officials representing the United States and the Chippewa Indians.

" Mothers of the Disappeared " is a song by rock band U2 . It is the eleventh and final track on their 1987 album The Joshua Tr

ilogy . The song was released as the B-side to the single " One " .
The song is about the fate of the 1970s and 1980s " disappeared " in Chile . This is part of a long tradition in Latin American music of songs about the disappeared .
The song's lyrics are sung by Bono in Spanish . Spanish lyrics were written by U2 and musician/producer Daniel Lanois .
The song was written following the experience of Bono and U2 guitarist The Edge in Chile during a 1986 tour when they met with Chilean human rights activist Maria Teresa Echaurren. Bono, The Edge, and Lanois recorded the song with a Chilean group called Inti-Illimani , which had been banned from playing under Augusto Pinochet's regime, but later allowed to perform again.
The song was recorded in Los Angeles , California , Brazil, London, and Dublin .
" Mothers of the Disappeared " is a slow-tempo song with acoustic guitar and a piano keyboard. The melody is a simple, repeated three-chord sequence. Bono sings the song in Spanish . The song's lyrics are about the disappearance of people during the Dirty War in Chile. Bono wrote the lyrics, and Daniel Lanois wrote the Spanish lyrics.
The song is written from the perspective of the disappeared, and the title refers to the mothers whose children disappeared or were killed by the Pinochet dictatorship. Bono toured Chile with guitarist Carlos Alomar in 1986. They met with Maria Teresa Echaurren and her group Mothers of the Disappeared . Bono told Flavorpill : "From the moment I met her, I was just blown away by her. Here was this woman who had buried her son, and she had a daughter who had been tortured and raped by the security forces."
The song was written largely to celebrate the announcement that Inti-Illimani, a folk group that had been banned under Pinochet, would be allowed to perform in Chile again. Bono said, "I thought it would be a nice gesture to have a member of the band sing in Spanish. I'm not a fluent Spanish speaker and I thought Dan [Lanois] would be a better candidate. He got the lyrics down in one day." The song is about the fate of the 1970s and 1980s " disappeared " in Chile , and it is the final song of The Joshua Trilogy . The song is part of a long tradition in Latin American music of songs about the disappeared , and it has been described as being in the "mestizo" genre, a blend of folk music and rock.
The song is about the disappeared people of Chile, and it was written during U2's 1986 tour. In 1987, U2 recorded a song with Inti-Illimani. Inti-Illimani had been banned from performing by Augusto Pinochet, the Chilean dictator, during the Dirty War. The band had been underground for years and had reunited, but were not allowed to perform. Bono told the BBC , "I went to Chile because all the people we met and spoke to were so brave and so wonderful. And then I got to meet the Mothers of the Disappeared and they're heartbreaking. It's an honour and a privilege to have been able to be a small part and to try and help in some way."
The song was performed on U2's 1987-1988 World Tour.
The song was released as the B-side to the single " One " , and it was included on The Joshua Trilogy , Achtung Baby , and U218 Singles .

In 1848 when the Minnesota Territory was formed there were four major " white " settlements : Saint Paul , Saint Anthony ( part

of present-day Minneapolis ) , Fort Snelling , and Marine-aux-Élan . [2] In 1849, the territorial capital was moved from Saint Paul to Saint Anthony because of the latter's better access to water transportation, and the city was renamed Minneapolis by a unanimous vote of the territorial legislature. [3] In 1852 Minnesota became the 32nd state of the United States of America. [4] Minneapolis was incorporated as a city in 1867. [5]
The West Bank neighborhood of Minneapolis in 1937.
See also: History of Minneapolis
The city of Minneapolis is named after the city of Minneapolis , Minnesota in the United States. The name is of Native American origin and meant "city of water". [6] [7] The Dakota people ( Sioux ) lived in the area for hundreds of years. In the 1600s they were joined by Ojibwe (Chippewa) bands that had moved west out of Michigan. The Dakota and Ojibwe were trappers, hunters, and farmers. [8]
Water was a key to the survival of the Dakota, who lived in small family-based villages in the area. They called the area Ikedagnug, meaning "where the waters reflect the clouds", referring to the many lakes in the Minneapolis area. [9] The Dakota initially called the city of Minneapolis Bdeota Owaki Ska ("the skies are far away") from the Dakota phrase Wadota Owaki Ska ("Sky Scrapers"), which is a reference to the city's skyscrapers. [10]
However, the name Minneapolis is derived from the Dakota phrase for "city of waters" [11] [12] [13] or "water falling in ladder-like fashion". [14] The Dakota people used this expression to describe Saint Anthony Falls, which were named after Anthony of Padua, the patron saint of the city. [15] The city of Minneapolis was incorporated on May 11, 1867. [16]
See also: History of Minneapolis (1867–1950)
Downtown Minneapolis, 1909
The earliest settlers to the area that now contains Minneapolis were Native American hunter-gatherers from the Sioux ( Dakota ) and Anishinaabe (Ojibwe) tribes, who had a major village on the banks of the Mississippi River . European-American fur traders first arrived in what became Minneapolis in the early 1820s. The city of Minneapolis was founded in 1852, when Major Thomas L. Smith of the U.S. Army of the Tennessee built a flour mill on St. Anthony Falls on the Mississippi River. The mill was called Pancratia. [17] The city of Minneapolis incorporated in 1867 and is one of the oldest cities in the state.
In 1878, Minneapolis and St. Paul were linked together by the Minnesota Street Railway. [18] [19] The two cities became known as the Twin Cities. [20] The economy of Minneapolis was initially based on milling and flour production. The city grew rapidly over the years. [21]
In 1978, Minneapolis and St. Paul were linked together by the Minnesota Amtrak line. [22] [23] The two cities became known as the Twin Cities. As of the 2010 census, Minneapolis had a population of 382,578. [24] It is the county seat of Hennepin County . [25]
Minneapolis has a mix of neighborhoods ranging from industrial areas to residential areas, from downtown to lakeside. It is the larger of the Twin Cities, the 48th-largest metropolitan area in the United States, and the 21st-largest in the U.S. The city lies on both sides of the Mississippi River, just north of the river's confluence with the Minnesota River , and adjoins Saint Paul, the state's capital. With a land area of 59.2 square miles (153 km2), Minneapolis is the 16th-largest city in the United States and the sixth-largest in the state.

cers are obliged to take measures to reduce waste production. The collection of household waste is free of charge and is subject to the Waste (England and Wales) Regulations 2011 . These regulations specify that the local authority must provide the following collection services to its residents:

1. A weekly collection of dry recyclables
2. A fortnightly collection of food waste
3. A collection of garden waste

The local authority may make a charge if a household produces more than 180 kg of waste per annum and this is deemed to be excessive.

Most commercial waste is collected by private operators. In Greater Manchester there is a wide range of private waste collection operators, but the bulk of the waste produced by businesses is collected by Biffa Group PLC , which is the largest collection and disposal operator in the region. Commercial waste is also collected by the local authority in some circumstances.

### Household collection

Household waste is collected fortnightly. The contents of the blue wheeled bin are collected and sorted separately at a Materials Recovery Facility where the recyclable material is separated from the rest of the waste and subsequently used to create new products.

### Other waste types

In Greater Manchester, any waste not collected by the local authority is collected by private waste collection operators who operate on a commercial basis. Commercial waste is typically collected weekly or fortnightly depending on the volume of waste produced.

### Recycling

Greater Manchester is a member of the Greater Manchester Waste Disposal Authority, which is responsible for the disposal of the region's waste.

In Greater Manchester, there is a weekly collection of dry recyclables and a fortnightly collection of food waste. Recyclables include paper, card, glass, metal and plastic, and food waste includes cooked food and food contaminated with liquids. Residents are able to separate these wastes and place them in the appropriate receptacle for collection. Householders are responsible for producing the correct recyclables and sorting them into the appropriate container.

The region's recycling rate is 22.9% (2010/11).

### Waste to energy

Waste to energy is a form of waste management that involves the transformation of waste into energy, for example by burning the waste. There are two ways to do this: 

* Thermal treatment of waste, e.g. incineration
* Chemical treatment of waste

Waste to energy is a form of waste management that can be used to reduce waste and to generate energy. There are two ways to do this: 

* Thermal treatment of waste, e.g. incineration
* Chemical treatment of waste

Waste to energy is considered to be a form of waste treatment. The energy that is generated may be used for the purposes of heat and/or electricity generation. The energy that is generated may also be used in other ways, for example, to generate steam for industrial processes.

### Landfill

The Greater Manchester Waste Disposal Authority is responsible for the landfill of the region's waste.

### Recycling centres

There are a number of recycling centres in Greater Manchester where householders are able to dispose of their waste.

### Commercial waste

The collection of commercial waste is subject to the requirements of the Waste (England and Wales) Regulations 2011 . These regulations apply to any waste produced by a business or other commercial operation.

### Bulky waste

There are a number of bulky waste collections in Greater Manchester.

### Treatment and disposal

Waste is treated and disposed of at the Greater Manchester Waste Disposal Authority's five waste management centres, which are: Bury, Littleborough, Rochdale, Salford and Wigan.

### Hazardous waste

Hazardous waste is waste that is defined as hazardous under the Hazardous Waste Regulations 2005 . Hazardous waste can be:

* Radioactive waste
* Dangerous infectious waste
* Special waste

Antimony is a chemical element with the symbol Sb and atomic number 51. A lustrous gray metalloid, it is found in nature mainly as the sulfide mineral stibnite (Sb 2 S 3). Antimony compounds have been known since ancient times and were powdered for use as medicine and cosmetics , often known by the Latin, stibium. The word "stibium" comes from the Greek στίβιoν, stibion, "a walnut", via the Arabic ستيبس sstagis. Antimony compounds were known in ancient Egypt, where the metal was mined in Nubia and used for medicinal purposes. The ancient Greeks and Romans applied it to wounds and sores. The metal was not isolated until 1540, by Valerius Cordus. Its most important compound, antimony sulfide, Sb 2 S 3, was also first isolated in this year, and was used in cosmetics and medicines. The metal is extracted from its ores by heating in the presence of air, producing antimony(III) oxide. The element reacts with oxygen in the air to form antimony(III) oxide, which is a white powder that ignites spontaneously at about 480 °C (896 °F). Antimony(III) oxide occurs naturally as the rare mineral valentinite. Antimony metal, which is obtained by reducing the oxide with hydrogen, is a hard, brittle, silvery grey metal with an earthy, garlicky odor. It has a face-centred cubic crystal structure with a melting point of about 630 °C (1,164 °F). Antimony is a semiconductor and is sensitive to light. It is a component of some alloy steels, and is used to harden lead. It is used in batteries, chemicals, pigments, and flame retardants. Its major use is in lead-acid storage batteries, where it makes up 8 % of the alloy used. Minor uses are in semiconductors, bearing metals, and alloys. The metal is toxic.
Antimony is used as an alloying agent in lead for storage batteries, and for bullets. In the manufacture of pewter , it is often added to harden the alloy.
Ammonium antimoniate is used as a topical antimicrobial agent to treat skin conditions such as athlete's foot. It is also used as a preservative in herbal medicines and in some toothpaste preparations.
There are no uses of antimony in the home.
Other uses include antimony chromate (AS 15), used in paints and wood preservatives, and di-antimony trioxide (AS 50), used as a flame retardant in plastics.
Antimony compounds are used as fire retardants in plastics and textiles. They are also used to increase the melting point of lead, thereby making it less prone to the formation of lead dust in industrial applications. Antimony and its compounds are widely used in the manufacture of lead-acid batteries, which account for about 67% of antimony use. Other uses include: antimony alloys, such as hardening of lead for containers; antimony compounds for use in flame retardants; and pewters, such as those used in jewelry and art.
Antimony trioxide is used as a component in the manufacture of flame-retardant polymers, rubber, plastics, and textiles. It is also used in the manufacture of batteries, alloys, and stabilizers for plastics. It is also used in paints, varnishes, enamels, and inks.
Certain antimony salts, such as antimony potassium tartrate (K 3 Sb 2 (C 4 H 4 O 6 ) 2), are used as astringents in ointments and liniments for burns and lacerations.
Antimony compounds are used in photography, electronics, and glassmaking.

Astraeus hygrometricus , commonly known as the hygroscopic earthstar , the barometer earthstar , or the false earthstar , is a

4-spored fungus in the order Agaricales. It is saprobic and fleshy, and grows in clusters or groups on the ground in coniferous, spruce, or mixed woods in summer and fall. The cap is 2–3 cm (0.79–1.18 in) in diameter, convex to bell-shaped to flat, and is dark brown to black. The dark brown gills are adnate to the stem, which is also dark brown to black. The spores are brown. The fruiting body is hygroscopic, becoming rounded, and pearly when moist. The species is similar to Astraeus hygrometricus var. accessibilis, which has a paler spore print, but can be distinguished from Astraeus hygrometricus var. hygrometricus by the thicker, more leathery flesh of the fruiting body, and the lack of a spherical pore when young.

## Taxonomy

The species was first described scientifically by French mycologist Louis René Tulasne in 1844 as Agaricus hygrometricus. The species was transferred to the genus Astraeus in 1876 by German mycologist Paul Kummer, who classified it as Astraeus hygrometricus.

### Varieties

A variety, Astraeus hygrometricus var. accessibilis, was described by the same author in 1871, based on specimens collected in the Baltic provinces of Russia. This species is distinguished from the type species by having paler spores, the fruiting bodies becoming rounded when moist, and having a spore print that is paler than Astraeus hygrometricus. There is some controversy over whether or not the variety is valid, and whether or not it is a synonym of the type species.

### Synonyms

The varieties of Astraeus hygrometricus have been synonymized with the type species.

The NDH authorities in Trebinje heard rumours that the Serbs could start an uprising there on 28 June , the feast day of Saint

Vasilije. As a result, they ordered the local gendarmerie commander, Captain Danilo Čolak, to meet with the chief of the local police, Lieutenant Nikola Pavi?i? and the chief of the local secret police, Lieutenant Predrag Markovi?, and instruct them to take precautionary measures. The commanders were further ordered to keep close watch over the activities of the local Catholic priest, Vlado Jokanovi?, and the Orthodox priest, Risto Jovi?i?.
After leaving the meeting, Čolak, Pavi?i? and Markovi? decided to show their alertness by sending a patrol to the nearby village of Rataje, where the population was of mixed nationality and where the Serbs had organised a cultural club in 1940. The patrol was to visit the club and learn about any  plans for mobilisation. Markovi? and Pavi?i? decided to join the patrol on their way to the village.
The patrol, consisting of eight members of the gendarmerie,  was stopped by Serbs coming out of the village of Rataje. The patrol informed the Serbs that they had received orders to check whether or not the club was planning a mobilisation. The Serbs recognized some of the gendarmes as members of the local gendarmerie. They approached the gendarmes with friendly expressions, but one of them told them that he was an activist of the Revolutionary National Movement and that he had been ordered to take them captive. As the Serbs advanced on the gendarmes, the gendarmes started shooting. The Serbs, in turn, opened fire. The gendarmes retreated into the nearby forest. The attacking Serbs pursued them, and a firefight ensued.
The next morning, the bodies of six gendarmes were found in the forest. Two gendarmes were missing. It was later found that they had been captured by the Serbs. One of the captives was later shot and the other was beaten to death.
The following day, the authorities in Trebinje received a letter from the Serbs in Rataje, informing them that they were in no way responsible for the incident in the forest. The letter stated that the gendarmes had been murdered by a group of Serb nationalists in the neighbouring villages of Bocari and Rataje.
 The local authorities reacted by arresting the Serbs from the villages of Bocari and Rataje. In the following days, the gendarmerie and the police started searching for the rest of the group of Serbs who were supposed to have participated in the attacks.
The Serbs were arrested at the homes of their relatives. Those who were found were taken to Trebinje. Among them was Vlado Jokanovi?, who was arrested in his home in Trebinje.

Governmental officials must be able to act effectively in the world of political reality . Scholars who were involved in politics too often had an outdated sense of the world and its problems , Innis believed . In the 1950s , Canadian public opinion and its effect on policy was of major interest to scholars in political science , and in 1954 Innis published his views on this subject with the publication of _Canadian Public Opinion and Policy_. In this book , Innis stated that the media exert a great deal of influence over public opinion . He also believed that public opinion is in fact simply the expression of elite opinion . Innis contended that the elite in a democracy is the group which controls the mass media . The media , he noted , have a tremendous power to influence public opinion . The media , Innis stated , are the most important institution of democracy . They are responsible for the dissemination of information and for the formation of public opinion .
The media , Innis argued , are controlled by the elite . These elite are commercial and corporate interests . They are also the media themselves . The media are dominated by those who control them . Innis believed that the public is far less likely to be influenced by the mass media than it is to be influenced by the elite . He claimed that the elite can use the mass media to influence public opinion , but this influence is usually indirect . Instead , they use the media to influence each other . The elite use the media as a means of communicating with each other . They are the ones who determine what is printed and broadcast . The public , Innis maintained , is not the target of the media .

British airline's licence to operate scheduled passenger flights. It was argued that the revocation was arbitrary and disproportionate, and that the revocation of the licence was in effect a prohibition on the airline operating and was there-fore a regulation that required parliamentary approval. The court disagreed, relying on the following passage from a speech of Lord Diplock in the unanimous House of Lords decision in British Steel Corp v Granada TV Ltd . It was argued, said Lord Diplock, that if the courts were to allow judicial review of the ministerial decision to revoke the airline's licence, 'the courts will then have acquired a jurisdiction to restrain the executive from doing things which Parliament has entrusted to the minister to do as his or her sole discretion'. This is quite unacceptable, for it would involve the courts in unjustifiably interfering in the affairs of government.
I do not think that the court should make any such interference. The executive and the legislature are not co-ordinate bodies, whose functions can be compared and matched in the same way that the functions of the courts and the executive are. The executive is not a subsidiary body of the legislature, but is directly responsible to the Queen and to the people. In carrying out the functions which the legislature has entrusted to it, the executive is required to maintain a certain degree of independence in order to ensure that the legislative policy of the day is effectively carried out by the government of the day. The courts cannot undertake to examine each decision of the executive in order to decide whether it is right or wrong. The courts are concerned only with the legality of the decision of the executive, and the only question they can ask is whether the decision is a decision which the executive had the power to make for itself.
The executive is therefore entitled to discharge its functions in a manner which is regarded by the legislature as in accordance with its wishes. It is for Parliament, and not the courts, to decide what are the executive's powers.
The court in Laker Airways decided that the revocation of the airline's licence was not a regulation that required parliamentary approval and therefore was not unlawful in the sense that it was in breach of the natural justice principle of the rule of law. The airline had argued that the revocation of the licence was in effect a regulation that required parliamentary approval. The court disagreed, saying that the revocation was a decision that the minister had made in the exercise of his discretionary powers, and that there was no requirement of parliamentary approval.

St Peulan 's Church , Llanbeulan is a disused medieval church in Llanbeulan , in Anglesey , north Wales . The nave , which is t

enth century , is the only part of the church remaining. The church was established in 1076 .
From the mid-seventeenth century until the mid-nineteenth century the church was in the care of the Carmelite Order . During its time there the church was known more commonly as Holy Trinity Church .
The church was the parish church of Llanbeulan , and was established in 1076 . It was also a chapel of ease to Llanfairpwllgwyngyllgogerychwyrndrobwllllantysiliogogogoch .
The church was disused in 1972 .
The church lies on the A5 , the main road connecting Menai Bridge to Holyhead . It stands in a field on the side of the road. The church is a Grade II listed building .
The church was built in the tenth century. There are some parts of the church that are from the late thirteenth century. The church has a nave and chancel, a south porch, a south aisle, a north aisle, and a small tower.
The church has a thirteenth century tiled roof, and timber framing. The church has a three-bay roof with a four-bay chancel.
The church used to have a bell turret. The bell turret was removed in 1889. The bell was then transferred to St Anthony's Church in Llanfechell . The bell is inscribed with the words "Fidei Defensor" and the date 1771.

The appearances of the main characters were inspired by those of actors and other entertainers , who were typically selected fr

om among the most handsome, most beautiful, most heroic, or most villainous men and women of the day.
The first such character was Richard III, the last of the Plantagenet kings. He was the subject of the first fully realized character in English literature. With the support of the actors and other entertainers who performed his story, Shakespeare created a profoundly memorable character who is likely the most villainous and most fascinating character in English literature.

In his early Munich years Busch 's attempt to write libretti , which are almost forgotten today , were unsuccessful . Up to 186

6 he worked with his friend Rudolf Baumbach on the libretto for his first opera _The Genie of the Golden Horn_. In 1868 he collaborated with the composer Wilhelm Kienzl , whose opera _The Bee , the Bird and the Butterfly_ (1881) he wrote the libretto for. In his later years his libretti for the operas of Alexander von Zemlinsky and Franz Schreker were also successful.
After the death of Richard Strauss , Busch was the most prominent librettist in Germany. In a total of 145 collaborations with 24 composers , he wrote 21 opera libretti , 20 operettas and 13 oratorios.
Richard Strauss's music theater works
The first collaboration between Richard Strauss and Busch was the opera _Feuersnot_ (1901) . It was followed by the opera _Salome_ (1905) , which caused a sensation with its realism and eroticism . This was followed by _Der Rosenkavalier_ (1911), which was very successful. The already 70-year-old Busch was still capable of challenging the new avant-garde in his libretto for _Arabella_ (1933). After the Second World War , he wrote an opera libretto for Hans Werner Henze , _The Bassarids_ (1961), which was not performed until 1966.
Busch and his brother Richard did not collaborate on operas or operettas. Instead, the two authors wrote together on the libretto for the oratorio _German Requiem_ of Johannes Brahms (1866).
As a playwright for the theater, Busch was successful at the end of the 19th century. He wrote the libretto to the "Sunday premieres" at the Stadttheater Munich between 1897 and 1906.
Busch also wrote the libretto for the operetta _The Silent Woman_ (1915) by Leo Fall . In his later years he wrote the libretto to the operetta _The Old Lady's Secret_ by Eduard Künneke (1923).
In addition, Rudolf Busch wrote the libretto for the opera _Das Mädchen aus der Feenwelt_ by Robert Planquette (1893) and the libretto for the opera _Tangokönigin_ by Edmund Eysler (1919).

Cyclone Omar (04L)
Hurricane Omar (04L) was the fourth named storm of the 2017 Atlantic hurricane season , and was the most significant tropical cyclone to impact the northern Leeward Islands of the Lesser Antilles and Puerto Rico in the 2017 Atlantic hurricane season. A tropical wave exited the west coast of Africa on September 23, and moved across the tropical Atlantic Ocean. It showed signs of organization early on September 29, and was designated Tropical Depression Fourteen at 21:00 UTC that day. The depression strengthened into Tropical Storm Omar later that night. On September 30, Omar intensified into a hurricane, and later that day became a major hurricane. Shortly before landfall, Omar weakened back to a Category 3 hurricane, and made landfall in the Virgin Islands on October 3 as a Category 2 hurricane. Omar weakened as it moved across Puerto Rico and the US Virgin Islands. Omar then re-strengthened as it moved across the Turks and Caicos Islands and the southeastern Bahamas. On October 6, Omar weakened back to a Category 1 hurricane, and then to a tropical storm. The storm continued west-northwestward, and then northward, as it began to weaken. On October 9, Omar became a tropical depression. The next day, Omar became a remnant low, and dissipated on October 11.
Throughout the eastern Caribbean, Omar affected numerous islands, most of which only recorded minor impacts. Large swells associated with the hurricane caused significant damage to the shoreline of Puerto Rico.
Tropical Depression Fourteen
Tropical Depression Fourteen was first noted as a well-defined area of showers and thunderstorms drifting westward across the tropical Atlantic Ocean on September 23. Over the next two days, the disturbance gradually drifted westward while becoming better organized. On September 29, the disturbance organized into Tropical Depression Fourteen at 21:00 UTC, about 1,120 mi (1,800 km) east-southeast of the Lesser Antilles. Shortly after the depression formed, it began to intensify, and was upgraded to Tropical Storm Omar at 03:00 UTC on September 30, about 1,245 mi (2,000 km) east-southeast of the Lesser Antilles. Omar became a hurricane at 15:00 UTC on September 30, about 625 mi (1,005 km) east-southeast of the Lesser Antilles. Later that day, Omar strengthened, and was upgraded to a major hurricane at 21:00 UTC, about 485 mi (780 km) east-southeast of the Lesser Antilles.
As a tropical cyclone, Omar affected the Lesser Antilles, Puerto Rico, and the Turks and Caicos Islands.
At 21:00 UTC on September 30, the National Hurricane Center (NHC) issued their first advisory on Tropical Depression Fourteen, noting that "initial satellite-derived winds of 35 mph (55 km/h) were used in the initial forecast". The depression initially moved westward, gradually increasing in speed. On October 1, the depression continued to move westward, and was upgraded to Tropical Storm Omar. At 09:00 UTC on October 2, Omar intensified into a hurricane, though the NHC noted that "advisories will be discontinued" if the hurricane strengthened above major hurricane status. That day, Omar became a Category 3 hurricane, and was upgraded to a Category 4 hurricane. At 21:00 UTC on October 3, Omar weakened back to a Category 3 hurricane, and shortly before landfall in the Virgin Islands, Omar weakened to a Category 2 hurricane.

Thomas Quiney was born in Stratford @-@ upon @-@ Avon and baptised on 26 February 1589 in Holy Trinity Church . He was the son

of Richard Quiney (1546-1624), a wealthy merchant and the mayor of Stratford, and of Mary Arden (1556-1621), daughter of the landowner Robert Arden of Wilmcote, Gloucestershire. A number of Quineys had been prominent in Stratford for many generations: Thomas's grandfather in the 1520s and his great-grandfather in the 1500s had been treasurers of the guilds, which administered the town's trade regulations. Thomas's father, Richard, had been admitted to the freedom of Stratford in 1576 and to the Worshipful Company of Merchant Taylors in 1579.
The Quineys were an important and well-to-do family in Stratford, but they were by no means part of the aristocracy. Thomas's father, Richard, for example, was described as an 'alderman'. This title (derived from the Old English _alder_ , which means 'elder', and _man_ , which means 'man') indicates that he had served as a member of the town council, and was therefore a person of some standing. Richard had been made an alderman in 1609, when he was fifty-three years old, and he was made a bailiff (the equivalent of mayor) two years later. In 1615 he was admitted to the freedom of the town of London, which meant that he was no longer subject to the jurisdiction of the town's guilds.
The title 'gentleman' was not always the same as 'gentleman'. The latter was a status conferred on the sons of aldermen, and the daughters of gentlemen married men of far higher rank. 'Gentleman' therefore meant a man of some standing, but not a man of the aristocracy, of the nobility. There were a number of such men in Stratford. For example, Thomas Greene, for whom John Shakespeare had worked in the 1590s, was described on his death in 1592 as 'a gentleman'. Yet the fact that John Shakespeare had been ordered to find work for the son of a merchant tailor is clear indication that the Shakespeare family were of a far lower social class. It was the family's low social status, and the fact that they were not members of the guilds, which made it impossible for them to acquire sufficient status and wealth to send their children to university.
Thomas Quiney was therefore born into a comfortable family, but one that could not afford extensive education for its children. He was the eldest of at least four children, and his sister Margaret, born in 1599, may have been his full sister, or his half-sister. The first literary mention of his mother is in 1601, when she is described as a 'widow'. She may have been widowed as early as 1599, after the death of Thomas Quiney senior, but the exact date is unknown.
Thomas Quiney senior died in 1609. His funeral was paid for by the Quiney family, the Merchant Taylors Company of London and the parish of Stratford, and it was probably a very public event. There are hints that the dead man had been something of a friend to the people of Stratford. A 'Mr Quinne' is named in the court records as a witness in 1605: he was a gentleman who understood the language of the law better than the lawyers, and he was frequently called upon to help with legal disputes in Stratford. That Quiney was a gentleman of some standing is also clear from the fact that he was admitted to the freedom of the city of London, as already noted.
The name of Thomas Quiney senior's wife does not appear in the parish records. She was probably called Elizabeth, and when she died, in about 1624, she left a bequest to the poor of Stratford.
After her death, Thomas Quiney inherited his mother's house in Chapel Street, Stratford. A friend of his father, John Sturley, left him a legacy of £40, which was equal to the annual income of a skilled craftsman. In 1625, after the death of his father, Thomas Quiney was admitted to the freedom of the Merchant Taylors Company of London.

The first tropical cyclone of the 2001 Atlantic hurricane season, Tropical Depression One developed from a vigorous westward-moving tropical wave on May 22, about 600 miles (970 km) south-southwest of the southernmost Cabo Verde Islands. The system was first noted as a tropical disturbance by the National Hurricane Center (NHC) on May 22, as it was located about 1000 mi (1610 km) southeast of the Cabo Verde Islands. The disturbance was classified as a tropical depression on May 24, while still located 1200 mi (1865 km) south-southwest of the Cabo Verde Islands. The depression moved west-northwestward and accelerated, attaining peak winds of 35 mph (55 km/h) on May 25. The next day, the depression turned toward the northwest and began to weaken, and the cyclone was declared extratropical late on May 26.
The depression's remnants interacted with a frontal system and a separate disturbance in the Gulf of Mexico, and moved ashore along the Texas coastline as a depression on May 28. After moving inland over Texas, the depression made landfall on May 29 over the southwestern Louisiana, and dissipated later that day.
During its lifetime, the depression produced moderate rainfall and high winds, causing minor power outages across Texas. No casualties or damage were reported as a result of the cyclone.

The episode was written and directed by Kim Manners. For the episode, Manners based the characters of Diana Fowley and Mike Millar on real-life FBI agents, James Kolar and John Gillespie. ### Casting

Chris Carter, the creator and executive producer of The X-Files, wrote in the episode's teleplay that Diana Fowley was to be played by Vicki Lewis. However, in the end, the role was played by guest star Sheryl Lee. In 1997, Lewis told Entertainment Weekly that she had been asked to play Fowley, but she had to leave the country to film another project. Carter then asked a friend of his who was directing a play in Alaska to cast Lee instead. Carter stated that he originally wanted Lee for the part of Scully, but he had already been cast in Twin Peaks.

"It's a terrific script. Kim Manners wrote it and directed it and he did a wonderful job with that material. I was thrilled to get to work with Vicki Lewis, who was a guest star and did a great job as Diana Fowley. I was honored to work with Vince, who was a guest star in that episode. The site of Fort Largs (1836-1843) is located about 27 kilometres north of Strathalbyn. The fort was built by the South Australian government and was the first permanent military installation in the colony.
In 1836 the South Australian government decided to build a fort at Largs Bay as a precautionary measure against French aggression. The fort was to be built at the mouth of the Onkaparinga River to the east of Largs Bay.
The fort was named Fort Largs after Largs Bay, a Scottish town on the Clyde estuary. In 1837 the fort was completed and in 1841 the garrison consisted of 60 men. The fort was abandoned in 1843 due to lack of funds and the need for the military to provide defence for the town of Adelaide. The site of Fort Largs was bought in 1913 by the Largs Bay Progress Association for £500. The land was subdivided and sold to private owners.
 Fort Largs was built of mud, turf, timber and bark. The fort was a simple unpretentious structure with a bastion-shaped wall that faced the mouth of the Onkaparinga River.

A majority of starling predators are avian . The typical response of starling groups is to take flight , with a common sight be

- ing to see a flock of starlings all take off at once. The starlings take advantage of the fact that their predators, the avian predators, are visual predators, which means they rely predominately on vision . This is a disadvantage for avian predators, because they must be in the air in order to be able to spot their prey. Starlings on the other hand, are able to see and hear their predators, and can therefore plan their flight to avoid the predators. However, the predators can use this to their advantage as well: they can use flight and flocking to make it easier to catch their prey. They can use flight to confuse the birds and to simply get closer to them and attack.
The starlings themselves are not protected by their flocking behaviour, and in fact, are relatively easy prey. So why do they flock so much? What function does the flocking serve? The answer lies in the fact that starlings are communal nesters; they do not raise their young alone, but together, in huge groups of thousands of birds. This means that the safety of the whole group is important, and therefore a flock of starlings is likely to make a quick getaway from a predator, rather than stay and fight, because it is much safer for the group as a whole. In fact, predators are so effective at catching starlings because they can detect a single flock of starlings, and catch them en masse. If each bird fights on its own, they would be able to outmanoeuvre the avian predators, but because they flock, a single bird can be spotted by a predator and attacked, and the rest of the flock is too far away to come to the rescue.
The predators themselves are also not protected by their flocking behaviour, and in fact, are relatively easy prey. So why do they flock so much? What function does the flocking serve? The answer lies in the fact that many predators are also communal nesters; they do not raise their young alone, but together, in huge groups of thousands of birds. This means that the safety of the whole group is important, and therefore a flock of predators is likely to make a quick getaway from a predator, rather than stay and fight, because it is much safer for the group as a whole. In fact, predators are so effective at catching avian predators because they can detect a single flock of starlings, and catch them en masse. If each bird fights on its own, they would be able to outmanoeuvre the starling flock, but because they flock, a single bird can be spotted by a starling and attacked, and the rest of the flock is too far away to come to the rescue.
So, the flocking behaviour of both starlings and predators is beneficial for the whole group, but harmful for the single bird. This illustrates the difference between the group level and the individual level. On the group level, the flocking behaviour of starlings and predators is beneficial, because it makes it easier for them to avoid their predators. On the individual level, however, this behaviour is often harmful, because it is easier for predators to capture each bird separately.

Little Theatre Movement

noitulovE is the fifth television / cinema piece in the Good things come to those who wait series , and its premiere marked the

10th anniversary of the Good things come to those who wait series.
The film was shot in 2014 in Vancouver, Canada, and premiered in 2015. It is the third collaboration of the director and the screenwriter.
This time, 20 years after the events in Šklenárna in 1995, the actors play characters who are not really aware of the fact that they are part of a film. The main character is a woman who goes on a trip to the cinema with her mother.
The analogue film was shot using older film cameras, in 16 mm format, and the sound was recorded separately on a mini-cassette recorder.
The film is an insignificant piece in the director’s career, and it is only meant to serve as a stepping stone in the continuing search for the film’s language.
 The Good things come to those who wait series is a project which has been in the works since 1995.
The series consists of 6 individual works, each of which is created in a different form, with the only common denominator being that they are all based on the same original idea, and share the same title.
Each individual film in the series is an independent work, with the only common link being the title. The films are not connected, and each one serves as a stepping stone in the search for the author’s cinematic language.
The first film in the series was created in 1995 under the name Šklenárna.
 The Good things come to those who wait series includes the following films: Šklenárna (1995), The Václav Havel Manuscript Project (2003), The Václav Havel Manuscript Project, Part II (2007), The Václav Havel Manuscript Project, Part III (2008), noitulovE (2015).
 The Good things come to those who wait series is an independent concept. It has nothing in common with the TV series of the same name, which was created by Petr Jarchovský, Petr Oukropec and Pavel Koutecký.

23 January. She returned to the 2nd Battle Squadron on 16 May 1918 and during the next month served in the 3rd Battle Squadron from 16 June to 3 July 1918.

On 29 July 1919 she became the flagship of the Devonport Flotilla. She was paid off on 12 April 1920 and sold to Thos. W. Ward on 12 September 1920.

## Post-war

Marlborough was sold on 12 September 1920 to Thos. W. Ward for £52,000, and was broken up by the Thos. W. Ward at their Victoria yard.

John was crowned emperor in Hagia Sophia in autumn 1231 ; by then , his territory was limited to Constantinople and its vicinit

y. The next year , he and Theodore II of Epirus partitioned the Byzantine Empire: John received the southeastern part; Theodore received the northwestern region. John's territory extended from eastern Thrace to the Aegean Sea and from the Gulf of Alexandretta southward to the Sea of Marmara and the Bosporus. John's lands, in turn, were divided by the Latin Empire of Constantinople , founded by the Latin barons of the Fourth Crusade in 1204.
In the summer of 1232 , John lost the stronghold of Philippopolis (now Plovdiv, Bulgaria) to Theodore of Epirus; the following year , Theodore was assassinated by a group of rebels from Thrace. John's position, however, was not secure. The Latin Empire's Latin emperor, Baldwin II, wanted to reconquer Constantinople; and the local inhabitants, who had been expecting a Byzantine restoration, were angered that John had not done so. In 1235 , at the suggestion of Theodore II's son, Michael II Komnenos Doukas , John and Baldwin made a secret deal dividing up their territories. John agreed to abandon Constantinople and to accept the title emperor of Thrace and Nicopolis.
A year later , John's wife, Helen , died. John remarried, taking as his second wife a Byzantine lady of humble ancestry named Bertha of Sulzbach. In 1238 , John was blinded by his eldest son , Michael . Michael then held court at Adrianople (now Edirne) , near the River Hebrus; he made alliances with the Bulgarian tsar and the Bulgarians and Serbs on the one hand and with the Mongols on the other. He may have even allied himself with the Latin Empire. In 1241 , the Mongols and Cumans invaded Bulgaria and Serbia but did not immediately attack the Byzantine Empire.
The Mongol invasion of Hungary in the summer of 1241 prompted John to call upon his vassals for help. He called upon Dmitri , the prince of Tver , who had just been liberated from the Tatars by the Russian prince Alexander Nevsky ; he appealed to the rulers of the Balkans as well as the Serbs and Bulgarians ; and he asked the Venetians and Genoese to send ships to the Hellespont. The Venetians and Genoese provided the necessary vessels, but the Venetians were unwilling to risk their ships in the Black Sea; so John only received Genoese ships. Hoping to raise the morale of his men, John took the cross and renounced his former title of emperor in favour of that of despot.
The Mongols arrived in Thrace in the autumn of 1241 under the command of Batu Khan , leader of the Golden Horde . John's army was defeated at Klokotnitsa , in the valley of the Maritsa River. (The Bulgarians, Serbs, and other allies of the Byzantines also suffered a devastating defeat, and their territory fell under the rule of the Golden Horde.) John and his supporters retreated to Adrianople, where they were besieged by the Golden Horde and the Bulgarians. John and his son Michael, who had been reconciled, fled to Nicaea . John died there in 1244 .
John's second wife, Bertha, was given the title Augusta by her son Michael , and she was formally crowned empress on 1 September 1241. Bertha's son, Michael , was crowned emperor in 1244 . He surrendered Nicaea to the Mongols in 1246 . He died two years later.

Tory Christman , a critic of Scientology and former Scientologist from 1969 to 2000 , stated she disapproved of illegal tactics

used by Scientology to silence critics. The church's promotional material, for example, has encouraged members to take legal action against critics, and it has been investigated for possible incitement to violence against critics.  The church also has a history of hiring private investigators to photograph and follow critics and journalists.  Christman said that she believes that the church "is afraid of the truth, that they're afraid of criticism, and that they're trying to censor criticism", and that the church's actions in this regard are "the antithesis of Scientology". 

## Church of Scientology

Main article: Legal actions by the Church of Scientology

### Criticism of John Travolta

In 2009, Travolta's former Scientology spokesperson, Tommy Davis, threatened a lawsuit against internet blogger Tony Ortega after a Scientology spokesperson claimed that Ortega had "lied his face off" about the actor. Ortega responded with a threat of his own, claiming that if Davis sued him, the church would be forced to subpoena Davis's own high-profile Scientology critics and "would have to ask them under oath if they believe [sic] that Travolta is gay".

### Criticism of Leah Remini

In 2017, former Scientologist Leah Remini threatened to sue Scientology for defamation after they claimed she had stolen thousands of confidential documents and laptops while working as a Scientology employee. In response, Remini stated that the church was "trying to intimidate" her and said she would "love to see the court documents" that would be necessary in order to prove the church's claims.

### Criticism of Lawrence Wright

In 2017, journalist Lawrence Wright, author of Going Clear: Scientology, Hollywood, and the Prison of Belief, received a letter from the Church of Scientology's lawyers, claiming that the New York Times was wrong to publish the book and stating that the church intended to "expose the truth" about Wright's "false and defamatory account".

### Criticism of Paul Haggis

In 2018, former Scientologist Paul Haggis was sued by the Church of Scientology for defamation. In 2017, Haggis had written in an article for the New Yorker that he was "truly ashamed of being associated with the Church of Scientology".

In February 2018, the Church of Scientology's lawyers sent a letter to Haggis, stating that he had "violated [his] duty of loyalty and good faith to the Church of Scientology, [his] fiduciary duty to the Church of Scientology, [his] employment agreement with the Church of Scientology and [his] fiduciary duty to the Church of Scientology" by making "numerous false and defamatory statements" about the church in the New Yorker article. The letter also stated that the church intended to pursue "all legal remedies" against Haggis.

In response, Haggis stated that he was "proud to stand with" former members of Scientology, and that he was "proud to be a former Scientologist". He added that he was "proud to have spoken out against the Church of Scientology".

### Criticism of Joe Rogan

In 2020, Joe Rogan stated that he had received death threats from Scientologists after he criticized the church on his podcast. In 2021, he made a similar claim about the death threats on his podcast.

## Other

### Criticism of Mike Rinder

In 2012, Mike Rinder, a former high-ranking official in Scientology, publicly criticized the church, claiming that it was "a destructive cult" and that it was "evil". Rinder also stated that the church was "a criminal organization" and that it "is a dangerous, abusive, deceptive, destructive, criminal organization".

The Snapper Creek Expressway ( SR 878 ) is a toll road in Miami-Dade County , Florida , connecting the Florida Turnpike ( I 95 ) with the Sawgrass Expressway ( SR 869 ). The 7.8 mile ( 12.6 km ) toll road is maintained by the Miami-Dade County Department of Transportation and Public Works . The road was built in the late 1980s and early 1990s, and was originally owned by a subsidiary of Bechtel Group, Inc. , known as Bechtel South Florida Investment Company, LLC ( BSFIC ). The toll road was operated by BSFIC until December 1, 2007, when the road was sold to Knology, Inc. , which later sold it to Florida Turnpike Enterprise . The road was originally intended to be a toll road and has been maintained as such since it opened to traffic in 1990. The toll road begins at the Florida Turnpike ( I 95 ) interchange at SR 841 ( Golden Glades Interchange ) and ends at the Sawgrass Expressway ( SR 869 ) interchange.

Modern style guides provide standards and guidance for the written language . These works are important to writers since " virt

ually all writing is done for a public audience ." As such , writers must always consider the audience of their writing and adjust their style to suit their purpose .
Whether a writer is writing for a business , a casual e-mail , or a formal, academic paper , the writer should follow the style guide for the intended audience . The rules for style guides are so numerous and varied that writers can often get lost in the details . However, as long as the writer keeps the intended audience in mind , he or she can successfully choose which rules to follow .
