On October 6 , 1993 , Jordan announced his retirement , citing a loss of desire to play the game . Jordan later stated that the

1993–94 NBA season was his last, but he returned to play in the 1994–95 season after a one-year sabbatical.
 In 2003, Jordan received a call from a close friend, former Chicago Bulls teammate and current Charlotte Hornets owner Michael Jordan , asking him to come out of retirement and return to the NBA to play for the Washington Wizards. Jordan agreed, signing a contract with the Wizards on January 13, 2004. On January 21, 2003 , Jordan made his return to the NBA, playing his first game with the Wizards against his former team, the Chicago Bulls. He received a standing ovation from the United Center crowd, and scored 19 points in a 91–89 loss to the Bulls. After playing four more seasons, Jordan retired for a second time on January 13, 2003.
 In 2007, Jordan was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame . In 2009, he was inducted into the FIBA Hall of Fame . In 2010, he was named the greatest North American athlete of the first quarter of the 21st century by ESPN , with the only other professional athlete to be named was Tiger Woods . In 2015, he was named the greatest NBA player of all time by ESPN, as well as the fifth greatest athlete of all time by the same network. In 2016, he was named the greatest North American athlete of the last 35 years by Sports Illustrated.
 Michael Jeffrey Jordan was born on February 17, 1963 in Brooklyn, New York . He grew up in Wilmington, North Carolina , where he was raised by his maternal grandparents, James and Sara Rae (Jefferson) Jordan. Jordan's father, James R. Jordan, Sr. , was a tool pusher. Jordan has two sisters, Deloris and Roslyn, and a younger brother, Larry. Jordan's parents divorced when he was one year old. Jordan's maternal grandparents saw his potential as an athlete when he was two years old, and they enrolled him in basketball courses. Jordan later stated that his grandparents were his role models and biggest influences in his life.
 Jordan attended Emsley A. Laney High School in Wilmington, where he played basketball for coach Robert Bridgeman. As a freshman, he was named the starter for the varsity team. In his sophomore year, he averaged 25 points per game, and led Laney to a 28–2 record and the state 4A championship. As a junior, he averaged 29 points per game and led Laney to a 31–2 record, and a 4A state runner-up finish. As a senior, Jordan averaged 37.6 points per game and led Laney to a 33–1 record and the 1980 state 4A championship. In 1984, Laney renamed its gymnasium the Michael Jordan Gymnasium.
 In high school, Jordan was also a standout baseball player and played American Legion baseball for the Wilmington Stars. He was a shortstop and batted over .400 in his senior season. In addition, he played minor league baseball for the Wilmington Waves.
 During his sophomore year, Jordan received a scholarship offer from North Carolina State , but he soon turned it down. Instead, he chose to attend the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill to play for head coach Dean Smith. After his freshman year, he was redshirted for the 1982–83 season due to NCAA rules, which required that freshmen be redshirted in their first season.
 In 1983–84, Jordan became a starter for the Tar Heels and was named ACC Freshman of the Year. He averaged 13.5 points and 5.7 rebounds per game, as North Carolina went 27–6, and won the ACC regular season and tournament championships. Jordan scored a then career-high 28 points in the championship game of the ACC Tournament, leading North Carolina to a 96–79 win over Georgetown. He also helped the Tar Heels advance to the 1984 NCAA Tournament, where they lost to Georgetown in the national championship game.

The Dust Bowl certainly was the most severe example of this problem, but the issue of soil erosion affected many other areas of the High Plains and the Canadian Prairie.
 The Great Depression was a severe worldwide economic depression that took place mostly during the 1930s, beginning in the United States. The timing of the Great Depression varied across nations; in most countries it started in 1929 and lasted until the late 1930s. It was the longest, deepest, and most widespread depression of the 20th century. In the 21st century, the Great Depression is commonly used as an example of how far the world's economy can decline.
 The Hoover Dam is a concrete arch-gravity dam in the Black Canyon of the Colorado River, on the border between the US states of Arizona and Nevada. It was constructed between 1931 and 1936 during the Great Depression and was dedicated on September 30, 1935, by President Franklin D. Roosevelt. Its construction was the key component of the largest public works undertaking of the era, the Tennessee Valley Authority.
The dam was named for Herbert Hoover, the 31st President of the United States. The dam produces vast amounts of hydroelectric power for public and private utilities in Nevada, Arizona, and California. It is possible that the reservoir formed by the dam will become an internationally famous tourist attraction, and the dam has been a national symbol of the United States since its completion.
 _The_ New Deal _was a series of programs, public work projects, financial reforms, and regulations enacted by President Franklin D. Roosevelt in the United States between 1933 and 1938. It responded to needs for relief, recovery, and reform, especially during the Depression of 1929. Major federal programs and agencies created by the New Deal include the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC), the Civil Works Administration (CWA), the Farm Security Administration (FSA), the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA), and the Works Progress Administration (WPA). New Deal programs provided relief to millions of unemployed Americans and families with low incomes. The projects put millions to work, and the regulations and reforms related to the banking system established consumer protection standards and prevented bank runs. The Supreme Court, in _Hammer v. The _National Labor Relations Act_ (1935) granted labor the right to bargain collectively. The _Fair Labor Standards Act_ (1938) set minimum wages, maximum hourly pay, and the first federal standards for overtime pay. The Social Security Act of 1935 gave federal support to the elderly, the unemployed, and the uninsured. The New Deal also created a new economic philosophy that came to be known as Keynesian economics. The New Deal influenced the creation of the European Union and the Atlantic Charter._

Private John HENDERSON was born in Horsford, Norfolk on 2nd April 1921. He joined the 1st Battalion, the Norfolk Regiment, which was part of the 1st Commonwealth Division.
On 18th September 1944, the 1st Battalion, the Norfolk Regiment, was involved in the RANKIN CHURCHILL Commando raid. The raid was part of Operation Commando, which was part of the Arnhem campaign. Operation Commando was a combined airborne and amphibious operation aimed at clearing a corridor across the Neder Rijn, the main waterway to the west of Arnhem. The operation was to be launched from the north of the Neder Rijn, with the main attack being launched from the south, via the Wilhelmina Canal.
The RANKIN CHURCHILL Commando raid, took place on the same day. The objective of the commando raid was to capture the bridge at RANKIN CHURCHILL, to the south of Renkin, in order to establish a second bridgehead near Arnhem, and thus provide the units of 1st Parachute Brigade with a second route into Arnhem.
The raid was successful, with the bridge at RANKIN CHURCHILL secured, and the nearby bridge over the Rijn Canal also secured. The Germans launched an attack on the bridge but were driven off, and the RANKIN CHURCHILL bridge remained in British hands, until it was secured by the 1st Parachute Brigade on 21st September 1944.
Private HENDERSON was wounded during the raid. He died of these wounds on 20th September 1944, and is buried in the RANKIN CHURCHILL Cemetery, located on the edge of the village of Renkin, to the south-east of Arnhem.

Purist critics in jazz complained about the music 's incorporation of danceable beats and electric guitar . In Stereo Review ,

1965, H. Owen Reed wrote, "The problem with Davis's 'electric' album is that it is not really electric. It is not as if he had gathered around him some of the best young electric guitarists and had them play some hot stuff. The guitar merely stands in as a substitute for the piano. The guitarist, John McLaughlin, is a fine player, but he seems lost in this music." In reference to Davis's use of electric guitar and electric bass, Louis Armstrong said, "There's no place in that music for the guitar or bass. At least, that's the way I feel. I'm not knocking it; I know that's the way Miles feels. Miles is a great musician, and he doesn't have to please everybody."

Among the musicians who played on the album were Herbie Hancock , Ron Carter , Tony Williams , Wayne Shorter , McLaughlin and Freddie Hubbard . One of the album's tracks, "Lonely Fire", was included on the soundtrack to the 1965 film The Pawnbroker , directed by Sidney Lumet and starring Rod Steiger.

## Reception and legacy

Professional ratings

In a retrospective review for The Village Voice, Robert Christgau called the album "a pleasurable, well-proportioned work" and concluded that "after nearly two years away from the studio, Davis had returned with a fine record." In similar fashion, Philip Clark of AllMusic wrote that the album "is much more than a mere flash in the pan – it's an extraordinary demonstration of Davis's artistic vision."

The album was ranked number 262 on Rolling Stone magazine's original list of the "500 Greatest Albums of All Time" in 2003, although it was not included in the magazine's updated list in 2020.

The M3 subtype of AML , also known as acute promyelocytic leukemia ( APL ) , is almost universally treated with the drug all @-

trans retinoic acid ( ATRA ).
ATRA is derived from vitamin A and is found naturally in the body.
 The treatment of APL was revolutionized in 1991 when the molecular basis of the disease was identified as an unbalanced translocation resulting in the formation of the chimeric RAR/PML fusion protein .
The RAR/PML fusion protein is produced by the fusion of the retinoic acid receptor ( RAR ) and the promyelocytic leukemia ( PML ) gene.
 The RAR/PML fusion protein is therefore found in all APL cells.
 Patients with the t (15; 17) translocation are considered to have M3 APL.
 The translocation is found in 85% to 90% of patients with APL.
 The remaining 10% to 15% of APL patients have other molecular abnormalities.

The Dangerously In Love Tour was the debut solo concert tour by American recording artist Beyoncé . The tour was intended to sh

ine spotlight on Beyoncé's solo career following her departure from the group Destiny's Child in 2005. Beyoncé began the tour on November 7, 2004 in Atlantic City, New Jersey to promote her debut solo album, Dangerously in Love (2003). The tour saw Beyoncé performing to sold-out crowds at various arenas and theatres across North America, Europe and Asia. The tour was declared a critical and commercial success as it was Beyoncé's first major tour and she became the first female artist to sell out Madison Square Garden three times in one year.
The tour was divided into two segments. The first leg of the tour, named "Dangerously in Love Tour", featured Beyoncé performing with a live band and a small dance troupe. The tour was extended following the release of Beyoncé's second album, B'Day (2006) and included songs from the album as well. The second leg of the tour, named "The Beyoncé Experience", was similar to the previous tour with two exceptions: it included more dance performers and the stage was larger. The tour was filmed in its entirety in Buenos Aires, Argentina and released as a concert film of the same name, The Beyoncé Experience (2007). The tour was Beyoncé's first major concert tour and led to her being named one of the top ten worldwide live acts of 2007 by Pollstar.
The first leg of the tour began on November 7, 2004 at the Atlantic City Boardwalk Hall in Atlantic City, New Jersey. The venues included Madison Square Garden in New York City, Radio City Music Hall in New York City and the MGM Grand Garden Arena in Las Vegas. The tour concluded on November 28, 2004 at the American Airlines Arena in Miami, Florida. Beyoncé's setlist included songs from her debut solo album, Dangerously in Love (2003), as well as songs from her former group Destiny's Child. Following the success of the tour, Beyoncé performed at the 2005 MTV Video Music Awards and the 2005 American Music Awards.
The second leg of the tour began on May 19, 2006 at the O2 Arena in London, England and concluded on March 31, 2007 at the MGM Grand Garden Arena in Las Vegas, Nevada. Included in the tour were numerous sold-out shows in the United States and Canada, as well as additional shows in Europe and Asia. The tour was extended following the release of Beyoncé's second album, B'Day (2006). The tour included songs from the album as well as songs from her former group Destiny's Child.

The Ottoman attack started in a disorganised fashion, with the Ottoman logistical trains being destroyed by the British, further hampering the Ottoman advance.
The Allies were able to quickly establish a line of defence at the Battle of Romani, and continued to defeat the Ottomans in subsequent engagements in the Sinai and Palestine campaigns.
The Battle of Romani (Arabic: معركة رماني‎) during the Sinai and Palestine Campaign of World War I, took place at Romani, Egypt, on 4–6 August 1916. The battle marked the first action of the Egyptian Expeditionary Force (EEF), which was formed in July 1916 under the command of General Sir Archibald Murray. The EEF consisted of the 52nd (Lowland) Infantry Division, the 53rd (Welsh) Infantry Division and the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps (ANZAC). The EEF's objective was to advance into Palestine to meet the strategic requirements of the Allied war effort. To its north, the EEF was opposed by the Ottoman 16th Army.
The EEF's advance began on 30 July 1916, with the ANZAC Corps crossing the Suez Canal at Romani. The Ottomans had deployed three Ottoman Army divisions in the Jazirat Tuzuk area, north of the Suez Canal, in anticipation of an attack by the British Indian Expeditionary Force. The Ottoman 16th Army had been formed in December 1915, in the Caucasus Campaign, and redeployed to the Sinai Peninsula in June 1916. The Ottoman 16th Army was commanded by German General Friedrich Freiherr Kress von Kressenstein. The Ottoman 16th Army consisted of the Ottoman 3rd Army and the Ottoman 4th Army.
On 3 August 1916, the ANZAC Corps commander, Lieutenant General William Birdwood, received intelligence that the Ottoman 16th Army was advancing from the direction of Rafah, and ordered the 53rd (Welsh) Infantry Division to advance towards Tel-el-Kebir. The ANZAC Corps' advance was halted by the Ottoman 153rd Infantry Brigade at the village of Katia, just east of Romani. The 53rd (Welsh) Infantry Division's advance resumed in the morning of 3 August, and the division's advance guards reached the Jazirat Dumayr area on 4 August.
The Ottoman advance resumed on 4 August, with the Ottoman 3rd Army's I Corps advancing towards Romani and the Ottoman 4th Army's II Corps advancing towards Katia. The Ottoman advance was screened by Ottoman cavalry, which was defeated on 4 August by Australian Light Horse. The advance of the 153rd Infantry Brigade and the 53rd (Welsh) Infantry Division was slowed on 5 August by the Ottoman 16th Army's 34th Infantry Division. The Ottoman advance halted at Romani, and the Ottoman 4th Army continued to advance towards Katia.
On the morning of 5 August, the 153rd Infantry Brigade and the 53rd (Welsh) Infantry Division were deployed to guard the Romani–Katia road. During the afternoon, the 153rd Infantry Brigade received orders to advance towards El Arish, which was defended by a small Ottoman force. During the night, the 153rd Infantry Brigade's 5th and 7th Battalions, Welch Regiment, advanced towards El Arish. The 7th Battalion, Welch Regiment, took El Arish and the 5th Battalion, Welch Regiment, was forced to retire by Ottoman forces. The 5th Battalion, Welch Regiment, withdrew to Romani, and the 7th Battalion, Welch Regiment, was forced to withdraw to the Romani–Katia road, which was being defended by the 53rd (Welsh) Infantry Division. The 53rd (Welsh) Infantry Division was relieved by the 52nd (Lowland) Infantry Division, which advanced into position between Katia and Romani.

en't the only ones called to the stand. The inspectors themselves, John R. Hutchinson and John B. Woodward, were called to account.
They came to the stand holding their heads high. They looked the committee members in the eyes, and they were not intimidated by the tense atmosphere in the room. They were confident, and they knew their testimony was going to help them.
The official transcript of the hearings before the House Committee on Merchant Marine and Fisheries is a long one, and much of it has been edited here. In this edited testimony, we learn that John R. Hutchinson had been an inspector for six years, and John B. Woodward for only four. Both were experienced men, and both were respected in the field. There is no evidence of impropriety in either of their lives.
The government inspectors were asked to explain their decision to inspect El Sol and Sac City on the same day at the same time. They explained that they had been on the Canyon de Chelly reservation, inspecting a ferry, when a message was sent to inform them that the steamboats were ready for inspection. They had turned around and headed back, and the inspectors had immediately begun to inspect the vessels. They stated that they had not made any compromises to the inspection process, and that they had taken their duties as seriously as any inspector would.

Cadmium occurs as a minor component in most zinc ores and is a byproduct of zinc production . Cadmium was used for a long time

in the preparation of a variety of paints , solder , and batteries, but it is now more commonly used in the preparation of semiconductor materials . The principal use of cadmium is in the production of nickel-cadmium batteries, as a component of metal-hydride storage batteries, and as a corrosion-resistant coating for steel. Cadmium salts have been used for a long time as a wood preservative, but this use has been discontinued in the United States since 1978. Cadmium chloride is used as a pesticide and as a component of the phosphate-based pesticides.
The U.S. Geological Survey has been collecting data on the production of cadmium and its compounds since 1965. This publication presents data on the production of cadmium and its compounds in the United States.
Fourteen companies operate 16 mining and six refining (ore concentrating) operations in the United States. Most cadmium recovered in the United States is recovered from byproducts of zinc mining and production. The mining and refining operations in the United States produce cadmium and cadmium compounds that are used in electronics and semiconductors, batteries and plastics, pesticides and other agricultural chemicals, and metal products.
In 2008, cadmium mines in the United States produced 10.6 million pounds of cadmium, valued at $12.6 million. The ore concentrating (refining) operations in the United States produced 9.6 million pounds of cadmium, valued at $12.6 million. More than 95 percent of the cadmium produced in the United States was imported from foreign countries.

The Early Neolithic people of Britain placed far greater emphasis on the ritualised burial of the dead than their Mesolithic fo

es. The two principal contemporary developments in Neolithic burial were the manifestation of the belief in a final journey to a transcendent realm beyond the grave (or at least into another world that was not completely beyond the grave) and the creation of large, architecturally elaborate chambered tombs, which in some parts of Britain were located in cemeteries that were the centres of social life.
The concept of the afterlife was central to the lives of Neolithic people, and it is expressed by the placement of people in post-mortem positions. The most spectacular examples comprise the bones of people who were deliberately placed in positions that would have been almost impossible to achieve in life, such as sitting on the edge of a bench, standing or leaning against a wall or lying on their backs with their arms and legs drawn up and visible. The bones of these people have been found in the Stonehenge area, with the most remarkable example of an individual named the Amesbury Archer, a man buried in a pit at Durrington Walls, just a few hundred yards from the great henge. He was laid on a bed of white chalk and was surrounded by a variety of artefacts, including a spear, a flint knife, a large polished flint axe, a bone comb and a wooden bowl. His body had been carefully mummified, and the flesh had been removed from his skull and the vertebrae of his spine. This was apparently done as a deliberate attempt to disguise his identity, but the mummification had failed, and his face could be clearly seen when the body was radiocarbon dated.
The Amesbury Archer had lived in the Late Neolithic period, around 2600 BC, and was buried around 1000 years before Stonehenge was built, but even then the belief in a transcendent realm was beginning to take hold. The people who had built Stonehenge, and who had built the great causewayed enclosure at Durrington Walls, believed that the dead should be ritually buried in fashion that would ensure that they were not forgotten. They created great mounds of earth in which they placed their dead, and they continued to visit these mounds to ensure that the dead were not forgotten.
A few years after the Amesbury Archer was laid to rest, a man called the 'Wycombe Beaker Man' was placed in a pit and buried with a flint knife, a copper awl and a necklace of beads. The beads were made from seashells. As a result, the grave is dated to around 2500 BC, and the burial took place just a few hundred yards from the River Thames, at a site in what is now Buckinghamshire. The grave was discovered at the end of the nineteenth century, but its position was not recorded at the time, and it was subsequently lost. However, in the 1970s it was rediscovered, and its location was recorded by modern surveying methods. The grave had been deliberately buried, and the entire pit was filled with water and then sealed with turf, as can be seen in the illustration.
These two graves are just two examples of the great variety that was seen in Neolithic burial. Indeed, each individual grave site had its own distinctive appearance. Although the graves were similar in the sense that they were architecturally complex and contained the remains of people who had been deliberately buried in pre-arranged positions, they varied enormously in terms of the types of grave goods that had been placed with the dead. Archaeologists divide Neolithic graves into two broad categories: those that are characterised by the fact that they contain a range of grave goods and those that do not.
In general, the graves that have no grave goods are those that were deliberately buried. These graves are characterised by the fact that they are square or rectangular pits, which are often associated with a stone structure and which are located close to a settlement. However, the graves that do contain grave goods are characterised by the fact that they are circular. These graves are associated with the construction of large, complex, architecturally elaborate structures that are built with stones that have been carefully worked to create a final resting place for the dead. The graves that contain no grave goods are often found in cemeteries, which were areas that were not occupied by people, whereas the cemeteries that have grave goods are located by settlements.

Lost Horizons is the second studio album from the British electronic duo Lemon Jelly , released on 7 October 2002 . Released by

the record label Off the Wall (subsequently part of EMI Records), the album was the group's second album, and peaked at No. 11 in the UK Albums Chart . It has been certified double platinum by the British Phonographic Industry (BPI) for sales in excess of 600,000. The album is a combination of the band's previous album, Lost in Translation , and new material. Two singles from the album were released. "Nice Weather for Ducks" was the first single to be released, peaking at No. 25 in the UK Singles Chart . The second single, "In the Sun", reached No. 3 in the UK Singles Chart . The album was reissued in 2004, featuring a bonus disc of B-sides and remixes.
The album was generally well received by critics, with the review aggregator website Metacritic recording an average score of 72 out of 100 based on 14 reviews. Allmusic gave the album four out of five stars, praising the album's "haunting melancholy" and "dreamy soundscapes".
The album's title track is a cover of the song "Lost Horizon" by the British band Everything but the Girl , which was released on their 1990 album Home. The track was originally intended to be a B-side to Lost in Translation , however a German record label that had licensed the track for a compilation album kept the track, and it was eventually added as a bonus track to the US and Canadian edition of Lost Horizons.
Lost Horizons was a commercial success, peaking at No. 11 in the UK Albums Chart and No. 81 in the US Billboard 200 . In the UK, the album had sold 606,804 units by November 2010. In Australia, the album peaked at No. 18 in the ARIA Albums Chart .

The history of draining and development of the Everglades dates back to the 19th century . During the Second Seminole War begin

to develop the first canals drainage, which started to drain the northern portion of the Everglades. The drainage canals were built by the U.S. Army in the 1890s and 1900s. The area drained was referred to as the Everglades Agricultural Area (EAA).
The Kissimmee River, which is the largest river in the EAA, was the first river to be dredged and relocated in 1907. The water in the Everglades was drained by pumps, which was all hand-powered equipment, until 1931 when the water was diverted by a 4000-acre-foot (5,000,000 m 3) Federal dam. The diverted water was used to irrigate sugarcane fields.
The drainage of the EAA was not completed until 1932, when the Tamiami Trail (U.S. 41) was built across the Everglades. The roadway was constructed with bridges that blocked the flow of water. The drainage canals were connected by a network of levees, which formed a drainage network.

Bama HBCU Varsity Program
The National Association of Collegiate Directors of Athletics (NACDA) named Alabama Athletics' HBCU Varsity Program the 2012 winner of the prestigious Roy F. Kramer Award.
The Roy F. Kramer Award, which is named in honor of the late NCAA President, recognizes the HBCU varsity program that best exemplifies the mission of HBCUs and the NCAA, which is to provide opportunities for student-athletes to compete and learn.
Alabama Athletics' HBCU Varsity Program, which has been in operation for 10 years, is comprised of an annual football game between Alabama and Florida A&M, an annual baseball game between Alabama and Tuskegee, an annual basketball game between Alabama and Alabama State, and a track and field competition between Alabama and Alabama State.
NACDA's HBCU Subcommittee selected Alabama's HBCU Varsity Program for the award based on its long-standing tradition of giving African-American students the opportunity to compete at the highest level of athletics, and for its ability to use sports as a vehicle to promote diversity and inclusion.
"I am proud of the HBCU Varsity Program we have here at Alabama," said Alabama Athletics Director Mal Moore. "It is a great program that has been a real asset to the University and to other HBCUs. I want to thank our athletics staff for their hard work and dedication in making this program a success."
Alabama's HBCU Varsity Program has raised over $100,000 for the HBCUs and Alabama Athletics since its inception in 2002. In addition to those donations, Alabama Athletics provides financial support for the HBCUs through academic scholarships and various other initiatives.
Alabama has won 11 national football championships, 14 national basketball championships and 15 national baseball championships. The Crimson Tide has also won 56 SEC championships and 67 national championships in men's and women's sports combined.

Hurricane Uleki was the first storm of the 1988 Pacific cyclone season. it formed from a low pressure area in the Pacific Ocean on the 24th of August.
Hurricane Uleki was first a tropical storm. It later became a tropical depression on the 26th of August, then a tropical storm again on the 27th.
Hurricane Uleki was at it's peak strength when it hit the Hawaiian Islands. The storm had a maximum sustained wind speed of 185 km/h (115 mph) and was a category 3 hurricane on the Saffir–Simpson hurricane scale.
Hurricane Uleki was the first storm to hit Hawaii in 10 years.

Simon Bradstreet ( baptized March 18 , 1603 / 4 – March 27 , 1697 ) was a colonial magistrate , businessman , diplomat , and th

irteenth Governor of the Massachusetts Bay Colony ( 1675 – 1679 ) .
Raised in England , Bradstreet was a graduate of Pembroke College , Cambridge and an early supporter of Oliver Cromwell . In his early years Bradstreet experienced financial difficulties and was involved in a legal dispute with the Massachusetts Bay Company . In 1636 he immigrated to Massachusetts and assumed a leadership position in the local government . Throughout his life he maintained a strong relationship with the Church of England and described himself as a "fellow-traveller" with the Puritans . During the English Civil War , Bradstreet was an active member of a group of colonial leaders who supported the Parliamentary cause . After the failure of the Royalist cause Bradstreet was elected Governor by the General Court of Massachusetts and held this position until his resignation in 1679 .
Bradstreet was a leading figure in the Massachusetts Bay Colony and a proponent of the idea of ​​colonial independence from England . He was a member of the General Court and the Governor's Council , and as Governor he played an important role in the creation of the Dominion of New England . Bradstreet was also active in the early stages of the Salem witch trials , and is one of the few colonial leaders who opposed the execution of alleged witches .
Bradstreet was born in 1603 or 1604 in London , England . He was the son of Simon Bradstreet and Katherine (née Culpeper) Bradstreet . Simon Bradstreet was an attorney and a personal friend of William Shakespeare . Katherine Bradstreet was the daughter of Sir Thomas Culpeper , a prominent member of the English nobility who was executed during the reign of Queen Mary I .
In 1618 or 1619 Bradstreet was enrolled at Pembroke College , Cambridge , where he received his bachelor's degree in 1623 . He later earned an MA degree from the College . While attending Cambridge he was involved in a legal dispute with the Massachusetts Bay Company , which resulted in his removal from the Company's membership roster in 1632 . This dispute caused Bradstreet to delay his departure for the Massachusetts Bay Colony .
Simon Bradstreet married Anne Marbury , daughter of Sir Robert Marbury , in 1637 . Anne Marbury was the widow of John Allen , a wealthy ship owner who had died in 1634 . Anne was a wealthy woman who brought land and property to the marriage . The couple had four children: Simon (1639 – 1642), Simon (1642 – 1696), John (died young) and Anne (1644 – 1712).
Bradstreet was elected to the General Court of Massachusetts in 1643 and he was reelected for several subsequent terms . In 1657 Bradstreet was elected to the governorship of the Massachusetts Bay Colony by the General Court , defeating John Winthrop the Younger . When he took office in 1657 he was the third governor of the colony, succeeding John Endicott .
The first term of the Governorship of Simon Bradstreet in Massachusetts lasted from 1657 to 1660 . During this time he was involved in ongoing disputes with the General Court of New England . At the end of his first term of office he was reelected by the General Court . He was then elected as the first President of the Governor's Council of the Massachusetts Bay Colony . He was reelected to the Governor's Council in 1663 .
In 1661 Bradstreet was elected a deputy to the General Court of Connecticut .
In 1666 Bradstreet was appointed as the Vice President of the Governor's Council of the Dominion of New England . The Dominion of New England was a colonial confederation that was formed by the four major English colonies in North America: Massachusetts Bay , Plymouth , New Haven and Connecticut . Governor of New England was Sir Edmund Andros , a member of the English Privy Council who was appointed by King Charles II .

Crown Fountain has both slits and a grate for drainage ( pictured above right ) to drain the 11 @,@ 520 US gal ( 43 @,@ 608 l ;

200 @,@ 3030 l ) of water into the ravine below. The fountain is surrounded by a 283 ft ( 86 m ) by 50 ft ( 15 m ) by 10 in ( 25 cm ) high concrete reflecting pool.
Crown Fountain is an interactive video sculpture consisting of two 50 ft ( 15 m ) towers, one on each side of the reflecting pool. Water spills out of the top of the towers and cascades to the ground below. A chilled mist is also sprayed from the bottom of the towers. The monumental sculpture is visible from State and Wabash to the north and south, and Congress and Madison to the west and east.
Each tower is 50 ft ( 15 m ) tall and is flanked by a pair of 50 ft ( 15 m ) mirrored glass panels. The mirrored glass panels are angled to reflect the surrounding cityscape and are layered with dichroic glass to enable the fountain to glow at night.
The towers are subdivided into 20 segments each, each with a 4 ft ( 1.2 m ) by 4 ft ( 1.2 m ) LED screen. The 20 segment LED screens are linked in pairs, with one vertical and one horizontal screen in each pair.
 The screens display a series of video projections of water spilling from the towers onto two groups of people. One group is shown in front of a blue background and is made up of people of mixed races, genders, and ages: the more "stereotypical" Chicagoan. The second group is shown in front of a red background and is made up of people of mixed races, genders, and ages: the "stereotypical" un-Chicagoan.
The image of the group on the screen changes every 15 minutes. The group on the screen is always flanked by an image of people of mixed races, genders, and ages.
When the towers are in operation, the LED screens are illuminated by a spotlight. The LED screens are visible from a distance of 1,000 ft ( 300 m ) away.
The fountain is surrounded by a three-foot deep, 200,000-gallon (757,000 L) pool. The fountain is programmed to spray jets of water up to 100 feet ( 30 m ) into the air.
When in use, the fountain is programmed to spray water up to 100 ft ( 30 m ) at 50 ft ( 15 m ) intervals. Water is chilled before being sprayed into the fountain, and the fountain is operated under a misting system. The chilled water is pumped from the fountain's base, through a 22 ft ( 7 m ) tall by 8 in ( 20 cm ) diameter underground well, up to the top of the fountain, and back down. The Missouri River originates from the confluence of the Jefferson, Madison, and Gallatin Rivers in Montana, near Three Forks . The stream then flows southwestwardly along the Continental Divide in southwestern Montana.
From its origins, the Missouri River is 3,767 miles (6,060 km) long, and drains a drainage basin of 519,000 square miles (1,340,000 km 2) in parts of ten U.S. states and two Canadian provinces. The Missouri River Basin is the fourth-largest drainage basin in the United States. The basin is bounded on the east by the Rocky Mountains and on the west by the Flathead, Spokane, and Columbia watersheds. The Missouri River is the longest river in the United States; its watershed encompasses about one-sixth of the conterminous United States.
The river is a major river of the American Midwest, supplying water to the states of Missouri, Kansas, Iowa, Nebraska, South Dakota, North Dakota and Montana as well as parts of Wyoming and Minnesota.
The Missouri River is sometimes considered the longest river system in the United States, as it flows through the Dakotas, Nebraska, Kansas, Iowa, Missouri, and Montana, and its many tributaries extend into Wyoming, South Dakota, Minnesota, and Colorado. It also forms part of the border between the states of North Dakota and South Dakota.
The river is fed primarily by the Rocky Mountains , with additional river flow coming from rain and snowmelt in the mountains, as well as streams flowing from the Great Plains .
The Missouri River begins at the confluence of the Jefferson, Madison, and Gallatin Rivers near Three Forks, Montana . The sculpture was donated to the City of Poughkeepsie by the State of New York in memory of all citizens who fought in the World War I.
The sculpture was designed to be located opposite the Veterans Administration hospital (now the Mid-Hudson Regional Hospital) on the east side of the City of Poughkeepsie.
The sculpture was originally sited on the lawn of the former Veterans Administration hospital (now the Mid-Hudson Regional Hospital) on the east side of the City of Poughkeepsie. In 1992, the sculpture was moved to the east side of the City of Poughkeepsie at the corner of North Clover Street and East College Street.

Star Trek: First Contact is a 1996 American science fiction action film directed by Jonathan Frakes, who also co-wrote the screenplay with Rick Berman, Brannon Braga, and Ronald D. Moore. It is the tenth film in the Star Trek film series and the second film in the Star Trek: The Next Generation film series, which is itself the second in the franchise. It was produced by Rick Berman, Howard L. Rosenman, and Robert W. Wertheimer. The film stars the cast of Star Trek: The Next Generation reprising their roles from the series, including Patrick Stewart, Jonathan Frakes, Brent Spiner, Michael Dorn, Gates McFadden, LeVar Burton, Marina Sirtis, and Whoopi Goldberg. Neal McDonough also reprises his role as Lt. Hawk in a brief cameo. The film also features James Cromwell, Alice Krige, and John de Lancie.
Star Trek: First Contact was released on November 22, 1996 in North America. It was well received by critics and audiences, and was the third highest-grossing film in the series. It was nominated for an Academy Award for Best Makeup.
In this film, the Borg, a cybernetic race that has assimilated other species into their Collective, have commandeered a large ship from the 21st century and have come to assimilate the 24th century. The Borg Queen, who has assimilated a humanoid from the 20th century, has established contact with a Borg cube and assimilated the crew of the Enterprise-E and the Earth. The crew of the Enterprise, with the assistance of the Borg Queen, attempt to stop the Borg from assimilating Earth.

Tintin is informed by Thomson and Thompson of a case involving the ramblings of a drunken man , later killed , found with a scr

ub brush and a broken glass in his hand. The two policemen have been assigned to investigate this case.  Tintin and his friends investigate on their own, and find a painting in the attic of the dead man, which they believe to be the work of a great artist.  They also discover the secret of the trunk.  The painting is stolen by the smugglers, but it is recovered by the police, although a piece has been cut out.
Tintin and Snowy go to the art dealer and the dealer asks them to come back the next day. The dealer is working with the smugglers to get the painting.  The dealer, however, is killed by the smugglers, and Tintin and Snowy find the dealer's body.  They go back to the art dealer's, but the smugglers have fled.  They are later arrested for the murder.  They are later released, as they have no proof of their innocence.  They find the smugglers' camp, and discover the mystery of the trunk.  The smugglers are arrested, and the painting is recovered.
The story was written in 1940, and was published in Belgium in 1941 and in France in 1942. It was the only book to be released during the occupation of Belgium by Nazi Germany.
The plot of the story is similar to that of the 1938 novel The Rasp by Georges Simenon, although Hergé's work was published a year later.  The story also has some similarities to the 1940 novel The Dark Forest by Georges Simenon.
The original French title, Le Manoir du Livre, is a play on words: 'manoir' is French for 'manor house', and in French the verb 'lire' means both 'to read' and 'to steal'.
The English title was translated by Frank P. Huxley.

" Don 't You Wanna Stay " is a duet recorded by American singers Jason Aldean and Kelly Clarkson from Aldean 's 2010 album , My

Kinda Party (2010). The song is written by Rhett Akins, Dallas Davidson, and Ben Hayslip and produced by Michael Knox. It was released on June 22, 2010, as the album's fourth single. The song has sold 3,123,000 copies in the United States as of July 2012.

He stated that he was nervous to work with Clarkson because he had never worked with a female artist before, but he also said that he thought they made a great pair.
Clarkson said that she was nervous to work with Aldean at first, because she didn't know what kind of reaction she would get from the country music audience. She said that she had never been to a Jason Aldean concert and that she wasn't sure what the fans would think of her. She said that she was surprised by the response she got from the fans and that she was happy that they seemed to like her version of the song.
The song is a duet between Aldean and Clarkson. It is written in the key of G major with a tempo of 100 beats per minute. It follows a chord progression of G–D–Em–C. It was written by Rhett Akins, Dallas Davidson, and Ben Hayslip, and produced by Michael Knox.

Tropical Storm Aka was the only tropical storm to form in the Central North Pacific during 1990 . An area of disturbed weather

725 miles (1,167 km) southwest of Manzanillo, Mexico, developed into a tropical depression on September 8. At 0000 UTC on September 9, the depression strengthened into Tropical Storm Aka. Early on the following day, the storm turned to the west-northwest. On September 11, the storm reached its peak intensity with maximum sustained winds of 60 mph (95 km/h) and a minimum barometric pressure of 997 mbar (29.4 inHg). Later that day, Aka began to weaken, and at 0000 UTC on September 12, the storm weakened into a tropical depression. During the early morning hours on September 14, the storm degenerated into a remnant low and later that day, the remnants of Aka were absorbed into a cold front.
Aka was the last tropical cyclone to affect Mexico until Hurricane Celia in 1999, and only the second to affect the country during the month of September. The storm brought 4 to 6 inches (100 to 150 mm) of rainfall to the southern portion of the state of Jalisco on September 10.

In September 1847 Busch began studying mechanical engineering at Hanover Polytechnic . Busch 's biographers are not in agreemen

on when he began his studies at the Polytechnic. Busch himself said that he began his studies there in October 1847, but some of his biographers believe that Busch began his studies in September 1847.
Busch began doing research at the Polytechnic in 1849. Busch 's biographers believe that his first research was done in the summer of 1849. The subject of his research was the cross-sectional strength of structural timber. It was in 1849 that Busch also joined the "Düsseldorfer Kaffee-Kreis" (Düsseldorf Coffee Circle), a group of German engineers and architects who met to discuss technical developments and the latest in science .
The result of Busch 's research was a paper titled "On the strength of timber in cross section" (Über die Biegeberechnung von Holz in der Querachse) which he presented to the "Engineers Advisory Board of the Prussian state" in Berlin on 8 July 1850. The paper, which described a method for calculating the strength of timber, was published in the "Centralblatt der Bauverwaltung des Königreichs Preußen" (Central Register of the Royal Prussian Building Authority) in 1850.
Busch graduated from the Polytechnic in 1852. His dissertation, "Elementary foundations of the theory of the cross-sectional strength of timber" (Grundlegendes zur Biegeberechnung von Holz in der Querachse), was published in 1852.  A more common method of avoiding the three seconds rule is known as "violating the rule " , in which the player does not dribble the ball while in possession of it.  More rarely, a player can "call for a time-out "  in which the player calls a time-out at any point during the game and is allowed to dribble the ball back up to the three second mark.   This is generally more difficult than trying to violate the rule as the player must be able to see the referee and be in a position to call for a time-out.

The selection of South Africa as host country was announced on 16 May 2004. South Africa became the first African nation to host the finals, and the third nation to host the World Cup on the African continent after the 1962 and 1998 tournaments in Chile and France respectively. South Africa was chosen by FIFA's executive committee at their meeting in Zurich on 15 May 2010. The finals involved 32 national teams, which competed for the title of World Champion. A total of 64 matches were played in 10 venues across 11 South African cities. The tournament also incorporated a brand new concept to the World Cup with the introduction of the Confederations Cup. The tournament was won by Spain, who beat the Netherlands 1–0 in the final after extra time. This was Spain's first World Cup title and third time in the final.

Even before Congress approved the Boulder Canyon Project , the Bureau of Reclamation was considering what kind of dam should be

built. The Army's engineer, Colonel George W. Snyder, had recommended a concrete arch dam (Figure 1.1), but Secretary of the Interior Ray Wilbur and the Bureau's commissioner, Floyd B. Olson, thought a concrete-and-masonry dam would be more economical. Olson was right, and the Bureau decided on a masonry dam.
The Bureau called for bids for a $10.3 million contract to build the dam in 1928, and awarded a contract for that amount to a Seattle-based contractor, Morrison-Knudsen. The dam was to be 267 feet high and 1,242 feet long, the largest such structure in the world. In addition, the Bureau wanted the dam to be as nearly self-supporting as possible, without using a government guarantee.
Rather than a traditional, rebar-reinforced masonry dam that would use a large amount of expensive steel, the Bureau asked Morrison-Knudsen to use a new system of facing and grouting that would use little steel. The result would be a dam that was economical to build but strong enough to withstand the force of the water behind it.
The Bureau's designer, John H. Hunt, had just come to the United States after studying in Italy, where he had seen reinforced-concrete arches being built. Beginning with the 1914 arch dam that is now the Hoover Dam, Hunt had been using arches with a steel core to build dams in the United States. The Bureau had decided it was too expensive to build a dam that way, and Hunt had worked with the Bureau's chief engineer, R. H. Wilson, to develop a method of using masonry to support the dam's weight.
In a paper prepared for the Bureau, Hunt described the new system as a "concrete arch dam without steel reinforcement." The Bureau's engineers decided that the arch dam would have to be much larger than the Bureau's previous arch dams, and they wanted it to be as strong as possible, so they found a way to increase the thickness of the arch. They also decided not to use a core of steel but to use a thin strip of steel to hold the masonry arch together. This was one of the first uses of the steel-wire-and-masonry system that allowed the Bureau to build a dam with almost no steel.
Morrison-Knudsen was responsible for building the dam. The Bureau paid for the dam by having the contractor sell bonds to investors. The contractor built the dam, then sold the bonds to the investors. Since the investors had already paid for the dam, they were paid back first when the dam began producing power. The Bureau was the last to be paid.
The dam was completed in 1936, and the Bureau turned it over to the federal Bureau of Power and Light, which operated it until 1986, when the dam and its power plant were transferred to the newly formed Southwestern Power Administration.

The photographs, illustrations, and maps in this book were taken by Bureau of Reclamation photographers, the Bureau of Reclamation's Office of History, and the Colorado River Commission. The drawings of the dam were prepared by the Bureau of Reclamation's drafting office and its predecessor, the United States Reclamation Service.

Despite being considered dissipated , a re @-@ analysis of satellite imagery indicated the circulation of Olaf persisted as tur

bulent convection continued to persist near the center of the circulation .  In addition , aircraft reconnaissance indicated Olaf was re-organizing itself as it moved closer to the coast of Mexico . 
Olaf's re-organization was also evidenced when it underwent an eyewall replacement cycle and attained additional wind shear through its eyewall and outer rainbands .  The system's cyclonic circulation organized once again , and it became a tropical storm on the morning of December 28 as a result of this process. 

### Tropical Storm Olaf

On December 28, the NHC upgraded Olaf to a tropical storm while it was located about 125 miles (200 km) south of Manzanillo , Mexico .  Olaf's core was characterized by a 50 mi (80 km) wide eye , and its maximum sustained winds were estimated at 50 mph (85 km/h) .  The cyclone's center of circulation was situated approximately 175 miles (280 km) south-southeast of Manzanillo , Mexico .  Olaf was forecast to move toward the west-northwest and dissipate by the next day as a result of its interaction with a trough of low pressure and a building high-pressure system .

As it moved away from the coast of Mexico, Olaf's circulation weakened and its winds lessened.  However, the cyclone maintained its hurricane-like characteristics, including a well-defined circulation and a visible eye.  Olaf's large eye was located 35 mi (56 km) northwest of the center of circulation as of 0600 UTC on December 29.  The cyclone's circulation was situated approximately 180 mi (290 km) south-southeast of Manzanillo, Mexico.  By 0000 UTC (1900 UTC) on December 30, Olaf was no longer classified as a tropical cyclone.  The system's remnants persisted west of Manzanillo for another day.

### Post-tropical cyclone Olaf remnants

On December 30, Olaf's remnants were absorbed by a frontal trough.  This trough, which was steered westward by a high pressure system, separated the remnant low-pressure system from the high pressure system.  This allowed the remnant cyclone to move westward and produce a significant amount of rainfall in the state of Jalisco , Mexico .  The remnant cyclone was located approximately 210 mi (340 km) southwest of Guadalajara , Mexico , and approximately 265 mi (425 km) south-southeast of Mazatlán , Mexico.  The remnant cyclone's circulation was characterized by a well-defined center of circulation and an eye.  The remnant cyclone was forecast to dissipate as it moved toward the west-northwest. 

## Impact

### Japan

Olaf caused $1.1 billion (1995 USD) in damage in Japan.

### Mexico

The remnants of Olaf caused approximately 200 mm (8 in) of rainfall in the Mexican state of Jalisco.  As a result of the rainfall, a large amount of flooding occurred in the state, which resulted in the death of 16 people.  In addition, approximately 600 people were left homeless and damage in the state totaled 295 million pesos ($10.4 million USD).

The city is the capital of Somalia. It's financial center is Merca by the Indian Ocean.
Mogadishu was founded by the Arabs in the 10th century, and was known as "Somalia's Islamic cultural centre". From 1277 to 1291, it was the seat of the Sultanate of Mogadishu, a Swahili sultanate, and was ruled by the Abu Bakr dynasty.
In the 17th century, Mogadishu was ruled by the Geledi Sultanate. In 1874, Mogadishu was made the capital of Italian Somalia.
Mogadishu was sucessfully recaptured by Somali forces under General Mohamed Farah Aidid in 1991, during the civil war in Somalia.
Mogadishu is home to the University of Mogadishu and the Somali National University.
The city has been at the center of the Somali civil war since the 1990s.
Mogadishu has a population of 914,000 (UN, 2005)
The Mosque of Hassan, built in 1926, and the Mogadishu Cathedral, built in 1927, are examples of the architecture of the 1920s.
The city has a very developed tourism infrastructure, including many hotels, guest houses, restaurants, travel agencies and shopping centers.
Mogadishu has the oldest known mosque in the city. It is named the mosque of Mogadishu.
The capital has a football team called Mogadishu City Club.

In 1853 the Royal Society 's project was concluded , and the observatory was set to be abandoned . After a lengthy debate , the

observatory was saved by the government , and the Observatory of the Cape of Good Hope was founded .
Before the end of 1853, the first four masts were erected and the instruments were installed.
The observatory remained in operation until 1971 , when the last instrument was removed to the nearby SAAO (South African Astronomical Observatory).
The observatory was built in the neo-Gothic style on 125 acres of land , which were bought by the government in 1857 . The design is based on the German observatories of Göttingen and Berlin . It consisted of a complex of buildings .
After the end of its astronomical work in 1971 , the building complex became the home of the Museum of the Royal Observatory, Cape of Good Hope . The observatory and the museum are still owned by the South African government.
The opening of the observatory was celebrated by the British governor of the Cape of Good Hope , Sir George Grey , and the astronomer royal , Sir John Herschel , with a small ceremony on 16 March 1829.

McCall represented Scotland at the European Championships in 1992 , when they again failed to go beyond the group stage after d

feating Wales in the opening fixture. 

McCall played for Scotland from U17 level. He made his debut against Wales in 1988, and played in the two clashes against England at the 1990 British Home Championship. He then became a regular for the national team, and was a part of the squad that reached the semi-finals of the 1992 European Championships on home soil.

He played the 1992–93 season on loan at Blackburn Rovers, and after returning to Scotland he became a regular first team player at Motherwell, playing over 200 times for the club. He skippered the team from 1994 to 1999, when he was replaced by Brian McLaughlin. 

In 1999, McCall signed for Everton, and became a favourite for the fans, and gained a reputation as one of the better defenders in the Premier League. After two seasons, he moved to Sunderland, with whom he won the Intertoto Cup and UEFA Cup in 2004. After a short spell at Birmingham City, he returned to Everton, where he played until 2008. He then joined Burnley, in a deal that saw the transfer of his former Everton team-mate Thomas Gravesen the other way.

He retired from football in 2010, after a short spell at Sheffield United.

rossover between the two game systems.   Suhrawardi's father was an obscure man named Shaikh 'Ali, who lived in the town of Bistam in northern Iran. His mother was the daughter of a Farshi man named Shaikh Jamal al-Din. Both of her parents were pious Muslims who had made the pilgrimage to Mecca. When she died, her body was taken to the shrine of the saint Shaikh Abu al-Abbas, where she was buried.
Suhrawardi's father was not a learned man, but he had a religious bent and was always fond of pious sayings. Once, when he was asked about the source of the sayings of the Sufis, he replied: "The words of the sages are like a mirror; the light of the sun is reflected in it, so that even if the sun should be obscured, the reflection will still be seen." He was also fond of proverbs, such as: "If you cannot find the truth, seek it in the truth."
Shaikh 'Ali was a coppersmith by trade. He had six sons: Suhrawardi, four years his senior; two others who died in their youth; and three younger brothers. Suhrawardi's mother, who lived in Samarqand, was the daughter of the philosopher and poet 'Abd al-Jabbar. She had married Shaikh 'Ali in Samarqand, where he subsequently died.
Shaikh 'Ali was very fond of his sons and always gave them good advice. He once said, "My sons, be pious and diligent in your studies, and never forget that the worries of this world and the next are the same."
His eldest son, Suhrawardi, grew up to be a pious and conscientious young man, who was proficient in Arabic and Persian. He was also well versed in the Qur'an, and could recite it in the style of the Zahiriyya.
  The Zahiriyya (or Zahiri) school of Qur'anic recitation, named for its founder, the eleventh-century _maddhab_ (school of jurisprudence) founder Abu al-'Ali al-Zahiri, is associated with highly ornate recitations of the Qur'an. In Banu 'Amir, Zahiriyya reciters are called _hassa,_ or "pierced."
The Zahiriyya style is characterized by the use of complicated _tajwid_ (rhythmic articulation) and melodious recitation of the Qur'an.
— M.J.
As a youth, Suhrawardi was very close to his mother, who was highly intelligent and had been well educated in Samarqand. She had also been a disciple of the philosopher and mystic Mulla Sadra, who was her father's teacher.
  Suhrawardi later said that his mother was so proficient in the sciences that the scholars of Samarqand were greatly impressed by her. She was well versed in medicine and logic, as well as in the _'ulama'_ 's works on the law. She had also studied astronomy and mathematics and was very knowledgeable in the Persian poetry of the time.
Samarqand, which lies in the foothills of the Hindu Kush, was a major center of learning in the twelfth century. It was here that the philosopher Mulla Sadra lived and taught. This was also the center where the philosopher Ibn Sina (known as Avicenna in the West) lived and taught.
Suhrawardi's mother was a devoted Muslim and at some point during his youth he was circumcised in her presence. It was she who first taught him the Fatiha (first chapter of the Qur'an) and some of the _adhan_ (call to prayer).

along the Nile Valley.

This article is about the bird. For the movie, see American Crake (film).

## Taxonomy

The American crake was formerly placed in the genus Zapornia with the rail-like coots, but is now placed in the monotypic genus Pellorneum.

## Description

The American crake is a small bird, measuring 14–16 cm (5.5–6.3 in) long. The male of the species has a grey-brown head, breast and back, and a white belly. The female is mottled brown above and below, and the young have a grey barred plumage with white flanks. The male's song is a loud, plaintive "kwek".

## Distribution and habitat

The American crake is found from Somalia in the east to South Africa in the west, and south to northeastern Namibia, Botswana, Zimbabwe, Zambia, Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

The American crake is a bird of marshes and other wetlands.

## Behaviour

### Diet

The diet of the American crake consists almost entirely of invertebrates, especially insects and their larvae.

### Breeding

The nest is a loose cup of grasses and other plant material, placed on the ground in a concealed spot. Clutch size is three to five eggs.

## Status

The American crake has a large range and is fast-breeding. It is therefore assessed by the International Union for Conservation of Nature as being of "least concern".

KLM , Norwegian Air Shuttle and Scandinavian Airlines applied for concession for a route from Oslo to Bodø via Narvik (Narvik Airport , Fram ) . They say that the route would be operated by the three airlines in rotation .

In 2006 , Norwegian Air Shuttle applied for concession for a route from Oslo to Bodø via Tromsø .

### 2010s

In 2011 , Norwegian Air Shuttle applied for concession for a route from Oslo to Bodø via Svolvær and Mosjøen .

In 2014 , Norwegian Air Shuttle applied for concession for a route from Oslo to Bodø via Steinkjer and Brønnøysund .

In 2016 , Norwegian Air Shuttle applied for concession for a route from Oslo to Bodø via Mosjøen .

The story takes place one year after the end of the previous series, and focuses on a new group of Transformers: the Autobots and the Decepticons. The series introduces a new human character, Jack Darby, who lives in Chicago and befriends the Autobots.
The series premiered on November 29, 2010 on The Hub. The first season of 26 episodes premiered on October 29, 2010 on The Hub. The second season of 26 episodes premiered on April 28, 2012 on The Hub, with the first five airing on HubWorld. The third season of 20 episodes premiered on October 18, 2012 on The Hub.

Transformers: Prime - The Game is a third-person shooter video game based on the TV series. The game is a cooperative experience featuring both single and multiplayer modes. Players can choose to play as either the Autobots or Decepticons. Both factions have the ability to transform into three alternate forms. Players are able to level up their characters and unlock new weapons and abilities. The game features four-player co-op local split-screen multiplayer, and a downloadable map pack featuring four new levels.

Torres ' parents are José Torres and Flori Sanz . He has two older siblings , Israel ( born 1977 ) and María Paz ( born 1976 )

## Career

Torres began playing football at the age of six, and joined Real Zaragoza in 1993. He made his first-team debut on 21 April 1996 in a 3–1 win over Sevilla at La Romareda, playing for the final 15 minutes as a substitute for Juan Crespo.

He moved to Real Madrid in the summer of 1997, but spent the 1997–98 season on loan at Real Valladolid. After returning to Madrid, he fell out of favour and was loaned out to Osasuna and Albacete.

In the 2001–02 season, Torres was loaned out to Elche CF. He was the top scorer in the Segunda División, netting 23 goals in 34 games. In the summer of 2002, he returned to Real Madrid, who had been relegated to Segunda for the first time in their history, becoming their top scorer with 16 goals in the season.

Torres remained at Real Madrid for the 2003–04 season, netting 24 goals in 34 games in Segunda Division. He spent the 2004–05 season on loan at CD Tenerife, scoring 11 goals in 31 games.

His final season as a professional was 2005–06, also on loan, this time at Real Murcia.

## International career

Torres made one appearance for Spain, coming on as a substitute in a 2–0 win over Russia at the 1998 FIFA World Cup.

After reaching Tanjong Priok on 10 February , the detachment found itself placed under Dutch command and formed into a composit

company of the Dutch 21e Regiment. The unit was equipped with rifles and ammunition and was placed under the command of Major J. P. van Alphen, the commander of the 1e Bataljon. The composition of the Dutch unit was as follows:
* 1st Bataljon, 21e Regiment: Major J. P. van Alphen
* 27 Bataljon Pantserauto's: Captain J. W. Kroon
* 322 Verkennings Compagnie: Captain J. G. G. van Tilburg
* 1e Bataljon, 22e Regiment: Captain J. G. H. L. Bosselaar

The Dutch command was put under the overall command of the British, with the South-east Asia Command in Singapore. When the Japanese invaded the Netherlands East Indies, the 1e Bataljon was placed in the 18e Division, under the command of Lieutenant-General Henry Gordon Bennett.

### Battle of Java

See also: Battle of Java

After the Dutch surrendered in early March, the unit was subjected to a relentless campaign of starvation, disease and torture by the Japanese. Some 2,000 members of the unit were sent to Kragan and the rest to Terezengjat. During this time, the Dutchmen were obliged to build fortifications and roads for the Japanese. They were finally liberated by the Australian 9th Division in August 1945.

The unit was re-formed in early 1946 as the 1st Battalion, Royal Netherlands East Indies Army (1e Bataljon, Koninklijk Nederlandsch-Indisch Leger) and was incorporated into the 1e Divisie.
The Catechism of the Catholic Church states that the death penalty is permissible in cases of extreme gravity . It is allowed i

us ad bellum , and does not amount to murder .
In 1692, Pope Innocent XI stated that in the cases of the most serious crimes, such as parricide, murder, rape, treason, heresy, and the like, there is no other recourse than death. His position was reiterated by Pope Pius XII in 1952, who proclaimed that the death penalty is in conformity with the doctrine of the Catholic Church.

fer ). This was the first computer program to demonstrate that a certain class of propositions ( " Logical Theorems ") could be deduced by a certain class of procedures ( " Logical Rules " ). The program used a very simple computer ( the IBM 650 ) to simulate a very simple machine ( Turing's " Universal Machine " ) to carry out a very simple task: to derive logical theorems.
 In 1956 , Newell and Simon created the " General Problem Solver " ( with help from J. C. Shafer and others ). This program used a Turing Machine to solve " General Problems " ( " problems in which the problem-solving procedures were specified in English " ).
In the 1950s and 1960s, Newell and Simon worked with the " Project MAC " group at MIT to construct a " Computer Science " capable of carrying out a wide variety of different tasks ( including " Artificial Intelligence " or " Human Intelligence " ).
 The " PEPS " project ( from the " Programme d'Etudes pour la Prospective Scientifique " ) was a project to build a computer capable of simulating the " Human Mind " . The " PEPS " project was led by Jacques Gauthier ( of the " Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique " ) and Jacques Perrin ( of the " Institut National de la Recherche Agronomique " ).
In 1963 , Gauthier and Perrin began a series of collaborations with Herbert A. Simon and Allen Newell.
In 1964 , Gauthier and Perrin asked Newell and Simon to design an " Intelligent System " capable of performing " Human Cognitive Tasks " on the " PEPS " computer.
Newell and Simon constructed the " Logical Theorist " and the " General Problem Solver " ( as Newell said, a " prototype " of the " Logical Theorist " and the " General Problem Solver " ).
In 1965 , Gauthier and Perrin asked Newell and Simon to design a computer capable of carrying out " Human Decision Making " ( including the ability to " Simulate Human Reasoning " ).
Newell and Simon constructed the " General Problem Solver " as a " prototype " of their " Intelligent System ". They modified the " Logical Theorist " to carry out " Human Decision Making ".
In the 1960s, the " Programme d'Etudes pour la Prospective Scientifique " was the first group to build a computer capable of carrying out a wide variety of different tasks.

St Mary 's is built of ashlar buff and red sandstone quarried locally at Alderley Edge , and the roof is of Kerridge stone slat

. The total cost of the building was £2, 000.
The architects were Henry Paley and Son of Manchester , and the builder was John Pritchard of Macclesfield . Work began in 1859 and the church was consecrated on 21 April 1861. It was built as the parish church for Cranage , Marton and Goostrey .
The main body of the church is 150 feet by 45 feet and 40 feet high to the eaves. The tower is 110 feet high. The church has a tiled roof and is a symmetrical design, consisting of a nave with aisles and a chancel with aisles and a chapel, with a western tower. The aisles are 40 feet wide and the roofs are covered with shingles. The main body of the church is built in three bays with an arcade between them. The aisles are wider than the nave, and the height of the church is diminished by the ashlar buttresses between the nave and aisles.
On the exterior of the church there are three groups of three lancet windows, two on each side of the tower and one above the west door. In the tower there are three lancet windows on each side. Inside the church there are pointed arched windows in the side walls of the chancel and the arches are filled with stained glass. The chancel arch and the arches leading from the aisles to the chancel are pointed and decorated. The arches leading from the aisles to the chapel are segmental pointed.
The altar and reredos are of oak and the pulpit is of marble. The altar and reredos are decorated with carved figures of the twelve apostles. The font is of stone, octagonal in shape and has a moulded edge. The pews are of oak, upholstered and cushioned.
The church is a Grade II listed building.
The churchyard also has listed buildings. In the churchyard is the war memorial, a stone cross with a bronze figure of St Michael. The cross has been listed as a Grade II building. The war memorial was unveiled on 8 May 1921 by Lieutenant Colonel P. A. A. Greenwood, DSO, MC.
On the south side of the churchyard is the stone gate piers and entrance gate to the churchyard. The piers are in brown sandstone and the gate is in wrought iron. The gate has been listed as a Grade II building.
Just outside the gate is a stone cross, known as the Way Cross. The cross is in sandstone and has been listed as a Grade II building.

lied air operations in Japan.

Between November 1945 and January 1946, RAAF Headquarters was heavily involved in the reorganisation of its Far East Air Force.
In addition, there was an increasing number of search and rescue operations to be carried out in the Pacific area, and a number of these missions were flown by RAAF aircraft operating from bases in the Philippines.
The end of the Pacific War also saw the disappearance of a number of the bases and operational units established during the war.
The 1st Fighter Wing, which had been formed in March 1945, was disbanded in early 1946.
The 109th Fighter Wing, which had arrived in Australia in October 1945, was disbanded in February 1946.
In addition, the 12th Air Defence Group, which had been formed in June 1945, was disbanded in January 1946.
With the end of the Pacific War, RAAF Headquarters' involvement in occupied Japan came to an end.

The surface composition of Ceres is broadly similar to that of C @-@ type asteroids . Some differences do exist . The ubiquitou

s and, in many cases, dominant "hydrated" mineralogy, indicates that Ceres was heated and altered to a significant degree during its evolution. Hydration is most commonly observed in the form of clay minerals, which indicate water alteration . Ceres is also enriched in phyllosilicates  and carbonates .
The surface of Ceres is also preserved from significant compositional evolution by its final state of being protected by an outer icy crust . The nature and extent of the outer crust of Ceres is an important question for Ceres geology, as the nature of Ceres' surface composition is not well constrained by high resolution images alone . The crust may preserve some information about the evolution of Ceres' interior, and may also be a record of Ceres' collisional history .
The lack of hazardous space weathering processes on Ceres is also likely due to Ceres' relatively low albedo, and may also help preserve Ceres' surface from other weathering processes . Ceres' moderate albedo may also explain why Ceres' surface composition is so similar to that of C-type asteroids .
This work is a study of the surface composition of Ceres as observed by the Dawn spacecraft. We study Ceres' albedo, surface morphology, and mineralogy using the high-resolution VIR (Visible and Infrared Spectrometer) and Framing Camera (FC) onboard Dawn. We use spectroscopy to constrain the mineralogy of Ceres at the spatial resolution of individual pixels, and use both spectroscopy and high-resolution topography to estimate Ceres' albedo.

Ceres was discovered on January 1st, 1801, by Giuseppe Piazzi .  It was at that time the first asteroid ever discovered, and was named after the Roman goddess of agriculture.  The discovery of Ceres and the subsequent discovery of the other asteroids in the same orbit (the "asteroid belt") led to the realization that the asteroid belt is a remnant of the solar nebula.  It was also the first body in the solar system to be observed remotely .
Ceres' orbit is highly eccentric, with an orbital semi-major axis of only 2.77 AU, and a perihelion of only 2.36 AU.  As a result, Ceres' orbit is highly inclined relative to the ecliptic, with an inclination of 17.2° .  The semimajor axis of Ceres' orbit is also much less than the average distance from the Sun to the Earth, and Ceres is thus a potential hazard to Earth.  Ceres has a diameter of 945 km, which places it among the largest objects in the asteroid belt .  Ceres' surface gravity is approximately 0.003 g, less than 1% of the surface gravity on Earth .
Ceres was discovered with a telescope of only 2.5 inch (64 mm) aperture .  This large difference in aperture size limits the resolution of the first observations of Ceres.  It was not until 1845 that Ceres was resolved into two distinct bodies .  These bodies were later referred to as 1 Ceres and 2 Ceres .
These early observations of Ceres led to the discovery of the asteroid belt.  This work was later followed up by the use of more powerful telescopes and the recognition of the distinction between asteroids and comets .  It was not until 1891 that the rotation period of Ceres was determined .
Ceres' orbit is relatively stable, and is unlikely to suffer major perturbations from gravitational interactions with other bodies.  As a result, Ceres is expected to remain in its current orbit for billions of years .

Joyce Kilmer 's reputation as a poet is staked largely on the widespread popularity of this one poem . " Trees " was liked imme

asurably more by the public than by most critics. Yet, as we shall see, it is a poem of many facets and complexities, and it bears closer examination than it usually gets from readers.
As a narrator, Joyce Kilmer is the _ego_ , the "I," the speaker in the poem. He is an unnamed man who tells us about his father's reaction to the poem. We learn that the poem was written by Kilmer when he was a boy. The father's "tone" is a bit diffident, almost embarrassed, for he does not want to seem impressed by the poem. The father is a _second_ narrator. He is not himself, but rather a passive representative of a class of people who are subdued by the poem.
The setting is a forest, but the time is not definitely given, as is the case with most of the other poems in _Trees._ There is no division into stanzas or into any other definite form, and the poem is written in the first person.
"Trees" is a poem for the ears, not for the eyes. Its musicality is obvious, but the poem has its own rhyme scheme, an intricate one in which the rhyme sounds are not always regular. "Trees," for instance, rhymes: "Many / Fell" and "ring" and "cling." Kilmer's music is the result of a combination of iambs and trochees, and the poem is written in anapestic tetrameter, a combination of iambic and trochaic feet. _Tetrameter_ is the name for lines of four feet.
Kilmer's skill with sound was not a matter of conscious study. He was not an expert in Greek and Latin, but he was a gifted student and he did have a strong ear for music and for rhythm, which is a talent of its own.
The poet's primary concern is to present a picture of a family, and he uses a variety of devices to do this. First, he begins by telling us about his family. He then describes the forest, and the poem concludes with a description of the man's family again.
"Trees" is a lyrical ballad with no consistent meter. The poem is written in one-line stanzas. Kilmer used many poetic devices in the poem, from alliteration to onomatopoeia, but he did not use a stanzaic or metrical structure.
In the first stanza, for example, the poet is telling us about his family. He uses a variety of devices, including alliteration, onomatopoeia, and the repetition of the _f_ 's.
In the second stanza, Kilmer begins with a simile, a comparison of the forest with a cathedral, a structure that has a roof and walls, and a floor. The use of the simile is a way of bringing the contrast between a natural scene and a man-made one, and it is consistent with the _lyrical_ nature of the poem.
The third stanza begins with a personification. The poet describes the trees as "enduring," a word that implies permanence. The personification is also an example of assonance, the repetition of the vowel sound _o._
The fourth stanza is another example of personification. Kilmer states that the forest is "a primeval world"—"primeval" means "from the earliest times." The trees are described as "kind" and "wise," traits that are not normally associated with inanimate objects.
The fifth stanza presents us with another personification. Kilmer describes the trees as "fellows." The poet uses this word for "men." It is another example of assonance.
In the sixth stanza, the poet is asking a rhetorical question. The answer to the question is "Yes," but the poet asks the question in the form of a statement in order to make a contrast between the natural and the man-made. The poet's statement is: "You are the companions of my joys." The word "joys" is a metonymy, a figure of speech that is a substitute for a larger concept. In this case, a replacement for the word "experiences."
In the seventh stanza, Kilmer again uses a rhetorical question. The answer to the question is "Yes," but the poet begins the stanza with the question in order to create a contrast between the natural and the man-made. The poet's question is "And you are the companions of my sorrows." The word "sorrows" is a metonymy.
