In South Africa , the common starling was introduced in 1897 by Cecil Rhodes . It spread slowly and by 1954 had reached Clanwil

gen in the Orange Free State province. In the 1960s, it began to spread to the north, soon reaching the northern parts of the Eastern Province by the end of the 1960s. It continued to spread north and was recorded in 1977 at Ladismith and Herold in the Western Cape. This was followed by scattered reports from as far north as Mossel Bay in the Western Cape and from the Eastern Cape's KwaZulu-Natal. By the 1980s, it was a common species throughout the Orange Free State, the Eastern Cape and the Northern Cape, where it is now most common. It was first seen in the Western Cape in 1994, when a pair was found near Clanwilgen. By the early 2000s it had spread to the Western Cape's southern and central parts and is now common there.
Common starlings were introduced into Australia in 1864 to control locusts and then in 1866 to control grasshoppers. They were found to be damaging to crops and fences, and a general pest. As a result, they were eradicated from Australia in 1905.
The common starling was introduced into the Cook Islands in the 1970s. It was found to be damaging to crops and the environment, and was eradicated in 1987.
 It is believed to be the species that started the Black Death .

SS El Sol was a cargo and passenger steamship launched on 11 May 1910 by the Newport News Shipbuilding and Dry Dock Co. of Newp

ork, Virginia, US. The ship was owned by the Reederei AG Norddeutscher Lloyd of Bremen, Germany. The vessel was 143 metres (469 ft) in length, had a beam of 18.1 metres (59 ft), a draft of 9.1 metres (30 ft), and a tonnage of 6,647 gross register tons (GRT). SS El Sol was powered by a triple expansion steam engine that drove a single screw propeller. She was capable of 12 knots (22 km/h) with a speed of 10 knots (19 km/h) at 200 rpm.

On 15 December 1911, the ship was chartered by the United States Government to take 1,000 troops to Veracruz, Mexico. On 16 April 1914, the ship was commandeered by the U.S. Navy for use as a troop transport during the Mexican Revolution. She was turned over to the US Navy on 15 May 1914. During the course of World War I, SS El Sol was a troop transport and was stationed on the US West Coast. On 30 December 1919, the ship was transferred to the Reconstruction Finance Corporation and was put on the market.

On 10 December 1920, SS El Sol was sold to the Chandris Line of Athens, Greece. The ship's registry was transferred to Athens, Greece. On 28 March 1925, the ship was renamed SS Chandris. During World War II, the Chandris Line operated the ship as a passenger and cargo liner and stationed her on the Mediterranean. On 11 September 1940, the ship was requisitioned by the Royal Navy. She was renamed HMS Calliope and was used as a hospital ship. The ship was released from service on 28 February 1946 and was returned to the Chandris Line.

On 29 September 1946, the ship was chartered by the Israeli government to transport 3,000 Jewish immigrants to Palestine. On 2 October 1946, the ship sailed from Haifa, Palestine with 480 passengers, including 22 Britons. The ship was struck by a gale while sailing in the Mediterranean Sea. At about 04:00 on 4 October 1946, the ship collided with an uncharted rock off the coast of Saverne, France, and sank. Of the 480 passengers, 22 were killed and 458 were rescued by the French destroyer Mogador and the British corvette HMS Hyacinth.

This article is about the file type. For the file structure, see Uniform Resource Locator § Technical implementation. For the WWW protocol, see Hypertext Transfer Protocol.
The Uniform Resource Locator (URL), colloquially termed a web address, is a reference to a web resource that specifies its location on a computer network and a mechanism for retrieving it. A URL is a specific type of Uniform Resource Identifier (URI), although many people use the two terms interchangeably. URLs occur most frequently to reference web pages (http) but are also used for file transfer (ftp), email (mailto), database access (JDBC), and many other applications. The most common URL syntax is the one used for hypertext system documents (HTTP), such as those on the World Wide Web (WWW).[1]
The protocol identifiers are case-insensitive.
The scheme is a sequence of characters beginning with a double slash (//), and may be followed by a single slash (/) or by another scheme. The two slashes together are the literal string "//", and do not count as part of the scheme.
The authority component may be "//" (empty authority) if the URL is a relative URL or if the URL is a scheme-specific URL.
The user information is optional and is a sequence of characters beginning with a single double slash (//), which is the literal string "//".
The hostname may be followed by a colon and a port number (as specified by the port number protocol identifier).
The path component consists of the remaining components, separated by a forward slash (/).
The file extension may be present, and indicates the content type of the resource if the resource is a file (e.g., a web page). A special form of URL is the "empty" URL, which consists of only a scheme but no authority, path, or query components. The empty URL is often used to specify a default resource, such as the "index.html" page of a web site.
The URL syntax is designed to allow the specification of hierarchical trees of resources. The authority component of a URL is a URI, which is further broken down as follows:
Scheme and registry
The first component of the URL is the scheme, which specifies a standard or de facto standard application-specific protocol. The scheme is a case-insensitive string, typically a DNS name, but may also be a registered number. For example, the URL http://example.com is a hypertext transfer protocol (HTTP) URL that references the server example.com at the IP address 127.0.0.1, and the file /index.html in the directory/folder index.html. The scheme is followed by a colon (:), which is optional. The remaining authority components consist of a user information component, a hostname, and a port number. The user information component may be present, and consists of a username and password, separated by a @ ("at" symbol) character. A user information component is only used for some protocols, most notably the FTP and HTTP URL schemes. The username and password are URI-encoded. Each user information component is followed by a colon (:), and may be followed by one or more authority component names, separated by a comma (,). The hostname is a sequence of characters, typically a domain name, but may also be an IP address. The hostname is followed by a colon (:), and then the port number, which is a number between 0 and 65535, inclusive.
The path component, which is the last component of the URL, includes the remaining components. The path component begins with either two forward slashes (//) or a single forward slash (/). A single forward slash (/) is the literal string "/", and is commonly used to reference the root of the tree. Two forward slashes (//) are the literal string "//", and do not count as part of the path. The path component may end with a forward slash (/). The path component may also include a query component, which is a sequence of characters following a question mark (?). The query component is a URI-encoded sequence of characters. The query component may include arguments, which are a sequence of characters following an ampersand (&) character. An argument is an encoded sequence of characters, and may include query component subcomponents, such as the filename, which is a sequence of characters following a pound sign (#) character.
The syntax of a relative URL is similar to that of a normal absolute URL, with the addition that the scheme component is omitted. The authority component is also optional.

In the summer of 1945 several hundred veterans of the battle were detached from operations in Norway and returned to Arnhem to

help the survivors of the battle. The veterans were drawn from the 1st, 2nd and 3rd Battalions, the Royal Regiment of Fusiliers, and the 2nd Battalion, the Oxfordshire and Buckinghamshire Light Infantry. After a brief period of rest they began a clean-up operation. By September the ruins of Arnhem had been cleared and the battlefield made safe for the growing numbers of Dutch civilians returning to their homes.
 The battlefield is now administered by the Netherlands War Graves Service, and a plaque on the memorial in the town reads: ' _In memory of the gallant soldiers of the British Empire who gave their lives during the battle for Arnhem. September 1944_.'
 I should like to record my thanks to Major R. M. C. Hall, late of the Fusiliers, for his help in the preparation of this chapter, to Mr. J. E. Freeman, of the Fusiliers Museum, and to Mr. H. C. Hooper, for permission to refer to their work.
CHAPTER ONE
#  _The Prelude_
THE SECRET of the battle of Arnhem, of which so little is known, lies in the fact that it was fought in the background of a very large and complicated operation. The plan was to seize the crossings of the Rhine and, by their use, to establish a lodgement from which the large-scale capture of Germany might be undertaken. It is, therefore, necessary to look at the whole plan and to see how the battle of Arnhem fitted into the scheme of operations.
The German Army in _West_ _Germany_
The German Army in _West Germany_ was a tough opponent. It had been trained to a high standard of efficiency, and its self-discipline was outstanding. In the autumn of 1944 this was particularly important, for the German Army was a tired one and had suffered a series of defeats. It had lost over 200,000 men in the battle of Normandy, and its morale had been further shaken by the valour and skill of the Allied air forces. The decision to invade was, therefore, taken with the full knowledge that the German Army was weak and in a state of flux.
The German Army was, however, still formidable. It possessed a large number of well-trained and well-equipped divisions; it had the bulk of its best armour and air force; and it was on a well-defended front which stretched from the Dutch border to the Swiss border. The Allies had to cross this front before they could hope to reach the Rhine.
The German Army was divided into several groups and armies. The _North_ _German_ _Army_ was the largest and most powerful group. Its three armies were the _1st_ _Panzer_ _Army_ (later the _Northern_ _Army_ ), the _12th_ _Army_ and the _21st_ _Army_. They were responsible for the defence of _North_ _Germany_ from the Baltic coast to the North Sea, a front of about 260 miles. The _Northern_ _Army_ , to the north and north-east of Hamburg, contained the bulk of the German armour in the _West_. The _12th_ _Army_ , to the south and south-east of Hamburg, was responsible for _South_ _Germany_ and held the _West_ _German_ _capital_ , _Frankfurt-_ _am_ _Main_. The _21st_ _Army_ , to the south of _Frankfurt-_ _am_ _Main_ , held _South_ _Germany_ from which it could thrust into the _South_ _of_ _France_ and _Italy_.
The Allies had to get through this formidable group of armies before they could reach the Rhine. In order to achieve this they planned to use three _Priorities_. The _Ruhr_ _Priority_ was to seize the _German_ _coal_ _mining_ _areas_ _of_ _the_ _Ruhr_ _Valley_. The _Rhine_ _Priority_ was to get across the Rhine and establish a lodgement. ## Meteorological history

On August 15, the National Hurricane Center (NHC) began to monitor a tropical wave that had moved off the coast of Africa. The wave slowly moved across the Atlantic Ocean, and on September 21 a tropical disturbance formed to the north of the Leeward Islands. On September 24, the disturbance developed enough to be classified as Tropical Depression Fifteen, and later that day it made landfall on Puerto Rico. The depression quickly moved over the mountains, and the next day the depression degenerated into a tropical wave. On September 27, the wave moved into the Caribbean Sea, and on September 29 the wave intensified into a tropical depression. During this time, the depression remained stationary for several days, and on October 3 the depression made landfall in Central America. The depression quickly moved inland, and the next day it degenerated into a tropical wave. The tropical wave moved across Nicaragua, and later that day the storm crossed into the Pacific Ocean.

## Preparations

Upon learning that the storm was expected to strike Puerto Rico, Governor Rafael Hernández Colón declared a state of emergency for the island. The governor also ordered the closing of schools, and urged residents to prepare for the storm. The storm also resulted in the evacuation of over 1,000 people from their homes. After the storm, President Ronald Reagan declared a state of emergency in Puerto Rico.

## Impact

Upon crossing Puerto Rico, the storm produced 3.07 inches (78 mm) of rainfall in San Juan, and 6.65 inches (170 mm) in Lares. In San Juan, the storm produced winds of 70 mph (110 km/h), gusting up to 85 mph (137 km/h). The storm also destroyed 1,000 houses and damaged another 10,000. It also destroyed 100 bridges, and flooded 25 percent of the island. Due to the storm, 11 people were killed, and 17 others were missing. The storm also resulted in $200 million in damage (1986 USD).

Frode Alfsen was born on 14 March 1898 in Hedmarken, Norway. He was the son of a laborer. Alfsen went to school in Dokka and then to the teacher education college in Hamar. Alfsen was active in the Norwegian Labor Movement from an early age. He was also active in the Social Democratic Youth League, where he was secretary.
In 1919, Alfsen was elected to the central committee of the Left Social Democrats. In the same year he was arrested and sentenced to two months in prison for having broken the law against public assemblies. He was also accused of having been active in the so-called counter-revolutionary organization. Alfsen was released in 1920, in the same year that the Left Social Democrats split from the mainstream Social Democrats. In the following years Alfsen was active in the Communist Party, and in 1923 he was elected as the party's first leader.
During the Spanish Civil War, Alfsen worked for the International Brigades. In 1937, he was arrested by the Nazis and sentenced to death. He was one of 1700 Norwegian communists that were imprisoned in Germany during the war. After the war, Alfsen worked as a journalist and writer. He wrote several books and a great number of articles for Arbeideren and Ny Tid. Alfsen was also a member of the Norwegian Writers' Union.

Edward Hasted , the local historian of Kent , has dismissed the story of the Biddenden Maids as a folk myth , claiming that the

maids' physique and wages would have made it unlikely that they were the offspring of the local gentry. There is no evidence for this, and it seems that Hasted was unaware that the family had been substantial landowners in the area for generations.
Many later writers have dismissed the story as a hoax. Yet it has persisted in the popular imagination. In 1976 a television programme, 'The Biddenden Maids', was aired. In 1999 the actor Simon Callow visited the village and gave a talk at the local pub. A monument to the maids was erected in the village square in 2006.
That is how the myth began. But how did it grow to become the best-known story in the world?
The first clue lies in the village itself. Biddenden is an attractive spot, where the Rother valley opens out onto the Weald. A swathe of green countryside stretches out as far as the eye can see. The village is very close to Ashford, and it was during the 1930s that the legend began to take hold, and take root.
In 1935, Cyril Rydal-White, an author from London, came to the village and fell in love with the place. He had been commissioned by _Punch_ magazine to write a tale of 'The Twins of Biddenden', and he chose to set his tale in the village. He wrote that
> The tiny church of St Mary the Virgin – 'the church of the two maids' – is one of the most remarkable in England. With its curious, crumbling tower, its tiny, miniature windows, its quaintly archaic porch and its tiny, twin Norman doorway, it is unique in the realm.
The issue of _Punch_ in which his story appeared (June 28, 1935) is a remarkable document. The cover shows a cartoon of the maids, one with a syringe in her mouth and one with her eyes closed. The cartoon is captioned 'The Legend of the Twin Sisters'.
The story itself is a straightforward tale of two girls who were born conjoined and who went on to lead separate lives. Rydal-White was using the 'true' story to create a fairy tale. He describes the maids as 'queer little twins', and the story is a 'legend'.
It was a nice, gentle, harmless tale. But it was the beginning of the legend.
The first person to publish a book about the maids was George W. Henty, one of the most popular authors of the Victorian era. He wrote historical adventure stories for boys, and his 1881 book, _Under Drake's Flag_ , describes a visit to Biddenden. He tells the story of the maids as he had heard it from a local priest, and he writes, 'As I have been told, the legend is as untrue as that of St George and the Dragon.'
But Henty did more than merely write a casual mention of the maids. He was a prolific writer, and his stories were published in the United States as well as in the United Kingdom. His books were often the first exposure to history many young people had. He wrote one hundred and thirty-seven books, which were translated into twenty-four languages and sold more than ten million copies.
Henty's interest in the maids was not a passing fancy. He returned to the story in his 1884 book, _The Dragon and the Raven_. In this book, also set in the reign of Henry VIII, the story of the maids is related to the story of the reign of Henry VIII. As such, it is one of the earliest examples of the maids being used as a metaphor for the Tudor dynasty.
It is odd that the maids were not more popular. It is true that Henry VIII had two sisters, Mary and Margaret, but they both died in infancy. There was no other royal family with conjoined twins. Later writers used the story as a metaphor for the Tudor dynasty. This was quite natural, as Henry and his sisters were all born in the same year. It seems that Henty was simply the first writer to use the story as a historical metaphor.

During the Royal Navy 's Second Battle of Heligoland Bight on 17 December 1914, Derfflinger was fourth in line astern of the battlecruisers Invincible , Indefatigable , Queen Mary and Lion .
At about 16: 10, the battlecruisers of the Second Battle Squadron opened fire on the German battlecruisers Von der Tann and Moltke at a range of 16,000 yd (14,600 m) but both missed. At 16: 11, the Germans opened fire on the British battlecruisers at a range of 15,700 yd (14,300 m). Derfflinger was turned away from the line of fire of the British battlecruisers by the use of smoke.
At 16: 12, when the battlecruisers were 14,500 yd (13,200 m) apart, the Germans and British began to exchange 11-inch shells. Derfflinger shelled the British battlecruisers for about a minute before the German vessels broke off the action.
At 16: 13, the British battlecruisers turned to the right and opened fire on the German battlecruisers. Derfflinger turned to starboard at 16: 14, and was hit by a 13.5-inch (340 mm) shell from Lion at 16: 15. The shell exploded aft of the forward funnel, demolishing the aft gunhouse and the aftermost funnel. The shell also hit the ship's steering gear and the torpedo control station. The steering gear was knocked out, and the ship was unable to turn. The torpedo control station was destroyed, but the torpedoes and depth-charge throwers were not damaged.
Derfflinger was hit a second time by a 13.5-inch shell from Lion at 16: 16. The shell exploded in the forward engine room, causing severe flooding.
At 16: 17, a 13.5-inch shell from the battlecruiser Black Prince struck Derfflinger, causing minor damage.
Derfflinger was hit for the fourth time at 16: 18 by a 13.5-inch shell from the battlecruiser Invincible. The shell exploded in the forward boiler room, killing the ship's executive officer. The boiler room was flooded, and the ship's speed was reduced to 14 knots (26 km/h; 16 mph).
Derfflinger was hit for the fifth time at 16: 18 by a 13.5-inch shell from the battlecruiser Lion. The shell exploded in the forward boiler room, destroying one boiler and killing eight of the ship's nine engineers. The damage to the boiler room was minor enough that the ship was able to complete the battle.
At 16: 19, a 13.5-inch shell from the battlecruiser Lion struck the ship's stern, killing eleven men and wounding several others.
Derfflinger was hit for the sixth time at 16: 20 by a 13.5-inch shell from the battlecruiser Queen Mary. The shell exploded in the ship's forward superstructure, killing 19 men and wounding 48.
Derfflinger was hit for the seventh and last time at 16: 20 by a 13.5-inch shell from the battlecruiser Lion. The shell exploded in the forward superstructure, killing 12 men and wounding 10.
At 16: 21, after having received 22 13.5-inch shell hits, Derfflinger was ordered to retire from the battle. The ship was towed to the Jade estuary, where it was repaired.

Following the German capitulation in November 1918 , Derfflinger was interned with a significant portion of the High Seas Fleet

at Scapa Flow . The internment of the fleet was opposed by the British Admiralty , and the German government requested that the fleet be returned to Germany. Once it was clear that Germany had lost the war, the German government ordered its fleet to scuttle itself. The ships were scuttled on 21 June 1919.  The German government had no intention of using the fleet in any future conflict, and had declared it a war grave. It was not until 30 November 1928 that the British Government returned the German battlecruisers to Germany.

1. The X-Files – The X-Files is an American science fiction horror drama television series created by Chris Carter. The program originally aired from September 10,1993 to May 19,2002 on Fox, the series revolves around FBI special agents Fox Mulder and Dana Scully who investigate X-Files, marginalized, unsolved cases involving paranormal phenomena. Mulder believes in the existence of aliens and the paranormal while the skeptical Scully is assigned to make scientific analyses of Mulders discoveries that debunk Mulder. The series starts with Fox Mulder as a tenant in a house, believing his sister Samantha. After his sisters disappearance, he began an investigation into her abduction. The series gradually reveals it is actually an alien invasion of Earth by a race of shape-shifting reptilian humanoids known as the Syndicate, with Mulder and Scully as some of the few who know the truth. The series is a blend of stand-alone stories and ongoing plots, many of the plot elements were open-ended, allowing for further expansion of the story arc in The Lone Gunmen spinoff, and the eventual 2008 film. The X-Files became the show of the 1990s. Series creator and producer Chris Carter, who wrote or co-wrote 16 of the 192 episodes, Carter originally wanted the series to be about the FBI, the conspiracy behind it, and the government cover-up. He wanted the lead character to be a man who would be in his 40s. It was not until Carter met David Duchovny, who was 28, that the character of Fox Mulder was born. Duchovny was almost not cast as he was unable to attend several auditions, the show reached more viewers after the airing of the third-season episode, Shadows. By the time the episode aired, viewers had already grown accustomed to the opening sequence, since that time, the opening has become an iconic part of the series. Compounds of the amphetamine and methamphetamine class , such as MDMA , DOC , and 2,4,5-TMP , also produce psychedelic effects , particularly at higher doses. Kashi Vishwanath Temple is a Hindu temple dedicated to Lord Shiva. It is considered the most sacred pilgrimage place of Hindus, and is referred to in the ancient Hindu scriptures as Kashi. It is also referred to as Shiv ki kashi or "the place where Shiva lives". The temple is believed to be the most sacred among the twelve Jyotirlingas. According to the Hindu epic Ramayana, when King Dashratha of Ayodhya was searching for a guru to teach his sons, Lord Rama and Lord Lakshman, the sons of King Dasharatha, Lord Rama received his training from the sage Vishwamitra. Lord Rama promised Vishwamitra that he would visit the sacred city of Kashi to worship Lord Shiva. Lord Rama visited Kashi and worshipped Lord Shiva. After Lord Rama's visit, the temple was known as Kashi Vishwanath Temple.

The toponymy of Oldham seems to imply " old village or place " from Eald ( Saxon ) signifying oldness or antiquity , and Ham (

12th century ), which is a modern dialect form of " home ". Oldham is first recorded in 1086 as Oldham in the Domesday Book. The earliest settlement was probably at " Oldham Edge" in Chadderton , where a Romano-British fort was sited. The fort was at 260m ( 850ft ) above sea level , near the confluence of the Irk and Medlock rivers .
The fort was strategically important at the intersection of five Roman roads, and the town grew up around it. It is unclear when "Oldham" became a separate town from "Chadderton", as they were always considered by the Saxons as one town.
Oldham's first reference in history was in the Domesday Book of 1086 as "Oldeham"  and the town's coat of arms was granted by the College of Arms in 1930. Oldham is one of the few towns in the United Kingdom that has a coat of arms.
The Domesday Book records that the ancient parish of Oldham covered the town and eight townships , three of which were absorbed into Oldham between 1894 and 1932 . These townships were Chadderton , Royton and Tonge with Haulgh , and a fourth, Kirklees, was added in 1894.
In 1848 Oldham became the county town of the newly formed county of Lancashire .
The town expanded rapidly in the 19th century , particularly after the coming of the railways , and in 1893 Oldham was granted a charter of incorporation and became a municipal borough.
A number of the town's civic buildings were designed by the Lancashire architect Alfred Waterhouse.
Oldham was also a county borough from 1894 to 1974 and then a metropolitan borough in Greater Manchester.
Oldham has a rich and diverse sporting history.
Oldham Roughyeds , formed in 1873 , are based at Bower Fold in the town centre .
Rochdale began as another Oldham club and also played at Bower Fold.
The Oldham club was also the first club to play rugby league in England in 1895 and, like Rochdale, continued to play at Bower Fold until 1999 when the ground closed.

Mirroring the role that track and field events have at the Summer Olympics and Paralympics , the sport is featured within the a

ims of the Commonwealth Games Federation (CGF), which describes it as the "central focus of the Commonwealth Games". The Commonwealth Games Federation is responsible for organising the games, and the International Paralympic Committee (IPC) manages the Paralympic events. Although the IPC has responsibility for overseeing the Paralympic events, it has no authority over the games themselves.
The Commonwealth Games were first held in 1930, then known as the British Empire Games, under the management of the British Empire Games Federation. The first official Commonwealth Games were held at the 1934 British Empire Games in London, England. The 1930 and 1934 games were essentially a multi-event British Empire Games, with teams from four countries.
Since the 1950 British Empire and Commonwealth Games the Games have been known as the British Empire and Commonwealth Games (1950–1966), British Commonwealth Games (1966–1974), British Commonwealth Games Federation Games (1974–1982), and British Commonwealth Games Council Games (1982–1999). In 1978, the Games were renamed the Commonwealth Games.
The first women's events were held at the 1990 Commonwealth Games in Auckland, New Zealand. The first Paralympic events were held at the 1994 Commonwealth Games in New Zealand.
 The Games are held every four years, and the program is a mixture of individual and team-based sports. The sport of lawn bowls is the only sport that has been contested at every Commonwealth Games.

## History

### First three Commonwealth Games (1930–1938)

The 1934 British Empire Games were held at the Empress Stadium in the London Borough of Wembley.

The first three editions of the Games were held under the auspices of the British Empire Games Federation, which was established in 1930 with the purpose of organizing the first Games. The first Games, known as the 1930 British Empire Games, were held in Hamilton, Ontario, Canada. The 1934 British Empire Games was held at the Empress Stadium in Wembley, England and the first women's events were held at the 1938 British Empire Games held in Sydney, Australia.

### Commonwealth Games Federation (1938–present)

The 1938 Commonwealth Games in Sydney, Australia

The Commonwealth Games Federation (CGF) was established in 1937 to oversee the future development of the Games. The CGF was established as the British Empire Games Federation, with Sir John Marks as its first president.

The CGF was established at the Commonwealth Games Federation's first annual general meeting, held on 16 July 1937, in London, England. The year of 1964 marked a decisive turning point in the Vietnam War . Following the ousting of President Ngô Đình Diệm in 1963

and the assassination of his brother Ngô Đình Nhu, the United States initiated a campaign of direct military intervention in South Vietnam from December 1963 onwards.  However, the conflict in Vietnam was neither purely a military one nor a civil war.  Instead, it was a conflict between two different political systems, the Soviet-backed "communist" system and the US-backed "democratic" system.  It was also a conflict between two different notions of nationhood, "indigenous" and "Americanized".  This book examines the impact of the cultural Cold War on the United States' intervention in the Vietnam War.  It focuses on how the United States' own internal Cold War struggles contributed to the escalation of the conflict in Vietnam.  It examines the role of cultural production in the United States in the policy-making process on Vietnam, and the role of cultural production in the United States in shaping American public opinion on the war.  It argues that the cultural Cold War in the United States in the 1950s and early 1960s fueled efforts to "Americanize" Vietnamese culture and to "democratize" Vietnamese society, and that these efforts contributed to the escalation of the conflict in Vietnam.  It also argues that American cultural production in the early 1960s contributed to the "Americanization" of Vietnamese politics and to the escalation of the conflict in Vietnam.  However, the United States' own internal Cold War struggles ultimately led it to direct military intervention in Vietnam.  The United States' involvement in the Vietnam War thus represents a turning point in the cultural Cold War in the United States, as it illustrates the limits of cultural production in the United States in shaping policy on Vietnam.  The book is divided into four parts.  The first part examines the cultural Cold War in the United States in the 1950s.  The second part examines the impact of the cultural Cold War on the United States' policy-making process on Vietnam during the early 1960s.  The third part examines the impact of the cultural Cold War on American public opinion on the war.  The fourth part examines the role of American cultural production in the early 1960s in the United States in the "Americanization" of Vietnamese culture.  The book concludes with an examination of how American cultural production in the late 1960s contributed to the escalation of the conflict in Vietnam.  The book is based on a wide range of primary sources, including government documents, foreign policy papers, interviews and oral histories, policy memoranda, and transcripts of congressional hearings, as well as publications by government officials, the media, and private citizens.  The book also draws on a wide range of secondary sources, including books and articles on the Vietnam War, cultural studies, and the cultural Cold War.

The first shock of the firing had been the realisation that the Germans were right there and shooting at the Australians. 'I was so close that I could feel the bullets bounce off me,' Smith said.
The Germans were now in the process of surrendering, although the Australians had no means of identifying who was surrendering and who was not. Nor did they know what to do with the men.

The play is a fictionalised account of the life of the English politician Robert Walpole, who was made the hero of the play by the 17th-century playwright William Congreve.

## Synopsis

The play follows the career of Robert Walpole, from his early days in London to his retirement from political life.

### Act I

Walpole is introduced to the audience as a poor lawyer's clerk, living on the first floor of a house not far from the Royal Exchange. He is in love with the beautiful, puritanious, virtuous, but poor, Miss Prue, but she does not return his love. The building shakes and a voice announces, "All is ready", and the angel of death comes to claim Walpole's soul, only to be repelled by the purity of his heart. Walpole is then granted a vision of the future, and is brought forward in time to be briefly introduced to many figures of note.

### Act II

Walpole returns to the present day, and is now a lawyer of some renown. He is introduced to Prue by her father, but Prue is now engaged to the dashing Viscount Davenant. Walpole is distressed by this, and the two men engage in a duel, with Walpole being wounded in the arm and Davenant being shot through the eye. Walpole is now regarded as a hero, and the two men are reconciled.

### Act III

Walpole is now a wealthy man. He is introduced to the Marquess of Buckingham, who is in love with Prue. Realising that he cannot have Walpole's hand in marriage, Buckingham beats Walpole to the ground, and is then himself beaten to death by Walpole. Walpole proposes to Prue, who accepts, and they are married.

### Act IV

Walpole and Prue are at their country house, where they have a visitor, the Marquess of Cumberland. Cumberland is in love with Prue and proposes to her, but Walpole is able to repel the advances of his rival. Walpole is now a powerful politician, and is able to persuade the Princess of Holland to leave the court of King James II in favour of George I. Walpole is now a member of the Privy Council and a friend of the King. Prue is now with child, but the baby dies, and Walpole is distraught. In the last scene, Walpole and Prue are visiting the Earl of Oxford, and Walpole is now the most powerful politician in England.

## Reception

The play was heavily criticised by contemporary reviewers, who wrote that the play was too long and drawn out, and that the play was not a good representation of any aspect of Walpole's life.

A large force of Persian cavalry was apparently defeated by Odaenathus in a pitched battle at the Battle of Resaena: this is the only known battle in the history of the Roman army in which the Persians are known to have been defeated. 

## Life

Odaenathus was the son of the Syrian governor Samaithis (Samus) and the grandson of Sisines, both of whom were the governors of Arabia. Odaenathus was a great-grandson of the Arabian king Malchus, the brother of the Jewish king Herod the Great.

Odaenathus was the 15th ruler of the Palmyrene Empire, which emerged as a centre of political power in the Syrian Desert during the 2nd century, with its capital at Palmyra. He succeeded his father as king of Palmyra and the neighboring provinces, and served as a provincial governor in the Roman province of Syria. During his reign, Palmyra became the most powerful state in the Eastern Mediterranean for a time. Odaenathus is likely to have been a member of a Christian family, based on the evidence that his wife, Zenobia, was also a Christian.

### War with Persia

The "Persian War" mosaic at Masada depicting the Roman victory at the Battle of Resaena against the Persians.

The Persian Empire under Sapor II, who had appointed Odaenathus, was threatening the Roman Empire in the East. In 260 AD, Shapur II sent an army to Syria to establish the Persian authority over the Roman province. Odaenathus led an army against the Persians and defeated them in a battle near Resaena. The battle is referred to as a conflict between the Persian and the Roman armies.

Odaenathus made peace with the Persian king by giving him the fortress of Callinicum, and the Roman garrisons of Damascus and Apamea, as well as the Palestinian town of Jerusalem as a wedding gift to his daughter Zenobia, who was married off to the Persian king. Shapur II, however, did not keep this agreement. Odaenathus responded by attacking the Persian Empire in 262 AD. He also captured the city of Bostra. Odaenathus then went to Antioch and made a treaty with the Emperor Gallienus.

The conflict between the Palmyrene Empire and the Persian Empire ended in 263 AD. Odaenathus took the Persian garrison of Jerusalem, and the Roman garrison of Apamea, near Damascus. In 263, he made an alliance with the Emperor Gallienus, and agreed to accept Gallienus' son, Valerian, as his son-in-law.

In 262, Odaenathus was assassinated by agents of Queen Zenobia, who succeeded him as ruler of Palmyra.

### Marriage and children

Odaenathus married Zenobia, who was the daughter of a prominent Arabian nobleman. They had three children: Vaballathus, the legitimate heir, and twins, named Zabdas and Maternianus. The children were all adopted by Odaenathus in succession, as heir apparent. Odaenathus then took the name Zabdas.

Anekāntavāda was often used by Jain monks to obtain royal patronage from Hindu Kings . Ācārya Hemacandra used anekāntavāda to g

ains support from the Chalukya King Someshvara III of Kalyani. The Jain monk Amoghavarsha was given the title of khalikara, or "one who wears the cloak of crown," by the Chalukya King of Karnataka.

The anekāntavāda is the essence of Jainism. The basic tenet of Jainism is the Anekantavada or the "doctrine of not accepting a doctrine as the only truth". Jainism teaches that the only reality is the soul, and that it should be understood in all of its aspects. To be successful in life, one must be able to view the world from all aspects and not be obsessed with any particular point of view. For Jains, the soul is the basis of all existence and not the worldly things which are transient. Jainism is a religion which believes in the existence of God, but it is a religion which believes that God does not do anything. Jainism is a religion which believes that the soul of every being is eternal.

## History

### Sources

The concept of anekāntavāda has been a subject of much debate among scholars. The debate has centred around the sources of the doctrine. According to some scholars, the doctrine is of Jaina origin, while according to others, it is a Hindu doctrine.

### Ancient sources

The earliest surviving references to anekāntavāda are in a Jain text, the Tattvartha-sūtra, and in the epic Mahabharata. The Jain text, written by the 2nd-century Jain teacher and philosopher, Umasvati, mentions the term anekāntavāda. The Mahabharata talks about the doctrine of anekāntavāda in the context of a debate between the Pandava prince, Arjuna, and the Jain monk, Nirvana, in the Virat-Parva.

According to Jain scholar Hermann Jacobi, the concept of anekāntavāda was known to the Buddha. He cites the following passage from the Mahavagga: "The Blessed One, the Lord, the Teacher, the Holy One, the Buddha, after having progressed for seven days, on the eighth day, early in the morning, before the sun rose, set out for the town of Savatthi. Here he sat down in the East in the Jeta grove. Here the Blessed One, the Lord, the Teacher, the Holy One, the Buddha, spoke thus to the Venerable Sariputta: 'Sariputta, this Dhamma is for one with only one view, not for one with two views.'"

### Modern sources

Monier-Williams defines anekāntavāda as "a principle of the Jaina philosophy which teaches that truth is only from a relative standpoint, and that the different doctrines from the different standpoints are equally true".

In 1860, the Jain scholar, Hermann Jacobi, published a book titled Die Lehre von der Unendlichkeit der Welt im Jainismus (The doctrine of the infinity of the world in Jainism). In this work, Jacobi stated that anekāntavāda was a doctrine of Jainism. According to Jacobi, the idea of anekāntavāda was first mentioned in the Jain text, the Tattvartha-sutra, which he attributed to the 2nd-century Jain teacher and philosopher, Umasvati. Jacobi also cited other Jain texts, such as the Tiloya-tara-sutra, to support his claim that the doctrine originated in Jainism.

During the 19th century, some Hindu scholars also acknowledged that anekāntavāda was a Jain doctrine. For example, in 1868, the Hindu scholar, S. K. De, wrote that "it is a remarkable fact that Anekāntavāda, which is in every respect a Jain doctrine, is, after the Buddha, the most prominent feature of the Hindu philosophy".

The Romanian Land Forces were reorganised in motorised and mechanised armies. The units of the 3rd Motorised Army were redesignated as follows:

  * 3rd Motorised Army (1st Mixed Army) (2nd and 3rd Mixed Divisions, 3rd Cavalry Division, 5th and 6th Rifle Divisions) – 1st Motorised Army
  * 6th Motorised Army (11th and 12th Rifle Divisions) – 2nd Motorised Army
  * 12th Motorised Army (17th and 18th Rifle Divisions) – 3rd Motorised Army
The Romanian Land Forces were organised in two corps:
  * 1st Corps (3rd and 4th Mixed Divisions, 3rd Cavalry Division)
  * 2nd Corps (1st, 2nd and 3rd Mixed Divisions, 5th and 6th Rifle Divisions)
In 1945, the Romanian Land Forces were organised as follows:
  * 1st Corps (1st, 2nd and 3rd Mixed Divisions, 4th Cavalry Division, 5th and 6th Rifle Divisions)

While it was moving little over the south @-@ central Caribbean , Omar brought prolonged tropical storm conditions to the ABC I

lands .
Omar became the 25th tropical cyclone to form in the Atlantic basin in 2010 and the 4th in the Caribbean Sea. The system became a tropical storm on November 17, 2010, and a hurricane on November 19. It did not maintain hurricane strength long and was downgraded to tropical storm status again on November 20. It became extratropical and dissipated on November 21.
 Omar's remnants produced rainfall of at least 6 inches across the U.S. Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico from November 16 to 18.
The system was first noted by the NHC on November 16 as a low pressure system located near 9.9°N 62.1°W. The system moved northwestward and was upgraded to Tropical Depression Sixteen on November 17. It moved west-northwestward and was named Omar on November 19. Omar reached peak intensity with winds of 60 mph (95 km/h) on November 20. Later that day, Omar was downgraded to a tropical storm. Winds increased to 70 mph (110 km/h) on November 21, and Omar became extratropical on November 22.

Late on 9 February , the Japanese made more landings , in the Causeway sector , held by the 27th Infantry Brigade . Despite hav

ing no air support , the brigade fought back with great courage , and in the face of overwhelming odds , managed to contain the enemy at the cost of more than 1,500 casualties .
The Japanese had intended to take the whole of the island by nightfall , but because of the resistance , the operation was suspended for the night .
The Japanese 18th Division attacked from the north in force , and during the night of 9/10 February , the 48th Regiment , supported by tanks and artillery , swept across the Nathu La and Mukhia La passes . The northern defenders , the 2nd Battalion , 7th Rajput Regiment , fought bravely only to be overwhelmed . The Japanese then advanced and overran the British air field at Mechuka , and one of the Indian battalions there.
The 1st Battalion , 7th Rajput Regiment , in the south , was also overrun. The 5th Battalion , 11th Gurkha Rifles , and the 13th Frontier Force Rifles , defending the southern part of the Shipki La position , were also overrun , but they had time to destroy their equipment , and the Japanese were then unable to use them as a stepping-stone for further advances.
The Japanese attacked again on 10 February , and the 1st Battalion , 7th Rajput Regiment , which was holding the Nathu La Pass , was able to delay the advance by a further 24 hours . But the passes were overrun and the line of defence along the Pangong Tso lake was also breached.
The next attempt to take the Chushul-Tawang road was made by the 18th Division on 11 February , and the 1st Battalion , 8th Gurkha Rifles , was forced back with casualties. The remainder of the 5th Battalion , 11th Gurkha Rifles , which was holding the Tawang-Chushul road , was then ordered to fall back towards Tawang on 12 February .
The 1st Battalion , 8th Gurkha Rifles , reinforced by a company of the 1st Battalion , 7th Gurkha Rifles , then made a final stand at Tawang , where the Japanese were held up until 15 February . The battalion was then withdrawn to Bomdila .
The British 14th Infantry Brigade was then ordered to take over the defence of the northern part of the frontier. The 1st Battalion , 2nd Gurkha Rifles , was moved to Tawang , and the 2nd Battalion , 6th Gurkha Rifles , to Bomdila . The 1st Battalion , 5th Gurkha Rifles , and the 4th Battalion , 14th Frontier Force , were then ordered to take up positions at Bomdila and Tenga respectively .
On 20 February , the 2nd Battalion , 5th Gurkha Rifles , moved to Tenga .
The Japanese then attacked the line of defence along the Tawang-Chushul road on 21 February , and the battalion was attacked by two battalions of the 38th Division , which were able to break through the position. The 2nd Battalion , 5th Gurkha Rifles , was then ordered to withdraw across the Tawang-Chushul road to the Chushul-Tawang road. This was successfully carried out , and the battalion then reorganised for the defence of Tawang.
The Japanese attacked on 24 February , and the battalion had to withdraw to Bomdila , where it was forced to surrender .
The 1st Battalion , 5th Gurkha Rifles , and the 1st Battalion , 8th Gurkha Rifles , were then ordered to take up positions at Bomdila. The 1st Battalion , 5th Gurkha Rifles , was then ordered to withdraw to Rangdum on 19 March , where a new defensive position was organised. The 1st Battalion , 8th Gurkha Rifles , was then ordered to withdraw to Lingti.
On their side , the Japanese 15th Division and the 15th Mountain Regiment then advanced on the Lingti-Jang-Chubi-Tawang road , and the 1st Battalion , 8th Gurkha Rifles , was again forced to withdraw from Lingti to Jang .

This campaign had two objectives: to force the North Vietnamese to negotiate a settlement that would bring an end to the conflict in the south, and to reduce the flow of men and supplies from the north to the south. The bombing was intended to force the North Vietnamese to stop supporting the Viet Cong and the NVA. The operation was a direct challenge to the North Vietnamese leadership to prove that it could not survive a major air campaign.

This rail is related to the New Guinea flightless rail , Megacrex inepta , and the chestnut rail , Eulabeornis castaneoventris

## Description

The rail is a slim, lanky bird with a long beak. It has a brown upper body and white underparts. The bill is dark, as is the face. The upperparts are marked with a black line. Juveniles are duller than adults. The bird's flight is fast and direct.

## Habitat

The bird is found in mangrove swamps and inland forests, where it eats insects, seeds, and small vertebrates.

## Reproduction

The birds breed between October and January. The female lays 1-2 eggs and incubates them for 23 to 24 days. Young birds are independent by 18 days.

Laborintus II is a recording of the 1965 composition of the same name by Luciano Berio , who wrote it for the 700th anniversary

of the foundation of the city of Venice. The work is a collection of 700 short melodies performed by 700 amateur singers. 

The first performance of Laborintus II took place in the Arsenale of Venice on 28 August 1965, a year after the first Laborintus. The 700 singers were divided into two choirs, each consisting of 350 men and 350 women. They sang in different choirs or simultaneously with each other. The performance lasted about 3 hours.

Berio is known for giving a fresh and positive view of the world. He sees music as a means of communication rather than a form of art. This is also evident in his concept of Laborintus II. In his composition he tried to show the world in a positive and cheerful way. In Laborintus II he wants to show the similarities between men and women in the choice of their music.

* 2003: Luciano Berio: Laborintus II – II Labirinti. Live recording from the performance in 2003 at the Teatro La Fenice in Venice, (released 2004)

Meyerbeer was always concerned to intensify the theatricality of his operas , even when new ideas emerged at a relatively late

171 stage in his career (op. 30 and later).
 Meyerbeer, in his recollection of the 1777 production of _Robert le diable_ , 218 says: 'it was the custom of the times to interpolate recitatives which were not in the original score, so that the vocal line contained no more than a mere canto. One would sing a _tempo di mezzo_ , then a _tempo di presto_ , and so on. But when the music resumed its original rhythm, the voice would fall into a _tempo di mezzo_ again, and this alternation of rhythms produced a perpetual flow of melody. This was the style of the operas of Giordano Berti, who was one of the most celebrated composers of his time. When I was in Paris, he was the director of the Italian Opera. I used to visit him as a friend, and he would show me the parts of his dramas that he was composing; I did not know at the time that they would be performed.'

Gakkai (the Black Dragon Society). In his gratitude, Sayuri invites him home for lunch, and Kōsaku sees that her father is a Shintō priest . Sayuri's father, Kōenji, is a devout believer in the government's plan to invade China, and he is a member of the Koku Gakkai. In return for his help, Kōsaku promises to visit Sayuri's father's temple. Sayuri's father, however, is not there, and Kōsaku learns that he has been kidnapped by the Koku Gakkai. Kōenji's disappearance is reported in the newspapers, and Kōsaku visits Sayuri's home to express his condolences.
On the day of Kōsaku's visit, he is warned by the police that the Koku Gakkai is planning to kidnap Sayuri. He realizes that the Koku Gakkai will try to take Sayuri to the temple to find her father. Kōsaku goes to the temple and finds Sayuri, but she is being held captive by the Koku Gakkai. Kōsaku escapes with Sayuri and runs away to Hong Kong. Kōsaku reports Sayuri's kidnapping to the police, but Sayuri refuses to testify against the Koku Gakkai. She also tells Kōsaku that if her father was still alive, he would not want her to testify against the Koku Gakkai.
Kōsaku and Sayuri escape to Hong Kong and become fugitives. They are chased by the Koku Gakkai and the police. Sayuri is captured by the police, and Kōsaku is attacked by the Koku Gakkai. He is the real Kōenji's father, and he is actually a priest of the buddhist temple Myōken-dō. He comes to the police station and identifies Kōsaku as his daughter's boyfriend. The Hokies also had a 500 yard receiver in Willie Jones who had 519 yards and 4 touchdowns.

Due to the rapid pace of operations , deployment , and redeployment , coordination of artillery units and their fires became a

critical factor in the airlift's success.  With the rapid tempo and fluid nature of operations , coordination and execution of artillery fires was difficult to achieve.  Artillery units had to be highly mobile and capable of rapid redeployment to support airlift operations.  Furthermore, in this environment, the artillery unit had to be able to communicate and coordinate with the civilian agencies and the airlift command in order to ensure the safety of civilians and to  avoid collateral damage.
The concept of a mobile, air-deployable artillery unit was tested during the airlift operations and found to be highly successful.  While the artillery unit had to be mobile, it still had to be organized, trained, and equipped to perform its primary mission of close air support, direct fire, and general support fires.  This meant that the size  of the unit had to be kept to a minimum so that it could be airlifted and deployed and sustained over a short period of time.  Using the size and weight of typical 105mm howitzers as a guide, the combat artillery unit  was 80 men strong, including both officers and enlisted personnel.  The unit was divided into three sections:  an  artillery section, a command section, and a maintenance section.  The artillery section consisted of the following subsections:  a firing section, a commander's section, and an observer section.  The command section consisted of the following subsections:  a commander's section, an assistant commander's section, and a forward observer section.  The maintenance section consisted of a maintenance section and a support section.  A total of 125 personnel were required to support the combat artillery unit.  The artillery section and the command section were attached to the combat artillery unit and fell under the overall command of the artillery battalion commander.  The maintenance section and the support section were attached to the combat artillery support battalion and fell under the overall command of the maintenance battalion commander.  The 105mm howitzer was the only weapon system which could be airlifted as a complete unit.  The M-48A2 tank was too heavy and too large to be airlifted, and the M-113 armored personnel carriers were too small to hold the number of personnel required for a combat artillery unit.  The M-48A2 tank and the M-113 armored personnel carrier fell outside the weight and size limitations for airlift and therefore had to be disbanded.  Furthermore, the M-48A2 tank and the M-113 armored personnel carrier were designed as tracked vehicles and were not suitable for jungle operations.  The M-113 armored personnel carrier could be used for jungle operations with the addition of a flotation system and a light armor package.  This would allow the M-113 to be airlifted on a C-130 cargo plane.  However, the M-113 armored personnel carrier was not airlifted because the M-48A2 tank was more suitable for the combat artillery unit.  There was one other factor that influenced the decision to use the M-48A2 tank in the combat artillery unit--the firepower and the survivability of the tank.  The tank had a 105mm main gun which provided the combat artillery unit with its primary firepower.  The tank could also be used for direct and counterfire missions.  The tank had two M-60 machine guns which could be used for counterfire and personal defense.  Furthermore, the tank had a crew of four men, which provided the combat artillery unit with a high level of safety.  The M-48A2 tank was designed as a tracked vehicle and could not be airlifted. The M-48A3 tank was used in the combat artillery unit until the M-48A3 tank could be replaced with the M-60A3 tank. In 1663 Scottish mathematician James Gregory had suggested in his Optica Promota that observations of a transit of the planet M

ecury across the Sun could be used to determine the parallax of the Sun, and thus the distance between the Earth and the Sun. The idea was not new. As early as 1617, Johannes Kepler had considered the possibility that the transit of Mercury might be employed to measure the distance between the Earth and the Sun. In 1639, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini had used the predicted transit of Mercury in 1661 to test the speed of light. However, he was able to determine only an upper limit to the speed of light. His estimate of 210,000 miles a second was 20,000 too high.
In the years following the publication of Gregory’s Optica Promota, and especially after 1672, when he inadvertently published a second edition of his book, the concept of using a transit of Mercury to determine the distance of the Sun from the Earth became a popular topic of discussion. Astronomers of the time agreed that the transit of Mercury would be an ideal means of determining the distance of the Sun—or at least the distance to Mercury.
Astronomers of the time had become interested in the mass of the Solar System, and they thought that the transit of Mercury might provide a way of determining the mass of the Sun. For that, they would need to know the mass of Mercury. Many of the astronomers reasoned that the distance to the Sun must be very nearly the same as the distance to Mercury.

2nd Battalion , 9th Marines ( 2 / 9 ) was an infantry battalion of the United States Marine Corps . Formed during World War I ,

it fought in the Pacific Ocean theater of World War II , and later saw action in the Vietnam War .

## History

### World War I

The 2nd Battalion, 9th Marines was commissioned on 16 September 1917 as the 1st Ammunition Company of the 2nd Brigade, 2nd Division, United States Marine Corps.

### World War II

The 2nd Battalion, 9th Marines was activated on 1 September 1942, at Camp Lejeune, North Carolina. After training, the battalion deployed to the Pacific theater of operations.

2/9's next mission was to participate in the landing of the 9th Marine Regiment on the island of Tarawa in the Gilbert Islands, 20 November 1943. The battalion assaulted Tarawa Beach 2. In the face of heavy fire from Japanese machine-gun nests, the battalion suffered 71 killed and 171 wounded. The Japanese were defeated on 23 November 1943, but the cost in American lives was very high. The battalion was awarded the Presidential Unit Citation for its actions in the landing.

The 2nd Battalion, 9th Marines was subsequently transferred to Guadalcanal and participated in the capture of Tulagi and Gavutu.

In April 1944, the 2nd Battalion, 9th Marines was transferred to the 2nd Marine Division and participated in the Battle of Saipan. During the Saipan operation, the battalion took heavy casualties during the bloody assault at Aslito Airfield. On 25 October 1944, the battalion was deactivated, and the personnel and equipment were reassigned to the 9th Marine Regiment.

### Korean War

After the war, the 2nd Battalion, 9th Marines was reactivated on 19 July 1952. Combat operations began in September 1952 when the battalion was assigned to the 2nd Marine Division and deployed to Korea. While serving in Korea, the battalion earned the Presidential Unit Citation and the Navy Unit Commendation for its actions in combat.

### Vietnam War

On 25 June 1963, the 2nd Battalion, 9th Marines was deployed to Danang, South Vietnam. The battalion was assigned to the 9th Marine Regiment.

From 1965 through 1966, the battalion was deployed to the Republic of Vietnam during Operation Shufly. The battalion was awarded the Presidential Unit Citation for its actions in combat.

On 26 June 1967, the battalion was redesignated as the 2nd Battalion, 9th Marines, Reconnaissance Company, and was reassigned to the 1st Marine Division. The battalion served in combat in the Republic of Vietnam until 18 July 1967, when the battalion was deactivated.

### Post-Vietnam War

Following the end of the Vietnam War, the battalion was reactivated on 15 July 1970, as part of the 2nd Marine Division.

The 2nd Battalion, 9th Marines participated in the Inchon Landing and the Battle of Chosin Reservoir in 1950, and the Battle of Iwo Jima in 1945. During the Vietnam War, the battalion earned the Presidential Unit Citation and the Navy Unit Commendation.

In 1991, the battalion deployed to Saudi Arabia to participate in Operation Desert Shield/Desert Storm.

### Global War on Terrorism

In 2003, the battalion deployed to Iraq to participate in the Iraq War. The battalion was awarded the Navy Unit Commendation for its actions in combat.

Furtado wanted to be more involved in the production of her third album, as she felt that her previous albums appeared to be more commercially produced. Commercially, the album debuted at number one on the Canadian and United States Billboard 200 . Its first three singles failed to match the success of her previous album's singles, but she scored her first number-one single in the United Kingdom with " All Good Things ( Come to an End) ".

that Brenda has apparently been missing for some time and Owen advises Jack that he will take him to see her . Jack is initially unconvinced by Owen's story, and when they arrive at the house, he is shocked to find that Brenda is not actually there . As they look around the house, they discover some very disturbing things, including a hidden room in the basement filled with bodies .
 concludes that the room is the work of a serial killer , but Jack insists that it is the work of an alien .
 Jack informs Rhys and Gwen that the alien is the man who abducted them, and they watch a video recording of him abducting two other people. Brenda is in the recording, and Jack is convinced that she is the alien's accomplice . He and Rhys go to see Brenda at the house and Jack learns that she has been drugged by the alien . The alien returns to the house, and Rhys and Jack struggle with him, ending with Rhys stabbing him. Afterwards, Jack takes the alien's body to the hospital and Rhys and Gwen inform the police of the murder . Jack is taken to a hospital ward and he is informed that he has been suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder and is under the care of Professor Rhys Williams ( Ken Bone ) . Jack grows suspicious of Rhys and he begins to investigate him, believing him to be the alien . When Jack arrives at Rhys' house, he is attacked by Rhys, who turns out to be the alien . Jack is knocked unconscious and he is taken to hospital .
 Jack is released from hospital and meets with Tosh, who tells him that Rhys has been arrested, and she asks for his help in developing an alien-detecting gadget . While they are working on it, Rhys telephones Jack and tells him that he is at the police station and he wants to talk to him . As Jack and Tosh work on the alien-detecting gadget, Rhys turns up at the Torchwood Institute and he is carrying a black box . He is shot by Tosh, but he quickly recovers and attacks her. Gwen arrives and Rhys knocks her out with a blow to the head . Jack arrives and is knocked unconscious, and Rhys takes the black box . Jack is taken to hospital and he is told that it is likely that he will suffer from brain damage . While he is in hospital, Jack dreams of the alien abducting people, and he wakes up to find that he is holding a power drill, which he uses to attack Rhys . He is captured by Rhys and taken to the hospital where Jack was previously unconscious . Rhys attacks Jack and they are separated by Tosh, who is holding a gun . As Rhys runs away, he is killed by a police officer . Jack is taken to the hospital, and he is told that he will make a full recovery, although he will be left with a small memory gap .

WASP @-@ 44 is a G @-@ type star ( the same class of star as the Sun ) that is located in the Cetus constellation . WASP @-@ 44

is a main sequence star at a distance of about 141.45 light years from the Sun . 

WASP @-@ 44

This article refers to a star, not to a planet. For the exoplanet, see WASP-44b.

WASP @-@ 44

## Nomenclature

WASP @-@ 44 is a G8V star that is named after the Wide Angle Search for Planets (abbreviated as WASP). In the case of multiple stars, the naming convention is to include the stellar type of the star followed by the star's GCVS designation (if the star is a member of a star system). Thus the star's name will be WASP G8V.

## Properties

WASP @-@ 44 is a main sequence star with a stellar classification of G8V. The star is currently around 4.20 billion years old. The star is 4.32 times more massive than the Sun and is radiating 18.9 times the luminosity of the Sun from its photosphere at an effective temperature of 5,229 K.

## Planetary system

This star has one confirmed extrasolar planet that orbits the star every 3.26 days. The planet has a minimum mass of 0.85 Jupiter masses and is a very hot gas giant.

In 1172 , the new pope , Alexander III , further encouraged Henry to advance the integration of the Irish Church with Rome . He

wrote to Archbishop Henry de Loundres , that he should maintain the primacy of the archbishop over the other bishops and that his authority should be as wide as that of other archbishops , except that he should not have metropolitan authority over Ireland .

The year 1172 saw the death of Archbishop Henry de Loundres , who had been in office for over 18 years and apparently preserved a good reputation. The canons of Limerick , who were met by the King at his approach to the city, were not in sympathy with him and had chosen a new archbishop who was in exile in Wales . The King, however, persuaded them to reinstate Henry de Loundres , who had been buried in the cathedral of Limerick . In 1173 , Henry de Loundres was succeeded by Archbishop Richard de Prendergast , who was consecrated on 23 March 1173.

In 1182 , Henry de Loundres wrote to the King saying that his desecrated churches needed the support of the King. He asked for a new castle and fortification at Burren and strengthening of the castles of Limerick and Clonfert . He also wanted three separate bridges for Limerick . Henry de Loundres had by 1188 , founded a monastery for Augustinian canons at Askeaton . The canons were to be under the protection of the King, the Lord of Thomond , and the Archbishop of Limerick . In 1189 , Henry de Loundres and the King died within a few days of each other and Henry was buried in the cathedral , where his tomb is still to be seen.

Notes may be used in any combination to form melodies and chords. Notes that are played at the same time form a chord. Notes that sounded consecutively form a melody.

Notes can be played individually or in chords, and can be sustained (sound for an extended period of time), or they can be played as a staccato (played very quickly, so that the notes are barely audible), or legato (played smoothly and continuously).

## Description

A note is a symbol that represents a relative pitch value in the context of a specific scale or key. It is often called the pitch of a note. Notes may also be called pitches, pitched events, or pitches events. Notes can be described as a sequence of intervals such as a step, an augmented second, or a major third.

In music, an octave (often called the octave register) is the interval between one note and another with double its frequency. The octave is the interval between the first and second harmonics of a vibrating string. The octave is the top of the musical alphabet; its note name is the first letter of the alphabet (A), which is not used in musical notation. Each note that is played on a violin or viola is played an octave higher when it is played on a cello or double bass.

He writes, "The Sxwem'cw are the most numerous division of the Secwepemc; they are found north of McLeery Lake and the Shuswap River, and are the common ancestors of all the Secwepemc."
It is unclear to me why Teit has chosen to refer to the Sxwem'cw as the "Upper" division, or why he has omitted the Uts'amcw from his analysis. Following the rejection of the 1909 " People 's Budget " , the House of Commons sought to establish its formal dominance over t

he Lords . In 1910 the House of Commons passed the Parliament Bill, which would have removed the Lords ' power to reject bills or amend them in a way that would be unacceptable to the Commons . After the 1910 general election the Liberal government introduced the Parliament Bill into the Commons, which it passed despite opposition from the Conservatives . However, the Lords rejected the bill, and the Liberal government called a general election. The Liberals were defeated in that election, and the Parliament Bill was defeated in the Lords in 1911 .
The second Home Rule Bill was passed by the Commons in 1912, and a referendum in Ulster on Home Rule was passed by a large majority in favour of the option of remaining within the United Kingdom . However, the House of Lords rejected the bill, and the government called another general election . The Lords rejected the bill again, forcing the government to call a third general election . The Liberal Party suffered a landslide defeat, and the House of Lords rejected the bill for the third time.
Under the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949 the Lords can only reject a bill passed by the Commons on two occasions, after which the Commons can override the rejection with a two-thirds majority in both houses and the bill becomes law without the Lords' consent. The two-thirds majority was not achieved until 1969, when the first Labour government rejected the Lords' amendments to the Race Relations Bill .
As the House of Commons is the dominant chamber, it is sometimes said that the Commons is sovereign and the House of Lords is a revising chamber. However, the Lords can block legislation that the Commons passes, forcing the government to call another election or to accept the Lords' amendments. This happened in the 1974–1975 " Winter of Discontent " . In the twenty-first century, the House of Lords is almost always in agreement with the House of Commons (although it can take several years for a bill to pass through the Lords, as the Lords can amend legislation at will).
 There are 702 members of the House of Lords, of which 26 are appointed by the Queen and 597 are life peers appointed by the Prime Minister, on the advice of the House of Lords Appointments Commission . Formerly, life peerages were awarded to prominent members of the governing party, or in recognition of public service, but since the life peerages created by Tony Blair 's Labour government in 1997, it is now possible to be appointed on merit alone.
 The 15 ultra-rare hereditary peers , whose number is limited by law, play no part in the passage of legislation.
 The Lords Spiritual are 26 bishops of the established Church of England , and sit as of right in the House of Lords and retain their seats even if they are not members of the government.
 The Lord Chancellor , a cabinet position, is legally a member of the Lords, but must remain an active member of the House of Commons. The position is currently held by the Conservative politician Liz Truss .
 The Lords Temporal are hereditary peers and life peers who are not members of the Government.
 Since the passing of the House of Lords Act 1999 , there are twenty-six hereditary peers who can remain members of the House of Lords, and, as of 2014, seventeen of these seats are occupied by members of the Conservative Party .
 The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council is not formally part of the House of Lords, but is often counted as one of the " houses " of Parliament.
 The House of Lords is not a court of law, but a legislative assembly, and as such, its members are not subject to judicial oaths of office.
 The Lords Spiritual have a two-seat majority, and the Lords Temporal a two-seat minority.
 House of Lords members are known as members of the House of Lords . The term "membership" can refer either to the current membership or to the membership as a whole, including members who have died, resigned or been removed from the House. The term "peer" refers to a member of the House of Lords, whether or not the member is a member of the Lords Spiritual.
Peers are styled with a title of nobility, usually inherited from a parent. Most peers are life peers, who hold their titles until death or resignation; they are not hereditary,

He struggles to find a way to cope with his mental health issues , and eventually resorts to using alcohol and illegal drugs to suppress the traumatic memories .

Comair Flight 5191 , marketed as Delta Connection Flight 5191 , was a scheduled United States ( US ) domestic passenger flight

​ 60 ​ from Blue Grass Airport in Lexington, ​ Kentucky ​ to Hartsfield–Jackson Atlanta International Airport in Atlanta, ​ Georgia ​ .  On August 27, 2006 , the 76-seat aircraft operating the flight crashed on takeoff from Blue Grass Airport, killing all 47 passengers and two crew members. The airplane was a Bombardier CRJ-200, operated by ExpressJet Airlines under a regional service agreement with Delta Air Lines .
The 2006 Lexington crash was the first fatal accident involving a Bombardier CRJ-200 passenger aircraft in the United States. The investigation revealed that the airplane's captain failed to recognize and act upon the presence of a potentially lethal aerodynamic stall condition during the takeoff, causing the airplane to crash.
On August 27, 2006 , Comair Flight 5191 ( DL 5191 ) was cleared for takeoff on Runway 5L at Blue Grass Airport in Lexington, ​ Kentucky . The captain, James Polehinke, 54, was a certified flight instructor and had flown CRJ-200s for eight years.  Polehinke had flown the aircraft 685 hours, and had logged 10,152 hours total as a pilot.  His first officer, James Steele, 41, was a 7,100-hour pilot who had flown CRJ-200s for five years.  Steele had logged 3,100 hours with ExpressJet.  The first officer conducted the takeoff and follow-through; the captain was seated in the right-hand seat.  There were 49 passengers and two crew members on board the aircraft.
The aircraft was cleared for takeoff at 10:40 EDT at an altitude of 1,100 feet (340 m) above ground level (AGL), and was cleared for takeoff at 10:43 EDT.  The aircraft accelerated to about 141 knots (163 mph, 263 km/h), and the captain said: "I think we're climbing."  The first officer responded: "Oh, I don't know. I think we're just about Vr."  The captain replied: "I don't think so, I think we're climbing."  The first officer then said: "Okay, I guess we are."  The captain replied: "I think we are. I don't know."  The first officer said: "I don't know. I'm not sure."  The captain replied: "I think we're climbing."  The first officer then said: "Yeah, I think we are."  The captain replied: "All right."
The airplane's climb angle momentarily increased to about 17°, then decreased to about 15°.  The increase in climb angle lasted about two seconds before the airplane fell back down to 10°.  This difference was caused by the airplane falling below the speed at which it could maintain its angle of climb.  The airplane continued to accelerate for another four to five seconds before the first officer abruptly called out "Vr" and the captain said "Whoa" and "Oh no" as the airspeed dropped and the nose pitched up.  The captain was not able to regain control of the aircraft and it crashed in a cornfield about 3,000 feet (910 m) short of the end of the runway.  The airplane crashed at an indicated airspeed of 160 knots (180 mph, 300 km/h), just above the minimum speed for a safe landing.
The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigation revealed that the captain failed to recognize and act upon the presence of a potentially lethal aerodynamic stall condition during the takeoff roll.  The crew failed to take the necessary corrective action.  The flight crew's failure to maintain airspeed while in a critical phase of flight was a probable cause of the accident.
The pilot's failure to recognize and act upon the presence of a potentially lethal aerodynamic stall condition during the takeoff roll was a factor in the accident.

It was the most scared I've ever been in my life."[16] Goldberg was initially nervous about the role because she did not think that she and Rachel were similar.[16] According to Goldberg, the producers wanted her to go to the hair salon and dye her hair blonde. She refused, as she did not want to change her appearance. In the end, the producers agreed to let her keep her hair brown and did not insist that she dye it.[17]
Goldberg initially received a three-year contract, with an option for a fourth year. Her contract was restructured after the first season to allow for the show to focus more on Rachel, as the producers found that the series was more successful with her as the main character. Goldberg was unaware that her character would become the focus of the show until the third season, when she was told that the show would "focus on Rachel".[16] She later said that she was glad she had not known beforehand, as she may have turned down the role. Her contract allowed her to star in six guest appearances on other television shows, which she took advantage of. She also turned down an offer to star in another series after Friends because she was worried about becoming typecast. She was paid $100,000 an episode in the last two seasons of the show, making her the highest paid female actor at the time.[18] She received $22 million for the first three seasons of Friends and $20 million for the last three seasons.[19]
Goldberg invited the other cast members to her wedding to David Crane , who had written three episodes of the show and produced its first season. She also invited the cast to her first child's birth, but not her second.[20]

RNA splicing , carried out by a complex called the spliceosome , is the process by which introns , or regions of DNA that do no

code for proteins, are removed from a pre-mRNA molecule to yield mature mRNA .
Somatic cells ( body cells ) get their genetic information from two copies of each gene, one from each parent. The first step in mRNA synthesis is the transcription of a gene into a pre-mRNA by the enzyme RNA polymerase . The pre-mRNA, though lacking introns, contains several sequences that are not part of the protein coding regions. These regions are removed from the pre-mRNA before it is utilized in protein synthesis.

island's capital town. It has a regular ferry service to Skye Bridge on the mainland and is the largest town on Skye. Portree is the island's only burgh. Portree is the main commercial centre and is popular with visitors due to its proximity to the Cuillin Mountains.
Portree is the only town on Skye with a secondary school. Skye High School is located on the outskirts of Portree. The town is host to the annual Skye Food and Arts Festival and Skye Blues Festival.
Portree High Street is the main shopping area. Portree has a supermarket and a variety of shops.
Portree is a fishing port and has many restaurants serving seafood. The town also has a number of hotels and guest houses. The town's fishing harbour is known as the Port of Portree. The main pier at Portree handles the island's ferries.
Many sailors left from the Port of Portree on their voyages of exploration. The harbour at Portree was damaged in a storm in 1917 and has not been rebuilt.
The town has an 18-hole golf course.
A number of bus services operate to Portree from Inverness, Elgin, Kyle of Lochalsh and Dunvegan.
