Two main languages are spoken in Ireland : Irish and English . Both languages have widely contributed to literature . Irish , n

atively known as Gaelic , is not the same as the language spoken in Scotland but more akin to the language of the Celts of Wales and Cornwall. Irish is the first language of approximately one-third of the Irish population . A minority of people in Ireland are bilingual , speaking both Irish and English .
 Irish-language literature had its roots in the 7th century . Christian missionaries who arrived in Ireland during the 5th and 6th centuries brought with them a Latin-based literature .
 In the 12th century , an independent Irish literature began to develop . The earliest evidence was in the form of stories preserved as oral tradition . These stories were collected by scholars and put into written form . The first of these was the ''Táin bó Cuailgne'' , which is still much read .
 The next major influence on Irish literature was the " Book of Kells " , a manuscript of the four gospels dated to around 800 A.D . It is now preserved in Trinity College in Dublin .
 The ''Acallam na Senórach'' , or ''The Conversation of the Old Men of Gaelic Ireland ,'' is a written record of a conversation between three old men who have been dead for many years . The text describes the history of Ireland and the story of the death of the hero Cuchulainn . This was written at the end of the 11th century .
 Gaelic poetry is the oldest form of Irish-language literature . The oldest manuscripts of this type include the ''Lebor na hUidre'', or ''Book of the Dun Cow'' . This is a manuscript of Irish myths and stories . The ''Yellow Book of Lecan'' contains poems of the mythical Fionn mac Cumhaill . The manuscript was compiled about 1390 .
 In the 15th century , the Irish-speaking community of Ireland was devastated by an outbreak of plague . The Irish-speaking nobility were especially hard hit . This caused a wholesale change in the nature of Irish-language literature . This was a time when the Irish-speaking people were under the rule of the English-speaking nobility . In response to this, Irish poetry and literature became more political in nature . The work of Eoghan Ruadh Ó Súilleabháin , known as O'Sullivan Beare , was a major contribution to this development in Irish-language literature .
 In the 16th century , the English language became more prevalent in Ireland . Irish-language literature was now written in both Latin and English . This writing was principally used for the instruction of the Irish people in their Catholic faith . The ''Book of the Cures of Evil Spirits'' contains prayers and instructions for the exorcising of evil spirits . It was written in 1581 .
 In 1607 , the Irish-language literary journal ''Cóip Dhubh'' was established . This became the first of several important Irish-language periodicals .
 In the 18th century , the Irish language was again at the centre of Irish life . This time, the Irish people fought for their independence from England . The Irish-language novel was now a major genre . The best known novel of this period was ''An Leabhar Mor'' , which means ''The Great Book'' . This took 11 years to write and was published in 1763 .
 The 18th century also saw the establishment of the first Irish-language newspaper . This was the ''Irish Press'' , which was founded in 1738 .
 In the 19th century , the Irish-language literary revival began . Literary clubs and societies were established all over Ireland to encourage Irish-language literature . These included the ''Gaelic Union'' and the ''Gaelic Journal'' . The ''Gaelic League'' was formed in 1893 .
 The ''Irish Review'' was first published in 1909 . This was the first Irish-language literary journal .
 The Irish-language theatre was established in 1902 by W. B. Yeats . This was called the " Irish Literary Theatre " .
 In the 20th century , the Irish-language literary revival continued to develop . It became popular for Irish-language writers to write in both English and Irish . Seán Ó Faoláin was one of the first Irish-language writers to do this . He was also the first Irish-language writer to be awarded the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1955 .

era.

The web is the most popular medium for consuming fonts, so that means that anyone who uses a web browser can use any font that their browser supports. All fonts are everywhere and anywhere, so the web is the most democratic place to use them.

By about 19 : 30 , Marlborough 's pumps had contained the flooding in the boiler rooms but she took on a list of around 7 – 8 d

m (2.5 – 3 ft) and was on an even keel.  At 20 : 00 a fire was started in the engine room to generate power for the pumps.  The starboard boiler room was flooded up to the waist of engineers.  The flooding was quickly made worse by the collapse of the port port-side boiler room bulkhead.  The boilers were disconnected from the engine room by severing the fuel lines.  The lower engine room was also flooded, but the pumps in the engine room kept it under control.

At 21 : 00 there was a sudden explosion in the engine room, which was caused by a rupture of the starboard boiler.  The death of the two engineers in the boiler room is believed to have been caused by this explosion.  The explosion resulted in the engine room flooding and the ensuing damage caused the boilers to fail from over-pressure.

A fire in the boiler room also resulted in smoke and steam rising to the surface.  A further explosion occurred in the engine room at 23 : 45 which severely damaged the bridge.

At 23 : 45 the port main steam pipe ruptured, resulting in a large explosion.  The explosion caused the port condenser to fail and the ship to flood rapidly.  At 23 : 52 the ship was ordered to abandon ship.  The order was given by the officer of the watch, Lieutenant Frederick Poore, who had just taken over the watch.  At 23 : 55 the bridge was destroyed and the top of the funnel fell into the sea.

After abandoning ship, the survivors clung to the ship's lifeboats and rafts for about two hours before being rescued.  The survivors were taken to the coastal town of Blyth in Northumberland, England, where they were accommodated in local hotels and public buildings.

### Sinking

The immediate cause of the explosion on Marlborough is unknown.  The main theory is that the boiler was over-pressurised and failed as a result.  The over-pressurisation may have been caused by the captain disconnecting the boiler from the engine room in an attempt to save the ship.

### Aftermath

The captain of Marlborough, Commander H.L. Gordon, was found guilty of negligence of duty and sentenced to 30 days' imprisonment.

The Admiralty Court of Inquiry found that Marlborough was lost because the boilers were over-pressurised and that the cause of the explosion was unknown.  The Court of Inquiry made various recommendations, including that all boilers should have pressure gauges and that boilers should not be disconnected from the engine room.

Reines had prepared for the possibility of measuring the distant events of a supernova explosion . Supernova explosions are rar

ities, the radiation of which is too weak for detection. However, the radiation emitted from the explosion of a supernova is sometimes so powerful that it overcomes the cosmic background radiation. These explosions are therefore detectable. Reines had calculated that the radiation emitted by a supernova would be detectable by the detector array.
During the course of the experiment, a supernova explosion was observed in the constellation of Scorpio. However, the radiation was so weak that it was not detected. The detection of the supernova was not until some time later. It was only then that the possibility of a supernova explosion being detected by a cosmic-ray detector array was considered.
But how could a supernova explosion be detected? It was not the supernova explosion itself that was detected, but only the radiation emitted thereafter. The radiation is emitted at a distance of about 326,000 light years from Earth. Any radiation travels at the speed of light. Therefore, the time interval between the radiation emitted from the supernova explosion and the detection of the radiation by the cosmic-ray detector array was equal to 326,000 years. This interval was measured to be 27 years. And so 1987A was detected.

In 1899 , Wheeler joined Bradford Grammar School shortly before his ninth birthday , where he proceeded straight to the second

year (under the old system) and he won a scholarship to Bradford Technical College in 1907. In 1912 he joined the Bradford City Police , although he attended classes at Bradford Technical College while still working as a police constable.
 In 1913, he returned to the Bradford Technical College to study mathematics and physics, where he studied for the Cambridge Local Examination in 1914. He obtained first class honours in both mathematics and physics. He continued his studies at the University of Manchester , where he graduated in 1920.
 In 1916, Wheeler met and fell in love with his future wife, the mathematician Kathleen Ollerenshaw , who was also studying mathematics at the University of Manchester at the time. They were married in 1920 .
 In 1920, Wheeler returned to the University of Manchester as a research fellow , where he was appointed to the chair of mathematics in 1924 . In 1947, he was appointed the first director of the newly established Institute of Mathematics and its Applications . Wheeler was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1930, and served as its President from 1958 to 1961.
 In 1961, Wheeler was appointed by the United Nations as a consultant in the field of mathematics education .
 In 1963, Wheeler was appointed to the chair of mathematics at the University of Oxford , and a fellow of Linacre College , Oxford. He retired from both positions in 1970.
 In 1973, Wheeler was appointed vice-president of the Royal Institution of Great Britain . He was elected to the Chair of the RI in 1977, serving until 1983.
 John Gribbin , in his biography of Wheeler, concludes that the main reason for his decline in popularity was his association with the Royal Institution.
 In 1952, Wheeler was appointed by the BBC to present the first television show devoted to mathematics, "Mathematics in Your World", which was repeated for three years. He wrote and presented a thirteen-part television series, entitled "Further Mathematics in Your World", in 1958, a book of the same title accompanied the series.
 In 1981, Wheeler was appointed to the chair of mathematics at the University of Durham , and a fellow of Hatfield College, Durham. He retired from this appointment in 1983, and he died on 13 April 1986, at the age of 86.
 Wheeler was honoured with the title of Officer of the Order of the British Empire in 1938, Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1958, and Companion of the Order of the Bath in 1962. He was made a Honorary Fellow of the Institute of Mathematics and its Applications in 1965.

The game allows players to command their squads via a top-down 2D strategy map , which can be zoomed in and out of .  Tagebuch vom Krieg (literally "Diary from the War" in German) is a Belgian-German television series produced by the German production company Brainpool , which was broadcast on ZDF and VTM .
 The game's story is set in a post-apocalyptic world in which a civil war has broken out between the Republic of Urdia and the Gallian Empire . The Republic is led by the mysterious "Commander" who has been at war with the Empire for over a decade . The game follows the story of the Eadna , a young girl who is taken prisoner by the Empire during the war . She is eventually rescued by the Republic's army and becomes a member of the resistance . The gameplay is a mix of third-person shooting and real-time strategy gameplay . Players can command a squad of units to fight against the Empire's forces . The game features a single-player campaign mode and a multiplayer mode . The game was met with mixed reviews upon release . Reviewers praised the game's graphics and sound design, but criticized the game's gameplay and controls . The game was nominated for several awards at the 2012 British Academy of Film and Television Arts Craft Awards , including Best Game Design and Best Animation . The game was also nominated for Best Sound Design at the 2012 BAFTA Awards .

A council of the 'godly' was set up in London, consisting of twenty-five ministers, and this further weakened the Assembly .
The Presbyterians ' hopes that Charles II would be restored to the throne were frustrated, and in 1647 the Assembly, in which there was a large majority of Independents, issued a remonstrance to the king, demanding a more suitable form of government. Charles replied that he would have to abdicate if he were to accept their proposals, and the Assembly was forced to abandon the idea of a Presbyterian form of government. As a result of its failure, the Assembly was dissolved in 1648.
The Independents, who had been very active in the war, continued to dominate the affairs of the nation. John Lilburne, the radical, was sent to prison, and Cromwell, who had been brought back to England from the Isle of Wight in 1647, was elected to Parliament. After the second Long Parliament, which opened in November 1648, Cromwell was chosen to be Speaker of the House of Commons .
In 1649, the Presbyterians, who had spent the last year of the war in Scotland, returned to England and were able to re-establish themselves in control of Parliament. Cromwell and the other Independents were removed from office, and the king was brought back to face trial. The army took over the government of the country, and, following the king's execution in January 1649, the Commonwealth of England was proclaimed.
With the abolition of the monarchy and the Presbyterian form of government, the Assembly was now in a position to serve as the main legislature of the nation. It was divided into two houses – the Commons and the Lords. The Commons consisted of 492 members, and the Lords had a total of 144 peers. The Commons had been elected to the Parliament which had met in May 1649, and although many of these had been dismissed when the king was brought back to trial, there was still a large number of them present, and the Lords were also largely composed of those who had been elected in 1649.
In 1653, the Committee of Safety, which had been set up to maintain the order of the nation, was abolished, and the Council of State was instituted in its place. The Council was divided into two sections, the Privy Council, which consisted of the leading members of the Commons, and the Council of State, which consisted of the leading members of the Lords. The Council of State was made up of 40 members, who were elected by the two Houses to serve for one year. At the beginning of each year, the members were chosen afresh. However, the orbits of most multiple @-@ star systems are not well-understood , and the majority of these systems have not been directly @-@ observed.  We report the detection of a new multiple @-@ star system with a high-quality orbit through long-term radial velocity observations.  The new system consists of a pair of main sequence stars that are 55 ± 100 yr old and separated by 27.4 ± 0.6 arcsec.  The spectral types of these stars are as yet undetermined, although they lie at the late K and early M type boundaries.  We also report a lower limit on the total absolute magnitude of the system of 13.1 ± 0.2 mag.  The companion star has a higher velocity than the primary star, and we report evidence for a structure in the radial velocity curve of the primary star.  If the structure is real, it could be caused by starspots or apsidal motion;  based on these evidence, we tentatively identify the companion star as a possible extrasolar planet.  However, further observations are required to confirm the planetary nature of this system.

Survivals from late Medieval church fittings and objects in Scotland are exceptionally rare even compared to those from compara

- ble English and Irish collections.1 The primary reason for this is that many medieval church communities were destroyed in the course of the Scottish Reformation and the Protestant Reformation of the sixteenth century, and their church buildings and the contents of their sanctuaries were either destroyed or removed.2 In addition, the survival rate for metal objects in Scotland is lower than in England, Ireland and Wales, because Scotland's metalwork was less highly prized as a result of the lack of a major metal-working tradition within the country.3 There were also distinct regional variations in the survival of metalwork in Scotland, which can be explained by a number of factors including the regional variations in the number of religious houses and the wealth of the communities and the local churches.4
Within this context, however, a significant group of early medieval metal objects have survived in Scotland, not only from royal and ecclesiastical contexts, but also from other sources. These include a group of objects that were originally retained by local communities as part of their treasury of church vessels when they were dissolved in the sixteenth century.5 These objects include a number of high-status pieces, such as a thirteenth-century processional cross, but also more everyday pieces, such as a group of eucharistic vessels that were retained by the parishioners of the church of St Mary the Virgin in Melrose in the Scottish Borders.6
Although the cross and the eucharistic vessels were separate, discrete collections, they formed part of the same group of objects that had been removed from the church on the orders of the commissioners appointed to oversee the dissolution of the monastery of Melrose in 1547.7 These objects had been removed from the church in the course of the Reformation and were held in a stone wall safe in the churchyard, where they were rediscovered in the nineteenth century.8 This rediscovery, which involved the excavation of the contents of the safe and the subsequent sale of the objects in modern times, has been described in a number of different ways. In his _History of the Parish of Melrose_ , James S. Ritchie describes the objects as having been 'buried under the churchyard wall'.9 In a recent article, Marijke Collins describes the objects as 'buried in the churchyard'.10 The reason for these differences is because the objects were not buried under the churchyard wall, but were instead buried under the floor of the church. In this article, the objects are therefore described as 'buried in the church'.
The objects were originally buried in the church of St Mary the Virgin, Melrose, which had been the church of the adjoining monastery of Melrose.11 The church had been founded in the twelfth century by the Cistercian monks of Melrose Abbey, who had also founded a number of other churches in the Borders, including the church of St Mary in Galashiels, which had been founded by the monks of Melrose in the twelfth century. The abbey church of Melrose Abbey had been one of the most impressive churches in the Borders, and had been built around a large central tower.12 The church was destroyed in 1544, during the war between the Scots and the English, and was not rebuilt until 1819.13
In the course of the Reformation, the church of St Mary the Virgin was closed and the churchyard was used as a burial ground for the community.14 The objects were buried in the churchyard as the church was being converted into a burial ground, and the objects were rediscovered in the nineteenth century when the churchyard wall was being moved.15
The objects were rediscovered by William Hood, a local farmer, who was the owner of the land in which the objects were buried.16 Hood was born in 1812, and in 1842 he married Ann Cairns, the daughter of the Reverend John Cairns, the minister of the church of St Mary the Virgin. Ann Cairns was born in 1821, and she was the daughter of the Reverend John Cairns, who was the minister of the church of St Mary the Virgin in Melrose from 1826 until 1855, and who was the minister of the church of St Mary the Virgin in Melrose from 1855 until 1893.17 William and Ann Hood and their children lived in the church, which was used as a dwelling for the minister and his family.18 The objects were buried under the floor of the church in the nineteenth century when the church was converted into a dwelling.19

The idea for a francophone unit came from a French national , François Cramer , who had business interests and connections in R

wanda. In 1922 he went to the Belgian Congo to seek a possible location for a French-run plantation in Rwanda. He met with the Belgian governor-general, Baron Albert Delcommune. While in Chifunabuli, the Belgian capital, Cramer met with representatives of the Rwanda government, including the Belgian-appointed Chief Minister, Prince Louis Rwagasore. In 1923 Cramer returned to Belgium to report on his mission. He made a documentary film that he showed to the Belgian government and to the French government, hoping to secure support for a francophone unit in Rwanda. On 31 March 1924, the Belgian government made a decision to establish a francophone colony in Rwanda. The Belgians were aware that the British were already in the country, and they were concerned about the effects of British colonialism on the future of Belgian rule in Congo. French colonialists were also interested in Rwanda. Cramer's film had been seen by French colonialists in the Belgian Congo and they hoped to establish a French-speaking colony in Rwanda, which would be friendly to French interests in Congo.
In 1925 Cramer and his wife returned to Rwanda and leased a 100,000 hectare area of land in the south-west of the country. He was granted a thirty-year lease by the Rwandan government. At that time, Cramer believed that the lease could be renewed indefinitely. In 1931, the Belgian government began an investigation of Cramer's activities in Rwanda. The report by a Belgian commission, published in 1932, stated that Cramer had sold the land to private parties without the knowledge or approval of the Belgian colonial government.
At the same time, Cramer had been selling Rwandan land to French colonialists. In 1931, he sold some of the land to a Belgian, Lucien Nothomb. Nothomb, a wealthy banker, had business interests in the Belgian Congo, including a plantation near the Rwanda border. It was not until 1936 that Nothomb filed an application for official recognition of his land title. Nothomb had initially planned to establish a large plantation, with his Belgian business partners, but he changed his plans in 1933 and sold the land to French colonialists. The land he sold to French colonialists included the area now known as Gisenyi, the area where the French plantation was later established.
In 1934, the French government established a commission to investigate the French claim for the title to the land in Gisenyi. The commission, composed of three Frenchmen, including Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza, a former governor of Middle Congo, provided the following account of the events that led to the French claim to Rwandan land: 'In 1923, Cramer, a Frenchman from Belgium, visited Rwanda. He met with the Rwandan government to discuss the possibility of establishing a French plantation in Rwanda. The Rwandan government told Cramer that the land near Gisenyi could be leased to him for thirty years. Cramer leased the land from the Rwandan government. The lease was renewed in 1930. In 1934, Cramer told us that although he had leased the land from the Rwandan government in 1923, he had sold the land to the French government in 1934. We believe that this is not true and that Cramer is still the owner of the land.'
The French government appointed a commission to investigate the French claim. The commission, composed of Frenchmen, was appointed by the French government in 1934. The commission travelled to Rwanda to investigate the French claim. The commission found that the land had been leased to Cramer by the Rwandan government in 1925. The commission also found that Cramer had sold the land to the French government in 1934. The commission concluded that the French government had a legitimate claim to the land.
In 1935, the French government sent a letter to the Belgian government requesting that the Belgian government recognise the French claim to the land in Gisenyi. In 1936, the Belgian government recognised the French claim. The Belgian government also gave the French government permission to establish a French plantation in Rwanda.

DuMont aspired to grow beyond its three stations , applying for new television station licenses in Cincinnati and Cleveland in

1949, and in Milwaukee, Minneapolis-St. Paul, Oklahoma City and Philadelphia in 1950. The company's motto, "Television for the Few," was intended to underline its belief that broadcast television should be available to the public in only the largest markets.
By the end of 1950, DuMont was operating eight networks, the most of any television company in any part of the world. The company's president, H. F. "Mac" Paley, had grandiose plans to create a national television network—plans that were nothing short of revolutionary.
The DuMont Television Network was launched on August 15, 1945, with the presentation of two programs, the first a live musical performance from the Hollywood Bowl and the second a long-distance telecast of the first baseball game ever broadcast nationwide, between the Brooklyn Dodgers and the Philadelphia Phillies, from Philadelphia's Shibe Park. The programs were seen simultaneously by millions of viewers in New York, Philadelphia and Chicago on the three stations affiliated with the DuMont Television Network.
On August 15, 1945, DuMont also made its debut as a major television manufacturer. At the debut of the DuMont Television Network, the company offered a Model 122 television set, which featured a 12-inch chassis and a 12-inch picture tube. The DuMont Model 122 sold for $495, and between 1945 and 1950, the company produced approximately 100,000 television sets.
The DuMont Corporation faced a number of problems in its early years. The DuMont Television Network was geographically limited. The company held licenses for only three television stations—WABD (now WNYW) in New York City, WTTG (now WDCA) in Washington, D.C., and WDTV (now WTTG) in Washington, D.C.
On July 1, 1951, the DuMont Corporation was acquired by Paramount Pictures.
DuMont was the first television network to establish a separate news division. In addition to the regular programming seen on the DuMont Television Network, the company produced several programs that were syndicated to local stations, including _The Ventriloquist_ with Edgar Bergen and his dummy, Charlie McCarthy, and _The Hank McCune Show_ , a weekly musical variety program that was also syndicated to stations in the United States and Canada.
In 1974, the DuMont television stations in New York, Washington, D.C., and Chicago were acquired by Metromedia Inc. Within a year of the acquisition, the DuMont name was dropped.
Today, DuMont is best remembered as the original home of _Captain Video and His Video Rangers_ , the first science-fiction television series. In its 1940s and 1950s heyday, the DuMont Television Network also aired several other firsts in the world of television, including the world's first color television series, _Police Call_ , and the first reality-based television series, _Moonlight Manhunt_.

Upon the retirement of the Keeper of the London Museum , Harmon Oates , Wheeler was invited to fill the vacancy . He had been c

ashier at the Royal Mint for most of the preceding twenty years , and had recently been appointed a Fellow of the Royal Society .
During the 1840s Wheeler was increasingly involved in the management of the Museum and its collections . He was appointed Assistant Keeper on 14 December 1842 , and a year later was given responsibility for the Department of Coins and Medals . This post , and a large salary , was awarded to him after he had "confirmed" his belief in the veracity of the (fake) _Cotton Rolls_ , which he had discovered in the early 1840s . He was given the additional task of examining the gold coins imported from Spain and Portugal under the new coinage laws .
Wheeler took a particular interest in the new regulations governing the exportation of gold coins from Britain . He was especially concerned about the "associations" that were formed in the early 1840s to export gold bullion to foreign countries . When the gold trade was first permitted in 1818 , the merchants of the London Mint Association were allowed to export the gold that was not required for coinage . When Wheeler was appointed to his post in 1843 , he was the only person responsible for the gold coming into the London Mint .
Wheeler's interest in the gold trade was heightened by the introduction of new counterfeit gold coins. The gold sovereign was counterfeited for the first time in 1843 , and the counterfeiters quickly moved on to the gold half-sovereign . Wheeler was responsible for the precise weight of the gold that was sent to the Prince Regent to form the new sovereigns . He was also responsible for the production of the sovereign as a coin .
The new gold coins were a popular success . During the 1840s the gold trade was expanded to include exports to China and the East Indies . Some of the gold sovereigns were sent to India , and some were sent to China . Wheeler was responsible for the coins sent to China , and worked with the merchants of the London Mint Association .
In December 1848, Wheeler was appointed Keeper of the London Museum . He held the post until his death in 1864 .
The story of the _Cotton Rolls_ is well known . The name of Wheeler is associated with the _Rolls_ because he had the idea of examining the _Rolls_ closely and identifying the mistakes in their fabrication . Wheeler was mistakenly thought to have been the first man to examine the _Rolls_ , but this was not the case . The idea of examining the _Rolls_ may have come to Wheeler from William Harness , or from John S. Harper . It was Harper who first suggested that the _Rolls_ were the work of a forger . Wheeler was probably the first to closely examine the _Rolls_ , but it was not until 1845 that he came to the conclusion that they were forgeries .
Wheeler's examination of the _Rolls_ may have been prompted by the visit to London of the _Rolls_ in early 1844 , and by the death of the _Rolls_ 's "discoverer" , the Reverend James Vibert . Wheeler's interest in the _Rolls_ was probably heightened by the new regulations governing the exportation of gold coins from Britain .

Both the apparent and absolute magnitude scales are logarithmic units : one whole number difference in magnitude is equal to a

2.55-fold difference in brightness.

## History

The term absolute magnitude was introduced in 1866 by John Herschel, who derived it from the mean distance between the Sun and a given star. Absolute magnitude is currently defined as the apparent magnitude of a star when viewed from a distance of 10 parsecs (32.6 light years).

## Definition

Absolute magnitude is a measure of brightness of a star, expressed in magnitude units. Magnitude of a star is a logarithmic measure of its brightness. Absolute magnitude is expressed in magnitude units.

Absolute magnitude depends on the distance to the star, not on the observer, unlike apparent magnitude. In other words, it is the apparent magnitude an observer would measure at a standard distance of 10 parsecs (32.6 light years).

Absolute magnitude is determined by measuring the brightness of a star from the Earth, then comparing the brightness of the star to the brightness of the Sun at 10 parsecs (32.6 light years).

\[M_{\text{V}}=m-5\]

where MV is the absolute magnitude, m the apparent magnitude, and 5 the absolute magnitude of the Sun.

The absolute magnitude of a star is often called simply its magnitude.

## Astronomical applications

Absolute magnitudes are frequently used to compare the brightness of stars. Comparing the absolute magnitudes of a star and the Sun allows one to determine the distance of the star using trigonometry.

### Astrometric parallax

Main article: Astrometric parallax

The parallax of a star is the angle between two points of that star as seen from two different points on Earth. This angle is one that is used to measure the distance to a star. The absolute magnitude of a star can be combined with the parallax to determine the distance to the star.

### Distance ladder

Main article: Distance ladder

The distance ladder is a hierarchy of different methods used to determine distances to objects in the universe. One of the methods is to use trigonometry to measure the parallax of a star and the absolute magnitude of the star.

### Precision

The Sun is the brightest object in the sky. At a distance of 1 AU from the Sun, the absolute magnitude is 4.83. The absolute magnitude of an object in the night sky is usually measured in comparison to the absolute magnitude of the Sun. For example, the absolute magnitude of the Moon is −12.75, which is 8.08 times more luminous than the Sun.

It is easy to see the reason why Wilde's ideas on art attracted the hostility of the literary establishment. Although aesthetics had already been the subject of a great deal of writing, Wilde's new theories were radically different from anything that had gone before. He argued that art should not be judged by its moral content, but by its "artistic" qualities. The artist should be judged by how well he or she created beauty. These views were criticized at the time by the mainstream critics. They were not only new, they were radical and expressed themselves in language that was often deliberately provocative.
In May 1894, a member of the public, Major Charles Johnston, wrote to _The Pall Mall Gazette_ , a newspaper, to complain about Wilde's latest work, _A Woman of No Importance_. Johnston wrote, " 'The Decay of Lying', by Oscar Wilde, is a piece of literary and artistic excrement, and nobody who has any regard for the English language or the English people should be guilty of even buying such a book." This letter was published in _The Pall Mall Gazette_ , and was followed up by a letter from Wilde himself in the same newspaper on 26 May 1894. Released in September 2012, Tempest is the 35th studio album by American singer-songwriter Bob Dylan. It is his first studio release in six years. The album was produced by Jack Frost and features 10 tracks, including four instrumentals. It is dedicated to the memory of Hank Williams, a major influence on Dylan.
The album was released on September 11, 2012, to generally positive reviews. It made the top 10 in the albums charts in eight countries and reached number two in the UK Albums Chart. It was certified Gold in the United States.

The Tempest is a 2010 film adaptation of William Shakespeare's play The Tempest, directed by Julie Taymor. The film stars Helen Mirren, Djimon Hounsou, Alan Cumming, Chris Cooper, Felicity Jones and Ben Whishaw.
The film premiered at the 2010 Toronto International Film Festival. It was released by Sony Pictures Classics in the United States on November 10, 2010, and on May 24, 2011 in the UK.
Caliban's mother, the witch Sycorax (Helen Mirren), dies and leaves her island to her son. When he is grown, his father, King Alonso of Naples (Jeremy Irons), is shipwrecked on the island. Prospero (Alan Cumming) and his daughter, Miranda (Felicity Jones), who was raised by Sycorax, learn of the shipwreck. Prospero uses Sycorax's magic and books to manipulate Alonso and his courtiers to fulfill his plan for revenge.
Caliban (Djimon Hounsou) is a force of nature in The Tempest, but it's not his size or strength that make him dangerous, it's his intellect, the way he can grasp ideas, and the way he can relay them.

The pyramid complex of Djedkare Isesi was one of the earliest pyramid complexes to be built. It was built on the site of the pyramid complex of Unas, and the new pyramid was built immediately adjacent to the southern side of the pyramid of Unas. Djedkare's pyramid was constructed in a similar way to those of the Old Kingdom. A step pyramid with a smooth outer casing was constructed on a base that measured 144 cubits by 124 cubits. Before meeting Beyoncé , Rich Harrison had conceptualized the beat of the song . He sampled the hook 's instrumentation from th

e 1983 single " Morning Train (9 to 5)" by The Manhattans .

## Composition

Beyoncé incorporated elements of 1980s funk and R&B into "Crazy in Love". She sings the song in a breathy, rasping tone. The song's instrumentation is a "swirling backdrop of funky guitars and snappy horns". The song also features a reggae beat and a "screeching, sampled sax". The song's chorus consists of the hook 's lyrics, "If you like it then you should have put a ring on it". According to the sheet music published at Musicnotes.com by Alfred Publishing, the song is written in the key of F major and has a tempo of 92 beats per minute. The song's vocal range spans from the low note of C  ₄ to the high note of C  ₅.

## Music video

The accompanying music video for "Crazy in Love" was filmed in New York City in March 2003; it was directed by Jake Nava and was released on April 7, 2003. Leighton Meester and Adamari López have small cameo roles in the video. In the video, the song's lyrics are illustrated by Beyoncé, a man (portrayed by Meester), and a woman (portrayed by López), who act out the lyrics with one another. The video begins with Beyoncé singing the song in the street. She then walks into a man's apartment. She sees the man and woman having sex in the bedroom, and she stands in the doorway watching them. The man then notices the woman and asks her what she is doing. She tells him that she is waiting for Beyoncé. The man says that he did not know Beyoncé was coming over. The man and Beyoncé then have sex in the room. The video ends with the man and woman still talking as Beyoncé walks out of the apartment.

The video received multiple music video nominations, including a nomination for Best R&B Video at the 2004 MTV Video Music Awards. "Crazy in Love" was ranked number two on Rolling Stone's list of the 100 Best Music Videos.

## Accolades

At the 2003 MTV Video Music Awards, the video for "Crazy in Love" won the awards for Best R&B Video and Best Choreography.

At the 2004 Grammy Awards, "Crazy in Love" was nominated for Record of the Year, Best R&B Song, and Best Rap/Sung Collaboration.

## Cultural impact

"Crazy in Love" was ranked number 14 on Rolling Stone's list of the 100 Best Songs of the '00s. In 2009, NME ranked the song number 5 on its list of the 50 Greatest Songs of the Decade. In 2011, VH1 named "Crazy in Love" the number one song of the decade.

British singer Robyn featured the song during the Kids In Glass Houses tour in 2008.

In 2009, Hot Chip covered "Crazy in Love" for the BBC Radio 1 series Live Lounge, changing the lyrics to "You're crazy, you're crazy in love... with a Hot Chip". The cover featured the band singing around a houseplant and was accompanied by a music video directed by Sophie Muller. The video received positive reviews and was included in the book 1001 Songs You Must Hear Before You Die.

In 2010, the song charted at number 8 on Rolling Stone's list of the 100 Best Songs of 2009.

In 2013, Young Love released a cover of the song on their album, Young Love. The cover was removed from the album due to legal issues. The song was re-released later that year on their EP Young Love EP.

In 2015, Kanye West sampled "Crazy in Love" for the song "FourFiveSeconds" from his album The Life of Pablo.

In 2016, Beyoncé performed a medley of "Crazy in Love" and "Déjà Vu" during her Formation World Tour.

Common starlings prefer urban or suburban areas where artificial structures and trees provide adequate nesting and roosting sit

- es. When the nesting season begins, the starlings search for a secure site that is near water. Nesting sites may be on telephone poles, buildings, ledges, or other man- made structures. The ideal site is usually a protected cavity located on a solid structure.
 Once a starling selects a nesting site, it begins to work on the nest. The nest may be built in a single day, although starlings often take several days to construct it. The nest is built in a shallow cavity, and the starling lines the inside with grasses, feathers, or fur. The nest may be lined with mud, grass, or leaves. The nest is usually around 6 inches deep, and is found in an upright position on the side of a building, in a small hole on a tree, or in an opening in a rocky ledge. The male and female work together to build the nest, but the male provides most of the grasses and feathers.
 Starlings eat a variety of invertebrates and fruit. They are especially fond of insects, and they may eat up to 50,000 insects in a day. They also eat fruit, seeds, berries, and the eggs and young of another bird.
 Starlings are sociable birds. During the breeding season, they can be found in large flocks. In winter, they form flocks that may contain more than 100,000 birds. They are also very protective of their nesting sites. They may drive away other birds or animals that get too close to their nest.
 Starlings are well known for their chattering calls. They also move in flocks and may use an assortment of antics to communicate with each other. Starlings can be aggressive, and will sometimes attack a person who gets too close to their nest.
 Starlings are easy to care for. They rarely need to be fed, and they can survive for a long time on insects alone.
 Starlings are monogamous, but they sometimes mate with other starlings outside the pair bond. A male starling may mate with up to 10 females.
 A female starling may lay 5 to 9 eggs in a single nesting. The eggs are white with brown spots. The eggs are incubated by both parents for around 12 days. The young hatch out and leave the nest within 14 days.
 Starlings are common birds, and their numbers are increasing. They were first introduced into the United States in 1890. They are widespread in both urban and rural areas throughout the United States.

The vault of the room has a mural painting that represents the Last Supper.
The chapel has also three main altarpieces that are placed in the interior of the room.
The chapel of the Saint Christ and of the Reliquaries has also some golden reliquaries, statues and a bust of Charles I of Spain .

The establishment of the University of Haifa in 1963 brought about an academic revolution and led to Haifa being featured in the top 10 of the world's most beautiful universities by Forbes . Haifa is home to the second-largest group of Jews of Middle Eastern origin in the world , after Israel . Haifa has been nicknamed "The Bay of the Sun" , "The City of the Mountain" , "The City of the Three Abrahams" , "The Rock" and "The City of Pearls" . Haifa is a chief seaport and a leading heavy industry center of Israel. The city is home to the country's petroleum refining facilities , and its chemicals , steel , and foodstuffs industries. Haifa has the second largest heart in Israel in terms of cultural activities after Tel Aviv . The city hosts the Israel Philharmonic Orchestra , the Israel Ballet , and Haifa Symphony Orchestra . Many musicians and artists live in the city , and it has been called "the city that never sleeps" . Haifa is the northern terminus of Israel's national railways.
Haifa is located in northern Israel on the slopes of Mount Carmel on the east coast of the Mediterranean Sea. It has a subtropical-mediterranean climate with mild rainy winters and hot semi-arid summers . The highest point in Haifa is Mount Carmel .
The city proper had a population of 276,715 in 2010 . It is situated within the Haifa metropolitan area which has a population of 680,932 .
Haifa's economy is based on the city's port and its oil refineries . The city is the home of the University of Haifa , the Technion - Israel Institute of Technology , and the University of Haifa Medical School . The city is also considered a major center of the high-tech industry in Israel , with many of the country's most successful high-tech start-up companies being founded in Haifa .
Haifa was selected as a Gamma- level Global City by GaWC in 2012 .

The Knights Templar , who were not allowed to own property, rented it from the Hospitallers. The Templars built the Templar Castle . In 1191, the city became part of the Ayyubid Sultanate of Egypt , and it was ruled by the Mamlukes during the 13th century. As if to underline this, in the summer of 1862 the Dakota and the Ojibway, believing that the American government was planning to invade Canada in the summer of 1862, retaliated by attacking isolated trading posts and punishing settlers, as well as destroying crops. The attacks were apparently motivated by a desire to deny the traders the means to pay for supplies from the tribe's enemies.
The US War Department immediately ordered a punitive expedition against the Dakota and the Ojibway. Although the expedition made little progress, it led to another treaty between the United States and the Dakota in 1863. Despite the promise of a reservation, the Dakota were still forced to sell the territory they had occupied for over a century.
In the early part of 1863, the Dakota were again provoked into attacking the whites. In May 1863, a party of 200 men from the Lower Sioux and the Yanktonais attacked a trading post near Mankato, Minnesota, killing the owner, his wife and eleven of his employees. On July 1, the Dakota, led by Little Crow, attacked the settlers along the Minnesota River. Although the settlers were able to resist, more than 400 were killed; 265 of the victims were women and children.
The resulting crisis led to a punitive expedition, which resulted in the deaths of approximately 800 Dakota. The majority were women and children who had sought sanctuary in a church and a schoolhouse. The remainder were captured and taken to a prison camp at Fort Snelling, where thousands more died of disease. The rest were taken to a reservation in Nebraska. The Indians were subsequently moved to Oklahoma, where they continued to live under the most difficult of conditions.
In 1864, Republican President Abraham Lincoln appointed William Tecumseh Sherman commander of the Department of the Missouri. It was intended that Sherman would use his military skills to control the Indian nations of the Plains. "The Indian, as an Indian, is doomed. He must be taught to change his habits, look for a new subsistence, and accept the condition of civilized life, or he will inevitably be exterminated. In a few years, he will either have become a civilized being, or he will be in the same condition as the buffalo—exterminated.
"The results will be the same as if the buffalo had to be done away with. It would be the same if the Indian tribes were organized into a strong and well-conducted nation. It would be the same if they had the best arms, the best horses, and all the other appliances of the white man. They would become a power. So far as they have done so, they have done so to their own destruction. They have done nothing to deserve our undying hatred."

In fact, the negotiations were hugely successful for the British Government. The Tobacco Advertising Control Act 2002, which had been opposed by British retailers, was repealed. The EU-US negotiations took place in the context of a larger argument over the regulation of tobacco advertising and promotion. The European Union had been attempting to restrict tobacco advertising since 1992. In 1992, the European Union adopted the Framework Decision on Smoking and Health. This document stated that member states should 'pursue a comprehensive approach to prevent tobacco consumption, in accordance with the Tobacco Advertising Directive 92/84/EEC, the Tobacco Products Directive 89/692/EEC and the Directive 90/659/EEC on the Technical Requirements for Tobacco Products'.
Member states were also required to 'apply a comprehensive ban on tobacco advertising, sponsorship and promotion' and to 'adopt measures to ensure that the tobacco industry does not mislead the public by creating the impression that tobacco use is safe, less hazardous than other tobacco products or less harmful than other substances'.
This declaration of intent was further clarified in 1996, when the Council of the European Union, in a joint letter sent to all the European Union's member states, re-affirmed that the European Union 'should adopt a comprehensive ban on tobacco advertising'.

The term Wicca was employed in an increasingly eclectic manner by authors like RavenWolf , who considered it to be a synonym fo

"Witchcraft" and defined it as "a modern Pagan religion based on the worship of the Goddess (Sky-Father & Mother Earth), Nature and the Elements". She also defined "Wicca as "a modern Pagan religion based on the worship of the Goddess (Sky-Father & Mother Earth), Nature and the Elements".
Paganism is one of those words that has many meanings, and a surprisingly large percentage of people who think they know what it means either don't, or are using an older meaning than is commonly known today.
I am not going to go into the various cultures that have had a belief in Nature Gods, or in the relationship between the forces of Nature and the creatures of Nature. I have not space to do so, and it would be beyond the scope of this book to do so. Instead, I will be concentrating on the origins of modern Paganism, and will be using the term Wicca to describe contemporary Paganism.
It has been said that Wicca is the most popular and widely practiced Pagan religion in the world today. Some have suggested that it is so new that it is not a religion, but more akin to a cult. For the purposes of this book I shall be using the term "Wicca" as a synonym for "contemporary Paganism" and as a collective noun for its various beliefs, traditions and practices.
#  **ORIGINS OF WICCA**
The origins of Wicca are shrouded in mystery and controversy. Wicca is first mentioned in J. F. C. Fuller's _Witchcraft and Witches_ (1927), where he linked it with Gerald Gardner (1884–1964), a writer and occultist who had been initiated into traditional witchcraft in 1939 by a coven of English witches. Following this, Gardner was initiated into the Gardnerian coven of witches by the High Priestess Doreen Valiente (1922–1998). Gardner immediately recognized the significance of Valiente's unique contribution to his coven and to the Craft, and in 1954 he was granted writing copyrights on the "Valiente Book of Shadows," the first manuscript to be preserved in the tradition of Wicca.
In the 1960s, Gardner initiated other covens and so Wicca began to spread rapidly, not only in England but also in the United States. Gardner was considered to be the leader of Wicca and the "Father of the Modern Wiccan Movement." By 1971, Gardner's coven numbered eight members.
In 1956, the Gardnerian Tradition was founded in the United States by Raymond Buckland (1934–2014), who was initiated into the Gardnerian Tradition by Gardner himself. The first book on Wicca, _The Witches' Bible_ by Gerald Gardner, was published in 1959.
The second book on Wicca was _The New Pagan's Handbook_ by Raymond Buckland, which appeared in 1974. In 1975, Buckland published _Witchcraft from the Inside_ , which was an account of his initiation into Gardnerian Wicca in England.
The most significant event in the history of Wicca was the founding of a new Wiccan organization in England in 1975 by the Aquarian Tabernacle Church. This new organization was led by Alex Sanders (1926–1988), a self-proclaimed "King of the Witches." Sanders's followers were known as the Sandersian Tradition, and his coven was called the Alexandrian Tradition.
The Alexandrian Tradition was founded on the principles of the first degree of Wicca as outlined by Gardner and was quite different from the Gardnerian Tradition. One of the most significant differences between the two traditions was that the Alexandrian Tradition did not require initiates to engage in ritual nudity.
